title: Fast Wave-optics Rendering of Multiplane Images for 3D Holographic Displays
summary: Recent advances in neural rendering have unlocked unprecedented capabilities in 3D reconstruction and novel view synthesis, giving rise to applications such as virtual fly-throughs of a 3D scene reconstructed from a set of sparse, casually captured images. However, these renderings are viewed on a computer screen or conventional VR headsets as 2D images, greatly limiting the perceptual realism and immersiveness of such experiences. The rapid development in novel 3D scene representations calls for dedicated rendering algorithms that convert these readily-available 3D contents into formats that are compatible with emerging 3D display technologies, such as holographic displays. In this paper, we propose a wave-optics rendering pipeline that works with multiplane images (MPIs) for efficient and high-quality hologram synthesis. Our MPI-based computer-generated holography algorithm greatly outperforms state-of-the-art primitive-based CGH algorithms in terms of runtime, achieving speedups up to 250,000x while achieving comparable image quality, and significantly outperforms conventional layer-based CGH algorithms in terms of image quality. We validate our method extensively on a wide variety of 3D scene datasets both in simulation and through experimentally captured results, showing exceptional 3D focal stack and 4D light field reconstruction performance without sacrificing efficiency.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a wave-optics rendering pipeline using multiplane images (MPIs) for efficient, high-quality hologram synthesis, achieving up to 250,000x speedup over state-of-the-art primitive-based CGH algorithms with comparable quality, and outperforming layer-based CGH in image quality.
AI.motivation: Current neural rendering advances produce high-quality 3D scene representations, but these are displayed as 2D images on screens or VR headsets, limiting perceptual realism and immersiveness. There is a need for dedicated rendering algorithms that convert these 3D contents into formats compatible with emerging 3D display technologies like holographic displays.
AI.method: A wave-optics rendering pipeline that works with multiplane images (MPIs) for efficient and high-quality computer-generated holography (CGH).
AI.result: Achieves speedups up to 250,000x over primitive-based CGH with comparable quality, and significantly outperforms conventional layer-based CGH in image quality. Validated on diverse 3D datasets in simulation and experimentally, showing exceptional 3D focal stack and 4D light field reconstruction.
AI.conclusion: The proposed MPI-based CGH algorithm provides an efficient bridge between neural 3D scene representations and holographic displays, enabling high-quality hologram synthesis without sacrificing efficiency.

title: LowPowAR: Power-Constrained Tone Mapping for Augmented Reality
comment: Accepted to TVCG 2026. 30 pages. Project page: https://horizon-lab.org/lowpowar/
summary: Everyday-wearable Augmented Reality (AR) glasses must meet strict power limits, making displays a key target for optimization. We cast display power optimization as a power-constrained tone-mapping problem and propose a human-vision-grounded, learning-based framework that maximizes perceptual quality under a given power budget. We introduce an optimization-friendly tone-mapping operator (TMO) parameterization along with a progressive optimization strategy to effectively navigate the quality-vs-power landscape. We distill the iterative optimization into a lightweight feed-forward neural network for real-time deployment. Subjective experiments show that our method yields better perceptual quality than prior work at the same power budget. Project page: https://horizon-lab.org/lowpowar/.

AI.tldr: Proposes a learning-based framework that optimizes perceptual quality of AR glasses displays under strict power constraints by formulating it as a power-constrained tone-mapping problem, using a novel TMO parameterization and progressive optimization, distilled into a lightweight neural network for real-time use.
AI.motivation: Everyday-wearable AR glasses face strict power limits, making display power optimization critical for practical adoption while maintaining visual quality.
AI.method: Formulates display power optimization as a power-constrained tone-mapping problem; introduces an optimization-friendly tone-mapping operator (TMO) parameterization with a progressive optimization strategy; distills the iterative optimization into a lightweight feed-forward neural network for real-time deployment.
AI.result: Subjective experiments demonstrate better perceptual quality compared to prior work at the same power budget.
AI.conclusion: The proposed human-vision-grounded, learning-based framework effectively maximizes perceptual quality under power constraints and is deployable in real-time on AR glasses.

title: CAPS: A Cascaded Reconstruction Model to Power Saving in Hearables Using Sub-Nyquist Sampling with Bandwidth Extension
comment: arXiv admin note: substantial text overlap with arXiv:2506.22321
summary: Hearables are wearable computers worn on the ear. Bone conduction microphones are used with air conduction microphones in hearables for multimodal speech enhancement in noisy conditions. Despite this potential, current models largely fail to explore how jointly reducing sampling bit resolution and sampling frequency in analog-to-digital converters (ADCs) of hearables impacts both power usage and audio quality. Furthermore, current frameworks cannot do sub-Nyquist sampling in hearables because they lack a method to reconstruct wideband signals from narrowband components. We therefore propose CAPS, which (i) intentionally employs sub-Nyquist sampling and low bit resolution in ADCs, achieving a 3.3x reduction in power consumption in hearables, and (ii) supports streaming operation on mobile platforms with an inference time of 1.36 ms and a memory footprint of 11.04 MB. CAPS ensures robust speech intelligibility in real-world settings, bridging the gap between efficiency and power savings.

AI.tldr: CAPS proposes a framework for hearables that uses sub-Nyquist sampling and low bit resolution ADCs to achieve 3.3x power reduction while maintaining robust speech intelligibility, with real-time streaming capability (1.36 ms inference, 11.04 MB memory).
AI.motivation: Current hearable models fail to explore how jointly reducing sampling bit resolution and sampling frequency in ADCs impacts both power usage and audio quality, and lack methods to reconstruct wideband signals from narrowband components for sub-Nyquist sampling.
AI.method: CAPS employs sub-Nyquist sampling and low bit resolution in ADCs, combined with a reconstruction method for wideband signals from narrowband components, enabling multimodal speech enhancement using bone conduction and air conduction microphones.
AI.result: Achieves 3.3x reduction in power consumption, 1.36 ms inference time, 11.04 MB memory footprint, and robust speech intelligibility in real-world noisy conditions.
AI.conclusion: CAPS bridges the gap between efficiency and power savings in hearables, enabling practical deployment on mobile platforms with streaming operation.

title: Understanding Developer Pain Points in Federated Learning: Insights from Stack Overflow and GitHub
summary: Federated Learning (FL) enables collaborative model training without centralizing raw data, but building and operating FL systems remains difficult due to distributed execution, rapidly evolving frameworks, and privacy and governance requirements. In this paper, we present an empirical study of FL developer challenges by independently analyzing 495 Stack Overflow posts and 9,116 GitHub issues and pull requests from 92 FL-related projects. Using BERTopic-based topic modeling and difficulty indicators such as unresolved rates and median resolution time, we characterize recurring problem areas and compare how they manifest across the two support platforms, Stack Overflow and GitHub. Our analysis surfaces nine dominant Stack Overflow topics and thirteen GitHub topics, with persistent difficulties concentrated in environment setup and dependency compatibility, API breakages and migration, training instability under non-IID data, evaluation and metric correctness, and the integration of privacy-preserving mechanisms. We also categorize posts by question intent to understand the kinds of help developers seek; this intent analysis shows that "How"-type questions dominate, reflecting strong demand for procedural guidance. Several topics, such as "TFF Installation and Environment Compatibility" and "Federated Feature Engineering and SecureBoost Issues," exhibit high unresolved rates and long resolution times, suggesting shortcomings in tooling, documentation, and debugging support. Based on these findings, we provide actionable implications for FL framework designers, documentation authors, and educators. Although our results are constrained to public discussions and a subset of widely discussed frameworks, the study offers a scalable method for continuously monitoring developer pain points and improving the usability, reliability, and deployability of FL systems.

AI.tldr: Analysis of 495 Stack Overflow posts and 9,116 GitHub issues/PRs from 92 FL projects using BERTopic modeling reveals nine dominant topics on Stack Overflow and thirteen on GitHub. Persistent difficulties include environment setup, API breakages, training instability under non-IID data, evaluation correctness, and privacy mechanism integration. "How"-type questions dominate, and topics like TFF installation and SecureBoost issues show high unresolved rates.
AI.motivation: Building and operating FL systems remains difficult due to distributed execution, rapidly evolving frameworks, and privacy/governance requirements, yet FL developer challenges have not been systematically studied at scale.
AI.method: Independently analyzed 495 Stack Overflow posts and 9,116 GitHub issues/PRs from 92 FL-related projects using BERTopic-based topic modeling and difficulty indicators (unresolved rates, median resolution time). Also categorized posts by question intent.
AI.result: Identified 9 Stack Overflow topics and 13 GitHub topics. Persistent difficulties in environment setup, API breakages, training instability under non-IID data, evaluation/metric correctness, and privacy-preserving mechanism integration. "How"-type questions dominate. TFF Installation and Federated Feature Engineering/SecureBoost issues show high unresolved rates and long resolution times.
AI.conclusion: Provides actionable implications for FL framework designers, documentation authors, and educators. The study offers a scalable method for continuously monitoring developer pain points and improving FL system usability, reliability, and deployability.

title: Detect Early, Escalate Rarely: Anytime Detection of AI-Generated Video from the Compressed Bitstream
summary: Detectors for AI-generated video are evaluated offline. A clip is decoded to pixels and scored once, increasingly by a large vision-language model. Detection, however, is deployed online. We recast the task as streaming perception and score the motion field the codec already wrote into the bitstream. Reading that field is a parse, not a pixel-domain forward pass. Because the running aggregate is monotone, one end-calibrated threshold is anytime-valid at the data-dependent decision time. Recalibrating at each prefix is not. Escalation is priced in closed form. A compute budget maps to a deferral window, on a frontier monotone exactly where the deferral condition holds. On matched GenVidBench the codec stage reaches full-length AUC 0.64 at five orders of magnitude less compute than a pixel CNN, on CPU. Its gate holds the stopping-time false-positive rate at target while the real data match its calibration, and drifts above it under distribution shift. Deferring 15% of clips lifts accuracy from 0.75 to 0.78 at $7\times$ less compute (paired: McNemar $p<10^{-6}$). The stage-1 ordering replicates on AIGVDBench. We introduce no new detector. The contribution is the reframing, two guarantees, and the measured frontiers. Code, configurations, and evaluation splits: https://github.com/KurbanIntelligenceLab/streamdet.

AI.tldr: This paper reframes AI-generated video detection from offline (pixel-level, single-pass) to online streaming perception by analyzing the motion field already present in the codec bitstream, requiring only a parse (no pixel decoding), achieving anytime-valid thresholds with monotone aggregates, and demonstrating 5 orders of magnitude compute reduction with competitive accuracy.
AI.motivation: Current AI-video detectors are evaluated offline (decode clip → pixels → score once), but deployment is online (streaming). This mismatch motivates a streaming perception reframing that leverages existing codec motion fields to avoid costly pixel-domain processing.
AI.method: The method reads (parses) the motion field directly from the compressed bitstream instead of decoding to pixels. A running monotone aggregate is computed, enabling one end-calibrated threshold that is anytime-valid at the data-dependent decision time (no recalibration needed per prefix). Escalation (compute budget vs. deferral window) is priced in closed form, yielding a monotone frontier where the deferral condition holds.
AI.result: On GenVidBench: codec stage achieves AUC 0.64 at 5 orders of magnitude less compute than a pixel CNN (on CPU). The gate maintains stopping-time false-positive rate under calibration and drifts under distribution shift. Deferring 15% of clips lifts accuracy from 0.75 to 0.78 at 7× less compute (McNemar p<10⁻⁶). Stage-1 ordering replicates on AIGVDBench.
AI.conclusion: The contribution is not a new detector but a reframing of video AI detection as streaming perception with two guarantees (anytime-valid threshold, monotone compute-deferral frontier) and measured frontiers. Code, configs, and splits are open-sourced.

title: Native Multi-Dimensional Subquadratic Operators via Input Dependent Long Convolutions
summary: Subquadratic alternatives to attention require compromises when applied to multi-dimensional data: standard convolutions lack global receptive fields and input dependency, while recurrent models require rasterizing data such as images, volumes, and partial differential equation (PDE) into an ad-hoc $1\rm D$ scan order that violates their spatial structure. We introduce \textit{HyenaND}, a subquadratic, global, input-dependent operator that acts directly on the native geometry of multidimensional data through convolutions with implicitly parametrized global, input-dependent multi-dimensional convolutional kernels. Our CUDA implementation, \texttt{nSubQ}, fuses the FFT-convolution path to turn HyenaND's $\mathcal{O}(L \log L)$ scaling into wall-clock speedups. Across long-context genomics, computer vision, medical imaging, and PDE modeling, pure HyenaND stacks match the accuracy of strong attention baselines, while hybrid configurations that interleave HyenaND and attention layers outperform both pure attention and strong recurrence-based hybrids.

AI.tldr: HyenaND is a subquadratic, global, input-dependent operator for multidimensional data that uses implicit parametrized global convolutions with FFT acceleration, achieving attention-level accuracy across genomics, vision, medical imaging, and PDE modeling while outperforming pure attention and recurrent hybrids in hybrid configurations.
AI.motivation: Subquadratic alternatives to attention (convolutions and recurrent models) require compromises when handling multi-dimensional data: convolutions lack global receptive fields and input dependency, while recurrent models force rasterization into 1D scan order, breaking spatial structure.
AI.method: HyenaND extends the Hyena operator to multidimensional data by using implicitly parametrized global, input-dependent convolutional kernels that operate directly on native data geometry. A CUDA implementation called nSubQ fuses the FFT-convolution path to achieve O(L log L) wall-clock speedups.
AI.result: Pure HyenaND stacks match strong attention baselines across long-context genomics, computer vision, medical imaging, and PDE modeling. Hybrid configurations interleaving HyenaND and attention layers outperform both pure attention and strong recurrence-based hybrids.
AI.conclusion: HyenaND provides a practical subquadratic alternative to attention for multidimensional data that preserves spatial structure while achieving global, input-dependent processing with wall-clock speedups.

title: FineServe: A Fine-Grained Dataset and Characterization of Global LLM Serving Workloads
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as always-on online services, making efficient LLM serving a critical systems challenge. Achieving low latency and high throughput under volatile demand requires deep understanding of real-world serving workloads, yet existing studies often rely on proxy traces or coarse-grained characterizations that fail to capture the heterogeneity of modern multi-model LLM platforms. We present FineServe, an in-the-wild, multi-model LLM serving workload dataset collected from a global commercial marketplace, enabling fine-grained characterization of real-world serving dynamics across heterogeneous models and tasks. Leveraging FineServe, we conduct a comprehensive analysis of arrival dynamics and token behavior, revealing fundamentally different fluctuation regimes across model architectures, scales and task intents. Building on these insights, we develop the FineServe workload generator, which composes fine-grained model-aware workloads into configurable mixtures tailored for benchmarking multi-model serving platforms. By exposing these fine-grained workload dynamics, FineServe provides a realistic foundation for evaluating routing, scheduling, and capacity-planning strategies in LLM serving systems. FineServe is available at https://github.com/hihiztc1/FineServe.

AI.tldr: FineServe is a real-world, multi-model LLM serving workload dataset from a global commercial platform that captures fine-grained dynamics across heterogeneous models and tasks. It reveals distinct fluctuation regimes based on model architecture, scale, and task intent, and provides a workload generator for benchmarking multi-model serving systems.
AI.motivation: Existing studies on LLM serving workloads rely on proxy traces or coarse characterizations that fail to capture the heterogeneity of modern multi-model LLM platforms, motivating the need for fine-grained, real-world workload data.
AI.method: FineServe collects an in-the-wild, multi-model LLM serving workload dataset from a global commercial marketplace. It performs fine-grained characterization of arrival dynamics and token behavior across heterogeneous models and tasks, and develops a workload generator that composes fine-grained model-aware workloads into configurable mixtures.
AI.result: The analysis reveals fundamentally different fluctuation regimes across model architectures, scales, and task intents, demonstrating that real-world serving dynamics are highly heterogeneous.
AI.conclusion: FineServe provides a realistic foundation for evaluating routing, scheduling, and capacity-planning strategies in LLM serving systems, enabling more accurate benchmarking of multi-model serving platforms.

title: A Splitting Architecture for Exact Reduced Coulomb Friction
comment: 14 pages. Accepted to SCA 2026 (ACM SIGGRAPH / Eurographics Symposium on Computer Animation); published open access in Computer Graphics Forum. DOI: 10.1111/cgf.70576. Project page: https://www.cs.ubc.ca/research/fbf-friction
summary: Existing approaches to frictional contact dynamics typically either modify the Coulomb law to improve numerical robustness or solve the exact law in a fully coupled monolithic form. However, in its reduced form, exact Coulomb friction can be written as a cone complementarity problem with an augmented velocity, which reveals a natural split between a cone-constrained linear response and a scalar non-associated coupling induced by tangential velocity. We exploit this structure in the solver design. Our method uses an outer iteration to update the non-associated coupling explicitly, and an inner solve for a strongly convex cone-constrained quadratic program. This separation also makes the inner solver modular, so different numerical schemes can be used without changing the outer iteration. We evaluate the method on rigid-body benchmarks with stick-slip transitions and frictional stacking, and show that it reproduces exact Coulomb complementarity without smoothing or relaxing the friction law.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a solver for exact Coulomb friction in rigid-body dynamics by splitting the problem into an outer iteration (updating non-associated coupling explicitly) and an inner cone-constrained quadratic program, enabling modular solver design without smoothing or relaxing the friction law.
AI.motivation: Existing frictional contact dynamics approaches either modify Coulomb's law for numerical robustness or solve it in a fully coupled monolithic form. The authors identify a natural split in the reduced form of exact Coulomb friction (a cone complementarity problem with augmented velocity) that separates cone-constrained linear response from scalar non-associated coupling induced by tangential velocity, which existing methods do not exploit.
AI.method: An outer iteration explicitly updates the non-associated coupling (tangential velocity effect), while an inner solve handles a strongly convex cone-constrained quadratic program. This separation makes the inner solver modular, allowing different numerical schemes to be used interchangeably without altering the outer iteration structure.
AI.result: The method reproduces exact Coulomb complementarity without smoothing or relaxing the friction law, validated on rigid-body benchmarks including stick-slip transitions and frictional stacking.
AI.conclusion: The proposed splitting strategy effectively handles exact Coulomb friction while maintaining solver modularity, offering a principled alternative to smoothed or relaxed friction models.

title: RIME: Enabling Large-Scale Agentic Post-Production
summary: Almost every piece of recorded music you have ever heard was modified before it reached you; commercial releases rarely spring fully-formed from the mind of a musician. Despite the promise of music generation models for one-shot output, such fine-grained iterative refinement workflows are a complementary problem, and largely out of their reach. There is also a gap for musicians: while they can express what they want to hear, not all have the facility with studio production tools to implement the complex set of actions needed to realize these intuitions. We formalize this task as agentic post-production, wherein individual aspects of a song are targeted, refined, and combined into a final track. We argue the bottleneck is data: existing corpora do not reflect how realistic post-production chains map onto the vocabulary musicians and engineers actually use. We argue there is a language for modifying recorded music that is dense, consistent, and learnable. We introduce the Rule-based Instructions for Music Editing (RIME) framework, which generates realistic paired edit-instruction data from any baseline music dataset grounded in canonical methods, design patterns, and constraints derived from real production workflows. RIME leverages POEMS, a new toolkit that combines stem separation, mixing, and common studio effects for use by multimodal agents. We use RIME and POEMS to generate 3,000 pairs of edit instructions and ground truth audio, and use this data to evaluate existing multimodal LLMs as agents on this task, showing persistent challenges in current models' post-production capabilities. We also demonstrate RIME's ability to improve post-production agent performance via supervised fine-tuning. We see RIME as an early step toward iterative musical agents, collaborative systems that could transform music production much as interactive coding agents have reshaped software engineering.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces RIME, a framework that generates realistic paired edit-instruction data for music post-production, and POEMS, a toolkit for stem separation, mixing, and effects. Using these tools, the authors create 3,000 edit-instruction/audio pairs, evaluate multimodal LLMs as post-production agents, and demonstrate improved performance via supervised fine-tuning, positioning this as an early step toward iterative musical agents.
AI.motivation: Existing music generation models produce one-shot outputs but cannot support the fine-grained iterative refinement workflows essential in real music production. Additionally, musicians often lack the technical studio production skills to implement their creative intuitions. There is no existing corpus that reflects how realistic post-production chains map onto the vocabulary used by musicians and engineers.
AI.method: The authors formalize agentic post-production, develop the RIME framework to generate realistic paired edit-instruction data grounded in canonical methods and real production workflows, and build POEMS (a toolkit combining stem separation, mixing, and common studio effects) for multimodal agents. They generate 3,000 instruction-audio pairs and evaluate multimodal LLMs on this task.
AI.result: 3,000 pairs of edit instructions and ground truth audio were generated. Evaluation of existing multimodal LLMs as agents on this task revealed persistent challenges in current models' post-production capabilities. Supervised fine-tuning using RIME data improved post-production agent performance.
AI.conclusion: RIME represents an early step toward iterative musical agents — collaborative systems that could transform music production, analogous to how interactive coding agents have reshaped software engineering.

title: PerfAgent: Profiler-Guided Iterative Refinement for Repository-Level Code Optimization
summary: Large language model (LLM) agents now perform well on correctness-oriented repository-level tasks, including SWE-Bench issue resolution and feature implementation in real codebases. However, they still struggle with repository-level code optimization, which requires preserving behavior while improving runtime performance. Passing tests is not enough in this setting; a patch must preserve behavior, implement code optimization, and approach expert speedups. Current agents often miss bottlenecks hidden behind abstraction layers and native extensions, stop after shallow speedups, or insufficiently test the code patches that thus may silently break edge cases. We present PerfAgent, a profiler-guided, verifier-in-the-loop workflow that gives an off-the-shelf coding agent the feedback needed to find real hotspots, improve beyond the first passing patch, and use profiler evidence rather than timing alone to decide what to optimize next. On two challenging optimization benchmarks, GSO and SWE-fficiency-Lite, PerfAgent more than doubles the rate of expert-matching patches over OpenHands with GPT-5.1, improving from 19.6% to 39.2% on GSO and from 26% to 74% on SWE-fficiency-Lite. It also surpasses an oracle best-of-five baseline at substantially lower cost, showing that the gains come from better feedback rather than additional test-time sampling.

AI.tldr: PerfAgent is a profiler-guided, verifier-in-the-loop workflow that improves LLM agents' ability to perform repository-level code optimization by providing targeted feedback from profiling and verification, more than doubling expert-matching patch rates on GSO (19.6%→39.2%) and SWE-fficiency-Lite (26%→74%) benchmarks compared to OpenHands with GPT-5.1.
AI.motivation: LLM agents perform well on correctness-oriented repository tasks (e.g., bug fixing, feature implementation) but struggle with repository-level code optimization, which requires preserving behavior while improving runtime performance. Current agents miss bottlenecks behind abstraction layers and native extensions, stop after shallow speedups, or insufficiently test patches that may silently break edge cases.
AI.method: PerfAgent uses a profiler-guided, verifier-in-the-loop workflow that gives an off-the-shelf coding agent feedback to find real hotspots, improve beyond the first passing patch, and use profiler evidence rather than timing alone to decide what to optimize next.
AI.result: On GSO, PerfAgent improves expert-matching patches from 19.6% to 39.2%; on SWE-fficiency-Lite, from 26% to 74%. It surpasses an oracle best-of-five baseline at substantially lower cost.
AI.conclusion: The gains come from better feedback through profiling and verification rather than additional test-time sampling, demonstrating that structured feedback loops are key to improving LLM agent performance on code optimization tasks.

title: Crowd4D: Scene-Aware Monocular 4D Crowd Reconstruction
summary: Recovering scene-consistent 4D crowd motion from monocular video in large-scale scenes remains challenging due to severe depth ambiguity and complex scene geometry. Existing monocular crowd reconstruction methods typically rely on single-plane assumptions, leading to unreliable metric scale and spatial drift under complex terrain. We propose Crowd4D, the first scene-aware 4D crowd reconstruction framework that jointly optimizes the crowd and scene from a monocular RGB video in large-scale scenes. Crowd4D explicitly incorporates scene geometry and ensures consistency across image and scene spaces via a multi-stage optimization strategy. A key bottleneck of this task lies in accurate human-scene alignment, particularly in scale and position. However, human and scene reconstructions are typically decoupled. To address this, we introduce the Human-Scene Interaction Proxy, abbreviated as HSIP, as an intermediate representation derived from Scene Interaction Point Clouds and a Scene Interaction Surface, abbreviated as SIPC and SIS. These representations encode explicit scene-aware geometric priors and redefine the optimization space for large-scale monocular 4D crowd reconstruction. To further improve temporal stability under occlusions, we introduce Crowd Structural Coherence Regularization, abbreviated as CSCR, which leverages HSIP-based spatial priors to impose soft temporal consistency on pairwise relative displacements and directions within local crowd neighborhoods. Extensive experiments demonstrate that Crowd4D consistently outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods and enables robust monocular 4D crowd reconstruction in complex, large-scale real-world scenes.

AI.tldr: Crowd4D is the first scene-aware 4D crowd reconstruction framework that jointly optimizes crowd and scene from monocular RGB video in large-scale scenes, using a Human-Scene Interaction Proxy (HSIP) with SIPC and SIS representations, along with Crowd Structural Coherence Regularization (CSCR), to overcome depth ambiguity and enable robust metric-scale reconstruction in complex terrain.
AI.motivation: Existing monocular crowd reconstruction methods rely on single-plane assumptions, causing unreliable metric scale and spatial drift under complex terrain. Human and scene reconstructions are typically decoupled, and accurate human-scene alignment (scale and position) remains a key bottleneck.
AI.method: Crowd4D employs a multi-stage optimization strategy that jointly optimizes crowd and scene. It introduces HSIP as an intermediate representation, composed of Scene Interaction Point Clouds (SIPC) and Scene Interaction Surface (SIS), encoding explicit scene-aware geometric priors. It further introduces CSCR, which uses HSIP-based spatial priors to enforce soft temporal consistency on pairwise relative displacements and directions within local crowd neighborhoods.
AI.result: Extensive experiments show Crowd4D consistently outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods and enables robust monocular 4D crowd reconstruction in complex, large-scale real-world scenes.
AI.conclusion: Scene-aware joint optimization with explicit geometric priors (HSIP) and structural temporal regularization (CSCR) is effective for recovering scene-consistent 4D crowd motion from monocular video in large-scale, geometrically complex scenes.

title: Bayesian Wind Tunnels for Model Selection
summary:
Prior work has shown that transformers can perform exact Bayesian filtering within a fixed
  hypothesis class. Can they also perform Bayesian model selection -- identifying the correct
  hypothesis class from data? We introduce model-selection Bayesian wind tunnels: controlled
  environments where ground-truth posteriors over hypothesis classes are available in closed
  form. Using fixed-point-free involutions -- whose defining property f(f(x))=x is purely
  relational -- a 2.8M-parameter transformer achieves 0.01-bit entropy agreement with the
  Bayesian optimum (3 seeds), with both integer tokens and opaque symbols whose meanings
  change every episode. This extends to non-nested comparisons: involutions vs. 3-cycles
  (where neither class is a subset of the other) achieve class-posterior MAE under 0.001,
  demonstrating genuine model selection beyond simplicity/subset bias. We then identify a
  sharp perceptual access condition: when the discriminative statistic requires arithmetic --
  modular addition (rotations) or multiplication (f(x)=cx mod p) -- model selection succeeds
  with integer tokens but fails completely with opaque symbols, and this boundary persists
  under 112x scaling (2.8M to 316M parameters). A stationarity control confirms the operative
  factor: opaque tokens with a fixed relabeling succeed (0.009-bit MAE), showing that stable
  semantics, not integer identity, enable circuit compilation. Header subtask diagnostics
  localize the failure to the composition of header inversion with arithmetic rather than
  header parsing itself. Probing frontier LLMs on the same tasks shows qualitative Bayesian
  behavior but a large calibration gap (~55x), measured through lossy probes and therefore
  directional rather than exact.

AI.tldr: Transformers can perform exact Bayesian model selection (not just filtering) using fixed-point-free involutions, achieving near-optimal entropy agreement, but fail when the discriminative statistic requires arithmetic with opaque symbols—a failure that persists under 112x scaling and stems from composing header inversion with arithmetic, not header parsing itself.
AI.motivation: Prior work shows transformers can do Bayesian filtering within a fixed hypothesis class, but whether they can perform Bayesian model selection—identifying the correct hypothesis class from data—remains unknown. This paper introduces controlled environments (model-selection Bayesian wind tunnels) to test this capability.
AI.method: The paper uses fixed-point-free involutions (f(f(x))=x) as a purely relational structure to test model selection. It creates Bayesian wind tunnels with closed-form ground-truth posteriors, tests transformers on integer tokens vs. opaque symbols (meanings change per episode), and compares nested (involutions vs. identity) and non-nested (involutions vs. 3-cycles) settings. It also probes scaling (2.8M to 316M parameters) and tests frontier LLMs.
AI.result: A 2.8M-parameter transformer achieves 0.01-bit entropy agreement with the Bayesian optimum for involutions. Non-nested comparisons achieve class-posterior MAE under 0.001. However, when arithmetic is required (modular addition/multiplication), model selection succeeds with integer tokens but fails completely with opaque symbols, persisting under 112x scaling. A stationarity control (fixed relabeling) succeeds, showing stable semantics enable circuit compilation. Frontier LLMs show qualitative Bayesian behavior but ~55x calibration gap.
AI.conclusion: Transformers can perform genuine Bayesian model selection beyond simplicity bias, but exhibit a sharp perceptual access failure: they cannot compose arithmetic with dynamically relabeled symbols, and this failure cannot be fixed by scaling. This reveals a fundamental architectural limitation in learning relational structures that require arithmetic on unstable token semantics.

title: Hybrid LSTM-Graph Neural Framework for Robust Financial Fraud Detection and Adversarial Resilience
summary: Financial institutions face significant challenges in detecting sophisticated money laundering patterns, such as smurfing and layering, due to extreme data imbalance (0.13% fraud rate) and evolving adversarial evasion tactics. This paper proposes FraudShield AI, a hybrid framework that integrates Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks with hand-crafted Graph Topological Features to capture both temporal sequences and structural relational context. By engineering network-centric features including PageRank Centrality, In-Degree dynamics, and a custom Flow Ratio, the system shifts the detection paradigm from isolated transaction analysis to network-level forensics. A Focal Loss objective is used to address class imbalance, and a dynamic thresholding mechanism is introduced to improve resilience against low-value smurfing attacks. Experimental evaluation on the PaySim dataset shows that the proposed hybrid model substantially outperforms Logistic Regression and XGBoost baselines in Precision, Recall, and F1-Score, particularly on hard-to-detect micro-transaction fraud patterns. An ablation study confirms the complementary contribution of both the temporal and topological components.

AI.tldr: FraudShield AI is a hybrid LSTM-Graph Topological Feature framework for detecting sophisticated money laundering patterns (smurfing/layering) under extreme data imbalance (0.13% fraud rate), using PageRank Centrality, In-Degree dynamics, Flow Ratio, Focal Loss, and dynamic thresholding, achieving substantial improvements over Logistic Regression and XGBoost on the PaySim dataset.
AI.motivation: Financial institutions struggle to detect sophisticated money laundering patterns (smurfing and layering) due to extreme data imbalance (0.13% fraud rate) and evolving adversarial evasion tactics, necessitating a shift from isolated transaction analysis to network-level forensics.
AI.method: The authors propose FraudShield AI, a hybrid framework integrating LSTM networks with hand-crafted Graph Topological Features (PageRank Centrality, In-Degree dynamics, custom Flow Ratio) to capture both temporal sequences and structural relational context. Focal Loss addresses class imbalance, and dynamic thresholding improves resilience against low-value smurfing attacks.
AI.result: On the PaySim dataset, the hybrid model substantially outperforms Logistic Regression and XGBoost baselines in Precision, Recall, and F1-Score, particularly on hard-to-detect micro-transaction fraud patterns. An ablation study confirms the complementary contribution of both temporal and topological components.
AI.conclusion: Shifting from isolated transaction analysis to network-level forensics with hybrid temporal-structural modeling significantly improves detection of sophisticated money laundering patterns under extreme data imbalance.

title: Black-Box Optimization for Identifying and Inverting Audio Dynamic Range Control Effects
summary: Dynamic Range Compression (DRC) is a widely used nonlinear audio effect whose parameters are often unknown, making blind estimation and inversion challenging. In this work, we formulate DRC parameter estimation as a black-box optimization problem in a perceptually motivated feature space. Given an observed signal and a reference representation, we estimate the parameters that minimize the distance between feature descriptors of the reconstructed and reference signals. Unlike gradient-based approaches, the proposed method does not require differentiability of the DRC model or the feature extraction pipeline, enabling the use of nonlinear and histogram-based descriptors. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method achieves competitive performance in blind parameter estimation and dry signal recovery, outperforming or matching state-of-the-art models in terms of reconstruction quality.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a black-box optimization approach for blind estimation of Dynamic Range Compression parameters using perceptually motivated features, achieving competitive reconstruction quality without requiring differentiability of the DRC model.
AI.motivation: DRC parameters are often unknown in practice, making blind estimation and inversion challenging. Existing gradient-based methods require differentiability of the DRC model or feature extraction pipeline, which limits the use of nonlinear and histogram-based descriptors.
AI.method: Formulates DRC parameter estimation as a black-box optimization problem in a perceptually motivated feature space, minimizing the distance between feature descriptors of reconstructed and reference signals without requiring differentiability.
AI.result: The proposed method achieves competitive performance in blind parameter estimation and dry signal recovery, outperforming or matching state-of-the-art models in reconstruction quality.
AI.conclusion: Black-box optimization with perceptually motivated features is effective for blind DRC parameter estimation and inversion, offering flexibility to use nonlinear and histogram-based descriptors that gradient-based methods cannot accommodate.

title: Context Matters: Improving the Practical Reliability of LLM-Based Unit Test Generation
summary: Automated unit test generation has recently benefited from advances in large language models (LLMs), yet our industrial deployments reveal a persistent gap between promising research results and practical usability. In real-world projects with complex frameworks and cross-file dependencies, LLM-generated tests frequently fail to compile, require costly manual repair, or provide unstable coverage improvements. This paper reports our experience in designing, deploying, and evaluating CATGen, a context-aware workflow for LLM-based unit test generation, informed by repeated industrial failures and refinements. Rather than relying on LLMs to infer incomplete project context, we found that compilation robustness critically depends on making project-level dependencies explicit, stabilizing test class scaffolding, and replacing iterative LLM-based repair with lightweight static analysis. These experience-driven insights shaped CATGen's multi-stage design, which combines structured context retrieval, deterministic test skeleton construction, and program analysis-based post-processing. We evaluate CATGen on real-world complex focal methods from proprietary industrial projects and additionally on the Defects4J benchmark to assess generalizability. Across both settings, CATGen substantially improves compilation success and structural coverage while significantly reducing generation time and token consumption compared to existing LLM-based approaches. Our results demonstrate that reliable LLM-based unit test generation in practice depends less on prompt engineering alone and more on systematic engineering support grounded in real-world development constraints.

AI.tldr: CATGen is a context-aware workflow for LLM-based unit test generation that significantly improves compilation success and structural coverage in real-world projects by using structured context retrieval, deterministic test skeleton construction, and static analysis-based post-processing, demonstrating that engineering rigor matters more than prompt engineering alone.
AI.motivation: Industrial deployments reveal a persistent gap between promising LLM-based unit test generation research and practical usability—LLM-generated tests frequently fail to compile, require costly manual repair, or provide unstable coverage improvements in real-world projects with complex frameworks and cross-file dependencies.
AI.method: CATGen's multi-stage design combines: (1) structured context retrieval with explicit project-level dependencies, (2) deterministic test skeleton construction for stabilizing class scaffolding, and (3) lightweight program analysis-based post-processing instead of iterative LLM-based repair.
AI.result: Evaluated on both proprietary industrial projects and Defects4J benchmark, CATGen substantially improves compilation success and structural coverage while significantly reducing generation time and token consumption compared to existing LLM-based approaches.
AI.conclusion: Reliable LLM-based unit test generation in practice depends less on prompt engineering alone and more on systematic engineering support grounded in real-world development constraints.

title: D3VL: Understanding Driving Scenes from 3D Time Series Data and Video with Language Models
summary: Recent advances in Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have triggered the development of end-to-end MLLMs for autonomous driving. However, the main emphasis to date has been for MLLMs using 2D images and videos. In contrast, this paper considers MLLM effectiveness using 3D sensors, particularly LiDAR and stereo cameras. LiDAR presents unique challenges to integration within an MLLM, largely because of data sparsity and lack of a grid structure for the data. For similar reasons, fusion of camera and LiDAR data within an MLLM pipeline is also uncommon. However, most autonomous systems rely on LiDAR-based sensing, and incorporating 3D data has been proven to improve performance in traditional 3D scene perception tasks. This paper presents D3VL, a novel MLLM framework that integrates 2D and 3D time-series data in a single but simple architecture. The model aims to answer questions involving traffic scene understanding and safety. D3VL shows an 11% improvement in the KITTI Question-Answering (QA) dataset compared to baseline methods in processing 2D and 3D time-series data. This paper further introduces the Waymo QA dataset extension, which assesses models' capabilities in processing 3D and time-series data under diverse driving conditions. D3VL implementation code and WaymoQA extension can be found on our supplemental website: https://automotivesafety-lvlm.github.io

AI.tldr: D3VL is a novel MLLM framework that integrates 2D images with 3D LiDAR/stereo time-series data for autonomous driving, achieving 11% improvement on KITTI QA and introducing the Waymo QA dataset extension for 3D and temporal reasoning evaluation.
AI.motivation: Existing MLLMs for autonomous driving focus predominantly on 2D images/videos, while LiDAR-based 3D sensing—critical in real autonomous systems—remains underexplored due to data sparsity and lack of grid structure, motivating the need for a framework that effectively integrates 3D sensor data.
AI.method: D3VL is a simple yet unified MLLM architecture that jointly processes 2D image and 3D LiDAR/stereo time-series data within a single pipeline, designed for traffic scene understanding and safety-related question answering.
AI.result: D3VL achieves an 11% improvement over baseline methods on the KITTI QA dataset for 2D and 3D time-series data processing; also introduces the WaymoQA dataset extension to evaluate 3D and temporal understanding under diverse driving conditions.
AI.conclusion: Integrating 3D sensory data (LiDAR/stereo) into MLLMs significantly boosts autonomous driving scene understanding and QA performance, and D3VL provides an effective, simple framework for this integration.

title: CruiseBench: A Real-Flight-Aligned N-CMAPSS Benchmark for Engine RUL Prediction
summary: Remaining useful life (RUL) prediction estimates how long an engine can continue safe operation and is central to maintenance planning. N-CMAPSS extends C-MAPSS by simulating run-to-failure aero-engine trajectories using recorded real-flight profiles and retaining complete within-flight time series rather than cycle-level snapshots. However, this added realism reduces evaluation control because full-flight records increase data volume and entangle degradation cues with operating-regime variation, complicating preprocessing choices and direct comparisons of RUL modeling performance. To mitigate this issue, this paper proposes CruiseBench, a cruise-stage RUL benchmark derived from N-CMAPSS. It introduces CPM-N-CMAPSS (Cruising-Period Mask for N-CMAPSS), a mask artifact that stores cycle-local cruising intervals identified by the common-altitude method for the nine accessible subdatasets. CruiseBench applies a fixed protocol to the masked rows, using scenario descriptors and measured sensors as inputs while excluding virtual sensors, health parameters, and auxiliary metadata from the feature tensor, preserving native-resolution windows, and applying dataset-wise RUL caps. Experiments with LSTM, GRU, TCN, and TSMixer provide baseline results for this setting. Under CruiseBench-eta5-W256-S10, TSMixer obtains the lowest average RMSE, $3.4\pm1.71$, and Saxena score, $(2.50\pm2.99)\times 10^{4}$. Ablation studies show that flight-stage selection, temporal downscaling method, and RUL-cap threshold affect reported results. With its fixed cruise-stage protocol, CruiseBench provides a reproducible sub-benchmark for controlled RUL model comparison and CPM-N-CMAPSS provides a stage-specific data foundation for future transfer-learning and domain-adaptation studies.

AI.tldr: CruiseBench is a cruise-stage RUL benchmark built from N-CMAPSS data, using a mask artifact (CPM-N-CMAPSS) to extract cruise intervals and a fixed preprocessing protocol. Experiments show TSMixer achieves the best performance (RMSE 3.4±1.71), and ablation studies confirm that flight-stage selection, downscaling, and RUL caps affect results. The benchmark enables reproducible RUL model comparisons.
AI.motivation: N-CMAPSS provides more realistic engine degradation data but introduces challenges: high data volume and entanglement of degradation signals with operating-regime variations, making preprocessing choices complex and direct RUL model comparison difficult. A controlled, reproducible sub-benchmark is needed to isolate degradation cues from regime effects.
AI.method: The authors propose CPM-N-CMAPSS, a mask that identifies cruise-stage intervals via the common-altitude method across nine N-CMAPSS subdatasets. CruiseBench applies a fixed protocol: uses scenario descriptors and measured sensors as inputs, excludes virtual sensors/health parameters/metadata, preserves native-resolution windows, and applies dataset-wise RUL caps. Four models (LSTM, GRU, TCN, TSMixer) are benchmarked.
AI.result: Under CruiseBench-eta5-W256-S10, TSMixer achieves the lowest average RMSE (3.4±1.71) and Saxena score ((2.50±2.99)×10⁴). Ablation studies confirm that flight-stage selection, temporal downscaling method, and RUL-cap threshold significantly influence results.
AI.conclusion: CruiseBench provides a reproducible sub-benchmark for controlled RUL model comparison under cruise-stage conditions. CPM-N-CMAPSS serves as a stage-specific data resource enabling future transfer-learning and domain-adaptation research.

title: OpenEvoShield: Dual Non-Stationary Continual Defense for Open-World Multi-Agent System Attacks
summary: LLM-based multi-agent systems (LLM-MAS) are increasingly deployed in safety-critical applications, where adversaries inject malicious instructions through inter-agent communication to propagate harmful behaviors. Unlike static threats, these attacks are doubly dynamic: adversaries refine injection strategies against deployed defenses while normal-agent behavior drifts with system expansion. Existing defenses treat deployment as a closed-world problem and degrade rapidly once either distribution shifts beyond training coverage. We propose OpenEvoShield, a co-evolutionary continual defense framework for LLM-MAS. An asymmetric rate controller (M1) decouples fast attack-side and slow normal-side learning rates from dual drift signals. A normal-boundary updater (M2) maintains a dynamic behavioral boundary at the slow rate, while an EWC-regularized policy ensemble (M3) fast-adapts without catastrophic forgetting. An energy-based multi-granularity detector (M4) fuses node-, subgraph-, and graph-level evidence to classify novel attacks as out-of-distribution. Experiments over 100 deployment rounds across five benchmarks and four MAS topologies show that OpenEvoShield outperforms static and continual baselines, detecting most previously unseen attacks while keeping false positive rates low.

AI.tldr: OpenEvoShield is a co-evolutionary continual defense framework for LLM-based multi-agent systems that handles dual dynamic drifts (fast attack adaptation and slow normal-agent drift) using an asymmetric rate controller, dynamic behavioral boundaries, EWC-regularized policy ensembles, and an energy-based multi-granularity detector, outperforming static and continual baselines across benchmarks.
AI.motivation: LLM-MAS are deployed in safety-critical settings where adversaries inject malicious instructions via inter-agent communication. Threats are doubly dynamic — adversaries refine attacks against defenses while normal-agent behavior drifts over time — yet existing defenses treat deployment as a closed-world problem and fail under distribution shift.
AI.method: OpenEvoShield comprises four modules: (M1) asymmetric rate controller decoupling fast attack-side and slow normal-side learning rates; (M2) normal-boundary updater maintaining dynamic behavioral boundaries at the slow rate; (M3) EWC-regularized policy ensemble enabling fast adaptation without catastrophic forgetting; (M4) energy-based multi-granularity detector fusing node-, subgraph-, and graph-level evidence for OOD attack classification.
AI.result: Evaluated over 100 deployment rounds across five benchmarks and four MAS topologies, OpenEvoShield outperforms static and continual baselines, detecting most previously unseen attacks while maintaining low false positive rates.
AI.conclusion: The co-evolutionary continual defense paradigm effectively addresses the dual dynamic drift challenge in LLM-MAS, offering robust and adaptive protection superior to existing closed-world defenses.

title: MR-Compare: A Mixed-Reality Framework for Spatially Grounded Visual Comparison of 3D Gaussian Splatting and Mesh Reconstructions with the Physical Environment
comment: 27 pages, 12 figures. Includes the full appendix
summary: We introduce MR-Compare, a mixed reality framework for spatially grounded visual comparison between 3D Gaussian splatting and mesh reconstructions with live video see-through (VST). Implemented on a PC-tethered Meta Quest~3, it combines a two-stage registration pipeline with a 3D Slider for cross-media comparison. We evaluated five representative desktop and mobile reconstruction workflows through a real-world benchmark with an exploratory user study ($n=30$) in two static indoor rooms. MR-Compare achieved centimetre-level translation error across all workflows. The two desktop 3DGS workflows showed the strongest overall pattern, with 3DGS-MCMC yielding the lowest registration error and strongest VST-referenced visual consistency. Room-session measures indicated high perceived usability and low workload. We further propose an anisotropy filter, a zero-shot module that leverages Gaussian anisotropies to improve 3DGS registration in MR-Compare. A controlled Replica threshold sweep shows that moderate pruning can improve robustness and reduce residual errors. These results establish system-level feasibility in the tested setting rather than task-level effectiveness or standalone deployment. The project is available at https://github.com/changruizhu96/MR-Compare.

AI.tldr: MR-Compare is a mixed reality framework for spatially grounded visual comparison between 3D Gaussian splatting and mesh reconstructions with live video see-through, achieving centimetre-level registration accuracy and high usability in indoor environments.
AI.motivation: To enable spatially grounded visual comparison between 3D Gaussian splatting (3DGS) and mesh reconstructions within a mixed reality environment using live video see-through, addressing the lack of tools for systematic cross-media reconstruction evaluation.
AI.method: MR-Compare combines a two-stage registration pipeline with a 3D Slider for cross-media comparison, implemented on a PC-tethered Meta Quest 3. It includes an anisotropy filter for zero-shot improvement of 3DGS registration. Evaluated with five reconstruction workflows (desktop and mobile) through an exploratory user study (n=30) in two static indoor rooms.
AI.result: Centimetre-level translation error across all workflows. 3DGS-MCMC achieved lowest registration error and strongest VST-referenced visual consistency. High perceived usability and low workload reported. Anisotropy filter with moderate pruning improved robustness and reduced residual errors.
AI.conclusion: Establishes system-level feasibility for mixed reality-based reconstruction comparison in controlled indoor settings, though not yet validated for task-level effectiveness or standalone deployment.

title: A Diagnostic Evaluation Framework for AI-Generated Cover Songs Using Music-Theoretic and Acoustic Features
comment: 16 pages, 3 figures, 8 tables. Code and analysis materials: https://github.com/TiaaL/songecho-cover-metrics
summary: AI-generated covers often fail through local musical errors that a global quality score cannot locate: the vocal contour may remain recognizable while the accompaniment uses the wrong harmonic function, or the output may stay in key while the arrangement remains incomplete. We present a five-dimensional diagnostic framework covering melodic pitch, harmonic progression, key consistency, style consistency, and arrangement/production quality. The benchmark contains 30 covers generated from 5 source songs by 6 systems, with expert severity ratings and 9 symbolic or acoustic features. Harmonic progression and arrangement had the highest severe-error rates (53% and 47%), whereas key consistency was better preserved. Six covers combined acceptable key consistency with severe harmonic errors. Large-leap ratio had a nominal association with melodic ratings (Spearman rho = -0.429, uncorrected p = 0.018), but no feature correlation survived the nine-test multiplicity reference. An interpretable percentile-rule pilot likewise failed to outperform a fixed majority baseline reliably across 16 dimension-level comparisons. The results separate useful diagnostic evidence from dependable automatic scoring: low-level and symbolic summaries can expose particular symptoms, but they do not replace context-aware musical judgment.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a five-dimensional diagnostic framework for evaluating AI-generated music covers, finding that harmonic progression and arrangement errors are most common, while key consistency is better preserved. However, automatic low-level features fail to reliably predict expert severity ratings after multiplicity correction, and interpretable rules cannot outperform simple baselines, highlighting the gap between symptomatic detection and context-aware musical judgment.
AI.motivation: Global quality scores for AI-generated music covers fail to localize specific musical errors (e.g., wrong harmony in accompaniment despite correct vocal contour, or incomplete arrangement while staying in key), motivating a need for fine-grained diagnostic evaluation.
AI.method: A five-dimensional diagnostic framework (melodic pitch, harmonic progression, key consistency, style consistency, arrangement/production quality) is introduced. 30 covers from 5 source songs by 6 systems are evaluated with expert severity ratings and 9 symbolic/acoustic features. Statistical analyses include Spearman correlations and an interpretable percentile-rule pilot compared against a fixed majority baseline across 16 dimension-level comparisons.
AI.result: Harmonic progression and arrangement had the highest severe-error rates (53% and 47%); key consistency was better preserved. Six covers had acceptable key consistency but severe harmonic errors. Large-leap ratio showed a nominal association with melodic ratings (Spearman rho = -0.429, uncorrected p = 0.018), but no feature correlation survived the nine-test multiplicity correction. The interpretable rule pilot failed to outperform the fixed majority baseline reliably.
AI.conclusion: Low-level symbolic/acoustic features can expose specific symptoms but do not replace context-aware musical judgment for automatic scoring of AI-generated covers.

title: Bridging Behavior and Implementation: Automated Java Glue Code Generation for Behavior-Driven Development
summary: Behavior-Driven Development (BDD) helps technical and non-technical stakeholders share a common understanding of software requirements through natural-language scenarios. Glue code makes these scenarios executable by mapping each step to the corresponding project code. However, developing and maintaining glue code requires knowledge of both the intended behavior and the underlying codebase, making it a labor-intensive part of BDD as requirements evolve. Although large language models (LLMs) have shown strong code generation capabilities, their use for automated glue code generation remains unexplored. This task requires reasoning over underspecified behavior, related BDD artifacts, and large project codebases. We present AutoGlue, a hierarchical multi-agent framework for automated Java glue code generation. AutoGlue follows a behavior-first workflow that separates behavior interpretation, context retrieval, and code generation. A Behavior Interpreter derives the intent of a step from its scenario context, while a Developer agent retrieves relevant BDD artifacts and project code before generating the final glue code. We evaluate AutoGlue on 1,307 steps from eight open-source Java projects. Compared with few-shot prompting, AutoGlue improves API F1 by 58.7% and CodeBLEU by 43.7%. It produces directly usable glue code for 46.1% of the evaluated steps, while most partially correct outputs require only minor revisions, such as adding missing actions or refining parameters. Ablation results show that behavior interpretation and project-aware context retrieval both contribute substantially to generation quality. These findings demonstrate that LLMs can effectively connect natural-language behavior specifications with project code and support specification-driven software development.

AI.tldr: AutoGlue is a hierarchical multi-agent framework for automated Java glue code generation in BDD, using LLMs with behavior interpretation and project-aware context retrieval. Evaluated on 1,307 steps from eight projects, it improves API F1 by 58.7% and CodeBLEU by 43.7% over few-shot prompting, producing directly usable glue code for 46.1% of steps.
AI.motivation: Developing and maintaining glue code in BDD is labor-intensive because it requires knowledge of both the intended behavior and the underlying codebase, especially as requirements evolve. LLMs have shown code generation capabilities but their use for automated glue code generation remains unexplored.
AI.method: AutoGlue is a hierarchical multi-agent framework following a behavior-first workflow with three components: (1) a Behavior Interpreter that derives step intent from scenario context, (2) a Developer agent that retrieves relevant BDD artifacts and project code, and (3) glue code generation based on the retrieved context.
AI.result: On 1,307 steps from eight open-source Java projects, AutoGlue improves API F1 by 58.7% and CodeBLEU by 43.7% compared to few-shot prompting. It produces directly usable glue code for 46.1% of steps, with most partially correct outputs requiring only minor revisions.
AI.conclusion: LLMs can effectively connect natural-language behavior specifications with project code, supporting specification-driven software development. Behavior interpretation and project-aware context retrieval both substantially contribute to generation quality.

title: Synthetic and Derived Training Images for Campus Waste Detection: A Multi-Seed Evaluation with YOLOv8n
summary: Incorrect disposal can contaminate campus recycling streams, and a bin-mounted camera could provide feedback as an item is discarded. We evaluated whether synthetic and derived images improve a YOLOv8n detector for this view. The real dataset contained 148 campus photographs: 86 for training, 31 for validation, and 31 for testing. Twelve joint-training configurations varied the amount and source of added images. We repeated seven principal settings with four matched seeds and computed bootstrap percentile intervals over those seeds. The real-only model reached a mean mAP@0.5 of 0.691 [0.665, 0.722]. Background replacement reduced the mean to 0.560 [0.499, 0.619], isolated-object images gave 0.680 [0.644, 0.724], and the full augmentation pool gave 0.487 [0.438, 0.537]. We also tested hand-and-forearm composites because every real photo showed a held object. Two cutouts in the initial composite set came from test photographs, so we discarded that experiment, rebuilt the set with training-split cutouts, and reran all four seeds. The corrected paired difference was +0.034 [-0.063, 0.199], which does not support a reliable hand-composite effect. Single-seed transfer experiments produced source-dependent rankings between joint mixing and sequential pretraining. None of the evaluated configurations exceeded the real-only baseline. The reported intervals quantify seed variation; the 31-photo test set remains too small for strong class-specific conclusions.

AI.tldr: Synthetic and derived images failed to improve a YOLOv8n detector for campus recycling stream contamination detection; the real-only baseline (mAP@0.5 = 0.691) outperformed all joint-training configurations, and a hand-composite experiment was invalidated due to data leakage from test split cutouts.
AI.motivation: To improve campus recycling stream contamination detection by evaluating whether synthetic and derived images, added during joint training, can boost a YOLOv8n detector's performance compared to a real-only baseline.
AI.method: Used a YOLOv8n detector with a real dataset of 148 campus photographs (86 train, 31 val, 31 test). Twelve joint-training configurations varied the amount and source of synthetic/derived images. Seven principal settings were repeated with four matched seeds; bootstrap percentile intervals were computed. A hand-and-forearm composite experiment was conducted but invalidated due to test-split leakage; it was rebuilt with training-split cutouts and rerun.
AI.result: Real-only model: mAP@0.5 = 0.691 [0.665, 0.722]. Background replacement: 0.560 [0.499, 0.619]. Isolated-object images: 0.680 [0.644, 0.724]. Full augmentation pool: 0.487 [0.438, 0.537]. Corrected hand-composite paired difference: +0.034 [-0.063, 0.199] (not reliable). No configuration exceeded the real-only baseline.
AI.conclusion: Synthetic and derived images did not improve detection performance over the real-only baseline; seed variation intervals reveal high uncertainty, and the 31-photo test set is insufficient for strong class-specific conclusions.

title: Air Quality Arena: A Large-Scale Multi-Region Ground Monitoring Dataset and Benchmark for Air Quality Forecasting with Time-Series Foundation Models
summary: Air pollution causes an estimated 7.9 million premature deaths annually, making accurate forecasting a critical public health priority. Machine learning is increasingly being applied to forecast air pollution levels, yet existing benchmarks remain narrow in both geographic scope and pollutant coverage, and fail to evaluate the latest generation of time series foundation models (TSFMs) on real world, large scale data. We present Air Quality Arena (AQA), a large scale multi-country and multi-pollutant dataset (AQA-Data) and benchmark (AQA-Bench) to address this gap. AQA covers 6 major pollutants over a three year period across 7 diverse countries and 4 continents, with more than 14,000 station-pollutant series, aiming to provide a comprehensive benchmark for air quality tasks. We benchmark this dataset across 11 leading time series foundation models and classical baselines to assess performance on short-term air quality forecasting. Our results demonstrate that TSFMs are effective zero-shot forecasters and consistently outperform classical baselines, with our top-performing model employing a cross-modal architecture that leverages a vision foundation model for time series forecasting. AQA is publicly released at AirQualityArena.github.io

AI.tldr: Air Quality Arena (AQA) is a large-scale, multi-country, multi-pollutant dataset and benchmark covering 6 pollutants across 7 countries and 4 continents with 14,000+ station-pollutant series. It evaluates 11 time series foundation models and classical baselines on short-term air quality forecasting, finding that TSFMs outperform classical methods, with the best model using a cross-modal architecture from vision foundation models.
AI.motivation: Air pollution causes 7.9 million premature deaths annually. Existing benchmarks are narrow in geographic scope and pollutant coverage, and fail to evaluate the latest time series foundation models on real-world, large-scale data. AQA addresses this gap with a comprehensive, multi-country, multi-pollutant benchmark.
AI.method: The authors construct AQA-Data covering 6 major pollutants (3 years, 7 countries, 4 continents, 14,000+ station-pollutant series). They benchmark 11 leading TSFMs and classical baselines on short-term forecasting tasks, including a cross-modal model leveraging a vision foundation model for time series.
AI.result: TSFMs are effective zero-shot forecasters and consistently outperform classical baselines. The top-performing model uses a cross-modal architecture (vision foundation model adapted for time series forecasting).
AI.conclusion: AQA provides a comprehensive, large-scale benchmark for air quality forecasting, demonstrating the superiority of modern TSFMs over classical approaches and the potential of cross-modal architectures. The dataset is publicly released.

title: Benchmarking Confidential GPU Inference on NVIDIA H100 under Intel TDX
summary: Confidential computing is becoming a practical deployment requirement for AI inference workloads that process sensitive inputs or protect proprietary model assets. However, the performance cost of enabling confidential execution for GPU-accelerated large language model serving remains workload dependent and operationally important. This paper presents a benchmark study comparing standard non-confidential execution with confidential computing mode on a single NVIDIA H100 80GB GPU hosted in an Intel TDX confidential instance. The evaluation uses two representative language models, Mistral-7B v0.1 and Qwen3-30B-A3B, and measures time to first token, end-to-end request latency, per-request token generation throughput, global token throughput, and closed-loop request throughput under increasing concurrency. In fixed request-rate experiments, confidential mode increases average TTFT by 21.8% for Mistral-7B and 27.8% for Qwen3-30B-A3B, while global token throughput drops by 17.7% and 21.1%, respectively. In closed-loop concurrency experiments, throughput gaps remain in the 11.5-20.2% range, but the larger model reaches its saturation knee earlier under confidential mode. The results suggest that confidential GPU inference can retain usable throughput under load, but capacity planning must account for both the steady throughput penalty and the earlier saturation behavior observed for larger models.

AI.tldr: This paper benchmarks confidential vs. non-confidential LLM inference on an NVIDIA H100 GPU in a TDX confidential instance, finding confidential mode increases TTFT by 21.8–27.8% and reduces throughput by 11.5–21.1%, with larger models saturating earlier.
AI.motivation: Confidential computing is increasingly required for AI inference workloads handling sensitive data or protecting proprietary models, but its performance impact on GPU-accelerated LLM serving is workload-dependent and operationally significant, motivating a systematic benchmark.
AI.method: Benchmark study comparing standard non-confidential vs. confidential execution on a single NVIDIA H100 80GB GPU in an Intel TDX confidential instance, evaluating Mistral-7B v0.1 and Qwen3-30B-A3B across metrics including TTFT, end-to-end latency, per-request token throughput, global token throughput, and closed-loop throughput under varying concurrency.
AI.result: Confidential mode increases average TTFT by 21.8% (Mistral-7B) and 27.8% (Qwen3-30B-A3B); global token throughput drops by 17.7% and 21.1% respectively. Closed-loop throughput gaps are 11.5–20.2%, with the larger model hitting saturation earlier under confidential mode.
AI.conclusion: Confidential GPU inference can maintain usable throughput under load, but capacity planning must account for both the steady throughput penalty and the earlier saturation behavior exhibited by larger models.

title: Split Radiance Cascades: Real-Time Global Illumination via Sparse Radiance Probes
summary:
Radiance probe methods are a popular and well-tested approach for approximating diffuse global illumination for real-time graphics, but they commonly suffer from a lack of detail due to the large spacing between probes. Radiance Cascade (RC) fixes this by increasing spatial resolution and reducing angular resolution for light and occlusion from closer objects, which allows it to provide details at all scales without noise or aliasing. However, leading implementations of RC either run in 2D or screenspace, due to the prohibitive costs of storing high-detail volumetric radiance information.
  In this work, we adapt Radiance Cascades for accurate real-time 3D diffuse global illumination using a sparse hashmap to store world-space probes. We introduce ray splitting, a method for calculating radiance intervals used in RC by tracing rays from visible surfaces and calculating their contribution to cascades based on their hit distance. We evaluate our algorithm, Split Radiance Cascades, on a variety of scenes, and demonstrate that it can provide high-quality indirect illumination in both single-frame and temporally accumulated contexts.

AI.tldr: Split Radiance Cascades adapts Radiance Cascades for real-time 3D diffuse global illumination by using a sparse hashmap for world-space probes and introducing ray splitting to compute radiance intervals from ray hit distances, achieving high-quality indirect illumination.
AI.motivation: Radiance Cascade methods in 2D/screenspace lack volumetric detail due to storage costs; the authors aim to enable 3D world-space Radiance Cascades efficiently for real-time diffuse GI.
AI.method: Uses a sparse hashmap to store world-space probes, and introduces ray splitting to calculate radiance intervals for cascades by tracing rays from visible surfaces and computing contributions based on hit distance.
AI.result: Provides high-quality indirect illumination in both single-frame and temporally accumulated contexts across various scenes.
AI.conclusion: Split Radiance Cascades enables accurate real-time 3D diffuse global illumination with detailed probe resolution previously infeasible in world space.

title: Ultra-Compact CNN Architectures for Tropical Bird Audio Detection on Microcontrollers
summary: Passive acoustic monitoring of tropical biodiversity is bottlenecked by the storage and battery cost of continuously recording soundscapes in which bird vocalisations typically occupy less than 10% of the audio. Autonomous recording units built on low-power microcontrollers (typically ARM Cortex-M with $\leq$256 kB of RAM) address this by triggering only on likely-positive segments, but the on-device options are unsatisfying: coarse frequency-energy triggers such as Goertzel filters flood SD cards with false positives at $\sim$71% precision, whereas neural detectors developed for temperate single-species tasks are either too large to deploy or transfer poorly to species-rich tropical settings. We present DrongoNet, a family of three INT8 CNN detectors sized for this envelope and validated on a 50,000-clip, 1,677-species Southeast Asian tropical dataset (SEABAD). The headline model, DrongoNet-Micro (919 parameters, 6.26 kB, 0.9810 AUC, 98.3\% mean recall at τ = 0.35), is a drop-in replacement for the Goertzel trigger used in commodity field recorders: at α = 0.10 tropical prevalence it captures 8 pp more bird vocalisations than Goertzel and extends a 32 GB card from $\sim$28 to $\sim$45 days of monitoring. DrongoNet-Nano (5.09 kB) bounds the ultra-low-flash extreme; DrongoNet-Edge (33.06 kB, 0.9991 AUC) targets Linux SBCs. On SEABAD, Micro matches a retrained TinyChirp CNN-Mel baseline within 0.1 pp AUC at 28$\times$ fewer parameters, confirming that the family is deployment-agnostic across mel-spectrogram bird corpora but requires per-environment retraining. Full INT8 quantisation costs $<$0.12% AUC across all three variants.

AI.tldr: DrongoNet is a family of three ultra-compact INT8 CNN detectors (Micro: 919 params, 6.26 kB; Nano: 5.09 kB; Edge: 33.06 kB) designed for on-device bird vocalisation detection on low-power microcontrollers (ARM Cortex-M with ≤256 kB RAM). It replaces coarse Goertzel filters (71% precision) in autonomous recording units, achieving 98.3% mean recall (Micro at τ=0.35) and 0.9810 AUC on a 50,000-clip, 1,677-species tropical dataset (SEABAD), extending SD card life from ~28 to ~45 days.
AI.motivation: Passive acoustic monitoring of tropical biodiversity is bottlenecked by storage/battery costs of continuous recording, as bird vocalisations occupy <10% of audio. Existing on-device triggers are either coarse (Goertzel filters with ~71% precision flooding SD cards with false positives) or too large/poorly transferable (neural detectors designed for temperate single-species tasks cannot fit on low-power MCUs with ≤256 kB RAM).
AI.method: DrongoNet is a family of three INT8 CNN detectors sized for ultra-low-power MCUs (Micro: 919 params, 6.26 kB; Nano: 5.09 kB; Edge: 33.06 kB). Models are validated on SEABAD (50,000 clips, 1,677 Southeast Asian species). Full INT8 quantization is applied (<0.12% AUC loss). Micro is a drop-in replacement for Goertzel triggers in commodity field recorders.
AI.result: DrongoNet-Micro: 0.9810 AUC, 98.3% mean recall at τ=0.35; at α=0.10 tropical prevalence captures 8 pp more bird vocalisations than Goertzel; extends 32 GB card from ~28 to ~45 days. Micro matches TinyChirp CNN-Mel baseline within 0.1 pp AUC at 28× fewer parameters. Full INT8 quantisation costs <0.12% AUC across all variants.
AI.conclusion: DrongoNet provides deployment-agnostic, ultra-compact neural triggers for tropical bird monitoring on severely resource-constrained devices, significantly outperforming Goertzel filters while fitting within the ≤256 kB RAM envelope. The family requires per-environment retraining but transfers well across mel-spectrogram bird corpora.

title: Towards Automated Formal Verification of zkEVMs Using LLM-Guided Constraint Synthesis
summary: Zero-Knowledge Ethereum Virtual Machines (zkEVMs) secure Ethereum rollups by generating zero-knowledge proofs that guarantee off-chain execution correctness. However, subtle implementation bugs (e.g., incorrect gas accounting) can lead to valid proofs certifying semantically faulty states, thereby silently defeating cryptographic guarantees.
