The derived discrete loss for training standard networks demonstrates robustness and consistent improvements over non-training and partial cross-entropy (PCE) baselines in experiments, achieving comparable performance without requiring ground-truth segmentation images.

AI.tldr: A unified variational framework for image segmentation with sparse pixel-level supervision, using a simplex-constrained Potts model with smooth perimeter regularization. Sparse labels are handled via fuzzy membership functions in RKHS. The loss improves weakly supervised learning over baselines.
AI.motivation: To address image segmentation under sparse pixel-level supervision without requiring dense ground-truth segmentation maps, improving upon existing weakly supervised and partial cross-entropy approaches.
AI.method: A simplex-constrained Potts model with a smooth perimeter regularizer is used as a convex, smooth energy functional. Sparse labels are incorporated via fuzzy membership functions derived from a function extension problem in an RKHS, capturing inhomogeneous intensity statistics. This functional serves as a training loss in weakly supervised deep learning or is optimized via iterative methods.
AI.result: The derived discrete loss improves robustness and achieves consistent improvements over non-training and partial cross-entropy baselines, with comparable performance to methods using full ground-truth segmentation images.
AI.conclusion: The proposed variational framework effectively leverages sparse supervision for image segmentation, offering a principled and practical loss function for weakly supervised deep learning.

title: Neural Operator Surrogates for Two-Dimensional Neutron Flux Estimation
comment: to be submitted to ANS Winter 2026
summary: This work extends our one-dimensional single-sweep neural-operator studies to two dimensions. We consider one-group transport with isotropic scattering. As in the one-dimensional work, we use Fourier neural operators (FNOs) to approximate the high-fidelity scalar flux. Additionally, we also investigate U-shaped neural operators (UNOs) in this study. We consider three surrogates. The first two map the material and source fields directly to the flux, one using an FNO and one using a UNO. The third is an FNO that additionally takes the scalar flux after one source iteration, the single-sweep approximation, as an input. Each case is solved to high fidelity with a verified discrete-ordinates solver, and an average relative L_2 error norm is used to characterize the quality of the inferred maps. We train every surrogate over three random seeds so that differences between them can be assessed against run-to-run variability. Two questions guide the study: whether the single-sweep input improves accuracy over the direct maps, and whether training on the logarithm of the flux improves accuracy in the strongly attenuated regions relevant to shielding.

AI.tldr: This paper extends 1D neural-operator studies to 2D transport problems, comparing Fourier (FNO) and U-shaped (UNO) neural operators as surrogates for high-fidelity scalar flux, with one variant incorporating a single-sweep approximation as input. Two key questions are: whether single-sweep input improves accuracy, and whether training on log-flux improves accuracy in strongly attenuated regions.
AI.motivation: To extend prior 1D single-sweep neural-operator studies to 2D transport problems, and to investigate whether incorporating a single-sweep approximation as input or training on the logarithm of flux improves surrogate accuracy, particularly in strongly attenuated regions relevant to shielding.
AI.method: Three surrogates are compared: (1) an FNO mapping material/source fields directly to flux, (2) a UNO mapping material/source fields directly to flux, and (3) an FNO that additionally takes the scalar flux after one source iteration (single-sweep approximation) as input. All are trained over three random seeds and evaluated via average relative L2 error norm against a high-fidelity discrete-ordinates solver.
AI.result: Not specified in the abstract; the paper evaluates average relative L2 error norms across three random seeds for each surrogate to assess accuracy differences relative to run-to-run variability.
AI.conclusion: The study addresses whether the single-sweep input improves accuracy over direct maps and whether training on the logarithm of flux improves accuracy in strongly attenuated shielding-relevant regions.

title: Profile-Graph Memory for LLM Agents: Implicit Cross-Entity Traversal through Narrative Profiles
comment: 11 pages, 2 figures, 7 tables. Code and MemHop benchmark: https://github.com/ShengtongZhu/ProGraph
summary: Long-term memory is essential for LLM agents that interact across sessions, yet current memory benchmarks primarily evaluate single-hop recall, leaving multi-hop association largely unmeasured. We make three contributions. First, we introduce MemHop, a multi-hop memory benchmark of 1,000 questions at hop depths 1-5 across 10 social-network scenarios, with per-hop evidence annotations. Second, we present Profile-Graph Memory (ProGraph), a two-layer memory architecture combining (i) profile expansion -- substring-matched traversal of entity names that naturally appear in LLM-written profile narratives, a minimal alternative to explicit knowledge-graph construction -- and (ii) compression residuals -- exact dates, quantities, and named items co-extracted with each profile update at zero extra API cost. Third, a full-grid ablation shows cross-benchmark mechanism specialization: profile expansion drives multi-hop reasoning (-22.6pp on MemHop when removed) while compression residuals drive precision recall (-8.6pp on LoCoMo when not co-extracted), with cross-effects under 3pp within a single architecture. ProGraph averages 80.1% on MemHop (matching the FullContext reference) and 78.4% on LoCoMo (exceeding FullContext by 11.3pp), outperforming Mem0, A-Mem, HippoRAG, and RAG on both. We release MemHop, ProGraph, and baseline implementations.

AI.tldr: Proposes MemHop (multi-hop memory benchmark) and ProGraph (two-layer memory architecture combining profile expansion and compression residuals), achieving state-of-the-art results on both MemHop and LoCoMo benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing memory benchmarks only evaluate single-hop recall, leaving multi-hop association across sessions largely unmeasured for LLM agents.
AI.method: Two-layer architecture: (1) Profile expansion — substring-matched traversal of entity names in LLM-written profile narratives, a lightweight alternative to explicit knowledge graphs; (2) Compression residuals — co-extracting exact dates, quantities, and named items with each profile update at zero extra API cost.
AI.result: ProGraph achieves 80.1% on MemHop (matching FullContext) and 78.4% on LoCoMo (+11.3pp over FullContext), outperforming Mem0, A-Mem, HippoRAG, and RAG. Ablation shows profile expansion drives multi-hop reasoning (-22.6pp when removed), compression residuals drive precision recall (-8.6pp when not co-extracted).
AI.conclusion: The proposed architecture demonstrates effective cross-benchmark mechanism specialization with minimal cross-effects, and the released benchmark (MemHop) enables future evaluation of multi-hop memory capabilities.

title: Cumsum-Composable Phase Transport for Low-Cost Streaming Keyword Spotting
summary:
State-space sequence models are attractive for streaming speech because they maintain compact recurrent state, but scan-style training kernels can have unfavorable constants for short audio tasks. We study cumsum-composable phase transport, a streaming-native temporal layer for keyword spotting. Each layer projects acoustic frames to complex channels, transports them by learned unitary rotations, accumulates a finite window using prefix differences, and applies a gated residual update. The same prefix representation gives exact batched training with ordinary cumulative sums and exact online inference with one prefix update per frame. Unitary transport is the key constraint: inverse rotations have norm one, keeping prefix terms well conditioned while memory is supplied by windows or block readouts.
  On Google Speech Commands v2 with 12 labels, mel+cumsum models retain competitive accuracy with compact baselines. The strongest single-seed run reaches 97.3\% test accuracy; a 51.6K-parameter tied model also reaches 97.3\%, and a 24.8K tied model reaches 96.8\% versus 97.1\% for a 25.6K MelCNNMaxPool baseline. In a matched cumsum-versus-scan benchmark, cumsum+window gives comparable accuracy, 94.82\% versus 94.33\%, while training 1.07x faster and reducing single-example latency from 7.09 ms to 5.01 ms on a Tesla T4. These results support cumsum phase transport as a simple low-cost temporal primitive for streaming keyword spotting.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes cumsum-composable phase transport, a streaming-native temporal layer for keyword spotting that uses unitary rotations and prefix cumulative sums to achieve fast batched training and efficient online inference, achieving competitive accuracy on Google Speech Commands v2 (up to 97.3%) with faster training (1.07x) and lower latency (5.01ms vs 7.09ms) compared to scan-style kernels.
AI.motivation: State-space sequence models are attractive for streaming speech due to compact recurrent state, but their scan-style training kernels have unfavorable computational constants for short audio tasks like keyword spotting.
AI.method: Each layer projects acoustic frames to complex channels, transports them via learned unitary rotations, accumulates a finite window using prefix differences, and applies a gated residual update. The prefix representation enables exact batched training with cumulative sums and exact online inference with one prefix update per frame.
AI.result: On Google Speech Commands v2, the model achieves 97.3% test accuracy; a 51.6K-parameter tied model also reaches 97.3%, and a 24.8K tied model reaches 96.8% vs 97.1% for a 25.6K MelCNNMaxPool baseline. In a matched benchmark, cumsum+window gives 94.82% vs 94.33% accuracy, trains 1.07x faster, and reduces latency from 7.09ms to 5.01ms on a Tesla T4.
AI.conclusion: Cumsum phase transport is a simple, low-cost temporal primitive for streaming keyword spotting, offering competitive accuracy with improved training speed and lower inference latency.

title: Don't Trust the Label: License Laundering in AI Supply Chains
summary: AI artifacts move through a multi-platform supply chain, spanning datasets and models on Hugging Face and applications on GitHub. While each artifact carries a license whose obligations should propagate through redistribution, no study has yet measured whether those obligations survive the chain or are stripped and replaced as artifacts move downstream. We trace 232,270 dataset$\rightarrow$model$\rightarrow$application chains and quantify two forms of license laundering: when artifacts with no declared license acquire definitive labels downstream, and when one declared license category replaces another during redistribution. We find that 62.3% of chains pass through at least one artifact with no declared license (concentrated in a small set of foundational datasets), and that every obligation-bearing license category falls below 7% end-to-end survival while the Permissive category reaches 95.1%. Based on these findings, we provide actionable recommendations for practitioners, model publishers, rights holders, and platform owners.

AI.tldr: This study traces 232,270 dataset→model→application chains in AI supply chains and finds widespread license laundering: 62.3% of chains pass through artifacts with no declared license, and obligation-bearing license categories have less than 7% end-to-end survival while permissive licenses survive at 95.1%.
AI.motivation: Despite AI artifacts (datasets, models, applications) moving through multi-platform supply chains with licenses that should propagate obligations downstream, no prior study has measured whether those obligations actually survive the chain or are stripped/replaced as artifacts move downstream.
AI.method: The authors trace 232,270 dataset→model→application chains across Hugging Face (datasets and models) and GitHub (applications), and quantify two forms of license laundering: (1) when artifacts with no declared license acquire definitive labels downstream, and (2) when one declared license category replaces another during redistribution.
AI.result: 62.3% of chains pass through at least one artifact with no declared license (concentrated in a small set of foundational datasets). Every obligation-bearing license category falls below 7% end-to-end survival, while the Permissive category reaches 95.1% survival.
AI.conclusion: The paper provides actionable recommendations for practitioners, model publishers, rights holders, and platform owners to address the license laundering problem in AI supply chains.

title: PhenSPINE: A Standardized Benchmark for Spine Pathology Diagnosis
comment: 12 pages, figures, Accepted at CITA 2026 (The 15th Conference on Information Technology and its Applications, Scopus)
summary: The accurate diagnosis of spinal pathologies depends heavily on radiological interpretation, yet automated systems are hindered by the lack of diverse, high-quality benchmarks. In this study, we present PhenSPINE, a Magnetic Resonance Imaging dataset comprising 16,813 images from 250 patients, curated to facilitate advanced deep learning research. We propose a robust diagnostic benchmark that integrates state-of-theart convolutional backbones with a Positional Encoding mechanism to explicitly model the anatomical context of intervertebral discs. Evaluating across four standard MRI sequences, our experiments demonstrate that the Sagittal T2-weighted sequence offers the most robust diagnostic value, achieving a superior Macro F1-score of 50.31%. We find that multisequence fusion strategies yield inferior performance compared to this single-sequence baseline, as the images across sequences in our dataset are significantly compromised by noise interference from surrounding anatomical regions. This work establishes a robust baseline and offers critical insights into sequence selection for spine analysis.

AI.tldr: PhenSPINE introduces a 16,813-image MRI dataset from 250 patients for spinal pathology diagnosis, using convolutional backbones with Positional Encoding. The Sagittal T2-weighted sequence achieves the best Macro F1-score (50.31%), outperforming multi-sequence fusion due to noise interference in other sequences.
AI.motivation: Automated spine diagnosis is limited by the lack of diverse, high-quality benchmarks; there is a need for a well-curated dataset and robust diagnostic methods that leverage anatomical context.
AI.method: Curated an MRI dataset (PhenSPINE) of 16,813 images from 250 patients; integrated convolutional backbones with a Positional Encoding mechanism to model intervertebral disc anatomical context; evaluated across four standard MRI sequences.
AI.result: Sagittal T2-weighted sequence achieved a Macro F1-score of 50.31%, outperforming multi-sequence fusion strategies, which were compromised by noise interference from surrounding anatomical regions.
AI.conclusion: The study establishes a robust baseline for spine analysis and provides critical insights into sequence selection, highlighting that single-sequence (Sagittal T2) can outperform multi-sequence fusion in noisy conditions.

title: The Orthogonalized Read Is a Removable Training Scaffold for Recurrent Memory
comment: 18 pages, 8 figures. Code, per-seed results, and checkpoints: https://github.com/no-way-labs/recurrent-memory-scaffold
summary: A recent report finds that orthogonalizing the mLSTM memory matrix at read time (five Newton-Schulz iterations, trained through) substantially improves noisy associative recall. The effect replicates, but it is not a memory improvement. Training on this task is a long chance plateau followed by a sharp escape, and the orthogonalized read acts by re-conditioning the learning problem during the plateau. Three properties establish this. It must be self-consistent: an exact recursive least-squares read (the Mesa layer) reproduces it, while straight-through halves, delta-rule writes, frozen random keys, and plain normalization all fail. It is uniform: across a learning-rate x hardness grid it multiplies the escape hazard roughly six-fold with no detectable hardness dependence, widening the workable learning-rate corridor that narrows for the baseline. And it is removable: applied to failed models at inference it rescues none, and annealed away on an escape-triggered schedule it leaves numerically stock mLSTMs at full accuracy. Much of the published gain needs no architecture at all -- solved-rate at a fixed budget measures escape hazard, which follows a heat/noise law (learning-rate elasticity +3.0, gradient-noise elasticity -1.65) under which the original vocab-96 result is a large-batch noise condition rather than a capacity one. Decoding the memory state directly shows failed models carry roughly half their associations in linearly recoverable form: the plateau is a readout failure over half-written storage. Two conclusions travel beyond the intervention: recall benchmarks used for architecture selection partly measure trainability, and the system is a fully instrumented model organism of "emergence," in which a sharp behavioral threshold demonstrably arises from a censored metric over gradually accumulating structure.

AI.tldr: Orthogonalizing mLSTM memory at read time doesn't improve memory but re-conditions learning dynamics during a training plateau, acting as a trainability enhancer rather than a storage fix. The effect is self-consistent, uniform across hyperparameters, and removable at inference. Published gains reflect escape hazard (heat/noise law) rather than capacity. Failed models store ~half of associations recoverably; the plateau is a readout failure.
AI.motivation: To understand why orthogonalizing the mLSTM memory matrix improves associative recall, and to determine whether the mechanism is genuinely memory improvement or a training dynamics artifact.
AI.method: Compared orthogonalized read (Newton-Schulz iterations) against exact recursive least-squares (Mesa layer), straight-through, delta-rule writes, frozen random keys, and plain normalization. Analyzed escape hazard across learning-rate × hardness grid. Conducted inference-only intervention and annealing experiments. Derived heat/noise law for escape hazard. Decoded memory states directly.
AI.result: Orthogonalization multiplies escape hazard ~6× uniformly across hardness, widens workable learning-rate corridor, but fails at inference. Gain follows heat/noise law: learning-rate elasticity +3.0, gradient-noise elasticity -1.65. Failed models store ~50% of associations linearly recoverably.
AI.conclusion: The orthogonalized read is a trainability intervention, not a memory improvement. Recall benchmarks partly measure trainability. The system serves as a model organism for "emergence" where sharp behavioral thresholds arise from censored metrics over gradual structure accumulation.

title: Lifted Representation Hypothesis in Language Models
comment: 20 pages, 6 figures, ICML 2026 Workshop: Philosophy Meets Machine Learning
summary: Large language models (LLMs) often answer queries by mapping individual observations to more general rule-like structures. However, it remains unclear how these structures are stored, selected, and revised. To study this process, we propose thelifted representation hypothesis: LLMs update memory through shared latent structures rather than isolated instance-level facts. This view frames lifting as an efficient use of symmetry across instances, and shattering as the refinement of coarse lifted structures into more specific subtypes. We evaluate LLMs' lifting and shattering through controlled exception-learning experiments across in-context learning, LoRA, and full fine-tuning. We find that LLMs are vulnerable to shattering failures when data are governed by nested rules and exceptions, while lifting often occurs prematurely. These results highlight the need to study the relation between data and rule structures in LLMs.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes the lifted representation hypothesis, where LLMs update memory through shared latent structures rather than isolated facts. Through exception-learning experiments across in-context learning, LoRA, and full fine-tuning, the authors find LLMs are vulnerable to shattering failures with nested rules/exceptions and often lift prematurely.
AI.motivation: To understand how LLMs store, select, and revise general rule-like structures derived from individual observations, as the mechanisms underlying this process remain unclear.
AI.method: Proposes the lifted representation hypothesis (lifting as symmetry across instances, shattering as refinement into subtypes) and evaluates it via controlled exception-learning experiments across in-context learning, LoRA, and full fine-tuning.
AI.result: LLMs exhibit shattering failures when data follow nested rules and exceptions, and lifting occurs prematurely in many cases.
AI.conclusion: Highlights the need to study the relationship between data structure and rule representations in LLMs, as current models show systematic weaknesses in handling hierarchical rule structures.

title: Audio-Zero: Label-Free Self-Evolution for Fine-Grained Audio Reasoning
summary: Large Audio Language models (LALMs) have made rapid progress on acoustic understanding, yet they still struggle with fine-grained audio reasoning (e.g., recognizing event order, repetitions and duration). Existing post-training methods heavily rely on expensive external labels or provide only coarse semantic signals. To bridge this gap, we introduce Audio-Zero, the first label-free self-evolution framework in the field of LALMs that improves fine-grained auditory perception and reasoning. Audio-Zero constructs an auditory self-play game from unlabeled audio contrast pairs: most players hear a reference audio, while one odd listener hears a subtle variant. The model first generates clues describing what it hears and then identifies the odd listener by reasoning over inconsistencies among clues. Since the odd listener is known by construction, the game provides verifiable rewards without any annotated answers. Experiments with Qwen2-Audio-7B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-Omni-7B on TREA, MMAU Test-mini and MMAR show that Audio-Zero improves fine-grained audio reasoning while preserving broad audio understanding. Evolutionary and diagnostic analyses further reveal that increasingly fine-grained auditory descriptions emerge naturally from game pressure.

AI.tldr: Audio-Zero is the first label-free self-evolution framework for Large Audio Language Models that improves fine-grained audio reasoning through an auditory self-play game with verifiable rewards, requiring no external annotations.
AI.motivation: Existing LALMs struggle with fine-grained audio reasoning (event order, repetitions, duration), and current post-training methods rely on expensive external labels or coarse semantic signals.
AI.method: Audio-Zero constructs an auditory self-play game from unlabeled audio contrast pairs, where most players hear a reference audio and one odd listener hears a subtle variant. The model generates clues and identifies the odd listener via reasoning over inconsistencies, using the known odd listener as verifiable reward without annotations.
AI.result: Experiments on Qwen2-Audio-7B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-Omni-7B across TREA, MMAU Test-mini, and MMAR benchmarks show improved fine-grained audio reasoning while preserving broad audio understanding.
AI.conclusion: Fine-grained auditory descriptions emerge naturally from game pressure, demonstrating the effectiveness of self-play for audio reasoning without external labels.

title: Multi-Source and Cross-Scenario Strategy-Guided Code Optimization
summary: Automated code optimization improves program performance by refactoring source code, and recent studies use LLMs to generate optimization patches. The newest approaches are strategy-guided: they summarize strategies from historical optimization commits as static analysis rules, and use these rules to match code locations for LLMs to optimize. However, these approaches have two limitations: (1) the strategies may come from other knowledge sources, such as textbooks and web pages, but the existing approaches cannot utilize them; (2) a strategy may be applicable to different scenarios, e.g., different programming languages, but existing approaches can only formalize strategies for the scenario to which the source commit belongs. To address these limitations, we propose MoST, an LLM-based code optimization framework that integrates multiple knowledge sources across scenarios. MoST uniformly represents items in different knowledge sources as evidence objects, clusters them in a cross-source and cross-scenario manner to identify strategies, and transfers them to the target scenario when necessary for generating static analysis rules. To implement this process, MoST employs a novel self-balanced weighted clustering algorithm to balance evidence objects from different knowledge sources, and a novel example transfer procedure to ensure the quality of the generated rules when transferring across scenarios. On a benchmark containing 151 C/C++, 150 Python, and 50 Rust historical optimization tasks, compared with SemOpt, MoST yields 24.44%-180.00% and 21.88%-37.50% more patches that are exactly the same as or semantically equivalent to developer patches, respectively. When optimizing 15 real-world projects, MoST achieves 19.72%-717.42% maximum improvements and 4.44%-258.17% average improvements for the performance tests in the projects, significantly outperforming SemOpt and Codex.

AI.tldr: MoST is an LLM-based code optimization framework that integrates multiple knowledge sources (textbooks, web pages, commits) across different programming scenarios using a novel self-balanced weighted clustering algorithm and example transfer procedure, significantly outperforming existing methods like SemOpt and Codex on C/C++, Python, and Rust optimization tasks.
AI.motivation: Existing strategy-guided LLM-based code optimization approaches have two limitations: (1) they can only utilize strategies from historical optimization commits, not from other knowledge sources like textbooks and web pages; (2) they can only formalize strategies for the specific scenario of the source commit, failing to generalize across different scenarios (e.g., different programming languages).
AI.method: MoST uniformly represents items from different knowledge sources as evidence objects, clusters them cross-source and cross-scenario using a self-balanced weighted clustering algorithm to identify strategies, and transfers them to target scenarios via an example transfer procedure for generating static analysis rules that guide LLM optimization.
AI.result: On benchmarks with 151 C/C++, 150 Python, and 50 Rust tasks, MoST produces 24.44%-180.00% more exact-match patches and 21.88%-37.50% more semantically equivalent patches than SemOpt. On 15 real-world projects, MoST achieves 19.72%-717.42% maximum and 4.44%-258.17% average performance improvements, outperforming SemOpt and Codex.
AI.conclusion: MoST effectively addresses the limitations of prior strategy-guided approaches by enabling cross-source and cross-scenario strategy extraction and transfer, leading to substantially better code optimization results across multiple programming languages and real-world projects.

title: SafeGen: Goal-Conditioned Video Diffusion of Safety-Critical Scenarios for VLM-Based Autonomous Driving
summary: VLMs are increasingly deployed in AD systems, creating an urgent need for rigorous safety evaluation under rare yet safety-critical scenarios. Among these, interactions with vulnerable road users represent a major source of real-world failures. However, existing safety-critical scenario generation methods predominantly rely on simulator-based pipelines, which suffer from a substantial sim-to-real gap and often fail to capture realistic, diverse, and unforeseen human-vehicle interaction dynamics. We present SafeGen, a goal-conditioned diffusion framework for safety-critical scenario generation in VLMADs. Our key insight is to formulate scenario generation as a goal-conditioned diffusion process, where a predefined catastrophic end-state serves as a strong supervisory signal, guiding the generation of temporally coherent video trajectories that naturally evolve toward safety-critical outcomes. Building on this formulation, we introduce Context Grounded End State Reasoning, which leverages VLMs to analyze benign driving contexts and infer latent vulnerabilities in human-vehicle interactions, producing structured end-state specifications that induce high-risk scenarios. Conditioned on these targets, we further propose End State Conditioned Video Evolution, which grounds semantic threats into physically plausible visual dynamics. Specifically, we instantiate high-risk agents within the scene via depth-aware geometric projection, followed by boundary-conditioned diffusion to generate intermediate frames with consistent motion patterns and temporal coherence. Extensive experiments across 3 VLMADs demonstrate that SafeGen increases the Judge Overall Score, a metric using a VLM judge to evaluate VLMADs' understanding and decision-making, by 24.25% on average compared to SoTA baselines. Furthermore, fine-tuning a VLMAD improves performance in real-world driving scenes by an average of 15.9%.

AI.tldr: SafeGen is a goal-conditioned diffusion framework for generating safety-critical traffic scenarios to evaluate Vision-Language Model Autonomous Driving systems (VLMADs). It formulates scenario generation as a diffusion process guided by catastrophic end-states, uses VLMs to infer vulnerabilities from benign contexts, and produces temporally coherent video trajectories. Experiments show 24.25% improvement in Judge Overall Score over baselines and 15.9% real-world driving improvement after fine-tuning.
AI.motivation: Existing safety-critical scenario generation methods rely on simulator-based pipelines with substantial sim-to-real gaps, failing to capture realistic, diverse, and unforeseen human-vehicle interaction dynamics. There is an urgent need for rigorous safety evaluation of VLMADs under rare yet safety-critical scenarios, especially involving vulnerable road users.
AI.method: SafeGen uses a goal-conditioned diffusion process where catastrophic end-states supervise video trajectory generation. It includes: (1) Context Grounded End State Reasoning, using VLMs to analyze benign driving contexts and infer latent vulnerabilities to produce structured end-state specifications; (2) End State Conditioned Video Evolution, grounding semantic threats into visual dynamics via depth-aware geometric projection of high-risk agents and boundary-conditioned diffusion for intermediate frames with temporal coherence.
AI.result: Across 3 VLMADs, SafeGen increases Judge Overall Score by 24.25% on average compared to state-of-the-art baselines. Fine-tuning a VLMAD using SafeGen-generated scenarios improves real-world driving performance by an average of 15.9%.
AI.conclusion: Goal-conditioned diffusion with end-state supervision is an effective paradigm for generating realistic, coherent safety-critical scenarios. The approach bridges the sim-to-real gap and enhances VLMAD safety evaluation and robustness.

title: LAARA: Layer-Aware Adaptive Rank Allocation for Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning
summary: Low-Rank Adaptation is widely used for parameter-efficient fine-tuning, yet existing methods typically assign the same adapter rank to every transformer layer despite their heterogeneous adaptation requirements. In this work, we show theoretically and empirically that uniform rank allocation is fundamentally suboptimal. Motivated by this observation, we propose LAARA (Layer Aware Adaptive Rank Allocation framework), a search-free framework that dynamically allocates ranks using lightweight diagonal Fisher estimates computed during training. LAARA combines projection-wise normalization, logarithmic compression, blended adapter importance estimation, and a vote-to-change dampening mechanism to produce stable and efficient rank adaptation. Experiments on GLUE and MathInstruct benchmark demonstrate that LAARA consistently matches or outperforms popular state of the art approaches such as LoRA, AdaLoRA, DyLoRA, and Bitfit while using significantly fewer trainable parameters. Our results show that Fisher-guided rank allocation provides a principled and effective foundation for adaptive parameter-efficient fine-tuning. The code is publicly available at: https://anonymous.4open.science/r/LAARA-D305/LAARA.py

AI.tldr: LAARA is a search-free framework that dynamically allocates adapter ranks per layer using diagonal Fisher estimates, outperforming uniform rank allocation methods like LoRA, AdaLoRA, DyLoRA, and Bitfit on GLUE and MathInstruct benchmarks with fewer trainable parameters.
AI.motivation: Existing low-rank adaptation methods assign the same adapter rank to every transformer layer, which is suboptimal because different layers have heterogeneous adaptation requirements.
AI.method: LAARA uses lightweight diagonal Fisher estimates computed during training, combined with projection-wise normalization, logarithmic compression, blended adapter importance estimation, and a vote-to-change dampening mechanism for stable rank allocation.
AI.result: LAARA matches or outperforms LoRA, AdaLoRA, DyLoRA, and Bitfit on GLUE and MathInstruct benchmarks while using significantly fewer trainable parameters.
AI.conclusion: Fisher-guided rank allocation provides a principled and effective foundation for adaptive parameter-efficient fine-tuning.

title: GraphContainer: A Unified Platform for Comparing and Debugging Graph RAG Methods
summary: Graph RAG mitigates hallucinations and stale knowledge in LLMs, particularly for multi-hop question answering. However, existing approaches remain highly fragmented and incompatible. The structural heterogeneity of graph formats across different frameworks and the lack of granular visualization tools make it exceedingly difficult to evaluate and compare retrieval behaviors. To bridge this gap, we propose GraphContainer, a novel platform designed to unify and visualize diverse graph RAG workflows. GraphContainer features two key components: (1) a Unified Graph Representation (UGR) layer that seamlessly standardizes multi-format graphs, and (2) a Graph Recorder that tracks and visually renders the step-by-step retrieval process. Through an interactive web interface, we demonstrate GraphContainer's ability to import heterogeneous graphs and perform live, traceable visual debugging of graph RAG methods. Ultimately, we show how GraphContainer enables controlled comparisons of various graph formats and retrieval strategies, lowering the barrier for researchers and practitioners to design optimal graph RAG pipelines. A demonstration video is available at https://youtu.be/O02eNJLwkU0.

AI.tldr: GraphContainer is a unified platform that standardizes and visualizes diverse Graph RAG workflows, enabling multi-format graph import, step-by-step retrieval tracing, and controlled comparison of graph formats and retrieval strategies to lower the barrier for designing optimal Graph RAG pipelines.
AI.motivation: Existing Graph RAG approaches are fragmented and incompatible due to structural heterogeneity of graph formats across frameworks, and lack granular visualization tools for evaluating and comparing retrieval behaviors.
AI.method: GraphContainer features a Unified Graph Representation (UGR) layer for standardizing multi-format graphs and a Graph Recorder for tracking and visually rendering the step-by-step retrieval process, exposed through an interactive web interface.
AI.result: Demonstrates ability to import heterogeneous graphs, perform live traceable visual debugging of Graph RAG methods, and enable controlled comparisons of various graph formats and retrieval strategies.
AI.conclusion: GraphContainer lowers the barrier for researchers and practitioners to design optimal Graph RAG pipelines by providing unified visualization and comparison capabilities.

title: Pushing the Frontier of Full-Song Generation: Hierarchical Autoregressive Planning Meets Flow-Matching Rendering
summary: In this report, we present a unified song generation framework capable of producing high-quality full-length music from lyrics, text descriptions, and musical attributes. The proposed framework supports three tasks: Lyrics-to-Song Generation, which generates complete songs from text descriptions, lyrics, and musical attributes; Instrumental Music Generation, which creates music without vocals; and Cover Song Generation, which reinterprets existing songs with different styles while preserving their melodic content. Architecturally, our system consists of four main components: a semantic-aware tokenizer, hybird-LM, FullDiT, and a two-level melody module. The tokenizer encodes audio into 8-codebook RVQ tokens for efficient discrete music representation. Based on these tokens, hybird-LM performs hierarchical autoregressive audio-token modeling for full-song generation. To improve audio fidelity, FullDiT performs full-song flow matching in a continuous VAE latent space conditioned on codec tokens, lyrics, and text captions. For cover song generation, the melody module extracts and discretizes melody cues from reference audio to guide generation while preserving the original melodic content. Finally, we investigate DPO, GRPO, and OPD as reward-based post-training strategies for hybird-LM and apply flow-based GRPO to FullDiT to improve musicality and rendering quality. Experimental results on a multilingual automatic benchmark, complemented by the Artificial Analysis Music with Vocals leaderboard, show that the proposed framework achieves competitive performance in the evaluated settings.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a unified song generation framework that supports three tasks (Lyrics-to-Song, Instrumental Music, and Cover Song Generation) using a four-component architecture (semantic-aware tokenizer, hybrid-LM, FullDiT, two-level melody module) with reward-based post-training strategies, achieving competitive performance on multilingual benchmarks.
AI.motivation: To develop a unified framework capable of producing high-quality full-length music from diverse inputs (lyrics, text descriptions, and musical attributes) across multiple generation tasks.
AI.method: The framework uses four components: (1) a semantic-aware tokenizer encoding audio into 8-codebook RVQ tokens; (2) hybrid-LM for hierarchical autoregressive audio-token modeling; (3) FullDiT for flow matching in VAE latent space conditioned on codec tokens, lyrics, and text; (4) a two-level melody module for extracting/discretizing melody cues for cover song generation. Post-training uses DPO, GRPO, and OPD for hybrid-LM and flow-based GRPO for FullDiT.
AI.result: The framework achieves competitive performance on a multilingual automatic benchmark and the Artificial Analysis Music with Vocals leaderboard.
AI.conclusion: The proposed unified framework with hybrid autoregressive and flow-matching components, plus reward-based post-training, effectively handles multiple song generation tasks with high quality.

title: The ICSE 2026 Shadow PC: Training the Next Generation of Reviewers Through Deliberate Practice
summary: Peer review is essential to software engineering research, yet reviewer training remains largely implicit. We describe the ICSE 2026 Shadow PC, a redesigned program emphasizing deliberate practice at scale. Key innovations include multi-phase structure with calibration and peer feedback, strict separation from the main PC, and a pathway toward leadership development. With 102 participants completing the program and reviewing 117 papers, 97% recommending the experience, and positive reception from authors (67% finding reviews helpful), the program demonstrates that rigorous reviewer training is achievable at scale. We share lessons learned and propose shadow PC area chairs as a mechanism for sustainable scaling and leadership development.

AI.tldr: The ICSE 2026 Shadow PC program demonstrates that rigorous reviewer training at scale is achievable through deliberate practice, multi-phase structure, and peer feedback, with 102 participants reviewing 117 papers and receiving 97% positive recommendations.
AI.motivation: Peer review is essential to software engineering research, yet reviewer training remains largely implicit, necessitating a structured approach to develop reviewing skills at scale.
AI.method: The program features a multi-phase structure with calibration and peer feedback, strict separation from the main PC, a pathway toward leadership development, and the introduction of shadow PC area chairs for sustainable scaling.
AI.result: 102 participants completed the program and reviewed 117 papers; 97% recommended the experience; 67% of authors found the reviews helpful.
AI.conclusion: Rigorous reviewer training is achievable at scale; shadow PC area chairs are proposed as a mechanism for sustainable scaling and leadership development.

title: Point-Selection Fine-Tuning Framework for Robust Point Cloud Classification
summary: Noisy and corrupted points can substantially degrade point cloud recognition performance, especially under challenging corruption settings. In particular, full fine-tuning of 3D pre-trained models may amplify the influence of outliers and overwrite robustness priors learned during pre-training, while naive parameter-efficient adaptation remains sensitive to corrupted tokens. To address this issue, we propose PSFT, a point-selection fine-tuning framework that improves robustness while remaining parameter-efficient. PSFT first estimates point-wise influence from pre-pooling features and adaptively retains minimally influential points to suppress outliers. Based on the selected subset, a prompt generation branch predicts layer-wise prompt tokens and injects them into a frozen backbone for lightweight downstream adaptation. To further mitigate residual noise after selection, we append a lightweight feature filter with bottleneck MLP transformation and Beta-gated residual blending to refine patch-token representations before prediction. Extensive experiments show that PSFT consistently reduces corruption error on ModelNet-C and ModelNet40-C across all tested 3D pre-trained backbones, while achieving the strongest ScanObjectNN-C results with ULIP-2 and Uni3D-B among the evaluated tuning strategies. Our implementation can be found at https://github.com/CVChMA/PSFT/tree/master.

AI.tldr: PSFT is a point-selection fine-tuning framework for 3D point cloud recognition that improves robustness against corruptions by selecting minimally influential points, generating layer-wise prompt tokens for parameter-efficient adaptation, and applying a Beta-gated feature filter to suppress residual noise.
AI.motivation: Noisy/corrupted points degrade point cloud recognition performance; full fine-tuning amplifies outlier influence and overwrites pre-trained robustness priors, while naive parameter-efficient tuning remains sensitive to corrupted tokens.
AI.method: PSFT first estimates point-wise influence from pre-pooling features and adaptively retains minimally influential points to suppress outliers. Then a prompt generation branch predicts layer-wise prompt tokens injected into a frozen backbone. Finally, a lightweight feature filter with bottleneck MLP and Beta-gated residual blending refines patch-token representations.
AI.result: PSFT consistently reduces corruption error on ModelNet-C and ModelNet40-C across all tested 3D pre-trained backbones, and achieves strongest ScanObjectNN-C results with ULIP-2 and Uni3D-B among evaluated tuning strategies.
AI.conclusion: PSFT effectively improves robustness against point cloud corruptions while maintaining parameter efficiency, outperforming existing tuning strategies on multiple corruption benchmarks.

title: Predicting Groundwater Arsenic Concentrations Using Graph Neural Networks
comment: 7 pages, 5 figures, 1 table, AAAI '26 AI4ES workshop acceptance
summary: Arsenic contamination in groundwater presents a longstanding public health crisis in the United States, especially for households depending on private wells. Accurate and spatially informed prediction of arsenic concentration is vital to identify high-risk areas and focus mitigation efforts. However, there is a lack of generalizable models for representing continuous variation in arsenic concentrations across regions. In this work, we pose arsenic prediction as a regression task and construct a spatially integrated dataset to aggregate over 74,000 arsenic samples from the Water Quality Portal (WQP), Mineral Resources Data System (MRDS), and Gridded National Soil Survey Geographic Database (gNATSGO). Specifically, we use a variety of techniques including kNearest Neighbors (k-NN) and Geographic Information Systems (GIS) to join arsenic measurement points from across the United States by location. Building on this dataset, we evaluate a diverse suite of machine learning models, including tree-based ensemble approaches, multilayer perceptrons, and spatially aware graph neural networks (GNN). Our findings show that while gradient-boosted trees are still considered state-of-the-art in the field of tabular data, GNNs are able to further account for spatial dependence to match or outperform the results of gradient-boosted trees. These results demonstrate that graph-based and spatially informed learning can enhance environmental prediction and provide a foundation for improved groundwater risk mapping and monitoring.

AI.tldr: This paper develops machine learning models, including graph neural networks, to predict arsenic concentrations in U.S. groundwater using a spatially integrated dataset of over 74,000 samples, showing that GNNs can match or outperform gradient-boosted trees by accounting for spatial dependence.
AI.motivation: Arsenic contamination in U.S. groundwater poses a public health crisis, especially for private well households, and there is a lack of generalizable models for representing continuous spatial variation in arsenic concentrations across regions.
AI.method: The authors construct a spatially integrated dataset of over 74,000 arsenic samples from WQP, MRDS, and gNATSGO using k-NN and GIS for location-based joining. They evaluate multiple ML models including tree-based ensembles, MLPs, and graph neural networks for regression-based arsenic prediction.
AI.result: GNNs match or outperform gradient-boosted trees (previously state-of-the-art for tabular data) by accounting for spatial dependence in arsenic concentrations.
AI.conclusion: Graph-based and spatially informed learning enhances environmental prediction and provides a foundation for improved groundwater risk mapping and monitoring.

title: AdaRoPE: Not All Attention Heads Should Rotate and Scale Equally
summary: Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE) is widely adopted in Transformers to encode positional information, yet standard implementations enforce a uniform frequency schedule and scaling across all attention heads. Using simplified retrieval tasks and length generalization scenarios, we show -- both empirically and theoretically -- that heads with different functional roles require distinct frequency ranges and attention scaling factors to operate effectively. Ignoring this structure leads to suboptimal utilization of embedding dimensions and degraded performance, particularly under long-context settings. To address these limitations, we propose AdaRoPE, which equips each attention head with learnable rotation frequencies and attention scaling factors. Pretrained LLMs with AdaRoPE consistently outperform existing RoPE variants, including partial RoPE and NoPE baselines. For context extension, we further show that uniform frequency and attention scaling, used in methods such as YaRN, are suboptimal. By applying head-specific scaling, AdaRoPE enables better context extension while better preserving short-context performance in both the extrapolation setting and the long-context continued pretraining setting. These results highlight the importance of optimizing rotary position embedding at the level of individual attention heads.

AI.tldr: AdaRoPE introduces learnable, head-specific rotation frequencies and attention scaling factors for Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE), outperforming uniform RoPE variants in both standard and long-context settings.
AI.motivation: Standard RoPE enforces a uniform frequency schedule and scaling across all attention heads, which is suboptimal because different heads require distinct frequency ranges and scaling factors for effective operation, especially under long-context settings.
AI.method: AdaRoPE equips each attention head with learnable rotation frequencies and attention scaling factors, replacing the uniform schedule used in standard RoPE.
AI.result: AdaRoPE consistently outperforms existing RoPE variants (including partial RoPE and NoPE baselines) in pretrained LLMs. For context extension, head-specific scaling enables better long-context performance while better preserving short-context performance compared to uniform scaling methods like YaRN.
AI.conclusion: Optimizing rotary position embedding at the level of individual attention heads is crucial; head-specific frequency and scaling schedules yield superior performance over uniform approaches.

title: Test Case Prioritization for DNNs via Neural Collapse Instability
summary: With the widespread deployment of deep neural networks (DNNs) in safety-critical domains, reducing the cost of model validation under limited testing budgets has become increasingly important. Existing test case prioritization techniques often rely on single-checkpoint confidence signals derived from output probabilities. However, DNNs can be confidently wrong, and the confidence margin between the predicted and competing classes is frequently small, which weakens early fault discovery. To address this limitation, we propose a Neural-Collapse-Inspired Prioritization (NCIP) framework that replaces absolute confidence with cross-checkpoint prediction variability in the terminal training regime, where model geometry becomes highly structured. NCIP introduces two key components. First, it selects an NC-guided representative subset of training checkpoints using an equiangularity score of classifier weights, quantified as the standard deviation of pairwise cosine similarities among class weight vectors. Second, it prioritizes test inputs by their prediction variability across the selected checkpoints, surfacing boundary-adjacent and failure-prone samples that are unstable under checkpoint-induced decision boundary shifts. Extensive experiments across multiple datasets and architectures show that NCIP achieves strong performance in early fault discovery compared with competitive baselines, with 1.5 to 16.6 percent RAUC-ALL gains and 4.9 to 20.6 percent RAUC-500 gains under the same testing budget. NCIP further attains the best average performance across all dataset-model pairs.

AI.tldr: NCIP replaces absolute confidence with cross-checkpoint prediction variability during terminal training for DNN test prioritization, achieving 1.5-20.6% gains in fault discovery.
AI.motivation: Existing DNN test case prioritization methods rely on single-checkpoint confidence signals that fail when models are confidently wrong or have small confidence margins, limiting early fault discovery under constrained testing budgets.
AI.method: NCIP selects NC-guided representative training checkpoints via equiangularity score (std of pairwise cosine similarities among class weight vectors), then prioritizes test inputs by their prediction variability across these checkpoints to identify boundary-adjacent, failure-prone samples.
AI.result: NCIP achieves 1.5-16.6% RAUC-ALL gains and 4.9-20.6% RAUC-500 gains over baselines, and attains the best average performance across all dataset-model pairs.
AI.conclusion: Leveraging Neural Collapse induced structural regularity in terminal training regime via cross-checkpoint prediction variability is an effective alternative to single-checkpoint confidence for test prioritization.

title: A Unified Tokenization Framework for Pain Recognition using Heterogeneous 3D Modalities
comment: Accepted at the 28th ACM International Conference on Multimodal Interaction (ICMI 2026)
summary: Pain is a complex and pervasive phenomenon affecting a large percentage of the population, and accurate assessment is essential for effective clinical management and intervention. Computational pain recognition systems enable continuous monitoring, support clinical decision-making, and help mitigate pain-related distress and functional decline. This study introduces a unified tokenization framework for heterogeneous 3D modalities in pain recognition that provides a single processing pipeline across behavioral and brain-activity 3D data, without requiring separate architectures for each modality or handcrafted inductive biases. The framework preserves spatial, temporal, and time--frequency structure while mapping diverse inputs into a shared token space. Extensive experiments show that the proposed approach effectively processes facial videos and fNIRS data in both raw-signal and spectrogram-based representations. On the AI4Pain benchmark dataset, the proposed framework achieves state-of-the-art performance while maintaining high computational efficiency and enabling real-time assessment on both GPU and CPU hardware.

AI.tldr: A unified tokenization framework for heterogeneous 3D modalities (facial video and fNIRS) achieves state-of-the-art pain recognition on AI4Pain benchmark with real-time computational efficiency on both GPU and CPU.
AI.motivation: Pain is prevalent and requires accurate assessment for effective clinical management. Computational pain recognition systems can enable continuous monitoring and support clinical decisions, but existing approaches require separate architectures for different 3D data modalities (e.g., behavioral vs. brain-activity data).
AI.method: A unified tokenization framework that processes heterogeneous 3D modalities (facial videos and fNIRS data) through a single pipeline. It preserves spatial, temporal, and time-frequency structure while mapping diverse inputs into a shared token space, supporting both raw-signal and spectrogram-based representations.
AI.result: Achieves state-of-the-art performance on the AI4Pain benchmark dataset while maintaining high computational efficiency and enabling real-time assessment on both GPU and CPU hardware.
AI.conclusion: The proposed unified tokenization framework effectively handles diverse 3D pain recognition modalities without needing separate architectures or handcrafted inductive biases, offering a practical solution for real-time clinical pain assessment.

title: Decodable but Not Detectable: A Leakage Fingerprint for Near-OOD Benchmarks
summary: While auditing a perturbation-based OOD detector on a document benchmark, we recorded an AUROC of 0.326 -- well below the 0.5 chance level. The cause is a benchmark leak: the designated "OOD" class is one the model was trained on, so its examples sit inside the in-distribution fit set and the detector is penalized for correctly ranking them as familiar. Deleting the class and retraining 35 models across two domains raises the score to 0.911. We distill the contamination into a leak fingerprint -- near-perfect supervised decodability (AUROC approximately 1) coupled with unsupervised detection collapsed below 0.65 -- and validate it on a controlled battery of 52 settings (20 leaked, 32 clean) across ResNet-50 and ViT-B/16 on CIFAR-10/100, achieving sensitivity 18/20 and specificity 31/32 in embedding space; the matched fit-set-exclusion controls are perfect at 20/20. An in-the-wild audit of 24 standard near/far OOD benchmark pairs fires on exactly one (the intrinsically hard CIFAR-100 vs CIFAR-10 pair) and on no far-OOD pair, confirming specificity and that standard cross-dataset construction is clean. Under the corrected protocol, perturbation signals are decodable but not detectable: a supervised reader recovers the OOD signal (AUROC 0.87-1.00) while no unsupervised detector does, and the perturbation method does not improve on plain Mahalanobis distance. We provide a theoretical account of why and, for transparency, retract an earlier circular correlation. The contributions are a corrected protocol and a validated leak diagnostic, not a new OOD method.

AI.tldr: A benchmark leak in OOD detection (training classes contaminating OOD sets) caused AUROC to drop below chance (0.326). Fixing it raised AUROC to 0.911. A leak fingerprint is proposed and validated across 52 controlled settings and 24 real-world benchmarks. Under corrected protocol, perturbation signals are decodable but not detectable, and the method doesn't improve on plain Mahalanobis distance.
AI.motivation: To identify and correct a benchmark leak causing spurious below-chance OOD detection performance, and to provide a validated diagnostic for detecting such contamination.
AI.method: Controlled experiments: deleting leaked class and retraining 35 models across two domains; proposing a leak fingerprint (near-perfect supervised decodability + unsupervised detection < 0.65); validating on 52 settings (20 leaked, 32 clean) with ResNet-50 and ViT-B/16 on CIFAR-10/100; auditing 24 standard near/far OOD pairs; providing theoretical analysis.
AI.result: Corrected protocol raises AUROC from 0.326 to 0.911. Leak fingerprint achieves sensitivity 18/20, specificity 31/32 in embedding space; fit-set-exclusion controls perfect 20/20. In-the-wild audit fires only on CIFAR-100 vs CIFAR-10. Under corrected protocol, perturbation signals are decodable (AUROC 0.87-1.00) but not detectable by unsupervised methods; no improvement over plain Mahalanobis.
AI.conclusion: The paper provides a corrected evaluation protocol and a validated leak diagnostic for OOD detection, not a new method. The earlier circular correlation is retracted.

title: Statistically Grounded Sparse-Feature Interventions for Activation-Space Control in Large Language Models
summary: Activation steering offers a lightweight alternative to fine-tuning for behavioral control of large language models, but SAE-based steering methods often rely on learned steering objectives or single-criterion feature selection. We introduce a transparent SAE-feature steering pipeline that first applies a six-condition reliability filter, then ranks sparse features through an unweighted Borda consensus over three complementary statistics: $F$-test, KSG mutual information, and Cohen's $d$. The resulting steering direction is constructed as a Cohen's-$d$-weighted combination of SAE decoder rows, providing an optimization-free direction motivated by Fisher-LDA under approximate SAE-feature decorrelation. Across three Gemma-family models, four behavioral domains, and 356 layer-strength configurations, the method produces measurable domain-specific shifts while revealing a substantial gap between raw attribute movement and quality-preserving generation. In the strongest configuration, logical-correctness steering reaches a primary-score delta of $+1.16$ in Gemma~2 9B; however, our broader finding is that usable steering is highly localized by model, domain, layer, and strength. These results argue that activation-steering evaluations should report quality-conditioned success alongside raw behavioral shift. Our code and data are available at https://github.com/Oshayer-Siddique/LLM-Steering-Using-SAE.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a transparent SAE-feature steering pipeline using a six-condition reliability filter, Borda consensus ranking over F-test, KSG mutual information, and Cohen's d, and a Cohen's-d-weighted steering direction constructed from SAE decoder rows. Testing across three Gemma models, four behavioral domains, and 356 configurations shows measurable domain shifts but reveals that usable steering is highly localized by model, domain, layer, and strength, with a gap between raw attribute movement and quality-preserving generation.
AI.motivation: Existing SAE-based steering methods rely on learned steering objectives or single-criterion feature selection, lacking transparency and principled, optimization-free construction of steering directions.
AI.method: A six-condition reliability filter for SAE features, followed by unweighted Borda consensus ranking over F-test, KSG mutual information, and Cohen's d statistics. The final steering direction is a Cohen's-d-weighted combination of SAE decoder rows, motivated by Fisher-LDA under approximate SAE-feature decorrelation.
AI.result: Across 356 layer-strength configurations on three Gemma models and four behavioral domains, the method produces measurable domain-specific shifts. The strongest result achieves a logical-correctness steering primary-score delta of +1.16 in Gemma 2 9B, but usable steering is highly localized by model, domain, layer, and strength.
AI.conclusion: The substantial gap between raw attribute movement and quality-preserving generation argues that activation-steering evaluations should report quality-conditioned success alongside raw behavioral shift.

title: ReFace: Reorganizing Facial Spatiotemporal Representations for Improved Pain Assessment
comment: Accepted at the 14th International Conference on Affective Computing and Intelligent Interaction (ACII 2026)
summary: Automatic pain assessment from facial video remains challenging due to the spatial heterogeneity of pain-related facial cues. This study proposes ReFace, a spatial reorganization pipeline that divides facial input into four spatial quadrants before tokenization, rather than processing the entire face as a single region. Evaluated on the AI4Pain dataset, the proposed approach achieves $56.00\%$ accuracy on the test set using video only, achieving the highest reported accuracy under the fixed AI4Pain benchmark protocol among the compared methods. Notably, the four-quadrant configuration processes the same total pixel budget as the full-face input, yet achieves higher accuracy, suggesting that spatial reorganization can improve performance under the proposed tokenization design. A single quadrant region, processing just one quarter of those pixels, remains competitive at a fraction of the computational cost.

AI.tldr: ReFace is a spatial reorganization pipeline for automatic pain assessment from facial video that divides facial input into four spatial quadrants before tokenization, achieving 56.00% accuracy on the AI4Pain dataset—the highest reported under the fixed benchmark protocol—while demonstrating that spatial reorganization improves performance over full-face input and that a single quadrant remains competitive with lower computational cost.
AI.motivation: Automatic pain assessment from facial video remains challenging due to the spatial heterogeneity of pain-related facial cues, motivating a reorganization strategy that better captures localized pain expressions rather than processing the entire face as a single region.
AI.method: ReFace divides facial input into four spatial quadrants before tokenization, rather than processing the full face as a single region, and evaluates on the AI4Pain dataset using video-only input.
AI.result: Achieves 56.00% accuracy on the AI4Pain test set, the highest reported accuracy under the fixed benchmark protocol; the four-quadrant configuration processes the same total pixel budget as full-face input yet yields higher accuracy, and a single quadrant (quarter of pixels) remains competitive at reduced computational cost.
AI.conclusion: Spatial reorganization via quadrant-based tokenization can improve pain assessment performance from facial video, and even a single quadrant offers a favorable accuracy-efficiency trade-off.

title: Cross-Subject Semantic Decoding with Shared-Space Alignment for Generalized Neural Representation Learning
summary: Generalizing across subjects remains challenging in invasive neural recordings because electrode configurations, anatomical structures, and neural signal patterns vary substantially across individuals. To investigate such inter-subject variability, we propose a cross-subject semantic decoding framework that aligns neural responses to speech perception from multiple subjects into a shared latent space and learns a mapping from the aligned neural representations to contextual embeddings. More specifically, using electrocorticography data collected during natural language comprehension, we estimate the shared space using the shared response model and train a decoder to predict contextual semantic embeddings from projected neural responses. For a held-out subject, we estimate a subject-specific projection into the predefined shared space, and directly apply the pretrained decoder without any retraining. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed framework consistently outperforms baseline methods across evaluation settings and exhibits a reduced performance drop from source subject to held-out subject testing, indicating improved cross-subject generalization. These results suggest that aligning neural activity into a shared latent space, while decoding in a semantic embedding space, provides an effective strategy for improving cross-subject generalization by reducing subject-specific differences in neural responses while effectively capturing shared stimulus-related representations.

AI.tldr: Proposes a cross-subject semantic decoding framework that aligns multi-subject ECoG neural responses to speech into a shared latent space via the Shared Response Model, then decodes contextual semantic embeddings without retraining, improving cross-subject generalization.
AI.motivation: Generalizing across subjects in invasive neural recordings is challenging due to inter-subject variability in electrode configurations, anatomical structures, and neural signal patterns.
AI.method: Uses the Shared Response Model (SRM) to estimate a shared latent space from multi-subject ECoG data during natural language comprehension, trains a decoder to map projected neural representations to contextual semantic embeddings, and applies the pretrained decoder to held-out subjects via subject-specific projection.
AI.result: The framework consistently outperforms baseline methods and shows a reduced performance drop from source to held-out subjects, indicating improved cross-subject generalization.
AI.conclusion: Aligning neural activity into a shared latent space combined with decoding in a semantic embedding space effectively reduces subject-specific differences while preserving shared stimulus-related representations, enabling better cross-subject generalization.

title: Logic-Guided Data Extraction with Answer Set Programming and Large Language Models
comment: 42nd International Conference on Logic Programming, to appear in Theory and Practice of Logic Programming (TPLP)
summary: When Large Language Models (LLMs) are used for semantic data extraction from unstructured text, producing candidate relational facts from natural language, they may remain unreliable for tasks requiring complex combinatorial reasoning and global consistency. This paper proposes a logic-guided data extraction framework combining LLM-based extraction with Answer Set Programming (ASP). The LLM produces candidate facts, whereas ASP performs validation, inference, consistency checking, and control. Unlike existing pipelines that query the LLM independently for all target predicates, the proposed approach uses ASP reasoning to identify which predicates are logically admissible at each stage and to guide extraction queries. By interleaving LLM calls with ASP derivation, the framework infers logically implied facts without further extraction and detects inconsistencies early. We formalize the pipeline and prove that, under mild assumptions, it is equivalent to the baseline approach with respect to the final extracted facts, while requiring fewer LLM calls. We also introduce a caching mechanism for logic-based control queries, exploiting monotonicity of conjunctive queries over incrementally constructed fact sets to reduce solver invocations. Experiments on ASP-derived benchmarks show that the framework reduces LLM calls and improves extraction quality by mitigating spurious outputs, demonstrating the value of non-monotonic logic programming for controlled semantic extraction.

AI.tldr: A logic-guided framework combining LLMs with Answer Set Programming (ASP) for semantic data extraction reduces LLM calls and improves extraction quality by interleaving LLM calls with ASP reasoning for validation, inference, consistency checking, and control, with theoretical equivalence guarantees and a caching mechanism.
AI.motivation: LLMs used for semantic data extraction from unstructured text are unreliable for tasks requiring complex combinatorial reasoning and global consistency, motivating the need for a logic-guided approach to enhance reliability.
AI.method: The framework interleaves LLM-based extraction with Answer Set Programming (ASP); ASP performs validation, inference, consistency checking, and control. It uses ASP reasoning to identify logically admissible predicates at each stage, guides extraction queries, infers logically implied facts, and detects inconsistencies early. A caching mechanism exploiting monotonicity of conjunctive queries over incrementally constructed fact sets reduces solver invocations.
AI.result: Experiments on ASP-derived benchmarks show the framework reduces LLM calls and improves extraction quality by mitigating spurious outputs. The framework is proven equivalent to the baseline approach under mild assumptions while requiring fewer LLM calls.
AI.conclusion: The framework demonstrates the value of non-monotonic logic programming (ASP) for controlled semantic extraction, offering efficiency gains and quality improvements over pure LLM-based extraction pipelines.

title: An Exploratory Analysis of Pain Localization via Explainable Computational Modeling
comment: Accepted at the 14th International Conference on Affective Computing and Intelligent Interaction (ACII 2026)
summary: Automatic pain localization, which involves identifying the anatomical origin of pain from peripheral physiological signals without patient self-report, is a clinically critical but largely unaddressed problem, particularly for non-verbal patients. This paper presents a systematic comparison of classical feature engineering and deep sequence learning for subject-independent three-class pain localization using the AI4Pain 2026 Challenge dataset, which comprises four synchronously recorded wearable modalities: electrodermal activity, blood volume pulse, respiration, and peripheral oxygen saturation recorded from 65 participants under controlled TENS-induced pain. A 115-dimensional hand-crafted feature set spanning time-domain, frequency-domain, modality-specific, and cross-modal descriptors is benchmarked against end-to-end deep architectures. Extremely Randomized Trees achieves the highest macro-F1 of 0.539, outperforming the best deep model by 7.4 percentage points, with EDA spectral features emerging as the dominant discriminators. A consistent 26-point gap between pain detection (F1\,=\,0.815) and localization (F1\,=\,0.552) across all models points to a fundamental ceiling imposed by the anatomical diffuseness of peripheral autonomic pathways at 10-second resolution.

AI.tldr: This paper benchmarks classical feature engineering (Extremely Randomized Trees) against deep sequence learning for three-class pain localization from wearable biosignals (EDA, BVP, Respiration, SpO2) using the AI4Pain 2026 dataset. Extremely Randomized Trees achieves the best macro-F1 of 0.539, outperforming deep models by 7.4 percentage points, with EDA spectral features being most discriminative. A consistent gap between pain detection (F1=0.815) and localization (F1=0.552) suggests a fundamental anatomical limitation at 10-second resolution.
AI.motivation: Automatic pain localization from peripheral physiological signals without self-report is clinically critical, especially for non-verbal patients, but remains largely unaddressed. This work aims to systematically compare classical and deep learning approaches for this problem.
AI.method: A 115-dimensional hand-crafted feature set (time-domain, frequency-domain, modality-specific, cross-modal) was benchmarked against end-to-end deep sequence models on the AI4Pain 2026 dataset (4 wearable modalities from 65 participants under TENS-induced pain). Extremely Randomized Trees was used as the classical method.
AI.result: Extremely Randomized Trees achieved the highest macro-F1 of 0.539, outperforming the best deep model by 7.4 percentage points. EDA spectral features emerged as the dominant discriminators. A consistent 26-point gap between pain detection (F1=0.815) and localization (F1=0.552) was observed.
AI.conclusion: Classical feature engineering outperforms deep learning for subject-independent pain localization from short-duration wearable signals. The consistent gap between detection and localization suggests a fundamental ceiling imposed by the anatomical diffuseness of peripheral autonomic pathways at 10-second resolution.

title: From Trajectories to Prefixes: Reusing Teacher Trajectories via Replayed Prefixes and Online Continuation
summary: Small language models are attractive backbones for interactive agents, but direct distillation from strong teacher trajectories often turns rich multi-turn behavior into one-shot imitation targets. This is inefficient in long-horizon environments, where early decisions shape later states and rewards. We propose Prefix-GRPO, a reinforcement learning framework that decomposes teacher trajectories into replay-aligned prefix queries and online continuations. Each prefix is replayed in the environment to recover a valid intermediate state, after which the student continues online interaction and receives task reward. Unlike response-only GRPO, Prefix-GRPO also applies clipped policy updates to historical assistant tokens inside the replayed prefix, using a policy-distilled SFT checkpoint to estimate their old log-probabilities. This unifies prefix learning and continuation learning within the same policy-optimization form. Experiments on TextCraft, BabyAI, and ALFWorld show that Prefix-GRPO improves small-model agents over distillation and standard RL baselines, while ablations show that replay alone is insufficient without explicit prefix-token optimization. The implementation and reproduction scripts are available at https://github.com/HappynessI/Prefix_GRPO.

AI.tldr: Prefix-GRPO is a reinforcement learning framework that improves small language model agents by decomposing teacher trajectories into replay-aligned prefix queries and online continuations, applying clipped policy updates to both prefix and continuation tokens. It outperforms distillation and standard RL baselines on TextCraft, BabyAI, and ALFWorld.
AI.motivation: Small language models are attractive for interactive agents, but direct distillation from teacher trajectories turns multi-turn behavior into one-shot imitation targets, which is inefficient in long-horizon environments where early decisions shape later states and rewards.
AI.method: Prefix-GRPO decomposes teacher trajectories into replay-aligned prefix queries and online continuations. Each prefix is replayed to recover a valid intermediate state, then the student continues online interaction. Unlike response-only GRPO, it applies clipped policy updates to historical assistant tokens inside the replayed prefix using a policy-distilled SFT checkpoint to estimate old log-probabilities, unifying prefix learning and continuation learning.
AI.result: Prefix-GRPO improves small-model agents over distillation and standard RL baselines on TextCraft, BabyAI, and ALFWorld. Ablations show that replay alone is insufficient without explicit prefix-token optimization.
AI.conclusion: Explicit optimization of prefix tokens via clipped policy updates within a replay-based RL framework is crucial for effectively training small language model agents from teacher trajectories in long-horizon environments.

title: Geometry-Guided Constraint Learning for LLM Safety Classification
summary: Safety as Polytope (SaP) learns linear half-space constraints in LLM hidden space but requires per-category tuning of the constraint count K. We show that sparse autoencoder (SAE) feature extraction resolves this: K=2 becomes optimal for 12/14 categories on Qwen3.5-9B, achieving 96-99% accuracy per category on our BeaverTails classification benchmark, largely eliminating the need for exhaustive sweeps (K=4-25 with random initialization). This convergence to two planes is consistent with the Linear Representation Hypothesis, providing suggestive evidence that safety boundaries in this setting admit a low-dimensional linear description in the SAE feature space. Building on this geometric perspective, we introduce a cone constraint whose learnable aperture adapts to each category's cluster concentration, stabilized by a three-phase training

AI.tldr: SaP learns linear half-space constraints in LLM hidden space. SAE feature extraction resolves per-category tuning of constraint count K, with K=2 becoming optimal for 12/14 categories on Qwen3.5-9B, achieving 96-99% accuracy. A cone constraint with learnable aperture is introduced, stabilized by three-phase training.
AI.motivation: To eliminate the need for per-category tuning of constraint count K in Safety as Polytope (SaP) by leveraging sparse autoencoder (SAE) feature extraction.
AI.method: Uses SAE feature extraction to simplify SaP: K=2 becomes optimal for most categories. Introduces a cone constraint with learnable aperture adapted to each category's cluster concentration, stabilized by a three-phase training process.
AI.result: K=2 is optimal for 12/14 categories on Qwen3.5-9B, achieving 96-99% accuracy per category on BeaverTails benchmark. Convergence to two planes supports the Linear Representation Hypothesis.
AI.conclusion: Safety boundaries in LLM hidden space admit a low-dimensional linear description in SAE feature space, and the proposed cone constraint with adaptive aperture improves performance.

title: Efficient Tracking and Understanding Object Transformations
summary: Tracking objects through state transformations is essential for understanding real-world dynamics. However, existing methods are computationally expensive. TubeletGraph recently showed impressive capabilities, but its inference cost (~$4.4$ seconds per object-frame on VOST) precludes any real-time deployment possibilities. We observe that TubeletGraph's overhead arises from building a spatiotemporal partition of the input video: (1) entity segmentation is computed densely for every frame regardless of whether a transformation occurs, and (2) every entity in the scene is tracked, scaling cost with scene complexity rather than the number of transformations of interest.
