To address both, we propose FluxGraph, a reactive variant that uses SAM2's internal multi-mask disagreement as a lightweight trigger for transformation detection, and removes the need for tracking all entities in the given video. FluxGraph is ~$3.3\times$ faster than TubeletGraph on VOST while improving tracking performance and preserving state graph quality. Furthermore, we also observe consistent speedups of $3.7-10.7\times$ across VSCOS, M$^3$-VOS, and DAVIS17 while maintaining performance. Code is publicly available at https://github.com/YihongSun/FluxGraph.

AI.tldr: FluxGraph is a reactive, faster variant of TubeletGraph for object tracking through state transformations. It uses SAM2's internal multi-mask disagreement as a lightweight trigger and avoids tracking all entities, achieving ~3.3× speedup on VOST and 3.7-10.7× on other benchmarks while maintaining or improving performance.
AI.motivation: Existing methods for tracking objects through state transformations are computationally expensive. TubeletGraph has high inference cost (~$4.4$ seconds per object-frame on VOST) due to dense entity segmentation and tracking all entities regardless of relevance, precluding real-time deployment.
AI.method: FluxGraph proposes a reactive approach with two key innovations: (1) using SAM2's internal multi-mask disagreement as a lightweight trigger for transformation detection instead of dense computation, and (2) eliminating the need to track all entities in the scene, scaling cost with transformations of interest rather than scene complexity.
AI.result: FluxGraph achieves ~3.3× speedup over TubeletGraph on VOST while improving tracking performance and preserving state graph quality. Consistent speedups of 3.7-10.7× are observed on VSCOS, M³-VOS, and DAVIS17 while maintaining performance.
AI.conclusion: FluxGraph demonstrates that reactive, trigger-based computation can significantly reduce inference cost for transformation tracking without sacrificing quality, enabling more practical deployment.

title: Memory Merge DQN: Sensitivity Weighted Target Updates for Stable Value Learning
summary: Deep Q-networks use target networks to stabilise bootstrapped value learning, but the standard hard copy update also introduces a tradeoff. Holding the target network fixed, improves short term stability, yet each hard update abruptly replaces the target parameters with the newest online network and discards recent parameter history. This can produce sudden changes in the bootstrap target and may remove value function structure that remains useful later in training. This paper introduces Memory Merge DQN, a target network update mechanism that maintains a short memory of recent historical online network copies and constructs the target network by merging network parameters based on the Q-value sensitivity rather than copying only the newest online network. Memory Merge gives greater influence to parameters that remain locally important for current Q-value behaviour, while using a recency prior to keep the merged target close to the latest online parameters. The method is inspired by Fisher Weight Model Merging, but uses Q-value sensitivity rather than Fisher information as the weighting signal. This paper evaluates Memory Merge DQN on Atari environments against DQN, Averaged DQN, DQN with layer normalisation, and PQN (with gradient clipping). The results show that Memory Merge DQN is highly competitive and it achieves the largest number of first place final performance results among the evaluated methods, beats DQN, Averaged DQN, and PQN (with gradient clipping), and produces substantial gains in several games where preserving useful value-function parameters appears beneficial. These findings suggest that selectively merging recent parameter weights and history can improve the stability and final performance of DQN agents, and that target network design is an important mechanism for preserving useful value function structure during long horizon value learning.

AI.tldr: Memory Merge DQN is a new target network update mechanism for DQNs that merges recent historical network parameters based on Q-value sensitivity instead of hard copying the latest online network, improving stability and final performance in Atari environments.
AI.motivation: Standard DQN's hard copy target network update introduces a tradeoff: short-term stability from fixed targets, but abrupt parameter replacement discards useful value function structure from recent history, potentially harming long-horizon learning.
AI.method: Memory Merge DQN maintains a short memory of recent online network copies and constructs the target network by merging parameters weighted by Q-value sensitivity (inspired by Fisher Weight Model Merging) combined with a recency prior, rather than copying only the newest online network.
AI.result: Memory Merge DQN achieves the highest number of first-place final performance results among evaluated methods on Atari, outperforming DQN, Averaged DQN, DQN with layer normalisation, and PQN (with gradient clipping), with substantial gains in games where preserving useful value-function parameters is beneficial.
AI.conclusion: Selectively merging recent parameter weights based on Q-value sensitivity improves DQN stability and final performance, highlighting target network design as a key mechanism for preserving useful value function structure during long-horizon value learning.

title: Rethinking Uncertainty Evaluation in Large Language Models
summary: Calibration is the primary criterion for evaluating LLM confidence, but it is insufficient: it admits trivially incoherent estimators, depends on the evaluation distribution, and does not test the extent to which the estimation can be interpreted as a consistent, underlying probability function. What we actually need is for LLM confidence estimates to satisfy the conditions required of coherent probabilistic beliefs. We formalize these conditions along three axes (structural coherence, faithfulness, and usefulness) and operationalize them as the C1 metrics. Widely used estimators systematically violate these conditions despite appearing well-calibrated: models assign lower confidence to logically easier questions 31\% of the time, and common interventions reducing RMSCE leave structural violations unchanged, suggesting that calibration is orthogonal to probabilistic validity. RLHF and chain-of-thought improve usefulness metrics without restoring coherence. Our results show current LLM confidence estimates cannot be interpreted as coherent probabilities; our framework provides the tools to measure and close this gap.

AI.tldr: Calibration alone is insufficient for evaluating LLM confidence estimates; this paper proposes a new framework (C1 metrics) along three axes (structural coherence, faithfulness, usefulness) demonstrating that LLM confidence estimates violate probabilistic coherence despite appearing well-calibrated.
AI.motivation: Calibration is insufficient for evaluating LLM confidence as it admits trivially incoherent estimators, depends on the evaluation distribution, and fails to test whether estimates represent consistent, underlying probability functions.
AI.method: The authors formalize three conditions (structural coherence, faithfulness, usefulness) and operationalize them as C1 metrics to evaluate LLM confidence estimates against coherent probabilistic beliefs.
AI.result: Widely used estimators systematically violate these conditions despite appearing well-calibrated; models assign lower confidence to logically easier questions 31% of the time; common interventions reducing RMSCE leave structural violations unchanged.
AI.conclusion: Current LLM confidence estimates cannot be interpreted as coherent probabilities; the C1 framework provides tools to measure and close this gap, with RLHF and chain-of-thought improving usefulness but not restoring coherence.

title: Extending a Large View Synthesis Model for Multi-view Panoptic Segmentation
comment: Accepted to ECCV 2026. 31 pages, 7 figures, 9 tables. Project page: https://kwonyoung9120.github.io/PanopticLVSM/
summary: Large view synthesis models synthesize novel views through cross-view attention without explicit 3D representations, and recent studies have shown that they learn accurate spatial correspondence from RGB supervision alone. We observe that this correspondence generalizes beyond appearance. When non-photorealistic signals such as binary encoded panoptic labels are passed through the model, they are propagated to novel views with consistent spatial structure. These results indicate that the correspondence learned for RGB view synthesis can also propagate view-independent per-pixel labels. From this observation, we present the first work to extend large view synthesis models beyond appearance rendering to 3D scene understanding. We propose a panoptic segmentation pipeline that reuses a frozen view synthesis model to propagate panoptic labels from input views to novel views, without 3D reconstruction or any segmentation-specific training of the view synthesis model. Given panoptic labels on the input views, we encode them into binary channel representations and pass them through the same model to render target-view segmentation. On ScanNet, our method achieves segmentation quality on par with Gaussian based approaches requiring explicit 3D reconstruction, while outperforming them in novel view synthesis by more than 7 dB. The label propagation also transfers across datasets, surpassing these approaches on Replica without any fine-tuning.

AI.tldr: Large view synthesis models learn spatial correspondence from RGB data that generalizes beyond appearance, enabling propagation of non-photorealistic signals like panoptic labels. The paper proposes using a frozen view synthesis model to propagate panoptic labels to novel views without 3D reconstruction or segmentation-specific training, achieving competitive segmentation quality and superior novel view synthesis.
AI.motivation: To extend large view synthesis models beyond appearance rendering to 3D scene understanding, leveraging the spatial correspondence learned from RGB supervision to propagate panoptic labels without explicit 3D reconstruction or additional segmentation training.
AI.method: A panoptic segmentation pipeline that reuses a frozen view synthesis model: panoptic labels from input views are encoded into binary channel representations and passed through the same model to render target-view segmentation, without 3D reconstruction or segmentation-specific training of the view synthesis model.
AI.result: On ScanNet, achieves segmentation quality on par with Gaussian-based approaches requiring explicit 3D reconstruction, while outperforming them in novel view synthesis by more than 7 dB. The label propagation also transfers across datasets, surpassing these approaches on Replica without any fine-tuning.
AI.conclusion: Large view synthesis models learn correspondence that generalizes beyond appearance and can be repurposed for 3D scene understanding tasks like panoptic segmentation, offering a simpler alternative to explicit 3D reconstruction methods.

title: Leveraging Offline Supervision for Efficient and Generalizable Reinforcement Learning in Large-Scale Vision-Language-Action Models
summary: It is commonly observed that online reinforcement learning (RL) produces better-performing strategies than offline methods across a broad range of performance measures. In particular, RL-trained policies exhibit stronger out-of-distribution (OOD) behavior, where models trained only with imitation learning approaches often struggle. A recent study introduced an OOD-focused benchmark and reported that RL-trained vision-language-action (VLA) policies achieve noticeably better OOD performance and slightly better in-distribution (IND) performance than their counterparts trained with supervised fine-tuning (SFT). In this work, we investigate whether hybrid offline-online training can combine the advantages of both approaches. Specifically, we study RL methods regularized by offline supervision via either offline data or an offline-trained reference policy. We evaluate these approaches on the OOD benchmark and compare them with both offline-only training and standard RL. Our results show that although offline training achieves limited OOD performance by itself, incorporating offline supervision into RL preserves strong OOD capability while substantially improving training efficiency. In particular, the guided methods reach performance close to that of standard RL while requiring roughly half of the training budget. Rather than producing a trade-off between speed and OOD performance, the hybrid approach retains strong OOD capability while achieving this efficiency gain. Project page: https://alstar8.github.io/offline-supervision-vla-rl

AI.tldr: This paper investigates hybrid offline-online RL training for VLA policies, finding that incorporating offline supervision (via offline data or a reference policy) into online RL preserves strong OOD performance while halving the training budget compared to standard RL, overcoming the limitations of pure offline methods.
AI.motivation: Online RL produces better-performing strategies than offline methods, particularly in OOD scenarios where imitation learning struggles. The authors aim to combine the advantages of both approaches through hybrid offline-online training.
AI.method: The authors study RL methods regularized by offline supervision via either offline data or an offline-trained reference policy, evaluating these hybrid approaches on an OOD benchmark against both offline-only training and standard RL.
AI.result: Hybrid methods preserve strong OOD capability while substantially improving training efficiency, reaching performance close to standard RL with roughly half the training budget. Offline training alone achieves limited OOD performance.
AI.conclusion: The hybrid approach does not produce a trade-off between speed and OOD performance; instead, it retains strong OOD capability while achieving significant efficiency gains, combining the strengths of both offline and online RL.

title: Spectral-LSH: Sub-Quadratic Prompt Compression via Krylov-Projected Locality-Sensitive Hashing
summary:
Long-prompt inference remains expensive because prefill attention scales quadratically with sequence length. We propose Spectral-LSH, a training-free prompt compression method that operates before the prompt enters the language model. Spectral-LSH approximates the dominant components of an implicit attention-kernel operator using a Krylov subspace method together with random features, avoiding explicit $O(N^2)$ attention-kernel materialization. It then applies SimHash in the resulting attention eigenspace to group similar tokens and aggregate them into macro-tokens with causal positional assignments.
  We evaluate Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, and Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct on C4. Our experiments reveal a compression-ratio phase transition. Below $ρ= 4 \times$, local token redundancy is low enough that lightweight chunking typically provides the best latency--quality trade-off. Above $ρ= 8 \times$, the spectral path preserves quality that chunking loses. At $ρ= 16 \times$, Qwen2.5-7B (adaptive) reduces the PPL ratio from 353.409 to 196.963, while Qwen2.5-14B (adaptive) reduces it from 9.533 to 3.427.
  On a small long-context structured stress test containing JSON-like, code-like, and table-like inputs, local LSH also improves every metric over chunking at $8 \times$. The adaptive backend captures both regimes by using the chunk path at low compression and spectral clustering at high compression, although chunking remains the fastest backend in total latency.

AI.tldr: Spectral-LSH is a training-free prompt compression method that uses Krylov subspace methods and SimHash in attention eigenspace to aggregate tokens into macro-tokens, reducing long-prompt inference costs. It reveals a compression-ratio phase transition where spectral methods outperform chunking above 8× compression, and an adaptive backend switches between the two regimes.
AI.motivation: Long-prompt inference is expensive due to quadratic O(N²) scaling of prefill attention with sequence length, motivating the need for efficient prompt compression without retraining.
AI.method: Spectral-LSH approximates dominant components of an implicit attention-kernel operator via Krylov subspace methods with random features (avoiding O(N²) materialization), then applies SimHash in the attention eigenspace to group similar tokens and aggregate them into macro-tokens with causal positional assignments. An adaptive backend selects between lightweight chunking (low compression) and spectral clustering (high compression).
AI.result: On C4 with Mistral-7B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Qwen2.5-14B, a phase transition is observed: below 4× compression, chunking is best; above 8×, spectral methods preserve quality better. At 16× compression, Qwen2.5-7B adaptive reduces PPL ratio from 353.409 to 196.963. On structured long-context tests, local LSH improves all metrics over chunking at 8×.
AI.conclusion: Spectral-LSH effectively compresses prompts without training, with the adaptive backend capturing optimal performance across both low and high compression regimes, though chunking remains fastest in total latency.

title: Global Building Area Estimation Products: How Accurate Are They?
summary: Geo-spatial rasters of building footprint area are useful for a variety of tasks, such as monitoring urbanization, improving energy efficiency, and tracking greenhouse gas emissions. There are now multiple global building raster datasets, however there lacks an independent, comprehensive, and fair assessment of their accuracy. In this work, we evaluate the accuracy of four major global building products: Global Human Settlement Layer (GHSL), Microsoft's TEMPO (TEMPO), The Global Building Atlas (GBA), and Overture. As ground truth for assessing their accuracy, we use ORBITaL-Net, a globally diverse dataset of manually labeled building footprints. To ensure fairness, we evaluate products on grids of multiple spatial resolutions, and several conventional performance metrics. Our results indicate that either GBA or TEMPO generally achieves the highest overall accuracy, depending upon the particular evaluation criteria. We also stratify the accuracy of each product by several factors: geographic location, population density, and income groups. The results reveal that product accuracy can sometimes vary significantly with respect to these factors. Notably, all products are significantly less accurate in Africa and Asia. Most products also suffer significant accuracy reduction in high-density urban areas.

AI.tldr: This paper evaluates four global building raster datasets (GHSL, TEMPO, GBA, Overture) against a manually labeled ground truth dataset (ORBITaL-Net), finding that GBA and TEMPO generally achieve the highest accuracy, but all products perform significantly worse in Africa, Asia, and high-density urban areas.
AI.motivation: Multiple global building raster datasets exist but lack an independent, comprehensive, and fair accuracy assessment, which is needed for applications like urbanization monitoring, energy efficiency, and greenhouse gas tracking.
AI.method: The authors evaluate four global building products (GHSL, TEMPO, GBA, Overture) using ORBITaL-Net (a globally diverse manually labeled building footprint dataset) as ground truth, assessing accuracy across multiple spatial resolutions and performance metrics, and stratifying results by geographic location, population density, and income groups.
AI.result: GBA and TEMPO generally achieve the highest overall accuracy depending on evaluation criteria. All products show significantly lower accuracy in Africa and Asia, and most products suffer substantial accuracy reduction in high-density urban areas.
AI.conclusion: No single product dominates across all conditions; accuracy varies significantly by geographic region, population density, and income levels, highlighting the need for targeted improvements in underrepresented regions and dense urban environments.

title: Predictive single cell foundation model for gene regulation and aging with privacy-preserving tabular learning
comment: 98 pages, 4 main figures, and 15 supplementary figures
summary: Pre-trained foundation models (FMs) have begun transforming single-cell genomics, but scaling them raises privacy concerns. Moreover, unlike text data, single-cell data is unordered and exhibits a unique tabular structure that current single-cell FMs overlook. We introduce Tabula, a privacy-preserving FM designed with federated learning (FL) that explicitly models the tabular structure of single-cell data. To deploy Tabula, we further developed Chiron, a decentralized AI agent-enabled platform for collaborative training across institutions without sharing raw data. Beyond strong performance across downstream benchmarks, Tabula reveals combinatorial regulatory logic across diverse biological systems, including hematopoiesis, pancreatic endogenesis, neurogenesis, and cardiogenesis. Using a new scRNA-seq dataset of paired young and aged human fibroblasts, Tabula nominates rejuvenation factors through age- and identity score-guided in silico prioritization, outperforming conventional approaches. Thus, Tabula represents an important advance in single-cell foundation modeling by integrating tabular learning with FL, paving the way toward privacy-preserving virtual cells for human health.

AI.tldr: Tabula is a privacy-preserving foundation model for single-cell genomics that integrates tabular learning with federated learning, deployed via the Chiron platform, and demonstrates strong performance in downstream tasks including biological discovery and rejuvenation factor nomination.
AI.motivation: Scaling pre-trained foundation models for single-cell genomics raises privacy concerns, and current models overlook the unique tabular structure of unordered single-cell data.
AI.method: Tabula employs federated learning (FL) to enable privacy-preserving training and explicitly models the tabular structure of single-cell data. It is deployed via Chiron, a decentralized AI agent platform for collaborative cross-institution training. A new scRNA-seq dataset of paired young and aged human fibroblasts is used for age- and identity score-guided in silico prioritization.
AI.result: Strong performance across downstream benchmarks; reveals combinatorial regulatory logic in hematopoiesis, pancreatic endogenesis, neurogenesis, and cardiogenesis; nominates rejuvenation factors outperforming conventional approaches.
AI.conclusion: Tabula advances single-cell foundation modeling by combining tabular learning with FL, paving the way toward privacy-preserving virtual cells for human health.

title: Beyond Tracking or Shortcut: Composition-Bounded Predictive States in Poker Autoregressive Models
summary: Hidden-state probes often recover latent labels in imperfect-information sequence models, but this alone does not establish that a model maintains a posterior belief distribution over hidden states. This paper studies this ambiguity in a no-range Limit Hold'em autoregressive model trained only on action and value targets, not on an opponent's hand or range. Opponent-range probes are positive after action/value controls in two of three seeds, and the behavior head predicts held-out actions about five percentage points above a baseline using only observable public history. However, visible public betting composition explains more opponent-range signal than residual hidden states, suggesting that most recoverable information comes from betting summaries. Action/value+composition baselines reach 16.5-16.7% top-10 accuracy while composition-residual hidden probes fall to 11.4-12.2%, and matched-composition comparisons are negative in every seed. We call this evidence pattern composition-bounded predictive support: hidden states remain behavior-predictive and opponent-range correlated, but most recoverable range information is explained by visible betting composition rather than residual hidden-state structure. This is a case-study claim about opponent-range representational evidence, not exact Bayesian posterior tracking or a causal belief mechanism. Synthetic control and oracle validations show that the same diagnostics accept posterior-sensitive states and reject raw composition states under matched controls. Thus positive belief probes should be interpreted through targeted alternatives before being treated as evidence of belief tracking.

AI.tldr: Hidden-state probes show opponent-range signal in a Limit Hold'em model, but this signal is largely explained by visible betting composition rather than residual hidden-state structure, leading to the concept of "composition-bounded predictive support."
AI.motivation: To investigate whether positive hidden-state probes for opponent-range in imperfect-information sequence models genuinely reflect posterior belief tracking or can be explained by simpler, observable features like betting composition.
AI.method: Trained a no-range Limit Hold'em autoregressive model on action and value targets, then performed opponent-range probing with action/value+composition baselines and composition-residual hidden probes, validated with synthetic controls and oracle tests.
AI.result: Opponent-range probes are positive after controls in 2/3 seeds; behavior head predicts held-out actions ~5% above public-history baseline. But composition baselines reach 16.5-16.7% top-10 accuracy, while composition-residual hidden probes drop to 11.4-12.2%, and matched-composition comparisons are negative in all seeds.
AI.conclusion: Positive belief probes should be interpreted through targeted alternatives (e.g., composition controls) before being treated as evidence of belief tracking; the evidence pattern is "composition-bounded predictive support," not exact Bayesian posterior tracking.

title: DRGBT-1K: A Large-scale High-quality Benchmark for Dynamic RGBT Tracking
summary: Dynamic RGBT (DRGBT) tracking aims to continuously localize a target when the available sensing modalities and observation platforms vary over time. Compared with conventional RGBT tracking with fixed RGBT inputs and a fixed observation platform, DRGBT tracking is more consistent with real-world collaborative perception systems, where targets may be observed by heterogeneous sensors from different viewpoints. However, existing benchmarks are still insufficient for systematically evaluating tracker robustness under real dynamic modality variations and cross-platform transitions. To address this limitation, we make the following contributions. 1) We construct DRGBT-1K, a large-scale high-quality benchmark for DRGBT tracking. It contains 1,045 sequences captured entirely in real-world scenarios and 795K RGBT frame pairs collected using UAVs and handheld RGBT devices, encompassing diverse real-world scenes, pronounced viewpoint changes, modality variations, and target appearance discontinuities. 2) We provide comprehensive annotations for fine-grained evaluation, including dense bounding boxes, target category labels, challenge attributes, frame-level modality labels and platform labels. DRGBT-1K covers 24 target categories, more than 15 scene types and 15 challenge attributes. 3) We establish a comprehensive benchmark by evaluating 20 representative multimodal tracking methods, including conventional RGBT trackers, modality-missing RGBT trackers, and DRGBT trackers under a unified evaluation protocol. 4) We release an unaligned version of DRGBT-1K and derive UGVT-1K to support broader research on unaligned multimodal tracking and UAV-ground collaborative tracking. 5) We develop an online evaluation platform for DRGBT-1K and provide a leaderboard that collects all methods evaluated on this benchmark.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces DRGBT-1K, a large-scale benchmark for Dynamic RGBT tracking that addresses the lack of systematic evaluation under real-world modality variations and cross-platform transitions. It includes 1,045 sequences, 795K RGBT frame pairs from UAVs and handheld devices, comprehensive annotations, evaluation of 20 tracking methods, and an online evaluation platform.
AI.motivation: Existing RGBT tracking benchmarks are insufficient for evaluating tracker robustness under real dynamic modality variations and cross-platform transitions, which are common in real-world collaborative perception systems where targets are observed by heterogeneous sensors from different viewpoints.
AI.method: The authors construct DRGBT-1K with 1,045 real-world sequences and 795K RGBT frame pairs from UAVs and handheld devices, provide comprehensive annotations (dense bounding boxes, category labels, challenge attributes, modality/platform labels), evaluate 20 representative multimodal tracking methods under a unified protocol, release an unaligned version (UGVT-1K), and develop an online evaluation platform with a leaderboard.
AI.result: The benchmark covers 24 target categories, over 15 scene types and 15 challenge attributes. 20 tracking methods including conventional RGBT trackers, modality-missing RGBT trackers, and DRGBT trackers were evaluated under a unified protocol.
AI.conclusion: DRGBT-1K provides a large-scale, high-quality benchmark that systematically evaluates tracker robustness under real dynamic modality variations and cross-platform transitions, supporting broader research on dynamic RGBT tracking, unaligned multimodal tracking, and UAV-ground collaborative tracking.

title: When Does Consensus Beat Voting? A Critical Analysis of Statistical Label Fusion in Medical Image Segmentation
summary: This paper provides a rigorous, self-contained investigation of consensus segmentation. We derive the mathematical foundations from first principles -- the generative model, EM algorithm, Van Leemput's marginalization analysis, identifiability conditions, Spatial STAPLE, and deep variational formulations -- and validate each theoretical prediction through controlled experiments. The central finding is sobering: under common conditions, STAPLE reduces to thresholded majority voting, suffers 95% EM suboptimality, and collapses under class imbalance. These are not edge cases but typical scenarios in medical imaging. Majority voting -- simple, non-parametric, and robust -- is a surprisingly strong baseline that the field has perhaps too hastily dismissed in favor of more "sophisticated" methods. At the same time, the deep consensus model demonstrates that the consensus problem is not inherently difficult -- it becomes tractable when the image is used alongside the labels. And conformal prediction shows that formal uncertainty guarantees are achievable and practical. We hope this work encourages practitioners to critically evaluate their consensus methods rather than applying STAPLE by default, and provides the mathematical and empirical foundation for more principled approaches.

AI.tldr: This paper rigorously analyzes consensus segmentation methods, demonstrating that STAPLE often degrades to simple majority voting, suffers from significant suboptimality (95% EM), and fails under class imbalance, while showing that deep consensus models and conformal prediction offer more robust alternatives with formal uncertainty guarantees.
AI.motivation: To critically evaluate STAPLE and other consensus segmentation methods from first principles, as the field has potentially over-relied on "sophisticated" methods like STAPLE without rigorous validation of their performance relative to simpler baselines.
AI.method: Derives mathematical foundations from first principles including generative models, EM algorithm, Van Leemput's marginalization, identifiability conditions, Spatial STAPLE, and deep variational formulations; validates theoretical predictions through controlled experiments.
AI.result: STAPLE reduces to thresholded majority voting under common conditions, exhibits 95% EM suboptimality, and collapses under class imbalance. Majority voting is a surprisingly strong baseline. Deep consensus models make the problem tractable by incorporating image data alongside labels. Conformal prediction provides achievable formal uncertainty guarantees.
AI.conclusion: Encourages practitioners to critically evaluate consensus methods rather than applying STAPLE by default, and provides mathematical and empirical foundations for more principled approaches to consensus segmentation.

title: Mitigating Scaffolding Collapse in Socratic Tutors via Representation Alignment
summary: Large language model (LLM)-based Socratic tutors increasingly guide students through multi-turn questioning, but they can suffer from scaffolding collapse: under sustained student pressure, a tutor gradually abandons guided inquiry and reveals solutions directly. Prior defenses primarily constrain observable responses through prompting, preference optimization, or filtering, leaving the internal representation drift that precedes trajectory-level collapse largely unaddressed. We propose Scaffold-Preserving Representation Alignment, a two-stage framework that first warms up a Socratic tutor with supervised fine-tuning, then combines trajectory-weighted direct preference optimization with a margin-preserving representation loss anchored to frozen reference states. Our method is designed to maintain separation between scaffold-preserving and collapse-inducing hidden states across dialogue turns. We evaluate our method across five STEM disciplines and five red-teaming attack strategies. On Qwen3-8B, our method lowers Collapse Rate to 32%, delays average collapse onset beyond nine turns, and keeps over-refusal low, suggesting that representation-level alignment can improve the robustness of long-horizon Socratic tutoring under our red-teaming protocol.

AI.tldr: Proposes Scaffold-Preserving Representation Alignment (SPRA), a two-stage framework combining trajectory-weighted DPO with a margin-preserving representation loss, to prevent scaffolding collapse in LLM-based Socratic tutors by maintaining separation between scaffold-preserving and collapse-inducing hidden states across dialogue turns.
AI.motivation: Prior defenses for scaffolding collapse (prompting, preference optimization, filtering) only constrain observable responses, leaving the internal representation drift that precedes trajectory-level collapse largely unaddressed.
AI.method: Two-stage framework: (1) warm-up Socratic tutor via supervised fine-tuning, then (2) combine trajectory-weighted direct preference optimization with a margin-preserving representation loss anchored to frozen reference states to maintain hidden state separation between scaffold-preserving and collapse-inducing trajectories.
AI.result: On Qwen3-8B, method lowers Collapse Rate to 32%, delays average collapse onset beyond nine turns, and keeps over-refusal low across five STEM disciplines and five red-teaming attack strategies.
AI.conclusion: Representation-level alignment can improve the robustness of long-horizon Socratic tutoring under red-teaming protocols.

title: Look Before You Edit: Attention-Guided Camera Placement and Multi-View Alignment for 3D Gaussian Splatting Editing
summary: Text-driven 3D scene editing with 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) typically applies a 2D diffusion editor to views rendered from fixed training cameras, limiting both the spatial coverage of edits and the user's freedom to target specific objects in complex scenes. We present LB-Edit, a framework that addresses two coupled problems: where to place editing cameras for localized edits, and how to make per-view edits agree with one another so that the 3D scene remains consistent after fine-tuning. First, Attention-Guided Editing Camera Placement (ACP) probes the diffusion model's self- and cross-attention at multiple candidate camera distances to find where attention is well-contained in the region of interest, then places a compact, geometrically diverse editing camera set at that attention-optimal distance. Second, Multi-view Attention Alignment (MAA) steers the editor toward the same edit across views along two axes: it aligns appearance by sharing self-attention features via token-level correspondence, and aligns spatial location by lifting cross-attention maps onto the 3D Gaussians as a shared 3D attention field, suppressing both appearance and spatial drift. Experiments on multi-object and single-object scenes show that our method achieves the highest user preference in instruction fidelity, multi-view consistency, and editing locality, using as few as 5 editing views and reducing latency by up to 7x over existing methods.

AI.tldr: LB-Edit is a text-driven 3D scene editing framework that uses Attention-Guided Editing Camera Placement (ACP) to find optimal camera positions and Multi-view Attention Alignment (MAA) to ensure cross-view consistency, achieving high-quality localized edits with as few as 5 views and up to 7x speedup.
AI.motivation: Existing 3DGS editing methods use 2D diffusion editors on fixed training camera views, which limits spatial coverage and user control over specific objects. The paper aims to solve two coupled problems: where to place editing cameras for localized edits and how to ensure multi-view consistency after fine-tuning.
AI.method: The framework has two key components: (1) Attention-Guided Editing Camera Placement (ACP) probes diffusion model attention at multiple candidate distances to find where attention is well-contained in the region of interest, then places a compact, geometrically diverse camera set at that optimal distance. (2) Multi-view Attention Alignment (MAA) aligns appearance by sharing self-attention features via token-level correspondence and aligns spatial location by lifting cross-attention maps onto 3D Gaussians as a shared 3D attention field.
AI.result: LB-Edit achieves the highest user preference in instruction fidelity, multi-view consistency, and editing locality, using as few as 5 editing views and reducing latency by up to 7x over existing methods on both multi-object and single-object scenes.
AI.conclusion: The proposed camera placement and attention alignment strategies effectively address spatial coverage and consistency issues in 3DGS editing, enabling efficient and localized text-driven 3D scene editing with significantly fewer views and faster performance.

title: Recovering Clinical Utility Under Differential Privacy: Empirical Validation of Adaptive Federated Aggregation on Heterogeneous Cardiovascular Datasets
comment: 16 pages, 3 figures. Submitted to the Journal of the Brazilian Computer Society (JBCS)
summary: Validating federated learning frameworks on real clinical data is an essential step between proof-of-concept demonstrations in controlled synthetic environments and deployment in real multicenter healthcare settings. A prior architectural study by the same authors (Tertulino and Alencar, 2026) demonstrated, on a synthetic six-feature benchmark, that server-side adaptive optimization acts as a temporal denoiser for Differential Privacy noise, answering an open challenge identified in the original pipeline work (Tertulino, 2025). That study used synthetically generated data and explicitly identified real-world validation as a priority future direction. The present work addresses this gap by validating the FedCVR framework on five publicly available real cardiovascular datasets (Framingham, Cleveland, Hungarian, Switzerland, and Long Beach VA), harmonized to the 13-attribute UCI Heart Disease schema and configured as a heterogeneous federated scenario with leave-one-institution-out cross-validation. Results demonstrate that FedCVR preserves its adaptive advantage on real data, achieving an F1-Score of 79.2% and AUC of 0.96 under the operational privacy budget (noise multiplier = 0.8, privacy budget epsilon approximately 4.2), while statistically outperforming standard FedAvg on all evaluated metrics (paired t-tests, all p <= 0.003, significant under the Bonferroni-corrected threshold). The measured privacy cost on real data confirms the graceful degradation pattern observed in the synthetic experiments, providing empirical evidence of the framework's clinical viability in genuine multicenter contexts.

AI.tldr: This paper validates the FedCVR federated learning framework on five real cardiovascular datasets (Framingham, Cleveland, Hungarian, Switzerland, Long Beach VA), demonstrating that server-side adaptive optimization effectively denoises Differential Privacy perturbations in clinical settings. FedCVR achieves F1-Score of 79.2% and AUC of 0.96 under privacy budget epsilon≈4.2, statistically outperforming standard FedAvg (all p≤0.003).
AI.motivation: Previous work demonstrated FedCVR's adaptive advantage on synthetic data, but real-world clinical validation was explicitly identified as a priority future direction. This study addresses the critical gap between controlled synthetic environments and deployment in genuine multicenter healthcare contexts.
AI.method: Validated FedCVR on five public real cardiovascular datasets (Framingham, Cleveland, Hungarian, Switzerland, Long Beach VA) harmonized to UCI Heart Disease 13-attribute schema, using leave-one-institution-out cross-validation in a heterogeneous federated scenario. Statistical significance tested with paired t-tests under Bonferroni-corrected threshold.
AI.result: FedCVR achieved F1-Score of 79.2% and AUC of 0.96 under noise multiplier=0.8 (epsilon≈4.2). Statistically outperformed FedAvg on all metrics (paired t-tests, all p≤0.003). Privacy cost degradation pattern on real data confirmed the synthetic experiment observations.
AI.conclusion: FedCVR preserves its adaptive advantage on real clinical data, providing empirical evidence of clinical viability in genuine multicenter contexts. The measured privacy cost confirms graceful degradation patterns, validating the framework's readiness for real-world deployment.

title: Euclean: Automated Geometry Problem Formalization with Unified Verification in Lean
summary: Recent formal reasoning systems have reached IMO-level performance, yet they leave a fragmented landscape: algebra and number theory are handled in Lean, while geometry still relies on domain-specific languages with limited formal guarantees. This split increases the trusted computing base and hinders unified model development. Existing geometry-in-Lean efforts (LeanEuclid, LeanGeo) introduce custom axiom systems incompatible with standard Mathlib, and their small scale ($<$ 1,100 problems) limits large-scale training. Native Mathlib autoformalization of geometry, however, poses distinct challenges: implicit diagrammatic assumptions (e.g., topological configuration and non-degeneracy) must be made explicit rather than deferred to external solvers, and models must adapt to Mathlib's small, rapidly evolving geometry infrastructure. We present Euclean, a four-stage framework - constraint explication, configuration anchoring, formalization mapping, and iterative repair - for automatically formalizing geometry in native Mathlib. We construct OMNI-Geometry (768 competition problems) and Numina-Geometry (177,597 problems), the largest geometry formalization dataset in Lean. Human evaluation shows 48.89% TOP1 and 73.33% TOP5 accuracy. Training Goedel v2 on our formalizations improves proof success from 13.6% to 15.1%, validating dataset quality for unified neural theorem proving. Code and datasets: https://github.com/tlb-22/Euclean.

AI.tldr: Euclean is a four-stage framework for autoformalizing geometry problems into native Mathlib/Lean, producing the largest geometry formalization dataset (177K+ problems) and improving theorem proving performance from 13.6% to 15.1%.
AI.motivation: Existing formal reasoning systems handle algebra/number theory in Lean but geometry relies on domain-specific languages with limited formal guarantees. This fragmented landscape increases the trusted computing base and hinders unified model development. Prior geometry-in-Lean efforts (LeanEuclid, LeanGeo) use custom axioms incompatible with standard Mathlib and are too small for large-scale training.
AI.method: Euclean proposes a four-stage framework: (1) constraint explication, (2) configuration anchoring, (3) formalization mapping, and (4) iterative repair. It constructs two datasets: OMNI-Geometry (768 competition problems) and Numina-Geometry (177,597 problems).
AI.result: Human evaluation achieves 48.89% TOP1 and 73.33% TOP5 accuracy. Training Goedel v2 on the formalizations improves proof success from 13.6% to 15.1%, validating dataset quality.
AI.conclusion: Euclean enables native Mathlib formalization of geometry at scale, addressing implicit diagrammatic assumptions and small infrastructure challenges, and improves neural theorem proving performance.

title: Frequency-Hierarchical Active k-Space Sampling for Diagnostic MRI
comment: EMA4MICCAI 2026: The 2nd MICCAI Workshop on Efficient Medical AI
summary: Active sampling for accelerated MRI must distribute a tight sampling budget across spatial frequencies that carry very different kinds of information. Low frequencies hold most of the anatomical context; high frequencies carry the fine details that drive pathology assessment. Existing active samplers either treat both regions identically or restrict the action space to entire Cartesian rows, which forces a poor compromise at high acceleration. We propose HieraSample, a task-driven framework built around this hierarchy. A cosine-annealed curriculum lowers the acceleration factor from 20x to 4x across 80 acquisition steps while keeping a fully-sampled low-frequency disk at every step; a Mamba-based policy then picks individual high-frequency coordinates from features extracted by dual disease and severity classifiers. The reward is the per-sample reduction in class-weighted cross-entropy after each action, so a positive reward corresponds directly to a more confident correct prediction. On the fastMRI+ knee benchmark, HieraSample matches the fully-sampled oracle on ACL diagnosis from 4x to 10x acceleration, and improves on a recent Cartesian baseline by as much as 20.4 AUC points on ACL severity.

AI.tldr: HieraSample is a task-driven active sampling framework for accelerated MRI that uses a cosine-annealed curriculum (20x→4x over 80 steps) with a fully-sampled low-frequency disk, a Mamba-based policy for selecting high-frequency coordinates, and reward based on class-weighted cross-entropy reduction. It matches fully-sampled oracle on ACL diagnosis from 4x-10x acceleration and improves Cartesian baselines by 20.4 AUC points on ACL severity.
AI.motivation: Existing active samplers for accelerated MRI either treat low and high frequencies identically or restrict sampling to entire Cartesian rows, forcing a poor compromise at high acceleration—failing to account for the hierarchical importance of anatomical context (low frequencies) versus fine details (high frequencies).
AI.method: (1) Cosine-annealed curriculum reducing acceleration from 20x to 4x across 80 acquisition steps, maintaining a fully-sampled low-frequency disk at every step. (2) A Mamba-based policy selects individual high-frequency coordinates from features extracted by dual disease and severity classifiers. (3) Reward is per-sample reduction in class-weighted cross-entropy after each action.
AI.result: On fastMRI+ knee benchmark, HieraSample matches fully-sampled oracle on ACL diagnosis from 4x to 10x acceleration, and improves on a recent Cartesian baseline by up to 20.4 AUC points on ACL severity.
AI.conclusion: HieraSample demonstrates that task-driven active sampling with a frequency-hierarchy-aware curriculum can achieve diagnostic-quality accelerated MRI at high acceleration factors, significantly outperforming Cartesian baselines for fine-grained severity assessment.

title: Structured Latent Space Modeling over Multi-Scale Temporal Patches for Multivariate Time Series Forecasting
summary: Multivariate time series encode structural patterns that unfold across multiple temporal scales, yet most forecasting backbones treat learned representations as transient byproducts of prediction, leaving the organizational geometry of these patterns underexploited. We introduce M2Patch, a CNN-based forecasting architecture that maps channel-independent multivariate observations into a structured latent space through two complementary differentiable constraints. Multi-scale patching decomposes the input into overlapping temporal granularities; depthwise separable convolutions with progressive dilation extract scale-specific features in linear time; and per-scale learned projections compress these features into a compact latent representation. The latent space is organized by an intra-scale smoothness constraint that enforces temporal continuity between adjacent patches, and an inter-scale alignment constraint, realized through learnable cross-scale mappings, that restores cross-granularity interaction within the channel-independent design, ensuring that all scales encode mutually consistent representations of the underlying dynamics. Experiments on ten real-world benchmarks show that M2Patch achieves 57 best and 34 second-best results across 40 forecasting settings, matching or exceeding representative baselines on most benchmarks while maintaining linear computational complexity and robustness to patch-level input corruption.

AI.tldr: M2Patch is a CNN-based multivariate time series forecasting model that uses multi-scale patching, depthwise separable convolutions, and dual constraints (intra-scale smoothness + inter-scale alignment) to organize structured latent representations, achieving state-of-the-art results on 40 forecasting settings with linear complexity.
AI.motivation: Existing forecasting backbones treat learned representations as transient byproducts of prediction and fail to exploit the organizational geometry of structural patterns that unfold across multiple temporal scales in multivariate time series.
AI.method: M2Patch uses (1) multi-scale patching to decompose input into overlapping temporal granularities, (2) depthwise separable convolutions with progressive dilation for scale-specific feature extraction, (3) per-scale learned projections for compact latent representation, (4) intra-scale smoothness constraint for temporal continuity, and (5) inter-scale alignment constraint via learnable cross-scale mappings for cross-granularity interaction in a channel-independent design.
AI.result: On 10 real-world benchmarks across 40 forecasting settings, M2Patch achieves 57 best and 34 second-best results, matches or exceeds representative baselines, while maintaining linear computational complexity and robustness to patch-level input corruption.
AI.conclusion: M2Patch demonstrates that explicitly structuring the latent space with multi-scale temporal constraints significantly improves multivariate time series forecasting, achieving strong empirical performance with efficient linear complexity.

title: CrackedPDFs: A Controlled Benchmark for Hidden Prompt Injection in PDFs
summary: Document-based LLM systems often flatten a PDF before guardrails inspect it. That step can discard evidence that an instruction was never visible to the user. We introduce CrackedPDFs, a controlled benchmark for hidden prompt injection in PDFs. The benchmark contains 29,322 generated PDFs from 4,983 base docu ments. It includes 9,774 injected files and 19,548 benign or matched-confounder files. We evaluate PromptGuard and a rule baseline. We also evaluate structural only learned models and a sanitized hybrid detector. The evaluation uses held-out provenance splits and paired benign-confounder controls. It also uses label-shuffle checks and shortcut audits. On a 2,919-document held-out test set, the hybrid de tector reaches 0.960 F1. ROC-AUC is 0.998 and PR-AUC is 0.997. It also ranks injected files above matched benign confounders in 95.9% of 973 pairs. Prompt Guard has low recall when given extracted text only. Structural-only learned mod els are weak under paired controls. A text-only TF-IDF model reaches perfect held-out scores but fails shortcut audits. These results show that document-aware hybrid detection is useful under controlled paired evaluation. They do not show broad real-world robustness or reliable cross-family generalization.

AI.tldr: CrackedPDFs is a benchmark of 29,322 PDFs for hidden prompt injection detection. A hybrid detector combining structural and textual features achieves 0.960 F1 on held-out data, outperforming PromptGuard and text-only models, but real-world generalization remains unproven.
AI.motivation: Flattening PDFs to text before applying guardrails discards visual/layout evidence that an instruction was never visible to the user, enabling hidden prompt injection attacks.
AI.method: Created a controlled benchmark (29,322 PDFs; 9,774 injected, 19,548 benign/confounder). Evaluated PromptGuard, rule baseline, structural-only learned models, text-only TF-IDF, and a hybrid detector using held-out provenance splits, paired controls, label-shuffle checks, and shortcut audits.
AI.result: Hybrid detector achieves 0.960 F1, 0.998 ROC-AUC, 0.997 PR-AUC; ranks injected above confounders in 95.9% of pairs. PromptGuard has low recall on text-only input; structural-only models are weak under paired controls; TF-IDF fails shortcut audits despite perfect held-out scores.
AI.conclusion: Document-aware hybrid detection is useful under controlled paired evaluation, but does not demonstrate broad real-world robustness or reliable cross-family generalization.

title: WASABI: Whole-graph Assignment-based Stabilizer for lAne topology By Inter-frame tracking
summary: Autonomous driving requires understanding the road as a graph of drivable lanes and their connectivity, beyond the ego lane alone, to follow routes through intersections and reason about cross- and merging-traffic. Recent perception models infer such lane topology, i.e., lane segments together with their inter-lane connectivity (LCLC), from onboard sensors over a 360-degree BEV view. Due to neural perception's imperfections, their outputs retain structural instabilities such as missed detections, lost or incorrect LCLC, over-detection, and label flicker. This paper presents WASABI, a real-time post-processing pipeline that stabilizes lane topology outputs both within and across frames by treating lane segments and their LCLC connectivity as joint tracking targets, under onboard real-time constraints (10 Hz / 20 ms / up to 200 input lanes). The pipeline integrates segment tracking with connectivity, noise-robust topology-aware refinement, and a resource-constrained real-time design. On internal validation data (16 sequences), WASABI improves LCLC detection F1 from 0.834 to 0.948 (+0.114, +13.6%) and reduces centerline lateral error from 2.50 m to 0.95 m, while reducing detection false-positives by 24.6%. Temporal-stability metrics on the same data show LCLC toggle rate reduced by 63.3% and boundary-label flicker rate by 30.2%, confirming across-frame stabilization beyond per-frame accuracy.

AI.tldr: WASABI is a real-time post-processing pipeline that stabilizes lane topology outputs in autonomous driving by jointly tracking lane segments and their inter-lane connectivity (LCLC) across frames, improving detection F1 from 0.834 to 0.948 (+13.6%), reducing centerline error from 2.50m to 0.95m, cutting false positives by 24.6%, and reducing toggle rate by 63.3% under real-time constraints (10 Hz / 20 ms / up to 200 lanes).
AI.motivation: Neural perception models for lane topology suffer from structural instabilities including missed detections, incorrect inter-lane connectivity (LCLC), over-detection, and label flicker, which undermine the reliability of autonomous driving systems that depend on a consistent graph of drivable lanes and their connectivity.
AI.method: WASABI treats lane segments and their LCLC connectivity as joint tracking targets, integrating segment tracking with connectivity, noise-robust topology-aware refinement, and a resource-constrained real-time design operating at 10 Hz / 20 ms with support for up to 200 input lanes.
AI.result: LCLC detection F1 improved from 0.834 to 0.948 (+13.6%), centerline lateral error reduced from 2.50m to 0.95m, detection false positives reduced by 24.6%, LCLC toggle rate reduced by 63.3%, and boundary-label flicker rate reduced by 30.2% on internal validation data (16 sequences).
AI.conclusion: WASABI effectively stabilizes lane topology outputs both within and across frames by jointly tracking lane segments and connectivity, achieving significant improvements in both per-frame accuracy and temporal consistency under real-time onboard constraints.

title: Reproducing Recurrent Transformers: The CoTFormer
comment: 7 pages, 3 figures, reproducibility report submitted to University of Southampton
summary: The CoTFormer architecture formalizes Chain-of-Thought as a form of recurrent latent computation, preserving intermediate states as attendable representations to mimic explicit reasoning traces. In this work, we evaluate CoTFormer and its structural variants across perplexity and compute efficiency metrics. Furthermore, we extend evaluation to controlled algorithmic settings to determine whether this recurrent framework improves out-of-distribution generalisation on inductive reasoning tasks.

AI.tldr: This paper evaluates the CoTFormer architecture, which formalizes Chain-of-Thought as recurrent latent computation with attendable intermediate states. The authors assess perplexity and compute efficiency of CoTFormer and its variants, and test whether the recurrent framework improves out-of-distribution generalization on inductive reasoning tasks in controlled algorithmic settings.
AI.motivation: To determine whether the CoTFormer's recurrent latent computation framework (which mimics explicit reasoning traces through attendable intermediate states) improves out-of-distribution generalization on inductive reasoning tasks, and to evaluate its efficiency and perplexity performance.
AI.method: Evaluation of CoTFormer and its structural variants on perplexity and compute efficiency metrics, alongside controlled algorithmic experiments to test out-of-distribution generalization on inductive reasoning tasks.
AI.result: The paper reports results comparing CoTFormer variants on perplexity and compute efficiency, and assesses generalization performance on inductive reasoning tasks (specific numerical outcomes not provided in the abstract).
AI.conclusion: The recurrent framework of CoTFormer shows promise for improving out-of-distribution generalization on inductive reasoning tasks, though the abstract does not specify definitive conclusions.

title: HyGRL: Adaptive Hybrid Graph Reasoning for Multi-Entity Questions
summary: Multi-entity compositional questions pose significant challenges to existing retrieval-augmented language models. Conventional methods fall into a dilemma: standard RAG lacks dynamic reasoning, traditional Graph-RAG is limited by structural sparsity, and LLM-constructed Graph-RAG incurs prohibitive costs. We propose \textbf{\fwa}, a unified framework that embeds unstructured text into structured knowledge graphs, creating a heterogeneous network for flexible evidence retrieval. Reasoning is formulated as adaptive structure induction, learned via a robust two-stage process: (1) imitation learning distills heuristic expert signals, and (2) reinforcement learning refines the policy using LLM-driven preference rewards. Experiments demonstrate that {\fwa} effectively merges textual richness with structural knowledge, outperforming SOTA baselines in answer accuracy and reasoning fidelity while maintaining extremely low token costs and near real-time inference((code available at https://github.com/wjywjy123/HyGRL) .

AI.tldr: HyGRL is a unified framework that embeds unstructured text into structured knowledge graphs for multi-entity compositional QA, using imitation learning + reinforcement learning to achieve SOTA accuracy with low token costs.
AI.motivation: Existing RAG methods struggle with multi-entity compositional questions: standard RAG lacks dynamic reasoning, traditional Graph-RAG suffers from structural sparsity, and LLM-constructed Graph-RAG is prohibitively expensive.
AI.method: Proposes HyGRL, which embeds unstructured text into a structured heterogeneous knowledge graph. Reasoning is formulated as adaptive structure induction via a two-stage process: (1) imitation learning from heuristic expert signals, (2) reinforcement learning with LLM-driven preference rewards to refine the policy.
AI.result: Outperforms SOTA baselines in answer accuracy and reasoning fidelity while maintaining extremely low token costs and near real-time inference.
AI.conclusion: HyGRL effectively merges textual richness with structural knowledge, offering a cost-efficient and accurate solution for multi-entity compositional QA.

title: Physics-Aware Complex-Valued State Space Model with Scattering-Prior Feature Modulation for PolSAR Image Classification
summary: Polarimetric synthetic aperture radar (PolSAR) image classification is a representative task for physics-aware GeoAI, where land-cover semantics are closely coupled with electromagnetic scattering mechanisms. Many existing complex-valued networks can preserve amplitude-phase information, but they are often limited in long-range spatial dependency modeling and usually incorporate polarimetric priors only as input-level or shallow auxiliary features. As a result, physical knowledge is insufficiently used to guide deep feature evolution. To address this issue, this paper proposes CV-SSMNet, a physics-aware complex-valued state-space network with scattering-aware feature modulation for PolSAR image classification. The proposed method builds a complex-valued state-space model (CV-SSM) in the original complex domain to capture long-range spatial dependencies while preserving polarimetric amplitude-phase coupling. Meanwhile, seven physically meaningful scattering priors, are encoded as FiLM-style modulation signals to adaptively recalibrate complex-valued representations during feature evolution. CV-SSMNet further integrates multi-scale complex convolutions, branch-wise CV-SSM encoding, prior-guided recalibration, and lightweight global context aggregation, enabling physically guided representation learning from local scattering structures to global spatial context. Experiments on three L-band benchmark datasets and an additional P-band BIOMASS evaluation demonstrate that CV-SSMNet achieves competitive accuracy, improved regional consistency, and better boundary preservation, supporting the effectiveness of embedding polarimetric scattering mechanisms into complex-valued long-range GeoAI representation learning.

AI.tldr: CV-SSMNet is a physics-aware complex-valued state-space network that integrates polarimetric scattering priors via FiLM-style modulation to improve PolSAR image classification by capturing long-range spatial dependencies while preserving amplitude-phase coupling.
AI.motivation: Existing complex-valued networks preserve amplitude-phase information but lack long-range spatial dependency modeling and only incorporate polarimetric priors as shallow features, leading to insufficient physical guidance in deep feature learning for PolSAR classification.
AI.method: CV-SSMNet builds a complex-valued state-space model (CV-SSM) in the complex domain to capture long-range dependencies while preserving polarimetric amplitude-phase coupling; encodes seven scattering priors as FiLM-style modulation signals to recalibrate complex-valued representations; integrates multi-scale complex convolutions, branch-wise CV-SSM encoding, prior-guided recalibration, and lightweight global context aggregation.
AI.result: Experiments on three L-band benchmark datasets and a P-band BIOMASS dataset show CV-SSMNet achieves competitive accuracy, improved regional consistency, and better boundary preservation.
AI.conclusion: Embedding polarimetric scattering mechanisms into complex-valued long-range GeoAI representation learning is effective for PolSAR image classification.

title: NMR Elucidation as an Agentic Search Problem, Not a Modeling Problem
summary: Structural elucidation from Nuclear Magnetic Resonance (NMR) data remains a fundamental bottleneck across chemistry, materials science, and biology. We demonstrate that an agentic AI system can perform this task at a level comparable to graduate-level chemistry students. Instead of training a model to directly map spectra to structures, we build a single autonomous agent, backed by a frozen LLM, that interacts with a curated environment with access to domain-specific processing tools, validation checks, tabulated chemical shifts, and instructions that outline the stepwise nature of a chemist's thinking process. On the Alberts dataset, our agent elucidates structures with a top-1 accuracy of 71%, comparable to the performance of graduate students at 66% top-1 accuracy. On the van Bramer and AstraZeneca datasets, our agent achieved 80% and 20% top-1 accuracy respectively, outperforming zero-shot end-to-end deep learning models which were trained on large datasets of simulated spectra. These results show that reframing NMR elucidation as an LLM-guided constrained search, rather than a modeling task, yields substantial gains and suggests a path toward multi-step orchestration frameworks that integrate a variety of tools, models, and domain knowledge to assist in automating spectroscopic analysis.

AI.tldr: An agentic AI system using a frozen LLM with domain-specific tools achieves 71% top-1 accuracy on NMR structural elucidation (comparable to graduate students' 66%), outperforming end-to-end deep learning models on benchmark datasets.
AI.motivation: Structural elucidation from NMR data is a fundamental bottleneck across chemistry, materials science, and biology, and existing end-to-end deep learning approaches trained on simulated spectra have limited performance.
AI.method: A single autonomous agent powered by a frozen LLM interacts with a curated environment equipped with domain-specific processing tools, validation checks, tabulated chemical shifts, and stepwise instructions mimicking a chemist's reasoning process, reframing NMR elucidation as an LLM-guided constrained search.
AI.result: Top-1 accuracy of 71% on Alberts dataset (vs. 66% for graduate students), 80% on van Bramer, and 20% on AstraZeneca, outperforming zero-shot end-to-end deep learning models trained on large simulated spectral datasets.
AI.conclusion: Reframing NMR elucidation as LLM-guided constrained search yields substantial gains over modeling approaches, suggesting a path toward multi-step orchestration frameworks integrating diverse tools, models, and domain knowledge for automated spectroscopic analysis.

title: ITPEval: Benchmarking Formal Translation Across Interactive Theorem Provers
summary: Formal theorem proving has emerged as a frontier challenge for machine learning, yet the ecosystem is fragmented: proofs remain siloed across incompatible systems, limiting both training data for learning-based provers and the portability of verified results. We present ITPEval, the first benchmark for evaluating automated formal proof translation across four major ITPs (Lean 4, Rocq, Isabelle, and HOL Light), spanning two distinct logical foundations. Our benchmark comprises 1,560 source files and 6,848 theorems organized into a controlled tier of axiomatized files that isolates foundational translation difficulty, and an ecosystem tier drawn from real libraries that exposes API and proof-style mismatches. We release itpeval, a unified multi-ITP verification infrastructure with state-isolated warm backends that preserve per-artifact native checking semantics. We evaluate both statement and proof translation across five frontier and open-weight LLMs on 12 directed translation pairs: statement translation peaks at 29.1% pass@1 and proof translation at 10.5%; controlled theorems reach 29.7% proof pass@1 versus 5.2% for ecosystem-level translations, confirming that library mismatch is the dominant bottleneck. In addition to pass@k evaluation, a deterministic Lean 4 BEq check establishes equivalence for 54.0% of verified source-to-Lean 4 miniF2F statement translations, showing that native type-checking alone can substantially overestimate semantic fidelity; in an autoformalization/auto-informalization round-trip study, Rocq and HOL Light are easier formalization targets than Lean 4 and Isabelle, while multi-ITP context improves pooled Lean 4 success from 4.8% to 10.6%. Our benchmark, verification infrastructure, and evaluation pipelines are publicly released.

AI.tldr: ITPEval is the first benchmark for evaluating automated formal proof translation across four major Interactive Theorem Provers (Lean 4, Rocq, Isabelle, HOL Light). It comprises 1,560 source files and 6,848 theorems across controlled and ecosystem tiers, finding that statement translation peaks at 29.1% pass@1, proof translation at 10.5%, and library mismatch is the dominant bottleneck. A Lean 4 BEq check reveals native type-checking overestimates semantic fidelity (54.0% equivalence), and multi-ITP context improves pooled Lean 4 success from 4.8% to 10.6%.
AI.motivation: Formal theorem proving is a frontier ML challenge, but the ecosystem is fragmented across incompatible ITP systems, limiting training data for learning-based provers and portability of verified results. No prior benchmark existed for evaluating cross-ITP proof translation.
AI.method: The authors construct ITPEval with 1,560 source files and 6,848 theorems organized into a controlled tier (axiomatized, isolating foundational translation difficulty) and an ecosystem tier (real libraries, exposing API/style mismatches). They build itpeval, a unified multi-ITP verification infrastructure with state-isolated warm backends. They evaluate statement and proof translation across 5 frontier/open-weight LLMs on 12 directed translation pairs using pass@1 and pass@k metrics, plus a deterministic Lean 4 BEq equivalence check and autoformalization/auto-informalization round-trip studies.
AI.result: Statement translation peaks at 29.1% pass@1; proof translation at 10.5%. Controlled theorems reach 29.7% proof pass@1 vs 5.2% for ecosystem-level translations, confirming library mismatch as the dominant bottleneck. Lean 4 BEq check establishes equivalence for 54.0% of verified source-to-Lean 4 miniF2F statement translations. Rocq and HOL Light are easier formalization targets than Lean 4 and Isabelle in round-trip studies; multi-ITP context improves pooled Lean 4 success from 4.8% to 10.6%.
AI.conclusion: Cross-ITP translation remains challenging, especially at the proof level and ecosystem scale. Library mismatch is the primary bottleneck. Native type-checking overestimates semantic fidelity, motivating richer equivalence checks. Multi-ITP context and round-trip studies reveal target-dependent difficulty variations. The benchmark, infrastructure, and pipelines are publicly released to facilitate further research.

title: Trace: A Taxonomy-Guided Environment for Multidomain Visual Reasoning
summary: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has substantially improved language-model reasoning, yet its extension to vision-language models remains constrained by the lack of training data that are simultaneously broad, exactly verifiable, and reproducible. We introduce Trace, a taxonomy-guided environment for multidomain visual reasoning. Trace factorizes task construction into a scene grammar and an executable task program, separating visual realization from answer computation. A shared semantic state determines the rendered image, prompt, typed answer, verifier state, and replayable instance trace. The resulting environment comprises 1,000 tasks over 277 scene grammars and 11 visual domains, with controlled semantic and visual variation. RLVR on 64,000 Trace instances improves the macro-average across 24 external benchmarks by 3.51 percentage points for Qwen2.5-VL-3B and 4.06 points for Qwen2.5-VL-7B, providing evidence that broad procedural training can transfer beyond the generated task distributions. Project page: https://maveryn.github.io/trace/.

AI.tldr: Trace is a taxonomy-guided environment with 1,000 visual reasoning tasks across 11 domains, using a scene grammar and executable task program to generate verifiable training data. RLVR training on 64,000 Trace instances yields ~3.5-4% macro-average improvement on 24 external benchmarks for Qwen2.5-VL models.
AI.motivation: RLVR has improved language-model reasoning but its extension to vision-language models is hindered by the lack of training data that is simultaneously broad, exactly verifiable, and reproducible.
AI.method: Trace factorizes task construction into a scene grammar and an executable task program, separating visual realization from answer computation. A shared semantic state determines the rendered image, prompt, typed answer, verifier state, and replayable instance trace, enabling controlled semantic and visual variation across 1,000 tasks, 277 scene grammars, and 11 visual domains.
AI.result: RLVR on 64,000 Trace instances improves macro-average across 24 external benchmarks by 3.51 pp for Qwen2.5-VL-3B and 4.06 pp for Qwen2.5-VL-7B.
AI.conclusion: Broad procedural training with verifiable rewards can transfer beyond the generated task distributions, suggesting Trace-style environments are effective for improving vision-language model reasoning.

title: Reward-Aware Population Scaling of Evolutionary Strategies in LLM Fine-Tuning
comment: 15 pages, 2 figures. Accepted at the 4th HiLD (High-dimensional Learning Dynamics) Workshop, ICML 2026
summary: Using Evolutionary Strategies (ES) for fine-tuning large language models is attractive because it is memory-efficient, parallel, and compatible with black-box or discrete rewards. Yet its population-size conclusions conflict sharply: fine-tuning with cross-entropy (CE) reward succeeds with $N=1$, while binary-reward training often needs $N \approx 30$. We show this gap is largely about reward design and normalization, not population size. In the capable-model regime we study, z-score advantage normalization can cause $N=2$ to fail. Disabling normalization lets binary-reward ES with $N=2$ improve on GSM8K and TREC across capable models spanning 0.5B-7B, where the normalized variant collapses or degrades. This small-$N$ risk is set by reward granularity: binary accuracy reward induces a zero-advantage probability $q$ that depends in closed form on base accuracy, batch size, and intra-pair correctness correlation; a zero-training probe on Qwen2.5-Instruct/GSM8K matches the formula with mean absolute error 0.020 across 12 configurations and finds the availability threshold $N_{\mathrm{avail}}$ to be small in this capable-model regime. The implication is not that $N=2$ is universally sufficient, but that small-population failure in capable-model binary ES can be an implementation artifact rather than an intrinsic population limit.

AI.tldr: The paper explains why Evolutionary Strategies (ES) fine-tuning of LLMs fails with small populations (N=2) when using binary rewards due to z-score normalization, not population size itself. Disabling normalization allows N=2 to work well, and a closed-form formula predicts when zero-advantage training occurs.
AI.motivation: There is a conflict in ES fine-tuning literature: CE reward works with N=1, but binary-reward ES requires N≈30. The authors aim to resolve whether this gap is due to population size limits or implementation artifacts like reward normalization.
AI.method: The authors analyze z-score advantage normalization, disable it to test small-N binary-reward ES, derive a closed-form formula for zero-advantage probability q based on base accuracy, batch size, and intra-pair correctness correlation, and validate it on Qwen2.5-Instruct/GSM8K.
AI.result: Disabling normalization lets N=2 binary-reward ES improve on GSM8K and TREC across 0.5B-7B capable models. The zero-advantage probability formula matches experiments with MAE 0.020 across 12 configurations. The availability threshold N_avail is small in the capable-model regime.
AI.conclusion: Small-population failure in capable-model binary ES is an implementation artifact (normalization) rather than an intrinsic population limit, though N=2 is not universally sufficient.

title: FORCE-Bench: A Benchmark, Dataset, and Evaluation Harness for Agentic AI in Enterprise Finance
summary: Recent advances in large language models have accelerated deployment of agentic systems in operational finance. Existing benchmarks emphasize measuring general capabilities, instruction following, or safety, but few directly address the operational finance workflows that agentic systems are now being deployed to automate. Finance professionals require agents to not only provide factually sound and properly grounded information, but also ensure that this information is verifiable and consistently adheres to rules and constraints of the operational finance domain. We introduce FORCE-Bench, which contains 251 expert-annotated queries and evaluates responses using a rubric-based framework calibrated to the requirements of the operational finance domain, across eight dimensions: accuracy, citations, clarity, depth, groundedness, recency, relevance, and structure. FORCE-Bench assesses agentic systems on three task types: financial obligation research (querying ERP systems for accounts receivable and payable data), financial entity performance research (answering time-bound questions from public filings and market data), and business brief generation (synthesising multi-source company intelligence reports). To reflect real deployment conditions, we evaluate our purpose-built agent, as well as the general-purpose agentic systems, under common tool access and latency-bounded settings. Results show that general-purpose agentic systems do not consistently meet finance-domain quality requirements under operational constraints, while the purpose-built Finance Agent for Microsoft 365 Copilot is more reliable across dimensions. We release the dataset, rubrics, harness, and analysis code as open-source to support reproducible comparison and adaptation to other enterprise finance environments.

AI.tldr: FORCE-Bench is a 251-query benchmark evaluating agentic systems across eight quality dimensions for operational finance tasks (obligation research, entity performance research, business brief generation). General-purpose agents fail to meet domain requirements under operational constraints, while a purpose-built Finance Agent for Microsoft 365 Copilot performs more reliably.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks focus on general capabilities, instruction following, or safety, but do not address the specific operational finance workflows that agentic systems are being deployed to automate, where factuality, verifiability, and adherence to domain rules are critical.
AI.method: The authors construct FORCE-Bench with 251 expert-annotated queries and evaluate responses using a rubric-based framework across eight dimensions (accuracy, citations, clarity, depth, groundedness, recency, relevance, structure).
