They assess three task types: financial obligation research (ERP queries), financial entity performance research (public filings/market data), and business brief generation (multi-source synthesis). Evaluations are conducted under common tool access and latency-bounded settings.
AI.result: General-purpose agentic systems do not consistently meet finance-domain quality requirements under operational constraints, whereas the purpose-built Finance Agent for Microsoft 365 Copilot demonstrates higher reliability across all eight dimensions.
AI.conclusion: Domain-specific benchmarks like FORCE-Bench are necessary to evaluate agentic systems in operational finance; general-purpose agents are insufficient, and purpose-built agents are more reliable. The dataset, rubrics, harness, and code are released as open-source to support further research.

title: Lean-SAM2: Target-Anchored Memory and Encoder Acceleration for SAM2
summary: The Segment Anything Model 2 (SAM2) has advanced temporal promptable segmentation, yet its deployment remains hindered by heavy memory cross-attention overhead and redundant full-frame visual feature extraction. While recent methods explore efficiency via heuristic memory pruning and window-based sparse routing, they typically suffer from catastrophic performance degradation in complex segmentation scenarios replete with occlusions and distractors. To resolve these limitations, we propose \textbf{Lean-SAM2}, a holistic lightweight framework designed to address the above vulnerabilities while systematically eliminating computational redundancies. Specifically, Lean-SAM2 integrates three collaborative mechanisms: (1) Target-Anchored Memory Pruning (TAMP) safeguards target tokens against deceptive attention by modulating raw attention significance with semantic consistency against prompt-derived foreground anchors; (2) Temporal Condensation with Insurance Memory (TCIM) condenses historical context via a visibility-gated fusion while conditionally archiving high-confidence entries in a parallel insurance bank; and (3) Target-Anchored Risk-Aware Routing (TARR) selectively activates the heavy image encoder for target-related windows based on anchor similarity, utilizing a risk-aware fallback policy to trigger full-frame refreshes during volatile transitions. Extensive evaluations across multiple challenging benchmarks demonstrate that Lean-SAM2 establishes a superior balance between accuracy and efficiency. For example, on the LVOSv2 validation dataset, Lean-SAM2 achieves overall inference speedups of $1.412\times$ and $1.417\times$ on the SAM2.1-Large and SAM2.1-Base+, respectively, significantly outperforming Efficient-SAM2 while boosting the corresponding $\mathcal{J}\&\mathcal{F}$ scores by $5.0\%$ and $3.6\%$. Code is available at https://github.com/DeawhaleQwQ/Lean-SAM2.

AI.tldr: Lean-SAM2 is a lightweight framework that reduces computational redundancies in SAM2 via three mechanisms (TAMP, TCIM, TARR), achieving superior speed and accuracy on complex segmentation benchmarks.
AI.motivation: SAM2 suffers from heavy memory cross-attention overhead and redundant full-frame visual feature extraction, while existing efficiency methods (e.g., heuristic memory pruning, window-based sparse routing) degrade catastrophically in complex scenarios with occlusions and distractors.
AI.method: Three collaborative components: (1) TAMP — modulates raw attention with semantic consistency against prompt-driven foreground anchors to protect target tokens; (2) TCIM — visibility-gated fusion for condensing historical context with a parallel insurance bank for high-confidence entries; (3) TARR — selectively activates image encoder for target-related windows via anchor similarity, with risk-aware fallback for full-frame refreshes during volatile transitions.
AI.result: On LVOSv2, Lean-SAM2 achieves 1.412× and 1.417× speedups on SAM2.1-Large and SAM2.1-Base+ respectively, outperforming Efficient-SAM2 while boosting J&F scores by 5.0% and 3.6%.
AI.conclusion: Lean-SAM2 establishes a superior accuracy-efficiency balance for temporal promptable segmentation, addressing both computational redundancy and robustness in complex scenarios.

title: Adaptive Multi-Expert Graph Transformer for Interpretable EEG-Based Diagnostics
summary: Electroencephalographic (EEG) abnormalities arise from dynamic changes in neural synchrony across spatial and temporal scales, yet many computational approaches reduce these dynamics to static features. We present a Spatial Multi-Expert Graph Transformer that models each EEG recording as a sequence of dynamic functional connectivity graphs. Time-resolved connectivity is estimated using the weighted Phase Lag Index (wPLI), and hierarchical graph encoding aggregates information from electrode to regional and global levels. A multi-expert transformer architecture enables subtype-aware reasoning, with a gating mechanism adaptively fusing expert outputs for global abnormality prediction. Experiments on the TUAB dataset show competitive abnormal EEG detection performance and demonstrate the potential of dynamic graph modeling with adaptive expert fusion for interpretable, subtype-aware spatial--temporal analysis.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a Spatial Multi-Expert Graph Transformer that models EEG recordings as sequences of dynamic functional connectivity graphs (using wPLI) and employs hierarchical graph encoding with multi-expert transformer for subtype-aware, interpretable abnormality detection, achieving competitive results on the TUAB dataset.
AI.motivation: EEG abnormalities arise from dynamic neural synchrony changes, but existing approaches often reduce these to static features, losing temporal and spatial richness.
AI.method: Models each EEG as a sequence of dynamic functional connectivity graphs (wPLI), uses hierarchical graph encoding from electrode to regional/global levels, and applies a multi-expert transformer with adaptive gating for subtype-aware abnormal EEG detection.
AI.result: Achieves competitive abnormal EEG detection performance on the TUAB dataset, demonstrating the effectiveness of dynamic graph modeling and adaptive expert fusion.
AI.conclusion: Dynamic graph modeling with multi-expert fusion is promising for interpretable, subtype-aware spatial-temporal EEG analysis.

title: The Chronos Vulnerability: A Taxonomy of Temporal Persistence and Memory-Based Deception in Agentic AI
summary: The transition from stateless generative models in artificial intelligence to stateful, autonomous agents represents an architectural evolution that, while providing the capabilities of long-term planning and the automation of enterprise workflows, also represents the introduction of a new form of security threat, the Chronos Vulnerability. The Chronos Vulnerability represents the threat of memory-based attacks, including the Memory Injection Attack (MINJA) and the sleeper agent, in which the internal belief system of the autonomous agent is compromised, effectively decoupling the attack vector from the final catastrophic event. This study formalizes the threat model for persistence-based attacks and the threat of Dynamics Blindness in the context of the World of Workflows benchmark, demonstrating that traditional endpoint content filters are insufficient for the current stateful architecture. Consequently, this study synthesizes a defense-in-depth landscape, categorizing emerging frameworks such as diagnostic trajectory guardrails (AgentDoG), formal temporal verification (Agent-C), immunological memory consensus (A-MemGuard), and hardware-anchored trust via GPU-based Trusted Execution Environments (TEEs) and Zero-Trust memory architectures.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies the Chronos Vulnerability—a new security threat from memory-based attacks (MINJA, sleeper agents) in stateful autonomous AI agents—and shows that traditional content filters are insufficient. It proposes a defense-in-depth framework using diagnostic guardrails, temporal verification, memory consensus, and hardware-anchored trust.
AI.motivation: The evolution from stateless generative models to stateful autonomous agents introduces persistent memory architectures that, while enabling long-term planning, also create novel attack surfaces not addressed by existing security measures.
AI.method: The study formalizes persistence-based attack threat models and Dynamics Blindness, evaluates traditional endpoint content filters against stateful architectures using the World of Workflows benchmark, and synthesizes a defense-in-depth taxonomy from emerging approaches.
AI.result: Traditional endpoint content filters are insufficient for stateful agent architectures. Emerging defenses include diagnostic trajectory guardrails (AgentDoG), formal temporal verification (Agent-C), immunological memory consensus (A-MemGuard), and hardware-anchored trust via GPU TEEs and Zero-Trust memory.
AI.conclusion: A multi-layered defense-in-depth landscape is necessary to address the Chronos Vulnerability, combining architectural, formal, consensus-based, and hardware-level protections against persistent memory attacks in autonomous agents.

title: MoAKE: Toward Unified All-in-One Action Quality Assessment via Mixture of Action Knowledge Experts
summary: Action Quality Assessment (AQA) aims to objectively evaluate performance quality from action videos. Most existing methods follow a ``one-by-one'' paradigm, training a separate model for each action type. This setting limits real-world deployment, as it requires prior action-type knowledge to select the corresponding model and suffers from poor generalization across diverse actions. To address these limitations, we study the challenging task of all-in-one AQA, which aims to assess heterogeneous actions within a single unified model. We propose a novel Mixture of Action Knowledge Experts (MoAKE) framework, designed to mitigate negative knowledge transfer caused by large semantic discrepancies among actions. MoAKE learns complementary experts that capture diverse action patterns within a shared semantic space and dynamically aggregates their knowledge to adapt the assessment to the input action. Each expert is tailored with segment-aware prototypes to handle varying temporal lengths, together with an Adaptive Intra- and Inter-Segment Relationship Modeling (AIISRM) module to model multi-granularity temporal dynamics. Furthermore, we establish comprehensive benchmarks for all-in-one as well as zero/few-shot AQA. Extensive experiments on three long-term datasets demonstrate that MoAKE significantly outperforms existing methods in the all-in-one setting, while also achieving consistent generalization on three short-term datasets under zero/few-shot evaluation. Code is available at https://github.com/XuHuangbiao/MoAKE.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes MoAKE, a unified Mixture of Action Knowledge Experts framework for all-in-one Action Quality Assessment that handles heterogeneous action types within a single model, overcoming the limitations of traditional one-by-one AQA approaches through complementary experts with segment-aware prototypes and adaptive temporal relationship modeling, achieving superior performance on both long-term and short-term action datasets.
AI.motivation: Existing AQA methods follow a "one-by-one" paradigm requiring separate models per action type, which limits real-world deployment due to the need for prior action-type knowledge and poor generalization across diverse actions. The authors aim to address these limitations by enabling all-in-one AQA within a single unified model.
AI.method: Proposes MoAKE (Mixture of Action Knowledge Experts) framework with: (1) complementary experts capturing diverse action patterns in a shared semantic space; (2) dynamic knowledge aggregation adapting to input actions; (3) segment-aware prototypes for handling varying temporal lengths; (4) Adaptive Intra- and Inter-Segment Relationship Modeling (AIISRM) module for multi-granularity temporal dynamics.
AI.result: MoAKE significantly outperforms existing methods in all-in-one setting on three long-term datasets, and achieves consistent generalization on three short-term datasets under zero/few-shot evaluation.
AI.conclusion: The MoAKE framework effectively mitigates negative knowledge transfer across heterogeneous actions, enabling a single unified model for diverse action quality assessment tasks with strong generalization capabilities.

title: Unlearning as Distribution Restoration: A Controlled Counterfactual Study, a Validated Selective Screen, and the Limits of Oracle-Free Certification
summary: Machine unlearning is commonly evaluated by matching a retrained oracle on trained probes. In a controlled nonce-fact testbed with a matched retraining reference, we find this criterion can favor methods that retain held-out knowledge: candidates it rates adequate score held-out forget facts $-2.82$ nats below the never-learned level (cluster CI $[-3.16,-2.48]$). We recast unlearning as restoration to the matched reference and audit oracle-free screens and certificate-style criteria across 45 model-seed cells spanning five open architecture families. The reference itself falsifies an absolute retain/round-trip certificate: the injected model, which retains the retain set by construction, fails the fixed retain threshold in 41/45 cells and its own round trip in 31/45, and the reference fully certifies in only 1/45. A base-anchored held-out screen remains strong as a selective necessary test: on a sealed challenge suite it rejects the injected model in 45/45 cells, accepts the reference in 44/45, and partially detects entity-routing suppression (35/45); it is a necessary test with measured sensitivity, not a sufficiency certificate. A damage-relative recalibration anchored to the reference's own operating point certifies a small subset in 15/45 cells; where it does not abstain, its picks lie within retraining noise (0.80 nats) on the axes it optimizes, while the common trained-probe criterion sits 5.17 nats away (a supporting comparison, not a head-to-head benchmark). A fixed-magnitude logit-suppression attack defeats the full forward battery in 12/45 cells, so forward-only certification is not sound; our method is an empirical selective test for methods-as-produced. An identifiability theorem delimits which facts admit an oracle-free forget threshold at all, with TOFU as the predicted boundary case.

AI.tldr: This paper challenges the common practice of evaluating machine unlearning by matching a retrained oracle, showing that this criterion can favor methods that actually retain held-out knowledge. The authors propose recasting unlearning as restoration to a matched reference, audit multiple evaluation criteria across 45 model-seed cells from five architecture families, and find that existing certificates often fail. They introduce a base-anchored held-out screen as a necessary (but not sufficient) test, a damage-relative recalibration method, and prove an identifiability theorem that delimits which facts can admit an oracle-free forget threshold.
AI.motivation: Existing machine unlearning evaluation criteria — particularly the common practice of matching a retrained oracle on trained probes — are flawed: they can favor methods that actually retain knowledge that should be forgotten. The paper aims to rigorously audit these criteria and develop more reliable evaluation methods.
AI.method: The authors use a controlled nonce-fact testbed with a matched retraining reference, evaluating across 45 model-seed cells spanning five open architecture families. They audit oracle-free screens and certificate-style criteria, propose a base-anchored held-out screen and a damage-relative recalibration anchored to the reference's own operating point, and develop an identifiability theorem for oracle-free forget thresholds.
AI.result: The common trained-probe criterion rated methods that score held-out forget facts -2.82 nats below never-learned level. The reference model falsified its own retain/round-trip certificate in most cells. The base-anchored screen rejected the injected model in 45/45 cells and accepted the reference in 44/45. The damage-relative recalibration certifies only 15/45 cells, with picks within 0.80 nats of retraining noise vs. 5.17 nats for the common criterion. Fixed-magnitude logit-suppression defeats forward-only certification in 12/45 cells.
AI.conclusion: Standard trained-probe criteria for machine unlearning are unreliable. A base-anchored held-out screen is a strong necessary (but not sufficient) test. Forward-only certification is unsound; instead, empirical selective testing for methods-as-produced is recommended. The identifiability theorem explains why TOFU is a boundary case for oracle-free forget thresholds.

title: Sophisticated Policies from Epistemic Priors
summary: Sophisticated Inference is a variant of active inference often associated with recursive belief modeling and tree search. We argue that its central computational role is simpler: within a planning horizon, it makes active inference closed-loop by allowing future actions to depend on future states and observations. This closed-loop structure can be represented in the epistemic-prior variational free energy framework. Epistemic priors supply the active-inference objective, while a joint posterior over future states and actions supplies the state-contingent control structure. We evaluate this decomposition in the Reactivity Maze, a stochastic benchmark designed to separate epistemic incentive from inner-horizon closed-loop control. The comparison includes three variational objectives with the same state-action posterior family, an action-state factorized active inference objective, Sophisticated Inference, and standard Expected Free Energy planning. The results show that neither ingredient is sufficient on its own. Methods without an epistemic component do not seek information, while methods that prevent future actions from depending on future states cannot turn information into reliable goal-reaching. By contrast, both Sophisticated Inference and full-joint epistemic-prior active inference solve the environment by combining epistemic drive with closed-loop inference. These results show that the advantage associated with Sophisticated Inference need not be specific to tree search itself. It arises from the closed-loop form of active inference, and this form can be represented in epistemic-prior variational inference when the posterior keeps future actions dependent on future states.

AI.tldr: Sophisticated Inference's advantage in active inference comes not from tree search but from enabling closed-loop control (future actions depend on future states). This can be captured by epistemic-prior variational inference with a joint state-action posterior, as demonstrated in the Reactivity Maze benchmark.
AI.motivation: To clarify the essential computational role of Sophisticated Inference in active inference—specifically whether its advantage stems from recursive belief modeling and tree search or from a simpler closed-loop control structure.
AI.method: The authors decompose active inference into an epistemic-prior variational free energy framework with a joint posterior over future states and actions (closed-loop). They compare three variational objectives and standard Expected Free Energy planning in the Reactivity Maze, a stochastic benchmark designed to separate epistemic incentive from inner-horizon closed-loop control.
AI.result: Neither epistemic drive alone nor open-loop control is sufficient. Methods lacking epistemic components fail to seek information; methods preventing future actions from depending on future states cannot turn information into reliable goal-reaching. Only Sophisticated Inference and the full-joint epistemic-prior active inference solve the environment by combining both components.
AI.conclusion: The advantage of Sophisticated Inference arises from its closed-loop form (state-contingent control) rather than from tree search per se. This closed-loop structure can be represented within epistemic-prior variational inference when the posterior maintains dependence of future actions on future states.

title: Memory-Augmented Multimodal Large Language Models for Small Object Understanding in Streaming Aerial Videos
summary: Language-guided aerial perception aims to understand user-specified tiny targets in complex unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) scenes. In real UAV deployment, the UAV must respond while it flies, so such perception runs in an online streaming manner, where frames arrive sequentially and the model responds to each one without access to future frames. However, applying current Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) to this setting raises two challenges. First, targets viewed from the air are often tiny, yet the visual compression in existing MLLMs treats all regions equally and discards their fine-grained details. Second, understanding a continuous stream requires past-frame context, yet retaining the entire history is infeasible on resource-constrained onboard hardware, whereas discarding it causes the target to drift or disappear. We address the tiny object and streaming challenges from both data and method perspectives. From the data perspective, we present \textbf{DroneEyes}, the \textbf{first} pixel-level and open-vocabulary referring-segmentation dataset for tiny aerial targets, comprising $2,140$ high-definition videos and $176,623$ pairs across Object Description and Referring Expression tasks, with dense per-frame masks. From the method perspective, we propose \textbf{SkyAnchor}, an MLLM with two designs to the above challenges: a Semantics-Aware Token Router that preserves small-target under a reduced visual-token budget, and a Hierarchical Memory Bank that keeps the target consistently understood on streams.

AI.tldr: The paper addresses the challenges of deploying MLLMs for real-time aerial perception of tiny targets in streaming UAV video, introducing DroneEyes (a pixel-level open-vocabulary dataset for tiny aerial targets) and SkyAnchor (an MLLM with a Semantics-Aware Token Router for preserving small-target details and a Hierarchical Memory Bank for consistent streaming understanding).
AI.motivation: Current MLLMs struggle in online streaming UAV deployment because (1) visual compression discards fine-grained details of tiny aerial targets, and (2) retaining full historical context is infeasible on resource-constrained hardware, causing target drift or loss.
AI.method: From the data side, they present DroneEyes, the first pixel-level open-vocabulary referring-segmentation dataset for tiny aerial targets (2,140 HD videos, 176,623 pairs, dense per-frame masks). From the method side, they propose SkyAnchor with two components: a Semantics-Aware Token Router that preserves small-target details under reduced visual-token budget, and a Hierarchical Memory Bank that maintains consistent target understanding across streams.
AI.result: DroneEyes is the first dataset of its kind for tiny aerial targets, and SkyAnchor addresses the tiny-object and streaming challenges through its two proposed designs.
AI.conclusion: The paper presents both data and method contributions to enable MLLMs for real-time, streaming aerial perception of tiny targets in UAV scenarios.

title: Marine Engine Fault Dataset: Open-Access Data under Controlled Reference and Fault Scenario Conditions
comment: submitted to a journal and currently is under review, 34 pages, 13 Figures
summary: Open-access datasets for marine-engine predictive maintenance remain scarce, particularly those from controlled fault experiments with documented operating conditions, subsystem-level interventions and system-level measurements. This work presents the Marine Engine Fault Dataset, an openly available dataset from a turbocharged, intercooled three-cylinder marine diesel engine operated on a testbed under both reference and fault-scenario conditions. The experimental campaign combined a reference-performance program across the 30-90% load range with scenario-based tests in which abnormal conditions were introduced after stabilized fault-free operation, enabling controlled comparison between baseline and fault-affected behaviour. Five anomaly classes were implemented through physical interventions affecting major engine subsystems: cooling-water pump cavitation, compressor air-filter clogging, air-cooler fouling, injection-valve nozzle clogging and turbine degradation induced through increased exhaust-side restriction. The released data comprise multi-sensor time-series of operating, thermal, pressure, flow and combustion-related variables, with a separate reference-performance record and metadata for structured reuse. Technical validation shows that the reference measurements remain physically coherent across the operating range and that the imposed anomalies produce interpretable response patterns consistent with the affected subsystems, including progressively distinguishable behaviour where different severities were implemented. By combining controlled fault realization, multi-load operation and system-level measurements within a real marine-engine platform, the dataset provides a well-documented benchmark for anomaly detection, fault diagnosis, degradation modelling and related condition-monitoring studies in maritime machinery.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces an open-access Marine Engine Fault Dataset from a three-cylinder marine diesel engine testbed, containing multi-sensor time-series data under both normal and five fault-scenario conditions (cooling-water pump cavitation, compressor air-filter clogging, air-cooler fouling, injection-valve nozzle clogging, and turbine degradation), providing a benchmark for predictive maintenance and condition-monitoring research.
AI.motivation: Open-access datasets for marine-engine predictive maintenance are scarce, especially those combining controlled fault experiments with documented operating conditions, subsystem-level interventions, and system-level measurements. This work aims to fill that gap.
AI.method: The authors operated a turbocharged, intercooled three-cylinder marine diesel engine on a testbed across 30-90% load range, conducting a reference-performance program and scenario-based tests with five physically implemented fault classes: cooling-water pump cavitation, compressor air-filter clogging, air-cooler fouling, injection-valve nozzle clogging, and turbine degradation via exhaust-side restriction. Multi-sensor time-series data were collected with metadata and reference records.
AI.result: Technical validation confirms reference measurements are physically coherent across the operating range, and imposed anomalies produce interpretable response patterns consistent with affected subsystems, with progressively distinguishable behavior at different severities.
AI.conclusion: The dataset offers a well-documented benchmark for anomaly detection, fault diagnosis, degradation modeling, and condition-monitoring studies in maritime machinery, combining controlled fault realization, multi-load operation, and system-level measurements on a real marine-engine platform.

title: Knowledge-Centric Self-Improvement
summary: Self-improving AI systems typically treat the agent as the object that improves, by optimizing prompts, workflows, harnesses, or even the agent's own code. This agent-centric view can make improvements expensive to maintain and difficult to transfer, because gains become tied to a particular agent design, task distribution, or adaptation run. We study a complementary paradigm: knowledge-centric self-improvement, in which agents remain generic and disposable while the persistent object is a curated knowledge base that agents can leverage for future tasks. We conduct controlled case studies to operationalize this idea via a simple protocol. Agents attempt one task, then contribute evidence-grounded insights to a shared knowledge base via task-level and cross-task forums, followed by knowledge distillation. Because self-improvement is contained in the knowledge rather than the agent, improvement can be more inspectable, transferable, and portable. Across abstract reasoning, coding, and terminal benchmarks, this protocol improves solve rates while reducing dollar cost relative to agent-centric baselines. The resulting distilled knowledge also transfers to held-out tasks and across LLM families, indicating that the improvement is not merely an LLM- or run-specific behavior. These results support a new view of self-improving agentic systems: progress can be driven primarily by the curated persistent knowledge. Code is available at https://github.com/recursive-knowledge/KSI.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces knowledge-centric self-improvement (KSI), a paradigm where AI agents remain generic and disposable, while improvement is concentrated in a curated, persistent knowledge base. Through a protocol involving task-level and cross-task forums followed by knowledge distillation, KSI improves solve rates and reduces costs compared to agent-centric baselines across abstract reasoning, coding, and terminal benchmarks, with gains transferring to held-out tasks and across LLM families.
AI.motivation: Traditional agent-centric self-improvement ties gains to specific agent designs, task distributions, or adaptation runs, making improvements expensive to maintain and difficult to transfer. The authors propose a complementary paradigm where improvement is contained in persistent knowledge rather than the agent itself, enabling greater inspectability, transferability, and portability.
AI.method: The authors operationalize knowledge-centric self-improvement via a simple protocol: agents attempt a task, then contribute evidence-grounded insights to a shared knowledge base through task-level and cross-task forums, followed by knowledge distillation. Agents remain generic and disposable while the knowledge base persists and accumulates improvement.
AI.result: Across abstract reasoning, coding, and terminal benchmarks, the protocol improves solve rates while reducing dollar cost relative to agent-centric baselines. The distilled knowledge transfers to held-out tasks and across LLM families, demonstrating that improvement is not merely an LLM- or run-specific behavior.
AI.conclusion: Progress in self-improving agentic systems can be driven primarily by curated persistent knowledge rather than by optimizing the agent itself. This supports a new view where knowledge-centric self-improvement offers a more inspectable, transferable, and portable alternative to traditional agent-centric approaches.

title: Robust Activation Map Rectification for Weakly Supervised Volumetric Segmentation: Temporal Coherence as a Free Lunch
summary: Weakly supervised segmentation relies heavily on class activation maps (CAMs) to initially localize target regions. However, CAMs are often noisy and prone to catastrophic failures. Existing remedies typically introduce additional training stages or prototype learning, increasing computational cost and reducing robustness. In this paper, we propose a training-free prototype-free framework that rectifies unreliable CAMs by exploiting temporal and structural coherence in volumetric data as a free lunch. Our approach is built on two key components. First, we introduce Variance-Reduced Activation Aggregation (VRAA) which suppresses noise and amplify coherent semantic signals. We provide a theoretical justification by modeling CAMs as high-dimensional random vectors and show that aggregation yields provable variance reduction. Second, we design a Bidirectional Extremity Rectification (BER) mechanism that detects and rectifies implausible activations through bidirectional extremity checks, effectively mitigating extreme-value failures without learning additional parameters. Our method is model-agnostic and can be seamlessly integrated with existing pipelines. Extensive experiments on multiple public benchmarks demonstrate substantial improvements over state-of-the-art weakly supervised methods, achieving up to 20% Dice and 40% mIoU gains while reducing inference time by more than 5 times. These results indicate that leveraging coherence as an implicit inductive bias yields a principled and efficient approach to stabilizing weakly supervised volumetric segmentation. Our code will be available.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes VRAA and BER, a training-free prototype-free framework that rectifies unreliable CAMs by leveraging temporal and structural coherence in volumetric data, achieving up to 20% Dice and 40% mIoU gains with 5x faster inference.
AI.motivation: Weakly supervised segmentation relies on CAMs, which are often noisy and prone to catastrophic failures. Existing remedies introduce additional training stages or prototype learning, increasing computational cost and reducing robustness.
AI.method: Two key components: (1) Variance-Reduced Activation Aggregation (VRAA) which suppresses noise and amplifies coherent semantic signals with theoretical variance reduction guarantees; (2) Bidirectional Extremity Rectification (BER) which detects and rectifies implausible activations via bidirectional extremity checks without learning additional parameters.
AI.result: Substantial improvements over state-of-the-art weakly supervised methods on multiple public benchmarks, achieving up to 20% Dice and 40% mIoU gains while reducing inference time by more than 5 times.
AI.conclusion: Leveraging coherence as an implicit inductive bias yields a principled and efficient approach to stabilizing weakly supervised volumetric segmentation. The method is model-agnostic and can be seamlessly integrated with existing pipelines.

title: Guardrails as Scapegoats: Auditing Unfaithful Safety Refusals in Tool-Augmented LLM Agents
comment: 10 pages, 3 figures. Accepted at the ACM KDD 2026 Workshop on Evaluation and Trustworthiness of Agentic AI
summary: Evaluation frameworks for tool-augmented LLM agents focus overwhelmingly on capability metrics or explicit tool crashes, leaving silent infrastructure failures and HTTP 200 responses with empty, null, or malformed payloads largely unaudited. We introduce a lightweight black-box auditing framework that injects four silent failure profiles across 12 production-adjacent tool stubs and classifies agent responses into three mutually exclusive behavioral classes: Honest Surrender (HSR), Fabrication (FAR), and Unfaithful Safety Refusal (USR). Evaluating two frontier and two open-source models at temperature zero under a neutral system prompt, we find that FAR dominates (56.6% of valid responses): agents treat empty payloads as real data, silently returning fabricated results. USR, in which an agent invents a policy or privacy rationale to explain the failure, is nearly absent at baseline (0.25%, one instance across 396 valid trajectories). Our key finding emerges from an ablation where we augment the system prompt with standard safety language ("prioritize user privacy and data security"), which amplifies USR by 15.6x (from 0.25% to 3.95%; 95% CI on ablation rate: 2.2%-6.4%; Fisher's exact test, p < 0.001). USR is a latent behavior, activated when safety vocabulary in the system prompt primes the model to reach for policy rationales when tools silently fail. Sensitive tools (fetch_medical_record, retrieve_contract, fetch_user_profile) account for the majority of USR instances. We propose a payload-response misalignment heuristic for production-level detection and discuss governance implications for safety-forward deployments.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a black-box auditing framework that injects four silent failure profiles into tool-augmented LLM agents, revealing that Fabrication (FAR) dominates at 56.6% of responses, and that adding standard safety language to system prompts amplifies Unfaithful Safety Refusal (USR) by 15.6x, with sensitive tools being the primary trigger.
AI.motivation: Existing evaluation frameworks for tool-augmented LLM agents focus on capability metrics or explicit tool crashes, ignoring silent infrastructure failures where HTTP 200 responses carry empty, null, or malformed payloads—a critical blind spot in agent reliability and safety auditing.
AI.method: The authors build a lightweight black-box auditing framework that injects four silent failure profiles across 12 production-adjacent tool stubs, classifying agent responses into three classes: Honest Surrender (HSR), Fabrication (FAR), and Unfaithful Safety Refusal (USR). They evaluate two frontier and two open-source models at temperature zero with a neutral system prompt, then perform an ablation adding standard safety language to the prompt.
AI.result: FAR dominates (56.6% of valid responses). USR is nearly absent at baseline (0.25%, one instance). Adding safety language amplifies USR by 15.6x (to 3.95%; 95% CI: 2.2%-6.4%; Fisher's exact test, p<0.001). Sensitive tools (fetch_medical_record, retrieve_contract, fetch_user_profile) account for the majority of USR instances.
AI.conclusion: USR is a latent behavior activated when safety vocabulary primes models to invent policy rationales for silent tool failures. The authors propose a payload-response misalignment heuristic for production detection and discuss governance implications for safety-forward deployments.

title: Edge Intelligence in Civil Aviation: Paradigms, Techniques, and Applications
summary: Civil aviation is safety critical and its operations, from flight decks and towers to ramps and maintenance, generate massive, heterogeneous data at the network edge. Yet cloud centric deployment of large Artificial Intelligence (AI) models often produces high task latency, lacks offline capability in communication denied environments, and requires centralizing sensitive data, raising privacy and sovereignty risks. Edge AI moves perception, prediction, and decision logic closer to the data producers via compression, collaborative inference, and split learning, thereby reducing latency, bandwidth, and exposure while enabling graceful operation during disconnections. This paper provides a panoramic view and a common understanding of edge intelligence tailored to civil aviation. We firstly articulate the operational motivations for edge AI, and then review recent techniques for edge inference and edge learning. We then introduce the organizational computing paradigms and the respective configurations in civil aviation environments; finally, we describe the emerging applications and the future research trends of edge intelligence in civil aviation. We argue that a refined edge solution can complement cloud foundations to deliver low latency, privacy preserving, and resilient AI services across the civil aviation lifecycle.

AI.tldr: This paper provides a comprehensive survey of edge AI tailored to civil aviation, covering motivations, techniques (compression, collaborative inference, split learning), computing paradigms, applications, and future trends, arguing that edge AI complements cloud to achieve low-latency, privacy-preserving, and resilient services across aviation operations.
AI.motivation: Cloud-centric AI deployment in civil aviation faces high latency, lack of offline capability in communication-denied environments, and privacy/sovereignty risks from centralizing sensitive data. Edge AI is needed to move perception and decision logic closer to data producers.
AI.method: The paper provides a panoramic review: (1) articulates operational motivations for edge AI in aviation; (2) reviews edge inference and edge learning techniques (compression, collaborative inference, split learning); (3) introduces organizational computing paradigms and configurations for civil aviation environments; (4) describes emerging applications and future research trends.
AI.result: A structured taxonomy and understanding of how edge intelligence (inference and learning) can be deployed in civil aviation settings, with identified configurations, emerging use cases, and open research directions.
AI.conclusion: A refined edge solution can complement cloud foundations to deliver low latency, privacy-preserving, and resilient AI services across the entire civil aviation lifecycle.

title: Current Injection Spiking Neural Network for Infrared and Visible Image Fusion
summary: Infrared and visible image fusion (IVIF) integrates the complementary information of two modalities into a single image with richer scene content. While existing methods are largely built on artificial neural networks (ANNs), which densely compute over all activations, spiking neural networks (SNNs) communicate through sparse binary spikes and compute only where and when a spike occurs, offering a route to more energy-efficient fusion. However, directly applying SNNs to IVIF creates a fundamental tension: cross-modal fusion relies on fine-grained responses from both modalities, whereas binary spikes can discard complementary cues that remain below the firing threshold. The membrane potential retains these subthreshold responses before firing, letting both modalities jointly shape the output when integrated at this stage. Building on this, we propose CIS-Fuse, a spiking network that performs cross-modal fusion directly at the membrane-potential level. At its core is the current injection spiking (CIS) operator, which injects one modality as a gated auxiliary current into the driving neuron of the other, so the two integrate before spike firing, with a per-channel learnable injection strength that adaptively regulates the modulation magnitude. Building on CIS, we construct a bidirectional cross-modal fusion (BCMF) module and deploy it on a dual-branch architecture with asymmetric stacking depths, where the two branches develop a clear functional specialization. Extensive experiments on four IVIF benchmarks and on downstream detection and segmentation show that CIS-Fuse achieves fusion quality on par with state-of-the-art ANN-based methods while inheriting the energy efficiency of spike-based computation, with roughly an order of magnitude lower inference energy than the similarly-sized ANN-based DCEvo. Code will be released upon publication.

AI.tldr: CIS-Fuse is a spiking neural network for infrared-visible image fusion that integrates cross-modal information at the membrane-potential level using a current injection spiking operator, achieving ANN-comparable fusion quality with ~10x lower energy consumption.
AI.motivation: Existing IVIF methods rely on ANNs which are energy-intensive. SNNs offer greater energy efficiency but struggle with cross-modal fusion because binary spikes can discard subthreshold complementary cues. The goal is to leverage SNN efficiency while preserving fine-grained cross-modal information.
AI.method: Proposes CIS-Fuse with a current injection spiking (CIS) operator that injects one modality as a gated auxiliary current into the other modality's driving neuron before spike firing, with per-channel learnable injection strength. A bidirectional cross-modal fusion (BCMF) module is built on CIS and deployed on a dual-branch architecture with asymmetric stacking depths for functional specialization.
AI.result: Achieves fusion quality on par with state-of-the-art ANN-based methods on four IVIF benchmarks and downstream detection/segmentation tasks, with roughly an order of magnitude lower inference energy than the similarly-sized ANN-based DCEvo.
AI.conclusion: Spike-based computation can match ANN fusion performance while being far more energy-efficient, validating subthreshold membrane-potential integration as an effective strategy for cross-modal fusion in SNNs.

title: REGEN: Replay-recycling for Expert-to-Generalist distillation with Offline Reinforcement Learning
summary: Large-scale online reinforcement learning (RL) is the predominant means of eliciting advanced abilities including long-term reasoning and agentic tool use in large language models (LLMs). However, continuing to scale it across vast task domains of interest remains challenging in both computational infrastructure and cost, especially when considering RL as merely a one-off learning stage. Recently, a widely used technique for distilling knowledge across various domains and training stages, multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD), helps to decouple the RL stage, saving costs, while maintaining generality across vast domains. Nonetheless, similar to online RL, MOPD requires coupled inference and backward passes, which continues to limit its scalability and computational efficiency. To address these challenges, we propose REGEN: Replay-recycling for Expert-to-Generalist Distillation with Offline RL. Instead of distilling from multiple teacher models, REGEN trains a generalist by simply recycling the replay memory -- the free by-product of the teachers' specialized RL training -- and employing offline RL algorithms. REGEN completely decouples the rollout sampling from the backward training process and thus greatly reduces the training cost. Across mathematical reasoning, code generation, and instruction following, REGEN matches the accuracy of MOPD at substantially lower cost. It potentially turns online RL into a data synthesis process instead of a one-off learning stage, and can potentially be extended to large-scale post-training without requiring heavy computational load.

AI.tldr: REGEN proposes using replay memory (by-products of specialized RL training) with offline RL algorithms to distill generalist LLMs, replacing costly multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD) while matching accuracy at substantially lower computational cost.
AI.motivation: Scaling online RL across vast task domains for LLMs remains computationally expensive and infrastructure-heavy, especially when treated as a one-off learning stage. MOPD helps decouple the RL stage but still requires coupled inference and backward passes, limiting scalability and efficiency.
AI.method: REGEN replaces multi-teacher distillation by recycling replay memory (free by-products of teachers' specialized RL training) and applying offline RL algorithms to train a generalist. This completely decouples rollout sampling from backward training, eliminating the need for coupled inference and backward passes.
AI.result: Across mathematical reasoning, code generation, and instruction following, REGEN matches the accuracy of MOPD at substantially lower training cost.
AI.conclusion: REGEN transforms online RL from a one-off learning stage into a data synthesis process, enabling scalable large-scale post-training without heavy computational load.

title: Symbol and Footprint Database for Electronic Components by Agentic Recognition and Generation
summary: A rich and recognizable component library is the cornerstone of printed circuit board (PCB) design and generation. Traditionally, engineers manually create symbols and footprints and design PCB schematics, which is time-consuming and error-prone. Leveraging multimodal large language models (MLLMs), we develop SFgen, an agentic recognition and generation flow of symbol and footprint for electronic components. SFgen achieves 86% accuracy for symbol generation and 80% accuracy for footprint generation. We use the SFgen method to create SFnet, a database of symbols and footprints. It now has 1000 components and is expanding constantly, which lays the foundation for automatic generation of PCB designs.

AI.tldr: SFgen is an MLLM-based agentic system that generates electronic component symbols (86% accuracy) and footprints (80% accuracy), and creates SFnet, an expanding database of 1000+ components for automated PCB design.
AI.motivation: Manual creation of PCB symbols and footprints is time-consuming and error-prone; there is a need for automated recognition and generation to accelerate PCB design workflows.
AI.method: SFgen leverages multimodal large language models (MLLMs) in an agentic flow to recognize and generate symbols and footprints for electronic components.
AI.result: 86% accuracy for symbol generation, 80% accuracy for footprint generation; SFnet database created with 1000 components (and expanding).
AI.conclusion: MLLM-based automated generation of component libraries is feasible and accurate, laying the foundation for fully automatic PCB design generation.

title: MTVDiff: Multimodal Conditional Latent Diffusion for Enhanced Thermal-to-Visible Face Translation
summary: Thermal-to-visible face translation presents fundamental challenges including geometric discontinuities, semantic attribute mismatches, and identity degradation. We propose MTVDiff, a novel multimodal latent diffusion framework that synergistically integrates depth and textual information to address these limitations while preserving identity characteristics. The MTVDiff framework presents three core technical contributions: (1) a Dual-Branch Cross-Attention Fusion (DBCAF) module for multi-scale thermal-depth feature extraction and fusion; (2) a Gated Text-to-Visual Feature Alignment mechanism for semantically-guided generation; and (3) Spatial Feature Transformations (SFT) for adaptive multimodal prior integration. Extensive experiments on the MCXFace and SpeakingFaces datasets demonstrate that our multimodal approach significantly outperforms existing GAN-based and diffusion-based approaches across multiple metrics, achieving substantial improvements in both image quality and face verification performance, with FID reductions of up to 48.3% and Rank-1 accuracy improvements of up to 8.9\%. Our work provides a robust solution for face recognition systems operating under varying illumination conditions and advances the state-of-the-art in cross-spectral facial image translation through effective multimodal integration.

AI.tldr: MTVDiff is a multimodal latent diffusion framework that integrates depth and text information for thermal-to-visible face translation, using DBCAF, Gated Text-to-Visual Feature Alignment, and SFT modules to achieve significant improvements in image quality and face verification performance.
AI.motivation: Thermal-to-visible face translation suffers from geometric discontinuities, semantic attribute mismatches, and identity degradation, which hinder face recognition systems operating under varying illumination conditions.
AI.method: MTVDiff proposes a multimodal latent diffusion framework with three core modules: (1) Dual-Branch Cross-Attention Fusion (DBCAF) for multi-scale thermal-depth feature extraction and fusion; (2) Gated Text-to-Visual Feature Alignment for semantically-guided generation; and (3) Spatial Feature Transformations (SFT) for adaptive multimodal prior integration.
AI.result: On MCXFace and SpeakingFaces datasets, MTVDiff outperforms existing GAN-based and diffusion-based approaches, achieving FID reductions of up to 48.3% and Rank-1 accuracy improvements of up to 8.9%.
AI.conclusion: MTVDiff provides a robust solution for face recognition under varying illumination and advances cross-spectral facial image translation through effective multimodal integration.

title: Predictive Extrema, Unprofitable Policies: An AI-Assisted Audit of Candle-Based Binance Spot Timing Models
comment: 23 pages, 5 figures, 8 tables. Simulation-only negative empirical study and human-supervised AI-assisted evidence audit. No live trading or investment advice. Code and available artifacts: https://github.com/AyoubJadouli/Quantbot-Research-Framework
summary: We audit whether candle-based machine-learning models can turn predictions of cryptocurrency extrema or short-horizon outcomes into positive Binance Spot paper policies after assumed costs. Numerical results come from scripted fixed-seed model runs and deterministic simulators; human-supervised AI agents supported the July 20 evidence-integrity revision through literature retrieval, separately tasked critique, artifact reconciliation, documentation, and source packaging, not trading decisions. The strongest later-period evidence, conditional on extensive predecessor search, is negative: an unchanged ten-pair mandatory-daily selector lost 6.72\% over 19 July cycles at an assumed 31-bps completed-cycle cost, with 3 wins and 16 losses. In short model-specific July evaluations, the validation-selected local-minimum policy returned -1.79\%, while the local-maximum sell-to-cash/re-entry policy underperformed continuous holding by 2.80\%; their gross mean advantages of 11.11 and 12.21 bps were below even the 21-bps stress. A Gurgul-inspired, OHLCV-only daily adaptation attained minimum/maximum ROC AUC of 0.874/0.896 but average precision of only 0.134/0.116 and lost 44.30\% over seven cycles, versus -41.20\% for buy-and-hold. A forensic audit also downgraded an earlier One4All "30-day holdout": its dates had influenced prior architecture work, its four-hour outcome horizon was not purged at split boundaries, it used same-close entry, and its raw result directories were absent. Across the tested, mostly exploratory protocols, event-ranking performance did not establish positive executable policy value. Every operational decision remains NO\_TRADE.

AI.tldr: Audit finds no evidence that candle-based ML models can generate positive cryptocurrency trading strategies after costs; all tested protocols failed to outperform buy-and-hold, with the best models losing 1.79-44.30% and the mandatory-daily selector losing 6.72% with only 3 wins out of 19 cycles.
AI.motivation: To determine whether candle-based machine-learning models can turn predictions of cryptocurrency extrema or short-horizon outcomes into positive net-of-cost trading policies on Binance Spot.
AI.method: Scripted fixed-seed model runs and deterministic simulators with human-supervised AI agents supporting evidence-integrity revision. Tested multiple protocols including a mandatory-daily selector, validation-selected local-minimum/maximum policies, OHLCV-only daily adaptation (Gurgul-inspired), and forensic audit of prior work.
AI.result: All protocols failed: mandatory-daily selector lost 6.72% (3/19 wins); local-minimum policy returned -1.79%; local-maximum policy underperformed holding by 2.80%; OHLCV model achieved ROC AUC 0.874/0.896 but average precision only 0.134/0.116, losing 44.30% vs -41.20% buy-and-hold. Prior One4All work was downgraded due to data leakage.
AI.conclusion: Across tested protocols, event-ranking performance did not establish positive executable policy value. Every operational decision remains NO_TRADE.

title: Silent Failures in Multimodal Agentic Search:A Diagnostic Taxonomy and Cross-Judge Evaluation
summary: Multimodal agentic search systems increasingly rely on external tools to answer knowledge-intensive visual questions. However, existing evaluations mainly focus on final-answer accuracy and may miss failures in the search trajectory. In this work, we study such hidden reliability issues as silent failures. We introduce a six-category taxonomy covering modality shortcuts, phantom grounding, wrong-evidence-right-answer cases, over-retrieval laundering, cross-modal contradiction, and provenance hallucination. Based on this taxonomy, we build a trajectory-level diagnostic pipeline that evaluates both answer correctness and evidence-grounding quality under a unified ReAct-style scaffold. Experiments on MMSearch-Plus trajectories across four frontier multimodal models show that surface accuracy consistently overestimates true trajectory-level correctness. We further use cross-judge validation, blank-image stress tests, and tool ablations to show that silent failures are capability-dependent and often shift rather than disappear. Home-page: https://github.com/DingWu1021/silent-failures-multimodal-agentic-search

AI.tldr: This paper introduces the concept of "silent failures" in multimodal agentic search systems—hidden reliability issues that surface accuracy metrics fail to capture. The authors propose a six-category taxonomy of such failures, build a trajectory-level diagnostic pipeline, and demonstrate through experiments that surface accuracy consistently overestimates true trajectory-level correctness across frontier models.
AI.motivation: Existing evaluations of multimodal agentic search systems focus primarily on final-answer accuracy, which misses hidden failures occurring along the search trajectory (e.g., incorrect evidence use, hallucination, or reasoning flaws that still happen to yield correct answers).
AI.method: The authors define a six-category taxonomy of silent failures: modality shortcuts, phantom grounding, wrong-evidence-right-answer cases, over-retrieval laundering, cross-modal contradiction, and provenance hallucination. They build a trajectory-level diagnostic pipeline evaluating both answer correctness and evidence-grounding quality under a unified ReAct-style scaffold. They perform cross-judge validation, blank-image stress tests, and tool ablations on MMSearch-Plus trajectories across four frontier multimodal models.
AI.result: Surface accuracy consistently overestimates true trajectory-level correctness. Silent failures are capability-dependent and often shift rather than disappear when system components change.
AI.conclusion: Trajectory-level evaluation is necessary to reveal hidden reliability issues in multimodal agentic search; silent failures are persistent and should be explicitly diagnosed rather than masked by final-answer metrics.

title: LAVIFT: Latent-Action-Guided Vision Fine-Tuning for Surgical Interaction Recognition
summary: Understanding instrument-tissue interactions is essential for context-aware surgical AI and autonomous robotic surgery. Pretrained vision-language models (VLMs) and vision encoders offer an alternative to conventional interaction classifiers by transferring broad visual and semantic knowledge. However, adapting them to fine-grained surgical interactions remains challenging: (1) freezing the vision encoder depends entirely on pretrained representations that may retain noise and provide weak spatial localization, while (2) full fine-tuning can improve global semantic alignment without ensuring that the encoder learns meaningful features in the correct action region. We address these limitations by introducing LAViFiT, an end-to-end latent-action-guided framework for vision-language fine-tuning. An inverse dynamics model captures the visual changes induced by each action, while a forward world model drives the encoder to represent action-relevant regions. A patch-level SIG Regularizer further prevents local feature collapse without additional supervision, such as bounding boxes or pseudo-labels. Experiments across multiple encoders and datasets improve recognition and image-text alignment, while representation analyses show stronger grounding over the complete instrument-tissue interaction region and more spatially coherent features.

AI.tldr: LAViFiT is an end-to-end latent-action-guided framework for fine-tuning vision-language models on surgical instrument-tissue interactions. It uses inverse dynamics and forward world models to improve action-relevant feature learning, plus a SIG Regularizer to prevent local feature collapse, achieving better recognition, alignment, and spatial grounding without extra supervision.
AI.motivation: Pretrained VLMs and vision encoders struggle to adapt to fine-grained surgical interactions because (1) freezing the encoder retains noise and provides weak spatial localization, and (2) full fine-tuning improves global alignment but fails to ensure the encoder learns meaningful features in the correct action region.
AI.method: LAViFiT introduces an end-to-end latent-action-guided vision-language fine-tuning framework with three components: (1) an inverse dynamics model that captures visual changes induced by each action, (2) a forward world model that drives the encoder to focus on action-relevant regions, and (3) a patch-level SIG Regularizer that prevents local feature collapse without requiring bounding boxes or pseudo-labels.
AI.result: Experiments across multiple encoders and datasets show improved recognition and image-text alignment. Representation analyses demonstrate stronger grounding over the complete instrument-tissue interaction region and more spatially coherent features.
AI.conclusion: LAViFiT effectively addresses the limitations of both frozen and fully fine-tuned VLMs for fine-grained surgical interactions, achieving better spatial grounding and feature coherence without additional supervision.

title: Generating Bearing Vibration Signals at User-Specified Fault Probabilities Using PR-GAN and Counterfactual Methods
summary: In bearing vibration datasets, most samples receive predicted fault probabilities close to 0 or 1, while samples with intermediate (gray-zone) probabilities are rare. Such borderline samples are important because they reflect conditions in which maintenance decisions may require additional inspection or a conservative response and are useful for studying decision boundaries. To address this scarcity, this paper proposes and compares two approaches that generate vibration signals whose predicted fault probability matches a target probability of 0.25, 0.50, or 0.75. We use the average output of a heterogeneous ensemble classifier with different architectures and random initializations as a fixed, gradient-accessible probability oracle. The first, training-based approach, Probability-Regularized Generative Adversarial Network (PR-GAN), extends Wasserstein Generative Adversarial Network with Gradient Penalty (WGAN-GP) and edits a real signal through a residual generator while pushing the classifier output toward the target probability. The second is a training-free, per-sample Wachter-style counterfactual (CF) procedure that directly optimizes each input signal to reach the target probability while remaining close to the source signal. We evaluate both methods on the Case Western Reserve University (CWRU) and Paderborn bearing datasets using mean absolute target-probability error, time-domain total variation, and frequency-domain log power spectral density (log-PSD) differences. Across all settings, CF reaches the target with a mean absolute probability error of 0.005-0.008 and a within-tolerance success rate of 1.000 on retained samples, whereas PR-GAN's mean error is 0.046-0.059 with success rates between 0.501 and 0.680. CF therefore steers the probability more reliably and requires smaller average L1 changes, whereas PR-GAN has a lower reported runtime in most settings.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes and compares two methods (PR-GAN and counterfactual optimization) for generating bearing vibration signals with intermediate predicted fault probabilities (0.25, 0.50, 0.75) to address the scarcity of boundary samples. The counterfactual approach achieves near-perfect target probability matching (error 0.005-0.008, success rate 1.000) while PR-GAN shows higher error (0.046-0.059) and lower success rates (0.501-0.680).
AI.motivation: Bearing vibration datasets overwhelmingly produce predicted fault probabilities near 0 or 1, lacking intermediate ("gray-zone") samples that are crucial for decision boundary analysis and conservative maintenance decisions. This scarcity limits the study of model behavior at decision boundaries.
AI.method: Two approaches: (1) PR-GAN, a training-based method extending WGAN-GP with a probability regularization that edits real signals via a residual generator toward target probabilities (0.25/0.50/0.75); (2) a training-free Wachter-style counterfactual procedure that directly optimizes each input signal to reach the target probability while minimizing L1 distance from the source. Both use a fixed heterogeneous ensemble classifier as a gradient-accessible probability oracle.
AI.result: CF achieves mean absolute probability error of 0.005-0.008 with 1.000 success rate on retained samples; PR-GAN achieves mean error of 0.046-0.059 with success rates between 0.501-0.680. CF requires smaller average L1 changes and more reliable probability steering, while PR-GAN has lower runtime in most settings.
AI.conclusion: The counterfactual approach is more reliable and precise for generating gray-zone bearing vibration signals at target probabilities, though at higher computational cost. PR-GAN offers faster generation but with less accuracy and reliability.

title: Rewarding Better Thinking for LLM Preference Alignment
summary: LLM preference alignment aims to optimize models toward human preferences across diverse user instructions. Reinforcement learning has become a major post-training approach for this goal, but existing proxy rewards are often outcome-level, mainly evaluating the final response while providing limited guidance for the reasoning trajectory. This can make credit assignment coarse when multiple responses receive similar final scores, leaving trajectory-level preferences under-specified. To address this limitation, we propose Thinking Checklist Reward (TCR), a process-oriented reward for RL-based preference alignment. TCR converts preference pairs into sample-specific thinking checklists and uses them to evaluate whether the generated reasoning trace addresses the preference-implied considerations. To reduce overlap with outcome-level supervision, TCR further introduces an exponential moving average (EMA) residual formulation to isolate a complementary thinking surplus beyond what is predictable from the outcome reward. Experiments on five models from three model families show that TCR consistently improves alignment performance across diverse benchmarks, with ablations further validating the importance of EMA-based residual formulation and sample-specific checklist supervision.

AI.tldr: Proposes Thinking Checklist Reward (TCR), a process-oriented reward that uses sample-specific checklists and EMA residual formulation to improve credit assignment in RL-based preference alignment beyond outcome-level rewards.
AI.motivation: Existing proxy rewards in LLM preference alignment are outcome-level, evaluating only final responses while providing limited guidance for reasoning trajectories. This leads to coarse credit assignment when multiple responses receive similar final scores, leaving trajectory-level preferences under-specified.
AI.method: TCR converts preference pairs into sample-specific thinking checklists to evaluate reasoning traces against preference-implied considerations, and uses an exponential moving average (EMA) residual formulation to isolate complementary thinking surplus beyond what outcome rewards predict.
AI.result: Experiments on five models from three model families show TCR consistently improves alignment performance across diverse benchmarks. Ablations validate the importance of EMA-based residual formulation and sample-specific checklist supervision.
AI.conclusion: Process-oriented, checklist-based rewards with EMA residuals effectively address trajectory-level preference alignment limitations, offering a complementary signal beyond outcome-level supervision.

title: OSVE: One Step Video Editing with One Step Diffusion Models
summary: Text-guided video editing with diffusion models is impractically slow, hindered by costly multi-step sampling and inversion. We present OSVE, the first framework to successfully adapt one-step Text-to-Image (T2I) models for high-quality video editing, addressing the core challenges of inversion, editability, and temporal consistency. To bypass slow iterative inversion, we train a learnable encoder that predicts the initial noise for each frame in a single forward pass. This encoder is trained with a novel Structure-Aware Editing (SAE) loss on a curated dataset of structurally-aligned image pairs, teaching it to preserve the source video's geometry during edits. For temporal coherence, we introduce Unified-Frame Editing (UFE), a technique that concatenates frame latents to facilitate cross-frame attention in a single generation step. Furthermore, for long videos, a sliding-window strategy with an anchor frame maintains global consistency. Our extensive experiments demonstrate that OSVE achieves editing quality comparable or superior to state-of-the-art multi-step methods, while operating approximately 155--171 times faster. This breakthrough paves the way for practical, real-time video editing applications. Code is available at https://github.com/KU-VGI/OSVE.

AI.tldr: OSVE is a one-step video editing framework that adapts one-step T2I diffusion models for fast, high-quality video editing, achieving 155-171x speedup over multi-step methods by using a learnable encoder for single-pass noise prediction (with Structure-Aware Editing loss) and Unified-Frame Editing for temporal consistency.
AI.motivation: Text-guided video editing with diffusion models is impractically slow due to costly multi-step sampling and inversion. The goal is to enable real-time, practical video editing by bypassing these bottlenecks.
AI.method: (1) A learnable encoder that predicts initial noise for each frame in a single forward pass (trained with Structure-Aware Editing loss on structurally-aligned image pairs). (2) Unified-Frame Editing (UFE) that concatenates frame latents for cross-frame attention in a single step. (3) A sliding-window strategy with an anchor frame for long video global consistency.
AI.result: OSVE achieves editing quality comparable or superior to state-of-the-art multi-step methods while operating approximately 155-171 times faster.
AI.conclusion: OSVE is the first framework to successfully adapt one-step T2I models for high-quality video editing, paving the way for practical, real-time video editing applications.

title: MoA-Structured Decode Attention DNF Derivation, KV-Cache Accumulation, GQA/MQA, and OpenACC Kernel
summary: We derive four memory-optimal inference artifacts for transformer attention using the Mathematics of Arrays (MoA), each following directly from the forward-pass Denotational Normal Form (DNF) of with the query-row index fixed to the current decode step. The artifacts are: (1)~a single-query decode DNF in which the $ψ$-reduction eliminates the $K^\top$ buffer algebraically, achieving $(d_k + nd_k+ nd_v+ d_v)\times4\,{B}$ Dynamic Random Access Memory (DRAM) traffic result numerically verified to $\|{err}\|_\leq2\times10^{-7}$; (2)~a C/OpenACC Graphics Processing Unit (GPU) kernel with Operational Normal Form (ONF) stride arithmetic and hardware-coalesced memory access, verified to $\|\mathrm{err}\|_\infty=0$ (exact IEEE-754 floating-point arithmetic); (3)~a multi-step KV-cache with $O(d_k+d_v)$ per-step append via MoA concatenation $\#$; and (4)~Grouped-Query Attention (GQA) and Multi-Query Attention (MQA) derived via $ψ$-selection, achieving a proven $\frac {h_q} { h_{kv} }$ reduction in KV traffic. All programs are verified against PyTorch scaled_dot_product_attention.

AI.tldr: Four memory-optimal inference artifacts for transformer attention derived via Mathematics of Arrays (MoA), including a single-query decode DNF, a C/OpenACC GPU kernel, a multi-step KV-cache, and GQA/MQA variants, all verified against PyTorch.
AI.motivation: To derive memory-optimal inference artifacts for transformer attention by eliminating redundant buffers (e.g., K^T) and reducing DRAM traffic through algebraic and array-theoretic methods.
AI.method: Using Mathematics of Arrays (MoA) to derive Denotational Normal Forms (DNF) and Operational Normal Forms (ONF) for attention, with ψ-reduction, MoA concatenation, and ψ-selection to produce memory-optimal artifacts.
AI.result: Achieved (1) (d_k + n d_k + n d_v + d_v) × 4B DRAM traffic with error ≤ 2e-7; (2) exact IEEE-754 GPU kernel; (3) O(d_k+d_v) per-step KV-cache append; (4) h_q/h_kv reduction in KV traffic for GQA/MQA.
AI.conclusion: The MoA framework enables provably memory-optimal attention inference artifacts with verified numerical accuracy.

title: Know Your Agent: Reconnaissance-Driven Pentesting of AI Agents
summary: Traditional pentesting uses reconnaissance at each step to uncover unseen weaknesses, build stronger attacks, and advance the objective; we argue that AI agents require the same treatment. We formalize agent reconnaissance by modeling the process and identifying the knowledge assets it seeks to extract: what they are, how they are used, and which agent weaknesses they exploit to give adversaries leverage in indirect prompt injection attacks. We instantiate these insights in Know Your Agent (KYA), a framework that automates black-box, reconnaissance-driven pentesting by probing agents, building target profiles, and using those profiles to craft stronger attacks. We evaluate KYA on agent-security benchmarks and a real-world coding agent, and release KYA, its benchmarks, and baseline implementations for reproducibility.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces KYA, a framework that performs automated reconnaissance-driven pentesting on AI agents to identify knowledge assets and exploit weaknesses through indirect prompt injection attacks.
AI.motivation: Traditional pentesting relies on reconnaissance at each step to uncover weaknesses and build stronger attacks, but AI agents lack such systematic reconnaissance. The authors argue that AI agents require the same treatment to expose vulnerabilities.
AI.method: The authors formalize agent reconnaissance by modeling the process and identifying knowledge assets (what they are, how used, which weaknesses exploited). They implement this in KYA, a framework that automates black-box reconnaissance-driven pentesting by probing agents, building target profiles, and using these profiles to craft stronger indirect prompt injection attacks.
AI.result: KYA was evaluated on agent-security benchmarks and a real-world coding agent. The framework and associated benchmarks and baseline implementations are released for reproducibility.
AI.conclusion: Applying reconnaissance-driven pentesting to AI agents, as demonstrated by KYA, can systematically uncover agent weaknesses and enable stronger adversarial attacks, mirroring traditional cybersecurity practices.

title: StrokeSeg2: Stroke Lesion Segmentation in Clinical Research Workflows
summary: Deep learning frameworks like nnU-Net achieve state-of-theart brain lesion segmentation performance but remain difficult to deploy in clinical research environments due to, among other reasons, software dependencies and computational requirements. We introduce StrokeSeg2, a lightweight, modular, cross-platform C++/Qt framework designed to adapt resource-intensive 3D stroke segmentation pipelines into portable and reproducible applications. To improve compatibility with standard clinical workstations, we investigate the combined effect of architectural compression through knowledge distillation and inference optimisation using ONNX Runtime with Float16 quantisation. Across heterogeneous hardware configurations (CPU, integrated GPU, and dedicated GPU) architectural distillation emerged as the primary contributor to efficiency gains, contributing to over 90% reduction in energy consumption and an average 84% reduction in inference time. Specifically, we identify a 0.84M-parameter student model as the most favourable trade-off, reducing the original 102.3M-parameter teacher architecture to a 2.1 MB disk footprint while preserving robust lesion localisation and competitive segmentation performance. This small footprint supports the development of a self-contained installer for clinical workstation targets. Finally, StrokeSeg2 packages these optimisations into standalone installers for Windows, macOS, and Linux. By providing both graphical and commandline interfaces without Docker or external environment dependencies, StrokeSeg2 facilitates deployment of high-performance segmentation workflows for routine clinical research pipelines.

AI.tldr: StrokeSeg2 is a lightweight, cross-platform C++/Qt framework that compresses 3D stroke segmentation models (from 102.3M to 0.84M parameters) via knowledge distillation and ONNX Runtime Float16 quantization, achieving >90% energy reduction and 84% faster inference while maintaining competitive segmentation performance, packaged as standalone installers for Windows/macOS/Linux without Docker dependencies.
AI.motivation: Deep learning frameworks like nnU-Net achieve state-of-the-art brain lesion segmentation but are difficult to deploy in clinical research environments due to software dependencies and high computational requirements.
AI.method: The paper introduces StrokeSeg2, a modular C++/Qt framework. It compresses a 102.3M-parameter teacher model via knowledge distillation to a 0.84M-parameter student model (2.1 MB disk footprint), combined with ONNX Runtime Float16 quantization for inference optimization, targeting heterogeneous hardware (CPU, iGPU, dGPU).
AI.result: Architectural distillation contributed to >90% reduction in energy consumption and average 84% reduction in inference time. The 0.84M-parameter student model preserved robust lesion localization with competitive segmentation performance. Self-contained installers were built for Windows, macOS, and Linux.
AI.conclusion: StrokeSeg2 facilitates deployment of high-performance segmentation workflows for routine clinical research pipelines by providing graphical and command-line interfaces without Docker or external environment dependencies.

title: Total Variation Distance Estimation in Autoregressive Models
comment: 39 pages, 11 figures, code is available at https://github.com/XunZhiyang/llm-tv-estimation
summary: Modern LLM deployments use a number of implementation choices and inference optimizations (e.g., batching, custom kernels, and quantization) on top of fixed weights, so two engines serving "the same model" can produce meaningfully different distributions. We study the problem of estimating the total variation (TV) distance between two length-$n$ autoregressive distributions to additive error $\varepsilon$, under three access models. (1) Under sample access, we use $\widetilde{O}(n^2 K/\varepsilon^2)$ queries, where $K$ is the maximum support of the next-token distribution. This improves upon the $\widetilde{O}(n^3 m/\varepsilon^5)$-query estimator of Meel et al. (2025), where $m \geq K$ is the total size of the token alphabet. (2) Under logit access, we use $O(n/\varepsilon^2)$ queries, and this is tight. (3) Under noisy logit access, we smoothly interpolate between the above two guarantees: if probability values are given to relative error $σ$, we use $\widetilde{O}((n+n^2σ^2)/\varepsilon^2)$ queries. We complement our theoretical results with an empirical evaluation of our algorithms, for example measuring the distance between SGLang and vLLM serving identical weights. Our experiments highlight the robustness and practicality of estimating the total variation distance, which remains estimable where the KL divergence is infinite. Our code is available at https://github.com/XunZhiyang/llm-tv-estimation.

AI.tldr: The paper studies estimating total variation (TV) distance between two autoregressive LLM distributions under three access models (sample, logit, noisy logit), providing query-efficient algorithms with improved theoretical guarantees and empirical validation on real inference engines (SGLang vs. vLLM).
AI.motivation: LLM deployments with different inference optimizations (batching, custom kernels, quantization) can produce meaningfully different output distributions from the same fixed weights, yet there is no rigorous way to quantify such discrepancies efficiently. Existing TV estimation methods are sample-inefficient or impractical.
