AI.method: The authors propose three algorithms for TV distance estimation under different access models: (1) sample access with $\widetilde{O}(n^2 K/\varepsilon^2)$ queries improving prior work; (2) logit access with $O(n/\varepsilon^2)$ queries (proven tight); (3) noisy logit access with $\widetilde{O}((n+n^2\sigma^2)/\varepsilon^2)$ queries interpolating between the two. Algorithms are theoretically analyzed and empirically evaluated.
AI.result: Improved query complexity for sample-access TV estimation. Tight lower bound for logit-access estimation. Smooth interpolation under noisy logit access. Empirical experiments demonstrate practical TV estimation between SGLang and vLLM serving identical weights, showing robustness where KL divergence is infinite.
AI.conclusion: TV distance is a practical and robust metric for comparing LLM distributions under implementation variations, with efficient estimation algorithms that work even when KL divergence fails.

title: DocOps: A Verifiable Benchmark for Autonomous Agents in Complex Document Operations
summary: As autonomous agents rapidly evolve, their ability to reliably manipulate ubiquitous digital documents has become critical for enabling general-purpose AI assistants and automating complex workspace workflows. In this paper, we introduce DocOps, a deterministically verifiable evaluation framework underpinned by a hierarchical taxonomy that deconstructs document operations inspired by real-world practices into atomic dimensions and escalating workflow complexities. Based on DocOps, we systematically evaluate representative closed- and open-source models across various agentic harnesses, revealing that even the most advanced frontier configurations still exhibit profound limitations when handling highly coupled, long-range tasks. Furthermore, a fine-grained analysis of existing agents' manipulation behaviors uncovers 3 key failure modes: long-term state tracking collapse, shallow semantic verification, and destructive editing of structural metadata. Ultimately, our work exposes the capability boundaries of agents in maintaining global document consistency, shedding light on the future design of robust, non-destructive agents for complex digital ecosystems.

AI.tldr: DocOps is a deterministically verifiable evaluation framework for assessing AI agents' ability to manipulate digital documents. It uses a hierarchical taxonomy to decompose document operations into atomic dimensions and escalating complexities. Evaluations of closed- and open-source models reveal significant limitations in handling coupled, long-range tasks, with three key failure modes: long-term state tracking collapse, shallow semantic verification, and destructive editing of structural metadata.
AI.motivation: As autonomous agents evolve, their ability to reliably manipulate ubiquitous digital documents is critical for enabling general-purpose AI assistants and automating complex workspace workflows, yet current capabilities are insufficiently evaluated.
AI.method: The authors introduce DocOps, a deterministically verifiable evaluation framework using a hierarchical taxonomy that deconstructs document operations into atomic dimensions and escalating workflow complexities. They evaluate representative closed- and open-source models across various agentic harnesses.
AI.result: Even the most advanced frontier configurations exhibit profound limitations in handling highly coupled, long-range tasks. Fine-grained analysis reveals three key failure modes: long-term state tracking collapse, shallow semantic verification, and destructive editing of structural metadata.
AI.conclusion: The work exposes capability boundaries of agents in maintaining global document consistency, shedding light on future design of robust, non-destructive agents for complex digital ecosystems.

title: MV-Bench: Benchmarking Multimodal Large Language Models for Coordinated Multi-View Interface Construction
summary: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) are increasingly expected to automate visualization development by generating code directly from visual designs. However, existing evaluations mainly focus on single-chart generation and overlook coordinated multi-view interface construction, which requires joint reasoning about data semantics, view coordination, and interaction logic. Consequently, MLLM capabilities in this setting remain underexplored, and the field lacks a dedicated benchmark for systematic assessment. We introduce MV-Bench, a benchmark for evaluating MLLMs on coordinated multi-view interface construction. Instead of relying on incomplete or inconsistent open-source implementations, we use Tableau workbook files as ground truth because they explicitly encode data bindings, visual mappings, and interactions. We develop a multi-stage pipeline that converts these specifications into executable web interfaces through structured intermediate representations. The benchmark contains 92 base interfaces and 1,048 verified instances created by recombining chart types, datasets, and interaction patterns. Each instance includes executable code, a rendered interface, a dataset, and interaction annotations. We evaluate five state-of-the-art MLLMs in a single-pass setting using metrics for visual fidelity, data binding correctness, and interaction completeness. The strongest model achieves 75.45 percent accuracy in visual layout reproduction, but only 21.71 percent in data binding and 11.68 percent in interaction completeness. These results show that current MLLMs can reproduce visual appearance but remain limited in generating the data semantics and interactive logic required by coordinated multi-view interfaces. Iterative refinement improves code executability but does not substantially reduce the gap in data binding and interaction generation.

AI.tldr: MV-Bench is a benchmark for evaluating MLLMs on generating coordinated multi-view interfaces from visual designs. Using Tableau workbooks as ground truth, it assesses five MLLMs on 1,048 instances. The best model achieves 75.45% in visual layout reproduction but only 21.71% in data binding and 11.68% in interaction completeness, revealing current MLLMs' limitations in semantic and interactive reasoning.
AI.motivation: Existing evaluations of MLLMs for visualization focus on single-chart generation and overlook coordinated multi-view interfaces requiring joint reasoning about data semantics, view coordination, and interaction logic. There is no dedicated benchmark for systematic assessment in this setting.
AI.method: The authors use Tableau workbook files (encoding data bindings, visual mappings, and interactions) as ground truth. A multi-stage pipeline converts these specifications into executable web interfaces via structured intermediate representations. The benchmark includes 92 base interfaces and 1,048 verified instances created by recombining chart types, datasets, and interaction patterns, each with executable code, rendered interface, dataset, and interaction annotations.
AI.result: Five state-of-the-art MLLMs were evaluated in a single-pass setting. The strongest model achieved 75.45% in visual layout reproduction, 21.71% in data binding correctness, and 11.68% in interaction completeness. Iterative refinement improved code executability but did not substantially reduce the gap in data binding and interaction generation.
AI.conclusion: Current MLLMs can reproduce visual appearance relatively well but remain severely limited in generating the data semantics and interactive logic required by coordinated multi-view interfaces, highlighting a significant gap in their capabilities for automated visualization development.

title: Do Sheaf Neural Networks Use Holonomy? A Measure--Intervene--Control Study
summary: Geometric architectures are often justified by internal mechanisms such as rotations, yet task performance alone cannot show whether those mechanisms drive predictions. Using sheaf neural networks (SNNs) as a testbed, we introduce the first basis-independent measurement of trained triangle-loop products, separating rotation, stalk-space area, and orientation. In a custom high-homophily GraphUniverse regime, Neural Sheaf Propagation (NSP) increases the triangle-weighted mean two-dimensional SO(2) loop rotation from 0.010 to 0.388 radians for triangle counting, while the community-detection comparison ends at 0.029 radians. Across the training-set-size experiment, replacing all learned SO(2) transports with identities sharply increases test error, establishing post-training sensitivity to the complete learned connection. However, a graph-summary ridge predictor is more accurate, diagonal maps also improve, and fixed-degree graphs develop increasing rotation without outperforming the training-mean predictor. This measure-intervene-control study separates geometric change, connection sensitivity, and evidence for triangle-specific computation.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces the first basis-independent measurement of learned geometric properties (rotations) in sheaf neural networks, showing that while models develop significant rotation for triangle-counting tasks, careful analysis reveals that this geometric change does not necessarily drive predictive performance, raising questions about whether internal geometric mechanisms are causally responsible for task performance.
AI.motivation: Geometric architectures (e.g., sheaf neural networks) are often justified by appealing to internal geometric mechanisms like rotations, but task performance alone cannot reveal whether these mechanisms actually drive predictions.
AI.method: Using sheaf neural networks (SNNs) as a testbed, the authors introduce the first basis-independent measurement of trained triangle-loop products, separating rotation, stalk-space area, and orientation. They conduct a measure-intervene-control study: measuring geometric properties, intervening by replacing learned transports with identities, and controlling via baselines like ridge predictors and training-mean predictors.
AI.result: Neural Sheaf Propagation (NSP) increases triangle-weighted mean 2D SO(2) loop rotation from 0.010 to 0.388 radians for triangle counting (vs. 0.029 for community detection). Replacing learned SO(2) transports with identities sharply increases test error. However, a graph-summary ridge predictor is more accurate, diagonal maps also improve performance, and fixed-degree graphs develop increasing rotation without outperforming the training-mean predictor.
AI.conclusion: The study separates geometric change, connection sensitivity, and evidence for triangle-specific computation, finding that while learned geometric structures (rotations) emerge and the model is sensitive to them, they are not necessarily the causal drivers of predictive performance—simpler explanations (ridge predictors, diagonal maps) can match or exceed performance.

title: JANUS: Foreseeing Latent Risk for Long-Horizon Agent Safety
summary: Agent safety is moving from content moderation toward preventing operational failures before tool-using agents act. We propose Janus, a foresight-oriented framework for long-horizon agent safety that trains guards to anticipate delayed risks from partial trajectories. Janus synthesizes diverse agent trajectories via multi-agent simulation and learns a shared policy with two coupled tasks: an anticipation task that forecasts safety-relevant futures and an adjudication task that decides safety from both the observed prefix and anticipated future. The two tasks are jointly optimized with CoAA-RL, which rewards forecasts by their utility for downstream safety judgment. The resulting guard model, Vanguard, blocks unsafe actions before execution. Across four agent-safety benchmarks, Vanguard improves average protection by 15.9 percentage points over baseline guards while increasing benign task completion by 5.1 percentage points.

AI.tldr: Janus is a foresight-oriented framework that trains guard models (Vanguard) to anticipate delayed risks from partial agent trajectories using multi-agent simulation and CoAA-RL, improving agent safety by 15.9 pp while increasing benign task completion by 5.1 pp.
AI.motivation: Agent safety is shifting from reactive content moderation to proactive prevention of operational failures before tool-using agents act, motivating a foresight-oriented approach for long-horizon safety.
AI.method: Janus synthesizes diverse agent trajectories via multi-agent simulation, learns a shared policy with two coupled tasks (anticipation forecasting safety-relevant futures, adjudication deciding safety from observed prefix and anticipated future), and jointly optimizes them using CoAA-RL which rewards forecasts by their utility for downstream safety judgment.
AI.result: Across four agent-safety benchmarks, Vanguard improves average protection by 15.9 percentage points over baseline guards and increases benign task completion by 5.1 percentage points.
AI.conclusion: The foresight-oriented approach of anticipating delayed risks before execution outperforms traditional guard methods, demonstrating that joint optimization of anticipation and adjudication improves both safety and task completion.

title: LoRFT: Benchmarking Long-Range Vehicle Trajectory Reconstruction from Fixed Highway Cameras
comment: 17 pages, 5 figures. Code and processed annotations: https://github.com/YvfanZhu/LoRFT
summary: Long-range vehicle trajectories provide important spatio-temporal evidence for traffic safety analysis, autonomous driving evaluation, and data-driven traffic management, yet continuously recovering them from fixed highway cameras remains difficult. As vehicles recede into distant road regions, perspective compression and scale decay often fragment or prematurely terminate automatic tracklets, even when their continuation remains identifiable from motion consistency across neighboring frames. We formulate this problem as recovering the far-range continuation of a vehicle trajectory from a reliable near-field tracklet. We introduce LoRFT, to our knowledge the first open benchmark dedicated to long-range vehicle trajectory reconstruction from fixed highway cameras. LoRFT comprises 22 expressway surveillance scenes, 366,109 video frames, 6,601 manually verified trajectories, 2,694,889 bounding boxes, road-geometry annotations, scene-level splits, and evaluation scripts. We further propose Map-RSTNet, a map-aware residual sequence-to-sequence model that reconstructs distant trajectories in a road-geometry-aligned state space and dynamically refreshes local road geometry during decoding. On LoRFT, Map-RSTNet reduces ADE, FDE, and 5-second RMSE by 11.0%, 15.4%, and 10.5%, respectively, relative to the strongest baseline. These results demonstrate that road-geometry-aware reconstruction can extend usable trajectory records from existing fixed-camera infrastructure. LoRFT provides a reproducible testbed for long-range vehicle trajectory reconstruction.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces LoRFT, the first benchmark for long-range vehicle trajectory reconstruction from fixed highway cameras, and proposes Map-RSTNet, a map-aware model that reduces trajectory error by over 10% compared to baselines.
AI.motivation: Long-range vehicle trajectories are crucial for traffic safety, autonomous driving, and traffic management, but perspective compression and scale decay in fixed highway cameras cause tracklets to fragment or terminate prematurely, even when motion consistency across frames could still support continuation.
AI.method: The authors propose Map-RSTNet, a map-aware residual sequence-to-sequence model that reconstructs distant trajectories in a road-geometry-aligned state space and dynamically refreshes local road geometry during decoding. They also introduce LoRFT, a benchmark with 22 expressway scenes, 366K frames, 6,601 trajectories, and 2.7M bounding boxes.
AI.result: On LoRFT, Map-RSTNet reduces ADE by 11.0%, FDE by 15.4%, and 5-second RMSE by 10.5% relative to the strongest baseline.
AI.conclusion: Road-geometry-aware reconstruction can extend usable trajectory records from existing fixed-camera infrastructure. LoRFT provides a reproducible testbed for this task.

title: Geospatial Diffusion-based Evolution Synthesis (GeoDES) for Storm-Centered Weather Augmentation
summary: While machine learning-based weather models hold significant promise, they struggle to predict the detailed structure of large-scale weather systems such as cyclonic storms. Regional models are constrained by limited historical records within fixed geographic boundaries, while global models are computationally expensive and often operate at resolutions too coarse to capture fine-grained storm dynamics. To bridge this gap, we introduce the Geospatial Diffusion-based Evolution Synthesis (GeoDES) model, a custom image-to-video diffusion model. By focusing generation strictly on the evolving storm structure, GeoDES synthesizes physically consistent, high-fidelity weather events suitable for stress-testing forecast models and expanding meteorological datasets. Evaluations demonstrate that GeoDES outperforms prior methods on key metrics, achieving $52\%$ lower Peak Vorticity Error and $8\%$ higher Anomaly Correlation Coefficient than the next strongest methods on the North Atlantic test set.

AI.tldr: GeoDES is an image-to-video diffusion model that generates physically consistent, high-fidelity cyclone evolutions, outperforming prior methods with 52% lower Peak Vorticity Error and 8% higher Anomaly Correlation Coefficient.
AI.motivation: ML weather models struggle with detailed storm structures; regional models are limited by short historical records and fixed boundaries, while global models are computationally expensive and too coarse for fine-grained storm dynamics.
AI.method: GeoDES is a custom image-to-video diffusion model that focuses generation on evolving storm structure, synthesizing physically consistent weather events for stress-testing forecast models and dataset expansion.
AI.result: Outperforms prior methods: 52% lower Peak Vorticity Error and 8% higher Anomaly Correlation Coefficient on the North Atlantic test set.
AI.conclusion: GeoDES effectively bridges the gap between regional and global models, providing high-fidelity storm evolution synthesis for meteorological applications.

title: Long-Term Sequential Decision Making under Risk
comment: Accpeted in Forty-Second Annual Conference on Uncertainty in Artificial Intelligence (UAI 2026)
summary: We study finite-horizon MDP planning under \emph{root-based} (resolute) risk objectives that apply a rank-dependent functional to the distribution of total returns. Such objectives are non-linear in the return distribution and generally break Bellman optimality, so direct optimization by scenario-tree enumeration is intractable. We propose \textbf{ERQDP}, an enumeration-free and sampling-free method that solves a rank--quantile surrogate via exact DP (Dynamic Programming), evaluates candidate policies exactly by DP over return Probability Mass Functions (PMFs) on a discretized return grid (with an explicit rounding bound), and refines the surrogate in an anytime loop that reports an explicit upper--lower gap (certificate) for the target objective up to discretization budgets. Across tested benchmarks, ERQDP returns certified solutions or explicit residual gaps, enables fast risk-parameter sweeps with substantial runtime gains, and supports both risk-averse and risk-seeking behaviors.

AI.tldr: ERQDP is an enumeration-free, sampling-free method for finite-horizon MDP planning under rank-dependent (resolute) risk objectives. It solves a rank-quantile surrogate via exact DP, evaluates policies via DP over return PMFs on a discretized grid, and iteratively refines the surrogate with an explicit optimality gap certificate.
AI.motivation: Finite-horizon MDP planning under root-based (resolute) risk objectives with rank-dependent functionals is challenging because the objectives are non-linear in the return distribution and break Bellman optimality, making direct optimization via scenario-tree enumeration intractable.
AI.method: ERQDP: (1) solves a rank-quantile surrogate via exact Dynamic Programming, (2) evaluates candidate policies exactly by DP over return Probability Mass Functions on a discretized return grid (with an explicit rounding bound), and (3) refines the surrogate in an anytime loop that reports an explicit upper-lower gap (certificate) for the target objective up to discretization budgets.
AI.result: Across benchmarks, ERQDP returns certified solutions or explicit residual gaps, enables fast risk-parameter sweeps with substantial runtime gains, and supports both risk-averse and risk-seeking behaviors.
AI.conclusion: ERQDP provides a tractable, certified approach to MDP planning under rank-dependent risk objectives, offering explicit optimality gaps and supporting flexible risk preferences without enumeration or sampling.

title: WearWow: Native 2K Multi-Garment Virtual Try-On via Adaptive Token Packing and Preference Alignment
summary: Synthesizing native 2K multi-garment virtual try-on is a formidable frontier in digital fashion, critically bottlenecked by two fundamental limitations: the O(N^2) memory explosion induced by 2k conditions, and the spectral bias of diffusion models that over-smooths high-frequency fabric details. We present WearWow, an end-to-end, mask-free generative framework that pioneers ultra-high-resolution multi-garment synthesis. To mitigate the memory explosion , we propose Adaptive 2D Token Packing (ATP). ATP leverages inherent garment sparsity to algorithmically pack heterogeneous items onto a unified 2D canvas and prune uninformative background tokens, minimizing the effective sequence length and subsequent memory overhead while rigorously preserving 2D spatial priors. To rectify texture degradation, we introduce the Multi-dimensional Try-on Reward (MTR) system. MTR synergizes a Semantic Guidance Reward to explicitly drive tactile restoration with a Cloth Distribution Reward to implicitly anchor the physical distribution, a joint formulation that effectively mitigates the severe reward hacking. Furthermore, we curate WearWow-2K, an extreme-quality dataset comprising native 2K triplets, providing physically correct spatial interactions that naturally empower the model's mask-free generation. Extensive experiments demonstrate that WearWow establishes a new state-of-the-art, exceeding existing commercial baselines in native 2K multi-garment synthesis.

AI.tldr: WearWow is an end-to-end, mask-free generative framework for native 2K multi-garment virtual try-on that solves memory explosion via Adaptive 2D Token Packing (ATP) and texture degradation via Multi-dimensional Try-on Reward (MTR), achieving state-of-the-art results on the curated WearWow-2K dataset.
AI.motivation: Existing multi-garment virtual try-on at 2K resolution suffers from two critical bottlenecks: (1) O(N²) memory explosion caused by processing 2K conditions, and (2) spectral bias in diffusion models that over-smooths high-frequency fabric details, preventing realistic ultra-high-resolution synthesis.
AI.method: WearWow proposes Adaptive 2D Token Packing (ATP) to exploit garment sparsity by packing heterogeneous items onto a unified 2D canvas and pruning background tokens, reducing sequence length and memory while preserving 2D spatial priors. It also introduces a Multi-dimensional Try-on Reward (MTR) system combining a Semantic Guidance Reward for tactile restoration and a Cloth Distribution Reward to anchor physical distribution, mitigating reward hacking. A new dataset WearWow-2K with native 2K triplets enables mask-free generation.
AI.result: Extensive experiments show WearWow establishes a new state-of-the-art, outperforming existing commercial baselines in native 2K multi-garment virtual try-on synthesis.
AI.conclusion: WearWow effectively addresses the memory and texture degradation bottlenecks in ultra-high-resolution multi-garment synthesis through adaptive token packing and multi-dimensional reward learning, validated by superior performance over commercial baselines.

title: SynPre-FL: Synthetic data-driven pretraining integrated Federated Learning training framework
summary: Federated learning (FL) offers a promising approach to privacy-preserving clinical risk prediction, but its deployment remains limited by restricted data sharing, client heterogeneity, class imbalance, and the lack of realistic tabular electronic health record (EHR) benchmarks. Synthetic data generation may alleviate data scarcity, yet its integration with federated optimisation has received limited systematic study. We propose SynPre-FL, a unified framework combining high-fidelity synthetic EHR generation with synthetic-pretrained FL for robust prediction under non-IID conditions. A latent autoencoder-diffusion model generates privacy-preserving synthetic cohorts, which are used to warm-start federated training. This pretraining is followed by heterogeneity-aware optimisation using class-balanced local objectives, proximal regularisation, and adaptive server aggregation. Post-hoc calibration and federated-safe explainability support reliable and interpretable risk estimates. Experiments show that the synthetic generator preserves univariate, bivariate, and multivariate structure while protecting against membership-inference and reconstruction attacks. The generated data achieve strong downstream utility under TSTR, TRTS, and model-based evaluations. Across federated settings with 5, 10, and 15 heterogeneous clients, SynPre-FL consistently improves robustness and scalability over baseline methods, especially under severe non-IID fragmentation. Calibration improves probability reliability, while SHAP analysis produces stable and clinically coherent feature attributions across federation sizes. SynPre-FL therefore provides a practical and reproducible framework for combining synthetic data with FL to enable privacy-aware, interpretable, and robust clinical prediction from distributed tabular EHR data.

AI.tldr: SynPre-FL is a unified framework combining high-fidelity synthetic EHR generation (via latent autoencoder-diffusion model) with synthetic-pretrained federated learning to enable privacy-preserving, robust, and interpretable clinical risk prediction under non-IID conditions across distributed tabular EHR data.
AI.motivation: Federated learning for clinical risk prediction is limited by data sharing restrictions, client heterogeneity, class imbalance, and the lack of realistic tabular EHR benchmarks. Synthetic data may help but its systematic integration with federated optimization remains understudied.
AI.method: SynPre-FL combines (1) a latent autoencoder-diffusion model for high-fidelity synthetic EHR generation with privacy guarantees, (2) synthetic pretraining to warm-start federated learning, and (3) heterogeneity-aware federated optimization using class-balanced local objectives, proximal regularization, and adaptive server aggregation, plus post-hoc calibration and federated-safe SHAP explainability.
AI.result: The synthetic generator preserves univariate, bivariate, and multivariate data structure while resisting membership-inference and reconstruction attacks. It achieves strong downstream utility under TSTR, TRTS, and model-based evaluations. Across federated settings with 5, 10, 15 heterogeneous clients, SynPre-FL consistently outperforms baselines, especially under severe non-IID fragmentation, with improved calibration and stable, clinically coherent SHAP attributions.
AI.conclusion: SynPre-FL provides a practical and reproducible framework for combining synthetic data with FL to enable privacy-aware, interpretable, and robust clinical prediction from distributed tabular EHR data.

title: MOF-Sleuth: Tool-Grounded Reward Alignment for Explainable Fine-Grained MOF CIF Auditing
summary: Large metal-organic framework (MOF) databases support simulation, screening, and machine learning through crystallographic information files (CIFs). Subtle chemical and structural errors in these inputs can compromise downstream results and hinder manual inspection. LLM advances in computational chemistry offer paths beyond predictive screening toward fine-grained diagnosis with evidence-grounded explanations. However, two challenges remain: (i) limited fine-grained attribution: MOF-specific validators and machine-learning models scale detection but provide fixed checks, readiness scores, or coarse labels rather than evidence-grounded explanations; and (ii) unreliable CIF reasoning: direct LLM auditing is costly and unreliable because chemical evidence is implicit across atom-site records and requires geometric, connectivity, occupancy, and charge calculations. Both stem from weak coupling between chemical evidence and language-model explanation. We introduce MOF-Sleuth, a reinforcement-guided CIF auditing agent with two modules: a deterministic Forensic Lab and a Sleuth reasoning engine. The Lab derives composition, geometry, connectivity, occupancy, coordination, and charge evidence, and Sleuth uses this evidence to produce an evidence-grounded explanation, error types, and a binary decision. Reward-guided reinforcement learning (RL) turns tool measurements into chemical explanation-level supervision, rewarding not only the final answer but also cited chemical evidence and evidence-supported diagnoses. We introduce Chemically Grounded Diagnosis (Chem-GD), a metric that assesses whether a correct diagnosis is explained by factual, relevant CIF-derived evidence. Across four benchmarks, MOF-Sleuth establishes state-of-the-art performance among LLM-based approaches and MOF-specific machine-learning methods, demonstrating gains in detection, attribution, and grounded explanation quality.

AI.tldr: MOF-Sleuth is a reinforcement-guided CIF auditing agent that uses a Forensic Lab to extract chemical evidence and a Sleuth reasoning engine to produce evidence-grounded explanations, error types, and binary decisions for detecting structural/chemical errors in MOF databases, achieving state-of-the-art performance across four benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Large MOF databases suffer from subtle chemical and structural errors in CIFs that compromise downstream simulations and machine learning. Existing methods (validators, ML models) scale detection but lack fine-grained, evidence-grounded explanations, while direct LLM auditing is costly and unreliable due to implicit chemical evidence across atom-site records.
AI.method: MOF-Sleuth consists of two modules: (i) a deterministic Forensic Lab that computes composition, geometry, connectivity, occupancy, coordination, and charge evidence from CIFs; and (ii) a Sleuth reasoning engine that uses this evidence to generate evidence-grounded explanations, error types, and binary decisions. Reward-guided reinforcement learning (RL) converts tool measurements into chemical explanation-level supervision, rewarding correct final answers, cited chemical evidence, and evidence-supported diagnoses.
AI.result: MOF-Sleuth achieves state-of-the-art performance among LLM-based approaches and MOF-specific machine-learning methods across four benchmarks, demonstrating gains in detection accuracy, attribution quality, and grounded explanation quality (measured by the novel Chem-GD metric).
AI.conclusion: The tight coupling of deterministic chemical evidence extraction with RL-guided LLM reasoning successfully addresses the weak coupling problem between chemical evidence and language-model explanation, enabling fine-grained, evidence-grounded CIF auditing beyond what either fixed validators or naive LLM approaches can achieve.

title: G-MAD: A Game-Based Data Generation Framework for Multi-View RGB-T Aerial Object Detection
summary: This work introduces G-MAD, an open-source framework that uses Arma3 to generate synchronized multi-view RGB-T data for aerial object detection. G-MAD addresses key limitations of real-world aerial dataset construction, including limited viewpoint control, imperfect RGB-T alignment and high annotation cost. The framework supports structured scenario specification, controllable multi-view camera placement, simultaneous visible/thermal capture, and automatic bounding box annotation using engine-level geometric metadata. These capabilities enable controlled studies of viewpoint variation, multi-modal fusion, and synthetic-to-real transfer in aerial object detection. Besides, using G-MAD, we construct and release AMOD, a new large-scale multi-view aerial RGB-T object detection benchmark. The source code and the dataset are available at https://unique-chan.github.io/G-MAD-Project.

AI.tldr: G-MAD is an open-source framework using Arma3 to generate synchronized multi-view RGB-T data for aerial object detection, addressing limitations of real-world datasets. It enables controlled studies and produces AMOD, a large-scale multi-view aerial RGB-T benchmark.
AI.motivation: Real-world aerial dataset construction suffers from limited viewpoint control, imperfect RGB-thermal alignment, and high annotation costs, motivating the need for a synthetic data generation framework.
AI.method: G-MAD leverages Arma3 to generate synchronized multi-view RGB-T data with structured scenario specification, controllable multi-view camera placement, simultaneous visible/thermal capture, and automatic bounding box annotation using engine-level geometric metadata.
AI.result: G-MAD produces AMOD, a large-scale multi-view aerial RGB-T object detection benchmark, enabling controlled studies of viewpoint variation, multi-modal fusion, and synthetic-to-real transfer.
AI.conclusion: G-MAD effectively addresses key limitations in aerial dataset construction and provides a useful open-source framework for multi-modal aerial object detection research.

title: The C-index illusion: discrimination without calibration in published survival models
summary: "Stop Chasing the C-index when Evaluating Survival Analysis Models" (ICML 2026, Spotlight) argued normatively, on synthetic data, that evaluating survival models by discrimination alone, i.e. the concordance index, produces systematically misleading model comparisons, because the metric ignores calibration and time-dependent accuracy. Whether this matters for real, published, non-clinical models has not been tested. We reproduce three published survival-ML models across three structurally distinct domains (hard-drive failure, peer-to-peer credit default, and user disengagement on digital platforms), validate our evaluation instrument against the anchor paper's own synthetic experiment, and test five pre-registered hypotheses under a Holm-corrected family-wise error rate. Three of five reject. A model that reproduces the published discrimination almost exactly (C = 0.9595 vs. 0.958 reported) fails a formal calibration test at p = 2.6e-136; a broad feature-ablation search finds no single attribute responsible for this discrimination, so the calibration failure is not an artifact of a trivial shortcut. A lender's estimated default risk is biased upward by roughly two percentage points, growing to nearly four points in the riskiest segment, when loan prepayment is treated as non-informative censoring rather than as a competing risk. A platform's churn model shows probability estimates that degrade with the prediction horizon even as its global discrimination stays within the pre-registered C-index band. A direct test of whether metric choice inverts which model is preferred does not reject, though with limited power given only two to three models per domain; the failure mode we document is better characterized as misplaced confidence in a chosen model than as choice of the wrong one. We release a reusable, pre-registered evaluation harness with full code and a single annotated notebook.

AI.tldr: Reproducing three published survival-ML models across three domains shows that evaluating solely by C-index (discrimination) is misleading: models with good C-index can fail calibration tests (p=2.6e-136), have biased risk estimates due to censoring assumptions, and show degrading probability estimates over time, even though C-index remains stable.
AI.motivation: To test whether the normative argument that evaluating survival models by C-index alone is misleading (from the anchor paper) holds for real, published, non-clinical models, not just synthetic data.
AI.method: Reproduced three published survival-ML models (hard-drive failure, P2P credit default, user disengagement), validated the evaluation instrument against the anchor paper's synthetic experiment, and tested five pre-registered hypotheses under Holm-corrected family-wise error rate.
AI.result: Three of five hypotheses rejected. Key findings: (1) A model matching reported C-index (0.9595 vs 0.958) fails calibration test (p=2.6e-136); (2) Treating prepayment as non-informative censoring instead of competing risk biases default risk estimates by ~2 percentage points overall, ~4 points in riskiest segment; (3) Churn model's probability estimates degrade with prediction horizon despite stable C-index. One hypothesis (metric choice inverting model preference) not rejected but had limited power.
AI.conclusion: Evaluating survival models by discrimination (C-index) alone is misleading for real models; the failure mode is misplaced confidence in a chosen model rather than selecting the wrong one. A reusable, pre-registered evaluation harness is released.

title: SenWorld: A Digital-Twin Simulation for Generating Context-Rich Evaluation Data
summary: Smartphone personal assistants reason over longitudinal personal data, yet evaluating them requires context-rich evaluation data whose correct answers are known, and real device traces are too privacy-sensitive to share. To address this challenge, we present SenWorld, a physically grounded, deterministic, event-sourced digital-twin simulation that generates such data with ground truth fixed by construction. In SenWorld, personas live through a full day in a world built from real map, weather, holiday, and network data; every observable signal is archived in full-system snapshots; and each evaluation case is labeled by a pointer to an existing record rather than by post-hoc annotation or a large language model (LLM) judge. We evaluate this method with 16 personas in Beijing. The generated data closely matches the held-out real-user benchmark in category distribution (Jensen--Shannon divergence (JSD) 0.070) and in the daily rhythm of communication records (JSD below 0.1), though generated records remain shorter than real ones. Without scripted interaction, personas form a fully reciprocated dialogue subgraph and differentiated behavioral repertoires. Projected into 717 evaluation cases, the generated data exposes 78 failures in a production smartphone assistant, concentrating on call and Short Message Service (SMS) records while contacts, schedules, and alarms never fail. The snapshot pointer confirms each failure as an assistant-side retrieval error, with no LLM judge involved. Overall, SenWorld offers a privacy-safe, reproducible, and distribution-checked path to evaluation data whose labels are fixed by construction.

AI.tldr: SenWorld is a privacy-safe, deterministic digital-twin simulation that generates labeled evaluation data for smartphone personal assistants by having personas live through full days in a physically grounded world, producing data that matches real-user benchmarks and reveals specific assistant failures without needing LLM judges.
AI.motivation: Smartphone personal assistants need context-rich evaluation data with known correct answers, but real device traces are too privacy-sensitive to share and existing evaluation methods rely on post-hoc annotation or LLM judges, which lack ground truth guarantees.
AI.method: SenWorld is a physically grounded, deterministic, event-sourced digital-twin simulation where personas live through full days in a world built from real map, weather, holiday, and network data. Every observable signal is archived in full-system snapshots, and each evaluation case is labeled by a pointer to an existing record rather than by annotation or LLM judge. The method was evaluated with 16 personas in Beijing.
AI.result: Generated data closely matches held-out real-user benchmark in category distribution (JSD 0.070) and daily communication rhythm (JSD below 0.1), though records are shorter. Personas form fully reciprocated dialogue subgraphs and differentiated behavioral repertoires. 717 evaluation cases exposed 78 failures in a production assistant, concentrated on call/SMS records; snapshot pointers confirmed each failure as an assistant-side retrieval error without LLM involvement.
AI.conclusion: SenWorld provides a privacy-safe, reproducible, and distribution-checked path to evaluation data whose labels are fixed by construction, avoiding the need for privacy-sensitive real traces or unreliable LLM judges.

title: SIINR: Structurally Informed Implicit Neural Representations for super-resolution with uncertainty quantification of clinical quality diffusion MRI datasets
summary: Diffusion Magnetic Resonance Imaging (dMRI) is a powerful tool for probing brain microstructure, but clinical acquisitions are often limited by low out-of-plane resolution, resulting in degraded structural information and reduced utility for advanced analysis. We introduce SIINR (Structurally Informed Implicit Neural Representations), a general framework for super-resoltion of clinical dMRI datasets while quantifying uncertainty in the reconstructed outputs. SIINR utilizes a supervised 3D U-net as a prior and combines it with a self-supervised implicit neural representation (INR) that fuses the high-resolution prior and the original low-resolution data. The INR enables joint modeling across spatial and angular domains, enforces data consistency, and provides analytic approximate posterior distributions for downstream uncertainty quantification. We validate the framework on a diverse set of open-access dMRI datasets, demonstrating that SIINR outperforms standard interpolation methods in both quantitative error metrics and qualitative anatomical fidelity. Experiments on clinical cases, including subjects with multiple sclerosis and brain lesions, illustrate the framework its ability to propagate intensity changes and flag uncertain regions in challenging scenarios. SIINR is flexible, modular, and can be adapted to different upsampling ratios and downstream tasks, providing a principled approach for enhancing clinical dMRI and supporting robust interpretation of derived neuroimaging metrics.

AI.tldr: SIINR is a framework that combines a supervised 3D U-net prior with a self-supervised implicit neural representation (INR) to super-resolve clinical dMRI data and quantify uncertainty, outperforming standard interpolation methods on diverse datasets including pathological cases.
AI.motivation: Clinical dMRI acquisitions suffer from low out-of-plane resolution, degrading structural information and limiting advanced analysis; there is a need for principled super-resolution that also quantifies uncertainty.
AI.method: SIINR uses a supervised 3D U-net as a high-resolution prior, fused with a self-supervised implicit neural representation (INR) that jointly models spatial and angular domains, enforces data consistency, and provides analytic approximate posterior distributions for uncertainty quantification.
AI.result: SIINR outperforms standard interpolation methods in quantitative error metrics and qualitative anatomical fidelity on open-access dMRI datasets; it propagates intensity changes and flags uncertain regions in clinical cases (multiple sclerosis, brain lesions).
AI.conclusion: SIINR is a flexible, modular framework adaptable to different upsampling ratios and downstream tasks, offering a principled approach for enhancing clinical dMRI and supporting robust interpretation of derived neuroimaging metrics.

title: Trustworthy Privacy-Preserving Multimodal Federated Learning for Personalised Breast Cancer Prediction
summary: Federated learning has emerged as a potential solution to privacy concerns associated with using sensitive health data for training predictive models, particularly in personalised cancer care. This research investigates whether federated learning can support the development of robust models for predicting tumour progression in breast cancer patients while addressing four critical deployment pillars: transparency, scalability, security, and fairness. This study evaluates a federated learning framework using multimodal data, including clinical information, tumour characteristics, biomarker data, and patient demographics, alongside medical imaging data such as MRI scans, to model changes in tumour characteristics over time. The performance of the federated approach was compared with that of a centralised model trained on aggregated data. The report then further examines strategies to enhance secure model updates, maintain performance across patient subgroups, and support scalability across institutions. The findings assess whether federated learning can achieve predictive performance comparable to centralised learning while preserving data locality. These results contribute to understanding the feasibility of privacy-preserving, multimodal predictive modelling and support future applications such as digital twins to assist clinicians and patients in personalised treatment planning.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates whether federated learning can support robust predictive modelling for breast cancer tumour progression using multimodal data while addressing transparency, scalability, security, and fairness. Federated learning achieved comparable performance to centralised learning while preserving data locality, supporting privacy-preserving personalised cancer care.
AI.motivation: To address privacy concerns associated with using sensitive health data for training predictive models in personalised cancer care, and to investigate whether federated learning can support robust tumour progression prediction while maintaining data locality.
AI.method: Evaluated a federated learning framework using multimodal data (clinical information, tumour characteristics, biomarker data, patient demographics, and MRI scans) to model changes in tumour characteristics over time. Compared performance with a centralised model trained on aggregated data, and examined strategies for secure model updates, performance across subgroups, and scalability.
AI.result: Federated learning achieved predictive performance comparable to centralised learning while preserving data locality, and addressed the four critical deployment pillars (transparency, scalability, security, and fairness).
AI.conclusion: Federated learning is a feasible approach for privacy-preserving, multimodal predictive modelling in breast cancer care, with potential applications such as digital twins for personalised treatment planning.

title: EvoThink: Evolving Thinking in Large Reasoning Models via Self-Pruning and Aha-Moment Preference Optimization
summary: Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) often suffer from overthinking due to redundant verification steps. Existing approaches for mitigating overthinking, such as fast-slow thinking switching and reasoning trajectory compression, fail to make a fine-grained distinction between beneficial and redundant steps within the LRM's reasoning process, and may thus impair reasoning capability in their pursuit of efficiency. To simultaneously improve reasoning efficiency and capability, we propose EvoThink, a framework that reduces redundant verification and encourages the exploration of new reasoning paths. EvoThink comprises two key components: Self-Pruning Training (SPT), an unsupervised method that iteratively prunes redundant reasoning steps and self-trains on the concise trajectories; and Aha-Moment Preference Optimization (AMPO), which, inspired by genetic algorithms, identifies valuable failed reasoning attempts, synthesizes from-wrong-to-right aha-moment data, and optimizes the model to internalize this reasoning pattern. Extensive evaluations across mathematical reasoning and code generation benchmarks demonstrate that EvoThink not only substantially reduces inference-time token usage but also improves the reasoning capability of LRMs.

AI.tldr: EvoThink is a framework that reduces redundant reasoning steps in Large Reasoning Models while improving both efficiency and capability through Self-Pruning Training and Aha-Moment Preference Optimization.
AI.motivation: LRMs overthink due to redundant verification steps. Existing methods (fast-slow switching, trajectory compression) lack fine-grained distinction between beneficial and redundant steps, potentially harming reasoning capability while pursuing efficiency.
AI.method: Two components: (1) Self-Pruning Training (SPT) - unsupervised iterative pruning of redundant reasoning steps with self-training on concise trajectories; (2) Aha-Moment Preference Optimization (AMPO) - inspired by genetic algorithms, identifies valuable failed reasoning attempts, synthesizes from-wrong-to-right aha-moment data, and optimizes the model to internalize this pattern.
AI.result: Substantially reduces inference-time token usage and improves reasoning capability across mathematical reasoning and code generation benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: EvoThink simultaneously improves both reasoning efficiency and capability, outperforming prior overthinking mitigation approaches.

title: ETPDesigner: Multi-Agent Orchestration for Interactive Multimodal Electronic Theater Program
summary: Electronic Theater Programs (ETPs) serve as critical promotional media in the performing arts, comprising a multi-page collection of heterogeneous visual assets such as theatrical posters, performance details, and character portraits. However, existing text-to-image paradigms struggle with such complex design tasks due to their inability to comprehend long-context narratives and maintain visual consistency across multiple distinct pages. To address this, we introduce ETPDesigner, a collaborative Multi-Agent framework that directly synthesizes high-quality ETPs from raw dramatic scripts. Emulating a professional design pipeline, our framework orchestrates specialized agents for semantic script analysis, core poster synthesis, functional background generation, and the stratified composition of character assets. Central to ETPDesigner is a global style anchor mechanism that extracts visual priors from the core poster to enforce strict aesthetic uniformity across all generated components. Furthermore, we elevate the ETP from a static publication to an immersive interactive companion. By integrating portrait animation, customized speech synthesis, and persona-grounded Large Language Models (LLMs), our system enables users to engage in real-time, voice-enabled conversations with the generated virtual characters. To rigorously benchmark this task, we construct ETP-Pro, a domain-specific benchmark of professional theater posters and high-quality character portraits. Extensive evaluations demonstrate our method's superiority in producing semantically faithful, aesthetically consistent, and highly interactive program sets.

AI.tldr: ETPDesigner is a Multi-Agent framework that generates interactive Electronic Theater Programs from scripts, featuring a global style anchor for visual consistency and animated character conversations.
AI.motivation: Existing text-to-image models fail at complex multi-page design tasks like ETPs because they cannot comprehend long-context narratives or maintain visual consistency across pages.
AI.method: A collaborative Multi-Agent framework (semantic analysis, poster synthesis, background generation, character composition) with a global style anchor mechanism for aesthetic uniformity, plus voice-enabled interactive characters via portrait animation, speech synthesis, and persona-grounded LLMs.
AI.result: Superior performance in semantic faithfulness, aesthetic consistency, and interactivity on the new ETP-Pro benchmark.
AI.conclusion: ETPDesigner effectively generates high-quality, interactive ETPs from raw scripts, outperforming existing methods on a dedicated benchmark.

title: Agent-Centric Animal Pose Forecasting
summary: Understanding animal behavior at an algorithmic level -- what animals attend to, how they form internal models and plans, and how this maps to action -- remains a central challenge in neuroscience and ethology. Data-driven generative models offer a path toward this understanding. We introduce a framework for training agent-centric autoregressive models of animal behavior from tracked pose, applicable to single animals and to groups in which each agent senses and responds to its conspecifics. Our models input egocentric sensory observations and output egocentric movements, mirroring the biological constraint that animals observe and act on the world from their own reference frame. Social behavior emerges from agents independently sensing and responding to one another. This agent-centric formulation requires managing many parallel representations of the same data, along with ML-specific transformations like discretization. We release a general-purpose library focused on the composable sequences of operations that translate between these representations. We show that trained models capture the distribution of social behavior in groups of courting Drosophila, and our library includes quantitative tools for measuring fit. We demonstrate how the library supports systematic comparison across input and output representations and that it adapts straightforwardly to a new domain.

AI.tldr: Introduces an agent-centric generative modeling framework for animal behavior using autoregressive models trained on tracked pose data, with a library for handling egocentric representations and parallel processing across agents.
AI.motivation: Understanding animal behavior algorithmically remains a central challenge in neuroscience and ethology; there is a need for data-driven models that respect biological constraints like egocentric sensing and action.
AI.method: Framework trains agent-centric autoregressive models from tracked pose data; agents use egocentric observations to predict egocentric movements. A library handles parallel representations, discretization, and composable transformations across multiple agents.
AI.result: Models capture the distribution of social behavior in groups of courting Drosophila; library includes quantitative tools for measuring fit and supports systematic comparison across input/output representations.
AI.conclusion: The agent-centric approach effectively models social behavior emergence from independent sensing and responding, and the library generalizes to new domains.

title: The Giant Hippocampus: From Structural Monoculture to a System of Systems
summary: AI researchers describe state-of-the-art models as one thing repeated at scale: the Transformer, wired identically for text, pixels, or speech. Neuroscientists describe the cortex as a mosaic - dense Layer 4 in visual cortex for spatial encoding, thick Layers 5/6 in motion cortex for temporal integration - different jobs solved by different structures. This paper argues the gap is a structural error, not a stylistic one, and is measurable. A century of cytoarchitecture, from Brodmann to single-cell Patch-seq, shows distinct cognitive functions are implemented by qualitatively different structures, not by rescaling one template. The convolutional neural network is the field's own proof: local receptive fields and hierarchical depth encoded this prior directly, reaching strong image recognition on far less data than later architectures needed. The paper traces how this lesson was discarded: the "Hardware Lottery" made the Transformer the path of least resistance, not the principled choice, and Mixture-of-Experts, often cited as diversity, in fact partitions parameters among identical experts. A functionalist analysis shows the Transformer is best understood as a functional analog of the hippocampal formation, not a general-purpose cortex - the same mistake as treating cortex as one giant Broca's area, except the field has now standardized on a giant hippocampus, applied to tasks it was never built for: audition, executive gating, working memory. The paper closes with an alternative: a Heterogeneous Topological Network, a System of Systems in which distinct modules keep the inductive bias their computation demands and communicate through standardized interfaces. This is a design discipline for AI architects, not cognitive science: specify modularity before training, using structural evidence as a design input rather than reverse-engineering architecture from a trained model's behavior.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that the AI field has made a structural error by using homogeneous Transformer architectures for all tasks, ignoring neuroscientific evidence that different cognitive functions require different neural structures. It proposes Heterogeneous Topological Networks with specialized modules as an alternative design discipline.
AI.motivation: The gap between AI's uniform scaling approach (one architecture repeated) and neuroscience's structural diversity (different cortical structures for different functions) is not stylistic but measurable and detrimental to progress.
AI.method: The paper provides a functionalist analysis of the Transformer as a hippocampal analog, traces the historical loss of structural priors (from CNNs to Transformers), and proposes Heterogeneous Topological Networks as a System of Systems with specialized modules communicating through standardized interfaces.
AI.result: The Transformer is functionally analogous to the hippocampal formation, not general-purpose cortex; Mixture-of-Experts does not provide true architectural diversity; and CNNs succeeded because they encoded structural priors that later architectures abandoned.
AI.conclusion: AI architects should specify modularity before training, using structural evidence from neuroscience as design input rather than reverse-engineering from trained model behavior.

title: OffNadirLoc: Benchmark and Framework for Challenging UAV-to-Satellite Geo-Localization under Large Off-Nadir Views
summary: Cross-view geo-localization between UAV and satellite imagery remains a fundamental yet highly challenging task, especially under large off-nadir views where drastic perspective distortions, occlusions, and appearance gaps occur. Existing benchmarks and methods primarily focus on near-nadir scenarios and often overlook the importance of structural scene understanding and intra-domain relational constraints, limiting their performance in real-world deployments. In this work, we introduce OffNadirLoc, a new benchmark for large off-nadir UAV-to-satellite geo-localization. To tackle the unique challenges posed by off-nadir perspectives, we further propose ONLoc, a framework that incorporates a structure-aware contextual weighting mechanism to dynamically emphasize reliable local features while suppressing ambiguous or repetitive regions. Additionally, we design a view-coherent learning strategy, which treats one satellite image and the corresponding UAV images from multiple views as a cohesive semantic group. This set-level supervision enables the model to learn viewpoint-invariant and discriminative features, making it more effective at capturing multi-view consistency than conventional pairwise contrastive learning. Extensive experiments on the OffNadirLoc benchmark and four near-nadir datasets demonstrate that our method consistently outperforms state-of-the-art approaches while exhibiting strong zero-shot generalization to unseen datasets without additional training. The code will be released at https://montalario.github.io/offnadirloc/.

AI.tldr: OffNadirLoc introduces a new benchmark for large off-nadir UAV-to-satellite geo-localization, and proposes ONLoc, a framework with structure-aware contextual weighting and view-coherent learning that outperforms state-of-the-art methods on both off-nadir and near-nadir benchmarks while showing strong zero-shot generalization.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks and methods focus on near-nadir scenarios and overlook structural scene understanding and intra-domain relational constraints, limiting performance in real-world large off-nadir deployments.
AI.method: ONLoc incorporates (1) a structure-aware contextual weighting mechanism to emphasize reliable local features and suppress ambiguous/repetitive regions, and (2) a view-coherent learning strategy that treats one satellite image and multiple-view UAV images as a cohesive semantic group, using set-level supervision for viewpoint-invariant feature learning.
AI.result: The method consistently outperforms state-of-the-art approaches on the OffNadirLoc benchmark and four near-nadir datasets, and exhibits strong zero-shot generalization to unseen datasets.
AI.conclusion: The proposed benchmark and framework effectively address the challenges of large off-nadir UAV-to-satellite geo-localization, and the code will be released.

title: End-to-End Differential Privacy in Training Deep Neural Network Classifiers
summary: Differentially private machine learning enables model training on sensitive data while ensuring that individual data is unlikely to be recoverable from the parameters of the resulting model. However, existing work often privatizes both training inputs and their labels, and these protections may be conservative when labels are public or can be safely made public. Therefore, in this work we propose a novel private training framework that instead privatizes training inputs while keeping labels public. We consider neural networks with softmax output layers, and thus the mapping from training inputs to the output of the softmax layer is a mapping onto the unit simplex. We randomize softmax outputs during training by applying the Dirichlet mechanism to enforce differential privacy for the training inputs, hence the ``end-to-end'' label. Because training data is reused across multiple training epochs, we use the notion of \Renyi differential privacy to formulate tight bounds on the strength of privacy provided by the Dirichlet mechanism across repeated uses. We show empirically that we attain new state-of-the-art accuracy when training from scratch on CIFAR10, MNIST, MedMNIST, FashionMNIST, and SVHN across all privacy budgets evaluated. Notably, when implementing $(ε, δ)$-differential privacy with $δ=10^{-5}$, we improve the prior state-of-the-art accuracy from $78.37\%$ to $88.17\%$ at $ε=4$ on CIFAR10, and our approach has $82.96\%$ accuracy even for $ε=1$, which significantly outperforms prior work.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a differentially private training framework that privatizes only training inputs while keeping labels public, using the Dirichlet mechanism on softmax outputs to achieve state-of-the-art accuracy across multiple benchmarks including CIFAR10 (88.17% at ε=4).
AI.motivation: Existing differentially private machine learning methods privatize both training inputs and labels, which can be overly conservative when labels are public or can safely be made public.
AI.method: The framework privatizes training inputs while keeping labels public; it applies the Dirichlet mechanism to randomize softmax outputs during training, using Rényi differential privacy to bound privacy loss across repeated epochs.
AI.result: Achieves new state-of-the-art accuracy on CIFAR10, MNIST, MedMNIST, FashionMNIST, and SVHN across all evaluated privacy budgets; notably 88.17% at ε=4 and 82.96% at ε=1 on CIFAR10 with δ=10^{-5}.
AI.conclusion: Privatizing only inputs while keeping labels public yields significantly better accuracy than prior work, demonstrating that label privatization is unnecessary when labels can be safely made public.

title: Coordinating from Memory: Graph-Structured Experience Reuse for Multi-Agent Adaptation in Dynamic Manufacturing
summary: Dynamic manufacturing environments require multi-agent systems to coordinate effectively under frequent operational disturbances such as machine failures, urgent job arrivals, and processing time variations. Existing multi-agent reinforcement learning approaches treat each disturbance episode independently, discarding valuable coordination experience that could accelerate future adaptation. In this paper, we propose a Graph-Structured Experiential Memory (GSEM) framework for multi-agent coordination in dynamic manufacturing. The framework encodes historical coordination episodes as heterogeneous relational graphs that capture task dependencies, machine states, and inter-agent collaboration patterns. When a new disturbance occurs, a graph neural network-based retrieval mechanism identifies structurally similar past episodes, enabling experience-guided policy adaptation rather than learning from scratch. Experiments on dynamic flexible job-shop scheduling benchmarks with three disturbance types show that GSEM reduces makespan by 4.1%-10.0% and adaptation time by 33%-38% compared to the strongest memory-augmented baseline, with the advantage increasing under higher disturbance frequency. Ablation studies and cross-disturbance transfer experiments further validate the necessity of graph-structured encoding and similarity-based retrieval and demonstrate the cross-disturbance generalizability of learned coordination patterns.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a Graph-Structured Experiential Memory (GSEM) framework that uses heterogeneous relational graphs and GNN-based retrieval to enable experience-guided multi-agent coordination in dynamic manufacturing, achieving 4.1%-10.0% makespan reduction and 33%-38% faster adaptation compared to baselines.
AI.motivation: Existing multi-agent reinforcement learning approaches treat each disturbance episode independently, discarding valuable coordination experience that could accelerate future adaptation in dynamic manufacturing environments.
AI.method: GSEM encodes historical coordination episodes as heterogeneous relational graphs capturing task dependencies, machine states, and inter-agent collaboration patterns. A graph neural network-based retrieval mechanism identifies structurally similar past episodes to guide policy adaptation during new disturbances.
AI.result: Experiments on dynamic flexible job-shop scheduling with three disturbance types show GSEM reduces makespan by 4.1%-10.0% and adaptation time by 33%-38% over the strongest memory-augmented baseline, with advantages increasing under higher disturbance frequency.
AI.conclusion: Graph-structured encoding and similarity-based retrieval are necessary for effective memory reuse; learned coordination patterns demonstrate cross-disturbance generalizability.

title: Forecasting the Number of Harvest-ready Fruits of Sweet Peppers Using Multimodal Time-Series Data
summary: Accurate yield forecasting at the individual-plant level is critical for precision agriculture and supply-chain planning, yet public datasets capturing both visual growth dynamics and per-plant measurement labels are scarce. In this paper, we introduce a novel, annotated image time-series dataset of 691 sweet pepper plants monitored over two growing seasons, comprising 4837 images with per-plant fruit counts categorized by maturity. We propose a multimodal deep learning framework that fuses high-dimensional image features, extracted using the DinoV3 encoder, with numerical count measurements. Our architecture utilizes a Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) network to model temporal dependencies and handles irregular sampling intervals common in greenhouse monitoring. Through quantitative experiments, we demonstrate that this multimodal approach reduces RMSE over a persistence baseline by 33% and 38% in the 2022 and 2023 seasons, respectively, with a further 1.2% average gain over a measurement-only model. Furthermore, we employ Deep Ensembles and Gaussian Negative Log-Likelihood (NLL) to provide calibrated uncertainty estimates, with an Uncertainty Calibration Error (UCE) ranging from 0.39 to 0.89 depending on the cross-season evaluation direction, offering a principled confidence signal for real-world agricultural decision-making. We release the dataset and code to support reproducible research and to accelerate development of data-driven yield forecasting methods for horticultural crops.

AI.tldr: A multimodal LSTM-DinoV3 framework with uncertainty estimation for individual-plant yield forecasting, supported by a new annotated time-series dataset of 691 sweet pepper plants, achieving 33-38% RMSE reduction over persistence baselines.
AI.motivation: Accurate per-plant yield forecasting is critical for precision agriculture and supply-chain planning, but public datasets with both visual growth dynamics and per-plant measurement labels are scarce.
AI.method: Multimodal deep learning framework fusing DinoV3 image features with numerical count measurements via LSTM networks handling irregular sampling intervals, plus Deep Ensembles and Gaussian NLL for calibrated uncertainty estimates.
AI.result: RMSE reduction of 33% (2022) and 38% (2023) over persistence baseline; 1.2% average gain over measurement-only model; UCE ranges 0.39–0.89 across cross-season evaluations.
AI.conclusion: The multimodal approach significantly outperforms baselines, provides calibrated uncertainty for real-world decision-making, and the released dataset/code enables reproducible research in horticultural yield forecasting.

title: The Mechanism Matters: When Knowledge Graphs Help Reinforcement Learning
summary: Knowledge graphs (KGs) are widely used to inject prior knowledge into reinforcement learning (RL), yet the literature is dominated by single-domain, positive-result method papers, so we lack a systematic account of when KG structure helps an agent, when it is neutral, and when it hurts. We conduct a controlled study that independently varies the RL task, the injection mechanism (state features, action masking, or potential-based reward shaping), and KG quality. Using a synthetic, fully controllable KG over MiniGrid environments, we report three findings. First, on compositional sparse-reward tasks structured KG guidance improves sample efficiency and solve reliability (70% to 97% of seeds), and a shuffle control that permutes the KG's edges while preserving their count collapses the benefit toward baseline (masking p=0.0001; shaping p=0.006), so the gain is structural rather than generic regularization. Second, KG value scales with the amount of task-relevant knowledge the graph contains. Third, and most consequential, safety depends on the mechanism: soft, optimality-preserving injection benefits from correct knowledge and harmlessly ignores incorrect knowledge, whereas hard masking is brittle, forbidding essential actions when the KG is incomplete or corrupted and making a wrong KG worse than none. A UMLS-derived clinical case study on sepsis management under offline RL is a careful null, underscoring that benefits require task structure the chosen mechanism can exploit. Our results give practitioners concrete guidance on how, and how much, to trust a KG when using it to guide RL.

AI.tldr: A controlled study of how KG structure affects RL performance, finding that KG benefits depend on task relevance and injection mechanism, with soft methods being robust while hard masking can be harmful with incorrect KGs.
AI.motivation: Existing KG-in-RL literature lacks systematic understanding of when KG structure helps, is neutral, or hurts RL performance, being dominated by single-domain positive-result method papers.
AI.method: Controlled study varying RL tasks, injection mechanisms (state features, action masking, potential-based reward shaping), and KG quality using synthetic MiniGrid environments and a UMLS-derived clinical sepsis case study.
AI.result: (1) Structured KG guidance improves sample efficiency and solve reliability on compositional sparse-reward tasks (70%→97% success), with shuffle controls confirming structural benefit (p<0.01). (2) KG value scales with task-relevant knowledge. (3) Soft injection tolerates incorrect KG, but hard masking is brittle and can make wrong KG worse than none.
AI.conclusion: Provides concrete practitioner guidance on how and how much to trust a KG when using it to guide RL, emphasizing mechanism-dependent safety considerations.

title: CLARK: Closed-loop Learning for Adaptive Reasoning over Knowledge Graphs
comment: 18 pages, 3 Figures, 1 algorithm, 3 tables, submitted to The International Semantic Web Conference'26
summary: Machine Learning models are widely used for automating classification tasks by extracting statistical patterns from data. However, their performance deteriorates if the data distribution changes, making them ill-suited to handle uncertain and evolving information. Moreover, they provide limited support for integrating prior knowledge. To address these limitations, we present CLARK (Closed-loop Learning for Adaptive Reasoning over Knowledge Graphs), a framework that integrates knowledge graphs, symbolic rule mining, and probabilistic reasoning under the Logic Programs with Markov Logic Networks (LP$^{\text{MLN}}$) formalism. Starting from CACTUS-derived KGs, CLARK translates graph structure into an LP$^{\text{MLN}}$ program and iteratively enriches it with candidate rules proposed by symbolic learners. These rules are calibrated through probabilistic weight learning, enabling reasoning under uncertainty and refinement of the underlying graph structure. We evaluate CLARK on two medical datasets, analysing both rule quality and downstream classification performance. Results demonstrate that CLARK leads to improved classification performance and more generalisable inference. Overall, CLARK provides a principled approach to constructing adaptive, interpretable, knowledge-driven models for classification.

AI.tldr: CLARK integrates knowledge graphs, symbolic rule mining, and probabilistic reasoning (LP^MLN) to create adaptive, interpretable classification models that handle distribution shifts and incorporate prior knowledge, showing improved performance on medical datasets.
AI.motivation: Standard ML models deteriorate under data distribution changes and offer limited support for integrating prior knowledge, motivating a more adaptive and knowledge-driven approach.
AI.method: CLARK translates CACTUS-derived knowledge graphs into LP^MLN programs, iteratively enriches them with symbolically mined candidate rules, and calibrates rules via probabilistic weight learning to enable reasoning under uncertainty and graph refinement.
AI.result: Evaluated on two medical datasets, CLARK achieves improved classification performance and more generalisable inference compared to baselines.
AI.conclusion: CLARK offers a principled framework for constructing adaptive, interpretable, knowledge-driven classification models that combine symbolic and probabilistic reasoning.

title: STEREOFLOW: Progressive Stereo Matching with StereoDiT and Transition Flow Matching
summary: Stereo matching is a fundamental task in 3D reconstruction. Despite remarkable advances, the prevailing paradigms formulate stereo matching as a deterministic regression problem, collapsing the multimodal distribution modeling into a single-point estimation. This formulation suffers from a regression-to-mean bias, frequently struggling with ambiguous regions. In contrast, we introduce a prior-guided generative framework that integrates deterministic matching regression and generative distribution modeling within a complementary formulation. Built upon this formulation, we introduce StereoFlow through three key components: (i) a two-stage progressive cascade matching network that progressively produces multi-resolution stereo conditions with complementary matching cues; (ii) a pixel diffusion transformer (termed StereoDiT) with a frequency-decoupled architecture for modeling correspondence ambiguity; (iii) a few-step flow matching objective (termed Transition Flow Matching) for efficient optimization. In summary, \textsc{\textbf{StereoFlow}} achieves strong geometric consistency and rich fine-grained details in ill-posed, discontinuous regions and under zero-shot generalization. Extensive experiments demonstrate that the proposed StereoFlow establishes multiple state-of-the-art results across benchmarks, including Scene Flow, KITTI, ETH3D, and Middlebury.

AI.tldr: StereoFlow introduces a prior-guided generative framework for stereo matching that combines deterministic regression with generative distribution modeling, using a progressive cascade matching network, a pixel diffusion transformer (StereoDiT) with frequency-decoupled architecture, and a few-step Transition Flow Matching objective, achieving SOTA results on Scene Flow, KITTI, ETH3D, and Middlebury.
AI.motivation: Traditional stereo matching methods treat the task as deterministic regression, collapsing multimodal disparity distributions into single-point estimates, which leads to regression-to-mean bias and poor performance in ambiguous regions.
AI.method: Proposes a prior-guided generative framework combining deterministic matching regression and generative distribution modeling via: (i) two-stage progressive cascade matching network for multi-resolution stereo conditions; (ii) StereoDiT, a pixel diffusion transformer with frequency-decoupled architecture; (iii) Transition Flow Matching, a few-step flow matching objective for efficient optimization.
AI.result: Achieves strong geometric consistency and fine-grained details in ill-posed/discontinuous regions and under zero-shot generalization, establishing multiple SOTA results on Scene Flow, KITTI, ETH3D, and Middlebury benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: The generative formulation effectively addresses the regression-to-mean bias of deterministic stereo matching, particularly excelling in ambiguous regions while maintaining geometric consistency.

title: SCPP: A Unified Python Library for Soft Clustering
summary: In this paper, we present SCPP (Soft Clustering Python Package), an open-source Python framework for soft clustering. SCPP establishes a canonical, scikit-learn-compatible estimator interface that standardizes model training, prediction, membership representation, evaluation, and benchmarking across heterogeneous soft clustering methods, including fuzzy, probabilistic, graph-based, matrix factorization, and deep learning methods. The framework currently integrates 40 representative algorithms together with a comprehensive benchmarking comprising datasets, clustering quality metrics, and standardized runtime, memory, and scalability evaluation. SCPP further provides extensive documentation, practical examples, automated testing, and seamless integration with the scientific Python ecosystem, enabling reproducible experimentation and straightforward extension with new algorithms. The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/soft-clustering/soft-clustering.

AI.tldr: SCPP is an open-source Python framework for soft clustering that standardizes 40 algorithms (fuzzy, probabilistic, graph-based, matrix factorization, deep learning) with a scikit-learn-compatible interface, benchmarking tools, and seamless ecosystem integration.
AI.motivation: To address the lack of a standardized, unified framework for soft clustering in Python that provides consistent interfaces, reproducible benchmarking, and easy extensibility across diverse soft clustering methods.
