AI.method: The authors developed SCPP as a canonical, scikit-learn-compatible estimator interface that unifies model training, prediction, membership representation, evaluation, and benchmarking for 40 soft clustering algorithms spanning fuzzy, probabilistic, graph-based, matrix factorization, and deep learning approaches.
AI.result: SCPP integrates 40 representative soft clustering algorithms with comprehensive benchmarking (datasets, clustering quality metrics, runtime, memory, scalability evaluation), extensive documentation, automated testing, and seamless scientific Python ecosystem integration.
AI.conclusion: SCPP provides a standardized, reproducible, and extensible open-source framework for soft clustering research and application, enabling consistent comparison and experimentation across heterogeneous methods.

title: Safe Remediation as Risk-Constrained Intervention Decision in Microservice Systems
summary: In modern IT operations (IT-Ops), the cost of an incorrect repair often exceeds the cost of no action at all. Yet existing automated remediation systems are designed to generate actions rather than to decide whether intervention is warranted, leaving safety as an afterthought enforced by manual approval. This paper makes three contributions to close this gap: (i) we reformulate safe remediation as a risk-constrained intervention decision problem and cast it as a Constrained Markov Decision Process (CMDP), in which the agent maximizes repair success subject to a bounded false remediation rate (FRR); (ii) we introduce a three-dimensional risk decomposition comprising blast radius, reversibility, and epistemic uncertainty, providing operators with an interpretable per-action safety interface; and (iii) we design a context-adaptive human-in-the-loop (HITL) gate that turns escalation from a binary failsafe into a bandwidth-aware control layer responsive to on-call load and business criticality. The full policy is learned offline from historical incident logs, enabling explicit control of the expected FRR. Experiments on the Train Ticket microservice benchmark with Chaos Mesh fault injection and an RCAEval-aligned fault taxonomy show that our framework reduces FRR by 39% while improving repair success by 2.5 points over a strong runbook baseline, and reduces on-call escalation load by 17% relative to a fixed-threshold variant.

AI.tldr: A risk-constrained CMDP framework for safe IT remediation that reduces false remediation rate by 39% while improving repair success by 2.5 points and reducing on-call load by 17%.
AI.motivation: In IT-Ops, incorrect repairs cost more than no action, yet existing automated remediation systems prioritize action generation over deciding whether intervention is warranted, leaving safety as an afterthought enforced by manual approval.
AI.method: The authors (i) formulate safe remediation as a risk-constrained CMDP maximizing repair success under bounded false remediation rate (FRR); (ii) introduce a 3D risk decomposition (blast radius, reversibility, epistemic uncertainty) for interpretable per-action safety; (iii) design a context-adaptive HITL gate that turns escalation into a bandwidth-aware control layer. The policy is learned offline from historical incident logs.
AI.result: On the Train Ticket microservice benchmark with Chaos Mesh fault injection and RCAEval-aligned taxonomy, the framework reduces FRR by 39%, improves repair success by 2.5 points over a strong runbook baseline, and reduces on-call escalation load by 17% relative to a fixed-threshold variant.
AI.conclusion: Safe automated remediation can be effectively achieved through risk-constrained decision-making with interpretable safety interfaces and adaptive human-in-the-loop escalation, outperforming both fixed-threshold and baseline runbook approaches.

title: Toward Seasonal Guidelines for Robust Deep-Learning Sentinel-2 Building Detection in Different Area Types
summary: Sentinel-2 imagery offers open access, global coverage, and frequent revisit times, making it attractive for practical building mapping at scale; however, its native 10m resolution makes building vs non-building classification challenging, particularly for small or sub-pixel buildings, and performance can vary with both seasonality and the heterogeneity of built-up environments. This paper introduces a Sentinel-2 building-detection framework designed to systematically quantify these effects and to support more formalised, practice-oriented model selection. We construct a dedicated multi-temporal Sentinel-2 dataset over the Warsaw region and derive binary ground-truth masks by rasterising official Polish topographic database (BDOT10k) building footprints onto the Sentinel-2 pixel grid. Using two established convolutional segmentation backbones (U-Net and DeepLabV3+), we first perform scene-specific fine-tuning to select a robust architecture and identify the best monthly models for L1C and L2A products separately. We then conduct cross-temporal inference by applying each best monthly model to all scenes, enabling an assessment of (i) which months provide favourable training and inference conditions, (ii) how performance transfers between seasons, (iii) the impact of processing level, and (iv) how these effects differ across built-up typologies. Based on these results, we provide practical guidance for routine Sentinel-2 building classification under varying acquisition periods and settlement characteristics.

AI.tldr: This paper develops a Sentinel-2 building-detection framework to systematically quantify the effects of seasonality, processing level, and built-up heterogeneity on classification performance, using U-Net and DeepLabV3+ over Warsaw, and provides practical guidance for model selection.
AI.motivation: Sentinel-2 imagery is attractive for large-scale building mapping due to its open access, global coverage, and frequent revisit times, but its 10m resolution makes building classification challenging, especially for small/sub-pixel buildings, and performance varies with seasonality and built-up heterogeneity. There is a need for a systematic framework to quantify these effects and support formalized model selection.
AI.method: Constructed a multi-temporal Sentinel-2 dataset over Warsaw with binary ground-truth masks derived from official Polish topographic database (BDOT10k) building footprints rasterized onto the Sentinel-2 pixel grid. Performed scene-specific fine-tuning using U-Net and DeepLabV3+ segmentation backbones to select robust architectures and identify best monthly models for L1C and L2A products separately. Conducted cross-temporal inference by applying each best monthly model to all scenes.
AI.result: The framework enables assessment of (i) which months provide favorable training/inference conditions, (ii) how performance transfers between seasons, (iii) the impact of processing level (L1C vs L2A), and (iv) how these effects differ across built-up typologies.
AI.conclusion: Provides practical guidance for routine Sentinel-2 building classification under varying acquisition periods and settlement characteristics.

title: HypEMBER: Hypernetwork-based Ensemble for Robust Policy Learning of Parametrized Dynamical Systems
summary: In this work we investigate reinforcement learning (RL) as a framework for the robust control of parametrized dynamical systems in presence of measurements and model uncertainties. High-dimensional state spaces, expensive numerical solvers, the partial knowledge of the governing equations, and the dependence on physical parameters that may be uncertain or difficult to estimate accurately, make the use of standard RL approaches computationally unfeasible. Indeed, lack of robustness and poor generalization across parameter variations are further amplified in presence of noisy or incomplete measurements, ultimately hampering control performance. To address these challenges, we introduce HypEMBER, a novel RL framework based on the combination of hypernetworks and ensemble learning. In the proposed approach, both the policy and value functions are represented through hypernetworks that generate the weights of the underlying models conditioned on the physical parameters of the system, thereby enabling parametric generalization across different dynamical regimes. In addition, an ensemble of policy and value approximators is employed to quantify epistemic uncertainty, leading to improved exploration strategies and enhanced robustness during and after training. The performance of the proposed framework is assessed on two representative parametrized control problems: (i) the one-dimensional Kuramoto-Sivashinsky equation and (ii) a particle-navigation task in a two-dimensional time-dependent gyre flow, focusing on robustness with respect to measurement noise and parameter misspecification. Numerical results demonstrate that HypEMBER consistently improves training stability and sample efficiency, while achieving superior robustness to uncertainties affecting both the system dynamics and the available observations, in comparison with state-of-the-art RL methods.

AI.tldr: HypEMBER is a reinforcement learning framework combining hypernetworks and ensemble learning to achieve robust control of parametrized dynamical systems under measurement noise and model uncertainties, demonstrating improved robustness, sample efficiency, and generalization across varying physical parameters compared to standard RL methods.
AI.motivation: Standard RL approaches are computationally unfeasible for parametrized dynamical systems due to high-dimensional state spaces, expensive numerical solvers, partial knowledge of governing equations, and uncertain physical parameters. Additionally, lack of robustness and poor generalization across parameter variations are further amplified by noisy or incomplete measurements, hampering control performance.
AI.method: HypEMBER combines hypernetworks (which generate weights of policy/value functions conditioned on physical parameters) with ensemble learning (multiple policy and value approximators to quantify epistemic uncertainty), enabling parametric generalization across dynamical regimes and improved exploration/robustness.
AI.result: Evaluated on the 1D Kuramoto-Sivashinsky equation and a particle-navigation task in 2D time-dependent gyre flow, HypEMBER consistently improves training stability and sample efficiency while achieving superior robustness to measurement noise and parameter misspecification compared to state-of-the-art RL methods.
AI.conclusion: The combination of hypernetworks and ensemble learning is an effective paradigm for robust RL control of parametrized dynamical systems under uncertainty, offering better generalization across parameter variations and resilience to noisy/incomplete observations.

title: EvoDRC: A Self-Evolving Agentic Framework for Automated DRC Violation Repair
summary: Design rule check (DRC) closure remains a major bottleneck in advanced-node physical design. Although detailed routers are rule-aware, residual design rule violations (DRVs) often require manual engineering change order iterations. Automating this process is challenging because repairs must account for complex geometric interactions, preserve circuit connectivity, and avoid introducing new violations. We present EvoDRC, a skill-evolution framework for agentic block-level DRC repair. EvoDRC initializes layer-specific repair skills using knowledge distilled from an unrelated reference design and continuously evolves these skills using traceable repair experience collected from the target design. EvoDRC decomposes the layout into bounded repair regions and assigns an LLM repair agent to each region. Local DRC analysis, connectivity-checking, and impact-preview tools provide feedback on proposed modifications. Repair operations and their resulting DRV changes are stored in a knowledge database and used to evolve the repair skills. Experiments on seven block-level designs from the DAC26 DRC Benchmark show that EvoDRC achieves a 73.5\% overall reduction compared to the reported baseline.

AI.tldr: EvoDRC is a skill-evolution framework for automated block-level DRC repair in advanced-node physical design. It initializes repair skills from a reference design, evolves them using traceable experience from the target design, and uses LLM agents with local DRC analysis tools to fix violations. Experiments show a 73.5% DRV reduction on DAC26 benchmarks.
AI.motivation: DRC closure is a major bottleneck in advanced-node physical design. Residual design rule violations (DRVs) after detailed routing require manual engineering change order iterations, which is time-consuming and labor-intensive. Automating this process is challenging due to complex geometric interactions, connectivity preservation requirements, and the risk of introducing new violations.
AI.method: EvoDRC initializes layer-specific repair skills via knowledge distillation from an unrelated reference design, then evolves these skills using traceable repair experience from the target design. It decomposes the layout into bounded repair regions, assigns an LLM repair agent per region, and uses local DRC analysis, connectivity-checking, and impact-preview tools to provide feedback. Repair operations and DRV changes are stored in a knowledge database to iteratively evolve repair skills.
AI.result: On seven block-level designs from the DAC26 DRC Benchmark, EvoDRC achieves a 73.5% overall reduction in design rule violations compared to the reported baseline.
AI.conclusion: The proposed skill-evolution framework effectively automates block-level DRC repair by combining knowledge distillation, iterative skill evolution, and LLM-based repair agents with local analysis tools, significantly reducing DRVs without manual intervention.

title: A Systematic Benchmark of Intensity Normalisation Methods for 3D Knee MRI Segmentation and Cross-Domain Generalisability
comment: This preprint has not undergone peer review or any post-submission improvements or corrections. The Version of Record of this contribution is published in 3Oth Annual Conference on Medical Image Understanding and Analysis, MIUA 2026. Code is available at https://github.com/oliverjm1/mri_normalisation
summary: Robust out-of-the-box performance is essential for the clinical deployment of deep learning models in medical imaging. An important but underexplored factor affecting model generalisability is intensity normalisation, particularly for magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), where image intensities vary across scanners and protocols. In this study, we systematically compared seven normalisation methods and their impact on the performance of a 3D U-Net model for meniscus segmentation from knee MRI. The methods included standard scaling approaches, histogram-based techniques, and a Gaussian Mixture Model (GMM)-based method. Models were trained on the IWOAI 2019 dataset and evaluated on both internal and external test sets (SKM-TEA) to assess generalisability. Performance was similar internally but differences were significant on external data, with Z-score, Nyúl histogram matching, and CLAHE showing greater robustness than other methods. However, these differences were small compared to the significant performance drop observed between datasets. Overall, while intensity normalisation had a measurable effect on model generalisability, its impact was limited relative to the effects of domain shift, highlighting the need for complementary strategies for robust deployment.

AI.tldr: This study compares seven intensity normalization methods for MRI-based meniscus segmentation using a 3D U-Net, finding that while normalization choices affect external generalizability, the performance drop due to domain shift across datasets far outweighs these differences.
AI.motivation: Robust out-of-the-box performance is critical for clinical deployment of deep learning in medical imaging. Intensity normalization is an underexplored factor affecting model generalizability, particularly in MRI where intensities vary across scanners and protocols.
AI.method: Seven normalization methods (standard scaling, histogram-based techniques, and GMM-based method) were systematically compared using a 3D U-Net for meniscus segmentation from knee MRI. Models were trained on IWOAI 2019 and evaluated on internal and external (SKM-TEA) test sets.
AI.result: Internal performance was similar across methods, but external data showed significant differences. Z-score, Nyúl histogram matching, and CLAHE demonstrated greater robustness. However, these differences were small compared to the large performance drop between datasets.
AI.conclusion: Intensity normalization has a measurable but limited impact on model generalizability relative to domain shift, highlighting the need for complementary strategies for robust clinical deployment.

title: Anatomy of a Sound Neural Reasoner: One-Shot Amortization, First-Pass Poisoning, and Search Inertness in Clue-Rich Completion
summary: Neural solvers are built to deduce, branch, and revise intermediate states. The Lattice Deduction Transformer (LDT) appears to do exactly that. In clue-rich Sudoku, it does not: one forward pass commits essentially the entire grid (every blank cell on standard 6x6, 94-96% on augmented 9x9), turning the iterative solver into a one-shot predictor wrapped in an exact verifier. All hard-slice failures are decided before search begins, when the first pass confidently deletes a value required by the true solution. We call this first-pass poisoning. Adding learned branching, MRV, backtracking, value exclusion, and shared nogoods (CoLT) does not change which Sudoku instances are solved; it cuts repeated invalid derivations 1,497-fold. At the frozen training budget, constraint-graph attention alone matches full-CoLT accuracy, while positional tables recover only under substantially longer training, indicating an optimization and sample-efficiency advantage rather than an absolute capacity difference. The diagnosis predicts two effective interventions. Digit-permutation augmentation raises 9x9 accuracy from below 1% to 96.5 +/- 0.3 across three training seeds on a symmetry-disjoint split. Test-time union over symmetry-transformed passes raises all three hard-slice checkpoints from 72.8-78.9% to 100% without retraining. On from-scratch graph coloring, one-shot behavior disappears and search changes accuracy. In clue-rich completion, LDT-like systems are one-shot amortized predictors rather than learned search procedures: accuracy is determined by calibration and symmetry, while search primarily removes computational waste.

AI.tldr: LDT neural solvers for Sudoku act as one-shot amortized predictors rather than true iterative search procedures: first-pass poisoning fixes errors before any search begins, learned branching only reduces redundant derivations without expanding solved instances, and accuracy gains come from symmetry augmentation and calibration, not from search mechanics.
AI.motivation: To determine whether neural solvers that claim to iteratively deduce, branch, and revise actually perform learned search, or instead function as one-shot predictors whose errors are locked in at the first forward pass.
AI.method: Analyze LDT's behavior on Sudoku by measuring first-pass commitment rates, comparing full CoLT (with branching/backtracking/nogoods) against constraint-graph attention alone, testing digit-permutation augmentation and test-time symmetry union, and contrasting with graph coloring to isolate the role of clue-richness.
AI.result: LDT commits 94-96% of augmented 9x9 grid in one pass; all hard failures originate from first-pass poisoning; CoLT search cuts redundant derivations 1,497x but solves no new instances; constraint-graph attention matches full-CoLT accuracy at frozen budget; digit-permutation augmentation raises accuracy from <1% to 96.5%; test-time symmetry union achieves 100% on all hard slices without retraining; one-shot behavior disappears on graph coloring.
AI.conclusion: In clue-rich completion tasks, LDT-like systems are one-shot amortized predictors whose accuracy is determined by calibration and symmetry exploitation, not by iterative search—search only eliminates computational waste. Effective interventions target input symmetries rather than improving search procedures.

title: Global Difference Constraint Propagation for Constraint Programming
summary: Difference constraints of the form $x - y \leq d$ are well studied, with efficient algorithms for satisfaction and implication, because of their connection to shortest paths. Finite domain propagation algorithms, however, typically do not make use of these algorithms, and treat each difference constraint as a separate propagator. Propagation does guarantee completeness of solving, but can be needlessly slow. In this paper we describe how to build a (bounds consistent) global propagator for difference constraints that treats them all simultaneously. SAT modulo theory solvers have included theory solvers for difference constraints for some time. While a theory solver for difference constraints gives the basis of a global difference constraint propagator, we show how the requirements on the propagator are quite different. Crucially, we show how to explain propagations by a global difference constraint propagator, in order to use it within a lazy clause generation solver. We give experiments showing that treating difference constraints globally can substantially improve on the standard propagation approach.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a global bounds-consistent propagator for difference constraints that treats them simultaneously rather than individually, and demonstrates how to generate explanations for propagations to integrate with lazy clause generation solvers, showing significant performance improvements over standard propagation.
AI.motivation: Standard finite domain propagation treats each difference constraint as a separate propagator, which is complete but needlessly slow. The authors aim to build a unified global propagator that handles all difference constraints simultaneously for better efficiency.
AI.method: The authors construct a bounds-consistent global propagator for difference constraints, drawing inspiration from SAT modulo theory (SMT) solvers. They adapt the theory solver approach to meet the different requirements of a constraint propagation context, and crucially develop methods to explain propagations for integration into lazy clause generation (LCG) solvers.
AI.result: Experimental results demonstrate that the global treatment of difference constraints substantially outperforms the standard approach of treating each constraint with a separate propagator.
AI.conclusion: A global difference constraint propagator with explanation capabilities can significantly improve solver performance compared to individual propagators, while maintaining soundness and completeness.

title: Importance-Aware OBS Pruning for Diffusion Models
summary: We propose importance-aware pruning for diffusion models, a training-free framework that prioritizes preserving parameters critical to semantically salient image regions. To do so, we incorporate spatial importance maps -- derived from conditioning signals or model attention -- into the pruning objective. This produces parameter rankings aligned with perceptual relevance rather than uniform reconstruction error. On MS-COCO dataset, our proposed approach consistently retains subject fidelity and structural correctness at high compression ratios where conventional pruning causes visible degradation. These results demonstrate that content-aware objectives are key to perceptually faithful compression of generative models.

AI.tldr: A training-free pruning framework for diffusion models that uses spatial importance maps to preserve parameters critical to semantically salient image regions, achieving better perceptual quality at high compression ratios compared to conventional pruning methods.
AI.motivation: Standard pruning techniques for diffusion models cause visible degradation in semantically important regions at high compression ratios, due to their uniform reconstruction error objective. This motivates a need for content-aware pruning that accounts for perceptual relevance.
AI.method: Incorporates spatial importance maps (derived from conditioning signals or model attention) into the pruning objective to produce parameter rankings aligned with perceptual relevance, rather than uniform reconstruction error. The framework is training-free.
AI.result: On MS-COCO dataset, the approach consistently retains subject fidelity and structural correctness at high compression ratios where conventional pruning causes visible degradation.
AI.conclusion: Content-aware objectives are key to perceptually faithful compression of generative models, demonstrating that importance-aware pruning outperforms conventional pruning for diffusion models.

title: Expert-Guided Forecast Editing for Time-Series Foundation Models
summary: Time-series foundation models can forecast across heterogeneous domains without task-specific training, but their forecasts are fixed once produced and cannot directly incorporate task-specific expert feedback. We study expert-guided forecast editing: a frozen foundation model generates candidate future trajectories, and an expensive expert evaluator scores them to guide forecast revision. Under a tight query budget, two natural strategies sit at opposite ends: best-of-$N$ purely exploits the foundation model's predictive distribution, while optimization approaches mostly explore the forecast horizon as an unstructured high-dimensional vector. Each extreme is individually sub-optimal. We introduce \textbf{DEFT}, an expert-guided forecast editing framework that balances the two by first exploiting the foundation model's predictive samples in a decomposed trend--seasonal space, then exploring around them via component-wise refinement. DEFT queries the expert only on complete trajectories, then reuses scores for the trend and seasonal components that appeared in the queried recombinations. This lets each expert query provide structured component-level feedback while keeping the foundation model frozen. We compare DEFT against direct search approaches, including best-of-$N$, cross-entropy methods, and Bayesian optimization, under matched expert-query budgets. Across two forecasting benchmarks consisting of 78 datasets, three time-series foundation models, four feedback types, and seven query budgets, DEFT consistently improves the effectiveness of expert guidance. A molecular-dynamics case study further suggests that the same principle extends to more physically grounded feedback, supporting the hypothesis that sparse test-time guidance should be spent balancing prior exploitation with structured exploration.

AI.tldr: DEFT is an expert-guided forecast editing framework that balances exploiting a frozen foundation model's predictive distribution (via best-of-N in trend-seasonal space) with structured exploration (via component-wise refinement), consistently outperforming pure exploitation or exploration approaches under tight expert query budgets across diverse benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Time-series foundation models can forecast across domains without task-specific training, but their forecasts are static and cannot incorporate expert feedback. Expert evaluators are expensive, and existing strategies either purely exploit the foundation model's predictive distribution (best-of-N) or treat the forecast horizon as an unstructured high-dimensional vector (optimization), both individually sub-optimal under tight query budgets.
AI.method: DEFT first exploits the foundation model's predictive samples in a decomposed trend-seasonal space, then explores around them via component-wise refinement. It queries experts on complete trajectories but reuses scores for the trend and seasonal components that appeared in queried recombinations, enabling structured component-level feedback from each query while keeping the foundation model frozen.
AI.result: Across 78 datasets, three foundation models, four feedback types, and seven query budgets, DEFT consistently improves the effectiveness of expert guidance over best-of-N, cross-entropy methods, and Bayesian optimization. A molecular-dynamics case study shows the principle extends to physically grounded feedback.
AI.conclusion: Sparse test-time guidance should be spent balancing prior exploitation with structured exploration. The trend-seasonal decomposition principle generalizes beyond standard forecasting to more physically grounded feedback domains.

title: Reading and Steering Representations of Materials-Science Mechanisms in an Open-Weight Language Model
summary: Large language models can answer scientific questions, yet a correct output does not reveal whether the model represents or uses the governing physics. Here we show that materials science mechanism information in the open-weight google/gemma-4-E4B-it model has three experimentally separable forms: concepts are readable in individual hidden states, constitutive orientation is carried by controlled transformations between states, and selected internal representations causally control engineering answers. We combine matched direct and Jacobian vocabulary readouts, option-free state geometry, a 60-law counterfactual benchmark and causal interventions. In 50 held-out materials descriptions, three independently fitted Jacobian lenses reproduced concept ranks, and target-free word sets from both readouts enabled blinded identification of 9 of 10 mechanism families. A separate 72-prompt benchmark produced mechanism-specific hidden-state neighborhoods, but an exact graph audit showed that this apparent physical organization was equally explained by numerical comparison. We therefore compared otherwise identical prompts in which only the direction of the physical input was reversed, asking whether the resulting hidden-state movement followed the supplied constitutive law. These state transformations ordered direct, physically neutral and inverse laws across 60 frozen relations and correctly oriented 39 of 40 directional laws, whereas lexical controls were near chance. Bidirectional interventions shifted answer probabilities toward or away from the physically appropriate outcome across all 12 matched cases, while counterfactual state patches transferred opposing decision signals across mechanisms and answer formats. Physical relationships were therefore more visible in controlled state changes than in absolute states alone.

AI.tldr: The paper demonstrates that physical mechanism information in LLMs exists in three separable forms: hidden states (concepts), controlled state transformations (constitutive orientation), and causally controlling internal representations. Using matched readouts, counterfactual benchmarks, and causal interventions on the google/gemma-4-E4B-it model, the authors show that physical relationships are more detectable through controlled state changes than through static state analysis alone.
AI.motivation: To determine whether large language models genuinely represent and use governing physics when answering scientific questions, rather than merely producing correct outputs through surface-level statistical patterns.
AI.method: Combined matched direct and Jacobian vocabulary readouts, option-free state geometry, a 60-law counterfactual benchmark, and causal interventions. Used independently fitted Jacobian lenses, blinded identification of mechanism families, directional reversal prompts, and bidirectional causal interventions with counterfactual state patches.
AI.result: Three experimentally separable forms of mechanism information found: readable concepts in hidden states, constitutive orientation via controlled state transformations, and causally controlling representations. Jacobian lenses reproduced concept ranks; 9/10 mechanism families identified blindly. Directional laws correctly oriented (39/40), lexical controls near chance. Causal interventions shifted answer probabilities appropriately across all 12 matched cases.
AI.conclusion: Physical relationships are more visible in controlled state changes than in absolute states alone, suggesting LLMs encode physics through dynamic transformations rather than static representations.

title: GaussianSeed: Hierarchical Gaussian Seeding for High-Resolution 3D Occupancy Prediction
summary: Vision-centric 3D occupancy prediction provides dense scene representations essential for autonomous driving and robotic navigation, yet existing methods struggle to scale to high voxel resolutions due to prohibitive computational costs. To address this, we introduce GaussianSeed, a progressive multi-scale Gaussian occupancy prediction framework that organizes primitives into a coarse-to-fine hierarchy. Benefiting from this hierarchical design, GaussianSeed effectively circumvents the memory bottlenecks inherent in dense representations, successfully scaling to a $0.1\text{m}$ spatial resolution while maintaining real-time inference capabilities. To comprehensively evaluate high-resolution geometric perception, we further construct TJScenes, a panoramic six-camera occupancy dataset with highly detailed $0.1\text{m}$ annotations. Extensive experiments on Occ3D-nuScenes and TJScenes demonstrate that GaussianSeed delivers the lowest latency among all evaluated methods while maintaining highly competitive accuracy, advancing the efficiency-quality frontier of high-resolution 3D occupancy prediction.

AI.tldr: GaussianSeed introduces a progressive multi-scale Gaussian occupancy prediction framework that scales to 0.1m spatial resolution with real-time inference, and the paper constructs TJScenes, a high-resolution panoramic six-camera occupancy dataset.
AI.motivation: Existing vision-centric 3D occupancy prediction methods struggle to scale to high voxel resolutions due to prohibitive computational costs and memory bottlenecks inherent in dense representations.
AI.method: GaussianSeed organizes primitives into a coarse-to-fine hierarchical (progressive multi-scale) structure using Gaussian representations, circumventing memory bottlenecks and enabling scaling to 0.1m resolution with real-time performance.
AI.result: GaussianSeed delivers the lowest latency among all evaluated methods while maintaining highly competitive accuracy on Occ3D-nuScenes and TJScenes datasets, successfully scaling to 0.1m spatial resolution in real time.
AI.conclusion: The proposed approach advances the efficiency-quality frontier of high-resolution 3D occupancy prediction, and the new TJScenes dataset enables comprehensive evaluation of high-resolution geometric perception.

title: Efficient Clustering with Provable Guardrails for LLM Inference at Scale
comment: Accepted for presentation at ICML HiLD workshop 2026 (non-archival)
summary: Scaling LLM-based applications to millions of users is bottlenecked by the inference cost and latency of modern foundation models. A natural fix is to cluster the inputs and call the LLM only on cluster representatives, letting other members inherit the output -- but this is only safe if each member is measurably close to its representative. Existing clustering methods do not offer such per-sample quality control at scale: none jointly guarantee a minimal within-cluster similarity, exact matching of categorical attributes, and scalability to tens of millions of samples. We propose a two-stage algorithm that generates initial clusters with Mini-batch K-Means, then greedily selects representatives within each initial cluster -- a step equivalent to the Johnson-Chvatal heuristic for Set Cover over alpha-balls in embedding space. The algorithm enforces the similarity and attribute guardrails exactly by construction, and runs in $O(nd + n^2 d/K)$ time and $O(nd + n^2/K^2)$ memory for $n$ samples, feature dimension $d$, and $K$ initial clusters -- linear in $n$ when $K$ grows proportionally with $n$. We provide benchmarks against common clustering methods on internal and public datasets: our method not only delivers per-sample guardrails but also runs 10-1000x faster and scales to data sizes where most standard methods become intractable. Deployed on 38 million customers for a persona-based recommender, the clustering method cut downstream cost and latency by 50-fold while preserving personalization and unblocked the production launch.

AI.tldr: A two-stage clustering algorithm (Mini-batch K-Means + Set Cover greedy selection) that provides per-sample quality guarantees (similarity and exact attribute matching), scales to tens of millions of samples in linear time, and reduced inference cost/latency by 50x in a production LLM-based recommender serving 38 million users.
AI.motivation: Scaling LLM-based applications is bottlenecked by inference cost and latency. Clustering inputs and calling the LLM only on representatives can reduce cost, but existing clustering methods lack per-sample quality control (guaranteed within-cluster similarity and exact categorical attribute matching) at scale (tens of millions of samples).
AI.method: Two-stage algorithm: (1) Initial clusters via Mini-batch K-Means (O(nd + n²d/K) time, O(nd + n²/K²) memory). (2) Greedy representative selection within each cluster, equivalent to Johnson-Chvatal heuristic for Set Cover over α-balls in embedding space, enforcing similarity and attribute guardrails exactly.
AI.result: Outperforms common clustering methods on internal and public datasets: provides per-sample guardrails while running 10-1000x faster and scaling beyond where standard methods become intractable. Deployed on 38 million customers, cutting downstream cost and latency by 50-fold while preserving personalization.
AI.conclusion: The proposed algorithm enables safe LLM inference cost reduction at massive scale with formal quality guarantees, unblocking production deployment that was previously infeasible.

title: PRO-LONG: Programmatic Memory Enables Long-Horizon Reasoning
summary: Long-horizon tasks require sustained perception, reasoning, and exploration, and are a persistent challenge for large language model (LLM) agents. This gap is reflected in their limited performance on continual learning benchmarks such as ARC-AGI-3, especially when models are evaluated out of the box. Various agent harnesses have been proposed to close this gap, and each commits to a strategy for handling long sequences of observations, i.e., what information to save from the environment and how to load it into model context, a choice we argue is particularly consequential. Existing methods for context management face a significant tradeoff, as preserving more information makes retrieving relevant details less tractable. We propose PRO-LONG, a minimal context management framework built around programmatic memory for LLM agents in long-horizon, exploratory settings. PRO-LONG addresses the tradeoff by keeping a complete, structured interaction log and capitalizing on recent progress in coding agents to search this history efficiently. On the full ARC-AGI-3 public game set, PRO-LONG improves over a base coding agent by an average of 18.0 percentage points across frontier models, and matches or exceeds state-of-the-art specialized harnesses (up to 76.1% pass@1) while using 4.2-5.8x fewer tokens. With Fable 5, PRO-LONG achieves 97.4% best@2 at a total cost of \$1,750. Relevant code and logs are available at https://github.com/alexisfox7/PRO-LONG.

AI.tldr: PRO-LONG is a minimal context management framework using programmatic memory to improve LLM agent performance on long-horizon tasks. It maintains a complete structured interaction log and leverages coding agents to search history efficiently, achieving 18.0% average improvement over base coding agents on ARC-AGI-3, matching/exceeding SOTA specialized harnesses (up to 76.1% pass@1) while using 4.2-5.8x fewer tokens.
AI.motivation: LLM agents struggle with long-horizon tasks requiring sustained perception, reasoning, and exploration, as evidenced by limited performance on continual learning benchmarks like ARC-AGI-3. Existing context management methods face a tradeoff between preserving more information and making retrieval tractable.
AI.method: PRO-LONG is a minimal context management framework built around programmatic memory. It keeps a complete, structured interaction log and capitalizes on recent progress in coding agents to efficiently search this history.
AI.result: On full ARC-AGI-3 public game set, PRO-LONG improves over base coding agent by 18.0 percentage points across frontier models, matches/exceeds SOTA specialized harnesses (76.1% pass@1) while using 4.2-5.8x fewer tokens. With Fable 5, achieves 97.4% best@2 at total cost of $1,750.
AI.conclusion: PRO-LONG effectively addresses the context management tradeoff in long-horizon exploratory tasks, demonstrating strong performance with significantly lower token consumption compared to existing methods.

title: Factor-Informed Uncertainty Distillation for Gaze Estimation
summary: Deep gaze estimation works well in controlled capture but degrades in unconstrained settings, where systems must reject unreliable predictions. Single-pass uncertainty (e.g., heteroscedastic regression) infers uncertainty from pixels without explicit input-validity cues, while sampling based methods are often too costly for real time use. We propose Factor-Informed Uncertainty Distillation (FIUD), a teacher-student framework that aligns uncertainty with interpretable image-quality failure modes. A gradient-boosting teacher predicts expected gaze error from factors such as illumination, sharpness, eye visibility and symmetry; a neural student distills these signals via curriculum learning and ranking supervision into a lightweight single-pass uncertainty head. Across ETH-XGaze, Gaze360, and MPIIFaceGaze (>300k samples), FIUD improves uncertainty, error rank correlation and selective prediction versus deterministic and sampling-based baselines, with the largest gains in unconstrained settings.

AI.tldr: FIUD is a teacher-student framework that distills interpretable image-quality factors into a lightweight uncertainty head for gaze estimation, improving selective prediction in unconstrained settings.
AI.motivation: Deep gaze estimation degrades in unconstrained settings where unreliable predictions must be rejected. Existing single-pass uncertainty methods lack explicit input-validity cues, while sampling-based approaches are too costly for real-time use.
AI.method: FIUD uses a gradient-boosting teacher to predict expected gaze error from interpretable factors (illumination, sharpness, eye visibility, symmetry), then a neural student distills these signals via curriculum learning and ranking supervision into a lightweight single-pass uncertainty head.
AI.result: Across ETH-XGaze, Gaze360, and MPIIFaceGaze (>300k samples), FIUD improves uncertainty quality, error rank correlation, and selective prediction versus deterministic and sampling-based baselines, with largest gains in unconstrained settings.
AI.conclusion: Factor-informed uncertainty distillation effectively bridges interpretable failure modes and efficient uncertainty estimation, significantly improving gaze prediction reliability in challenging real-world conditions.

authors: Venkata Naga Sai Vishnu Rohit Pulipaka
title: How Fast Can Reward Models Score? A Systems Study of C++ and PyTorch Inference Runtimes for RLHF
summary: In RLHF pipelines, reward scoring blocks policy updates. Slow scoring bottlenecks the entire loop, since no update runs until every rollout gets a score. And yet most setups just default to PyTorch eager mode or torch.compile, no one checks if that's actually fastest. Scoring itself is small. Rollout generation eats far more of a typical RLHF step. But scoring and generation fight over the same CPU and GPU resources, so a faster scoring engine doesn't shrink step time on its own. It mainly frees up capacity generation can use instead. We built a native C++ inference engine on ONNX Runtime. First step: confirm correctness. Output matched the PyTorch reference to 5.7 x 10^-6 on CPU and 4.2 x 10^-3 on GPU, close enough to trust. Then we tested it against PyTorch eager mode, torch.compile, and FastAPI, on both CPU and GPU. CPU was decisive. Our engine beat every baseline, confidence intervals didn't even overlap. GPU gave a different view: we beat PyTorch and FastAPI, but torch.compile came out ahead. Further testing traced the speedup to ONNX Runtime itself, not C++ as a language. And batching strategy mattered more than either the language or the runtime choice, more than we expected. The results are from repeated, independent runs, since single runs just aren't reliable enough to trust.

AI.tldr: The paper builds a native C++ ONNX Runtime inference engine for RLHF scoring, finding that CPU performance decisively beats PyTorch eager mode, torch.compile, and FastAPI (non-overlapping confidence intervals), while GPU trails torch.compile. Key finding: batching strategy matters more than language or runtime choice.
AI.motivation: In RLHF pipelines, reward scoring bottlenecks policy updates because no update runs until all rollouts are scored. Yet most setups default to PyTorch eager mode or torch.compile without checking if that's actually fastest. Scoring and generation also contend for the same CPU/GPU resources, so a faster scoring engine primarily frees capacity for generation rather than shrinking step time directly.
AI.method: Built a native C++ inference engine on ONNX Runtime. Confirmed correctness by matching PyTorch reference to 5.7e-6 on CPU and 4.2e-3 on GPU. Benchmarked against PyTorch eager mode, torch.compile, and FastAPI on both CPU and GPU. Used repeated independent runs for reliability.
AI.result: CPU: The engine beat every baseline with non-overlapping confidence intervals. GPU: Beat PyTorch and FastAPI but torch.compile performed better. The speedup was traced to ONNX Runtime itself, not C++. Batching strategy had a larger impact than either language or runtime choice.
AI.conclusion: A faster scoring engine doesn't directly reduce RLHF step time but frees capacity for generation. ONNX Runtime (not C++) drives CPU gains; torch.compile remains superior on GPU. Batching strategy is the most important optimization factor.

title: TRUST-ESD: A Risk-Calibrated and Governance-Aware AI Framework for Enterprise Strategic Decision Support Under Uncertainty
comment: 15 pages, 7 figures, 4 tables. Submitted to APWeb-WAIM 2026, Danang, Vietnam, September 7-9, 2026
summary: Enterprise strategic decision support requires AI systems that are not only accurate, but also uncertainty-aware, risk-calibrated, explainable, and governance-compliant. This paper proposes TRUST-ESD, a risk-calibrated and governance-aware framework for enterprise decision support under uncertainty. TRUST-ESD evaluates feasible counterfactual strategies through predictive utility estimation, conformal uncertainty calibration, CVaR-based downside-risk scoring, risk-memory retrieval, policy-as-code governance, explainability, and human oversight. Unlike prediction-only methods that select actions by maximum expected utility, TRUST-ESD recommends strategies that balance value, reliability, risk exposure, and compliance. Experimental results show that TRUST-ESD improves risk-adjusted utility by 7.95%, reduces risk exposure by 23.22%, reduces CVaR by 23.78%, lowers calibration error by 13.89%, improves explanation fidelity by 10.90%, and increases governance compliance by 9.76% compared with strong uncertainty-aware baselines, while maintaining competitive predictive accuracy. Ablation and case-study analyses further confirm that uncertainty calibration, downside-risk scoring, risk memory, explainability, and governance validation jointly improve trustworthy enterprise decision-making.

AI.tldr: TRUST-ESD is a risk-calibrated, governance-aware framework for enterprise strategic decision support that integrates conformal uncertainty calibration, CVaR-based downside-risk scoring, risk-memory retrieval, policy-as-code governance, and explainability to recommend strategies balancing value, reliability, risk exposure, and compliance, achieving significant improvements across multiple trustworthy decision metrics.
AI.motivation: Enterprise strategic decision support requires AI systems that are not only accurate, but also uncertainty-aware, risk-calibrated, explainable, and governance-compliant — attributes beyond standard prediction-only methods that select actions by maximum expected utility.
AI.method: TRUST-ESD evaluates feasible counterfactual strategies through predictive utility estimation, conformal uncertainty calibration, CVaR-based downside-risk scoring, risk-memory retrieval, policy-as-code governance, explainability, and human oversight.
AI.result: Improves risk-adjusted utility by 7.95%, reduces risk exposure by 23.22%, reduces CVaR by 23.78%, lowers calibration error by 13.89%, improves explanation fidelity by 10.90%, and increases governance compliance by 9.76% over strong uncertainty-aware baselines, while maintaining competitive predictive accuracy.
AI.conclusion: Uncertainty calibration, downside-risk scoring, risk memory, explainability, and governance validation jointly improve trustworthy enterprise decision-making, as confirmed by ablation and case-study analyses.

title: Development of an automated, reliable, and clinically meaningful artificial intelligence (AI) tool for diagnosing cardiac disease from conventional cardiovascular magnetic resonance (CMR) images
summary: Aims: Cardiovascular magnetic resonance (CMR) imaging enables non-invasive assessment of myocardial structure, function, and pathology, but requires substantial experience in interpretation of CMR images that could be supported by artificial intelligence (AI)-based models. However, use of AI models for enhanced CMR reading is limited by labor-intensive data curation, suboptimal model performance, and unclear implementation pathways. Methods and results: We developed an automated data curation pipeline for CMR-based cardiovascular disease (CVD) diagnosis, integrating open-source locally-run large language models (LLMs) to extract diagnostic labels from narrative CMR reports and preprocessing multimodal imaging data, including cine and late-gadolinium-enhancement (LGE) CMR sequences. Three vision foundation models (DINO, VST, UMedPT) were fine-tuned across these modalities in a two-stage approach. The dataset comprised hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM), dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM), ischemic cardiomyopathy (ICM), cardiac amyloidosis (CA), and normal controls (NOR). A total of 988 curated cases were randomly divided into 742 for training and 246 for validation. Fine-tuned AI-models achieved high discriminative diagnostic performance on an independent test set comprising 1067 patients , with individual AUC-ROC values of up to 0.937 for the correct diagnosis of HCM and 0.945 for cardiac amyloidosis. Ensemble strategies combining multiple models and modalities further improved AI-based diagnostic accuracy and robustness, achieving the highest overall diagnostic performance for HCM (AUC=0.959, CI [0.936-0.978]), CA (AUC=0.966, CI [0.939-0.986]), NOR (AUC=0.872, CI [0.852-0.894]), DCM (AUC=0.848, CI [0.808-0.885]) and ICM (AUC=0.840, CI [0.809-0.868]). All training and inference code, along with the trained model weights, are publicly available on https://github.com/sinaamirrajab/CMR_CVD.

AI.tldr: This paper presents an automated pipeline combining open-source LLMs for label extraction from CMR reports with fine-tuned vision foundation models (DINO, VST, UMedPT) for cardiovascular disease diagnosis. On 1067 patients, ensemble models achieved high diagnostic performance: HCM (AUC=0.959), CA (AUC=0.966), NOR (AUC=0.872), DCM (AUC=0.848), ICM (AUC=0.840). Code and weights are publicly available.
AI.motivation: CMR imaging interpretation requires substantial expertise, and AI-based support is limited by labor-intensive data curation, suboptimal model performance, and unclear implementation pathways. This work aims to address these barriers.
AI.method: An automated data curation pipeline using open-source LLMs to extract diagnostic labels from narrative CMR reports, combined with preprocessing of cine and LGE CMR sequences. Three vision foundation models (DINO, VST, UMedPT) were fine-tuned in a two-stage approach across 988 curated cases (742 training, 246 validation). Ensemble strategies combining multiple models and modalities were employed.
AI.result: On 1067 test patients, individual models achieved AUC-ROC up to 0.937 (HCM) and 0.945 (CA). Ensemble strategies improved performance: HCM AUC=0.959, CA AUC=0.966, NOR AUC=0.872, DCM AUC=0.848, ICM AUC=0.840.
AI.conclusion: AI models fine-tuned via an automated curation pipeline can achieve high discriminative diagnostic performance for multiple CVDs from CMR data. Ensemble approaches combining models and modalities enhance robustness and accuracy. Public code/model release facilitates further development and clinical translation.

title: Koopman Dreamer: Spectrally Constrained Latent Dynamics for Stable World-Model Imagination
summary: Latent world models improve sample efficiency in continuous control by optimizing policies over imagined latent trajectories, but common neural transitions offer limited direct control over modal persistence and error accumulation in long rollouts. We propose Koopman Dreamer, a Dreamer-style world model with a spectrally constrained deterministic latent dynamics core. Its Koopman-inspired backbone uses two-dimensional rotation--scaling blocks with bounded radii to represent damping, rotation, and near-periodic modes. Linear and low-rank bilinear action terms capture global and state-dependent control effects, while stochastic-state modulation supplies local correction information. To reduce the mismatch between posterior-conditioned training and prior-only imagination, the model combines posterior-conditioned EMA teacher targets with one-step consistency, multi-step rollout, and open-loop observation-prediction objectives. We further derive a multi-step rollout-error bound that separates amplification by the spectral backbone and bilinear interaction from the additive effects of stochastic-state mismatch and modeling residuals, clarifying the trade-off between error attenuation and long-term information retention. Experimental results on proprioceptive continuous-control tasks from the DeepMind Control Suite and UAV-LiDAR autonomous navigation demonstrate that Koopman Dreamer improves the stability of long-horizon latent rollouts and achieves stronger closed-loop control performance on tasks that rely on high-quality multi-step imagination.

AI.tldr: Koopman Dreamer improves long-horizon latent rollouts in model-based RL by using spectrally constrained Koopman dynamics (2D rotation-scaling blocks) combined with consistency and multi-step objectives, achieving stronger control on continuous tasks.
AI.motivation: Standard Dreamer-style world models suffer from limited control over modal persistence and error accumulation during long latent rollouts. The authors aim to improve stability and long-term prediction quality in imagination-based policy optimization.
AI.method: Proposes a Koopman-inspired deterministic backbone using bounded 2D rotation-scaling blocks to represent damping, rotation, and near-periodic modes under spectral constraints. Combines linear/low-rank bilinear action terms with stochastic-state modulation. Training uses posterior-conditioned EMA teacher targets with one-step consistency, multi-step rollout, and open-loop prediction objectives. Derives a multi-step rollout-error bound separating spectral, bilinear, stochastic, and residual error sources.
AI.result: On DeepMind Control Suite and UAV-LiDAR autonomous navigation tasks, Koopman Dreamer improves stability of long-horizon latent rollouts and achieves stronger closed-loop control performance compared to baselines, especially on tasks requiring high-quality multi-step imagination.
AI.conclusion: Spectral constraints on the latent dynamics backbone, combined with tailored multi-step training objectives, effectively mitigate error accumulation and improve the quality of imagined trajectories for model-based continuous control.

title: CUSUM-Shaped Inference-Time Monitoring and Targeted Re-Decoding for Quantized Small Language Model Reasoning
summary: Quantized small autoregressive reasoning models can enter long, repetitive, or unproductive trajectories, yet inference-time compute is usually allocated without observing how a trajectory develops. Building on an earlier token-level e-CUSUM controller, we develop MGT-B (Monitoring-Guided Test-time Backtracking), a revised external controller that maps overlapping windows of pre-sampling uncertainty and degeneration features to position-conditional empirical tail probabilities, accumulates mixture betting factors with a CUSUM-shaped reset, and responds to an alarm by estimating a rollback point, restoring token and key-value-cache state, and performing constrained re-decoding. To audit whether the effect persists on problem identities first observed after the manual choice of log threshold h = 10, we retrospectively exclude 260 IDs present in pre-threshold artifacts and retain the chronologically first post-threshold pair for each remaining ID, yielding a 240-pair chronology-audit set. On this set, accuracy changes from 82/240 to 88/240 (+2.50 percentage points; 13 corrections, 7 regressions; exact McNemar p = 0.2632; paired bootstrap 95% interval [-1.25, +6.25]). A broader 467-pair historical-coverage set of seed-matched pairs changes accuracy from 146/467 to 167/467 (+4.50 points; McNemar p = 0.000753), but includes 200 seed-1 IDs available before or during threshold selection and is reported only as an exploratory estimate. All 316 no-alarm outputs in the 467-pair set are identical to vanilla, while the 151 alarmed trajectories contain 29 corrections and 8 regressions. Neither analysis is confirmatory, and the empirical factors are not established as a valid e-process or e-detector. The results support a selective monitoring-and-repair mechanism for the studied MATH-500 setting, rather than a general or theoretically certified reasoning improvement.

AI.tldr: MGT-B is a monitoring-guided test-time backtracking controller that detects and corrects unproductive autoregressive reasoning trajectories by analyzing uncertainty and degeneration features, showing modest accuracy improvements (2.5-4.5 percentage points) on MATH-500 but with notable limitations in statistical significance and generalizability.
AI.motivation: Quantized small autoregressive reasoning models often produce long, repetitive, or unproductive trajectories, yet inference-time compute is typically allocated without monitoring how a trajectory develops, motivating the need for a selective monitoring-and-repair mechanism.
AI.method: MGT-B extends an earlier token-level e-CUSUM controller by: (1) mapping overlapping windows of pre-sampling uncertainty and degeneration features to position-conditional empirical tail probabilities, (2) accumulating mixture betting factors with a CUSUM-shaped reset, and (3) responding to alarms by estimating rollback points, restoring token and KV-cache state, and performing constrained re-decoding. A retrospective chronology-audit set (240 pairs) excludes pre-threshold IDs to reduce data leakage.
AI.result: On the 240-pair chronology-audit set: accuracy 82/240 → 88/240 (+2.50 pp, 13 corrections, 7 regressions, McNemar p=0.2632, bootstrap 95% CI [-1.25, +6.25]). On the 467-pair historical-coverage set: 146/467 → 167/467 (+4.50 pp, McNemar p=0.000753) but includes 200 seed-1 IDs available during threshold selection. All 316 no-alarm outputs are identical to vanilla; 151 alarmed trajectories contain 29 corrections and 8 regressions.
AI.conclusion: Results support a selective monitoring-and-repair mechanism for the MATH-500 setting but not a general or theoretically certified reasoning improvement. Neither analysis is confirmatory, and empirical factors are not established as a valid e-process or e-detector.

title: ENTRAP-VL: A Taxonomic Probe for Dual Contextual Entrainment in Vision-Language Models
summary: Contextual entrainment is the tendency of a model to let auxiliary context in its input pull its output, independently of whether that context is relevant, true, or even meaningful. Recently, it has been identified and given a mechanistic account in unimodal language models. Whether and how it manifests in vision-language models (VLMs) is, by contrast, largely unexamined, and the field lacks a purpose-built instrument with which to investigate it. We take the position that studying contextual entrainment in VLMs requires more than porting an existing text-only benchmark to the multimodal setting: it requires a taxonomically structured, dual-modality instrument whose conditions are constructed around the item at hand (the depicted image in the textual stream, the textual query in the visual stream). We argue that the move to VLMs is substantive rather than incremental. It makes entrainment a dual phenomenon, drivable independently by textual and by visual context, and it opens a veracity distinction (context that is false of the depicted scene yet possible in the world) that has no counterpart in the unimodal, world-knowledge-only formulation of prior work. To make this position concrete and actionable, we introduce ENTRAP-VL (ENTRainment Assessment Probe for Vision and Language), a manually curated dataset of 1,500 items across eight categories, organized by a taxonomy that spans two axes, i.e., the association of context with the item and its relationship to truth, and split into a textual-entrainment stream (eight context conditions) and a visual-entrainment stream (three context conditions). We do not claim to measure entrainment in any particular model; we provide the instrument, the taxonomy that motivates it, and the evaluation protocols it enables, so that the community can investigate the phenomenon rigorously. We will release the dataset and its documentation publicly.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces ENTRAP-VL, a taxonomically structured, dual-modality dataset for investigating contextual entrainment (the tendency of models to let auxiliary context pull their output) in vision-language models, going beyond simple porting of text-only benchmarks to the multimodal setting.
AI.motivation: Contextual entrainment has been studied in unimodal language models but remains largely unexamined in vision-language models (VLMs). The authors argue that studying this phenomenon in VLMs requires more than adapting text-only benchmarks—it needs a purpose-built, taxonomically structured instrument that accounts for dual-modality (textual and visual) context and introduces a veracity distinction not present in prior unimodal work.
AI.method: The authors construct ENTRAP-VL, a manually curated dataset of 1,500 items across eight categories, organized by a taxonomy spanning two axes: (1) the association of context with the item and (2) its relationship to truth. The dataset is split into a textual-entrainment stream (eight context conditions) and a visual-entrainment stream (three context conditions). They release the instrument, taxonomy, and evaluation protocols without claiming to measure entrainment in any specific model.
AI.result: The primary result is the creation of ENTRAP-VL itself—a structured, dual-modality probe for studying contextual entrainment in VLMs. The taxonomy reveals that multimodal entrainment is a dual phenomenon drivable independently by textual and visual context, and introduces a veracity distinction (context false of the depicted scene but possible in the world) absent in unimodal settings.
AI.conclusion: The move to studying contextual entrainment in VLMs is substantive rather than incremental, requiring taxonomically structured instruments like ENTRAP-VL. The authors provide this resource to the community for rigorous investigation of the phenomenon, without making claims about specific model behaviors.

title: Analytic Distribution of Classifier-Free Guidance for Schedule Design
summary: Classifier-free guidance (CFG) is the default mechanism for conditional generation in diffusion models, but the distribution sampled by its deterministic guided dynamics is not captured by the usual product-distribution heuristic $p_0^ωq_0^{1-ω}$. We analyze CFG through the probability flow ODE and derive exact analytic path-integral representations of the induced distributions for both constant and time-dependent guidance. The resulting formulas show that CFG modifies $p_{t_0}$ by an exponential path-integral correction, and that a time-dependent schedule enters this correction through the weight $ω(t)-1$. This characterization explains how score discrepancies accumulate along sampling trajectories and motivates Distribution-Guided CFG (DG-CFG), a schedule that balances timestep contributions while accounting for signal strength and low-noise score-error amplification. A toy model with analytic scores closely verifies the predicted distributions. On Stable Diffusion~1.5, DG-CFG improves generation and yields a stronger diversity--fidelity trade-off across guidance strengths, with especially clear gains when strong guidance causes saturation and quality degradation in constant and heuristic schedules. Across NFE budgets, DG-CFG reaches fixed image-quality targets with fewer sampling steps, reducing the sampling cost needed to achieve target metrics.

AI.tldr: The paper derives exact analytic path-integral representations for classifier-free guidance (CFG) in diffusion models, showing it modifies distributions via exponential corrections. This leads to Distribution-Guided CFG (DG-CFG), a time-dependent schedule that balances timestep contributions and accounts for score-error amplification, improving diversity-fidelity trade-offs on Stable Diffusion 1.5 and reducing required sampling steps.
AI.motivation: Current understanding of CFG via the product-distribution heuristic $p_0^\omega q_0^{1-\omega}$ is inaccurate for the actual deterministic guided dynamics. The paper aims to derive exact distributional characterizations of CFG to better understand its behavior and motivate improved guidance schedules.
AI.method: The authors analyze CFG through the probability flow ODE framework, deriving exact analytic path-integral representations for induced distributions under constant and time-dependent guidance. Based on this analysis, they propose DG-CFG, a schedule that balances timestep contributions while accounting for signal strength and low-noise score-error amplification. Validation uses a toy model with analytic scores and experiments on Stable Diffusion 1.5.
AI.result: DG-CFG improves generation quality with stronger diversity-fidelity trade-offs across guidance strengths on Stable Diffusion 1.5, particularly when strong guidance causes saturation. DG-CFG reaches fixed image-quality targets with fewer sampling steps across NFE budgets, reducing sampling cost.
AI.conclusion: The exact path-integral formulation provides a principled understanding of CFG dynamics, and the derived DG-CFG schedule offers practical improvements in efficiency and quality-quality balance for diffusion model sampling.

title: PoTRE: Test-Time Reasoning inspired by Cognitive Heterogeneity
comment: Accepted at Transactions on Machine Learning Research (TMLR 2026)
summary: While Large Language Models (LLMs) excel at many tasks, they frequently struggle with complex reasoning that requires long-horizon planning and iterative error correction. Furthermore, standard single-stream prompting proves brittle when models encounter novel abstractions or rigorous domain constraints. We introduce PoTRE (Poly-Topological Reasoning Ensembles), a heterogeneous framework that decouples inference into four agents: (1) Adversarial Refinement Agent, (2) Hierarchical strategic Planning Agent, (3) Spectrum Search Agent, and (4) Direct Chain Agent. A final Task-Adaptive Aggregation Layer dynamically reconciles these perspectives -- via final candidate selection, semantic synthesis, or neuro-symbolic verification -- to produce a robust global solution. We evaluate PoTRE on three frontier benchmarks: ARC-AGI-2, Humanity's Last Exam (HLE), and PRBench Finance. PoTRE achieves state-of-the-art accuracy of 49.92% on HLE, surpassing the previous best official score. We demonstrate that this architectural heterogeneity achieves improved reasoning performance using similar or fewer inference tokens compared to heavily scaled homogeneous baselines.

AI.tldr: PoTRE is a heterogeneous multi-agent framework using four specialized reasoning agents (Adversarial Refinement, Hierarchical Planning, Spectrum Search, Direct Chain) with a Task-Adaptive Aggregation Layer, achieving SOTA 49.92% on HLE with improved reasoning performance using fewer tokens than scaled homogeneous baselines.
AI.motivation: LLMs struggle with complex reasoning requiring long-horizon planning and iterative error correction, and standard single-stream prompting is brittle under novel abstractions or rigorous domain constraints.
AI.method: PoTRE decouples inference into four agents (Adversarial Refinement, Hierarchical Strategic Planning, Spectrum Search, Direct Chain) with a final Task-Adaptive Aggregation Layer that reconciles perspectives via candidate selection, semantic synthesis, or neuro-symbolic verification.
AI.result: Achieves SOTA 49.92% on HLE, surpassing previous best official score. Demonstrates improved reasoning performance with similar or fewer inference tokens compared to heavily scaled homogeneous baselines.
AI.conclusion: Architectural heterogeneity in multi-agent reasoning frameworks can outperform homogeneous scaling for complex reasoning tasks, achieving higher accuracy with greater token efficiency.

title: RIM: A Retrieval-In-Matching Framework for Cross-Domain Global Visual Localization of UAVs
comment: 56 pages, 10 figures, and 18 tables. Supplementary material is included
summary: Global visual localization of unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) using remote-sensing reference maps has attracted increasing attention. However, acquisition-time and imaging-platform differences between UAV and reference imagery induce substantial cross-domain appearance and viewpoint shifts, challenging robust six-degree-of-freedom (6-DoF) pose estimation. We address these shifts by sampling UAV-viewpoint reference views from Google 3D Tiles across locations, altitudes, and orientations. A two-stage cross-domain fine-tuning recipe adapts SALAD using pose-near positives and geographically distant hard negatives, while local geometric consistency re-ranks the Top-K candidates. We further propose Retrieval-In-Matching (RIM), which freezes the adapted DINOv2-B retriever and distils a local-descriptor decoder that reuses its token field alongside a shallow VGG19 detail stream. One query-side DINOv2-B forward thus serves both SALAD retrieval and local description, eliminating a second foundation-model backbone while preserving retrieval descriptors by construction. We evaluate RIM zero-shot on the reconstructed EPFL Urbanscape and self-collected Chang'an Park datasets, both geographically disjoint from the training data. RIM outperforms ten recent retrieval baseline families. At 25/50 m under the full 3D distance metric, it improves Recall@1 over SALAD by 8.55/13.77 percentage points on EPFL and 4.45/8.94 points on Park. At Top-K=5, the complete measured localization query, including retrieval, candidate matching, and robust geometric verification, takes 67.9 ms end-to-end: 1.8 times faster than the strongest separate sparse-matching baseline and over 40 times faster than RoMa, while achieving comparable re-ranking accuracy. These results establish an efficient and deployable pipeline for UAV global visual localization in GNSS-challenged environments.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes RIM (Retrieval-In-Matching), a method for UAV global visual localization that uses Google 3D Tiles to sample UAV-viewpoint reference views and a two-stage cross-domain fine-tuning recipe for SALAD with pose-near positives and hard negatives. RIM freezes an adapted DINOv2-B retriever and distills a local-descriptor decoder that reuses its token field alongside a shallow VGG19 detail stream, enabling a single query-side DINOv2-B forward pass to serve both retrieval and local description. Evaluated zero-shot on EPFL Urbanscape and Chang'an Park datasets, RIM achieves significant Recall@1 improvements over SALAD (8.55/13.77 pp on EPFL, 4.45/8.94 pp on Park at 25/50m), and a complete end-to-end localization query takes 67.9 ms — 1.8× faster than the strongest sparse-matching baseline and 40× faster than RoMa.
AI.motivation: Address acquisition-time and imaging-platform differences between UAV and reference imagery that cause cross-domain appearance and viewpoint shifts, which challenge robust 6-DoF pose estimation for UAV global visual localization using remote-sensing reference maps.
AI.method: (1) Sample UAV-viewpoint reference views from Google 3D Tiles across locations, altitudes, and orientations. (2) Two-stage cross-domain fine-tuning of SALAD using pose-near positives and geographically distant hard negatives, with local geometric consistency re-ranking of Top-K candidates. (3) Proposed RIM: freeze adapted DINOv2-B retriever, distill a local-descriptor decoder that reuses its token field alongside a shallow VGG19 detail stream, so one query-side DINOv2-B forward serves both SALAD retrieval and local description.
AI.result: Zero-shot evaluation on EPFL Urbanscape and Chang'an Park: RIM outperforms ten retrieval baseline families; at 25/50m under full 3D distance metric, improves Recall@1 over SALAD by 8.55/13.77 pp (EPFL) and 4.45/8.94 pp (Park). Complete end-to-end localization (Top-K=5) takes 67.9 ms — 1.8× faster than the strongest separate sparse-matching baseline and >40× faster than RoMa.
AI.conclusion: RIM establishes an efficient and deployable pipeline for UAV global visual localization in GNSS-challenged environments, eliminating a second foundation-model backbone while preserving retrieval descriptors by construction and achieving both superior accuracy and speed.

title: The World Model Remembers, the Actor Forgets: Dream Rehearsal for Continual Model-Based RL
comment: 11 pages, 2 figures. Code, pre-registration trail, and run data: https://github.com/gurpnijjer/dream-rehearsal
summary: Model-based reinforcement-learning agents of the DreamerV3 family forget catastrophically when trained on task sequences, even when an unbounded replay buffer preserves every earlier experience. We ask a question the continual-RL literature has assumed an answer to but never measured: which component forgets? Under never-clear replay, pre-registered component-level probes (n=3 seeds throughout) show that the world model retains essentially everything measurable about old tasks -- reward discrimination (retention ratio ~1.0), value estimates, and termination structure -- while the actor's behavior collapses. Forgetting in this regime is a channel problem, not a memory problem. We demonstrate this by intervention: with the world model frozen and identical imagined rollouts, reinforcement learning in imagination fails to recover a lost skill (0/3 seeds), while supervised self-imitation on the world model's own graded dreams recovers it on 3/3 seeds with zero environment interaction. Interleaved during training, this graded dream rehearsal yields a task-label-free, parameter-constant continual learner: 3/3 four-task chains retained where plain replay passes 0/3, 3/3 eight-task chains, and consistent gains over matched real-episode cloning (paired difference +0.13, bootstrap 95% CI [0.07, 0.24], complete seed separation). The dream-grading step is load-bearing: we characterize two scoring failure modes, provide an offline selection gauge that caught both before they contaminated results, and give a realized-first grading rule that closes them. All experiments were pre-registered with committed protocols; every refuted hypothesis is reported.

AI.tldr: DreamerV3 agents forget catastrophically on task sequences not due to world model failure but actor collapse. Freezing the world model and using graded dream rehearsal (self-imitation on the model's own dreams) recovers skills without environment interaction and enables continual learning across 4-8 task chains where plain replay fails entirely.
AI.motivation: To identify which component of model-based RL (DreamerV3) causes catastrophic forgetting in continual learning settings, challenging the assumption that replay buffer insufficiency is the root cause.
AI.method: Pre-registered component-level probing with n=3 seeds; world model freezing intervention; graded dream rehearsal (self-imitation on graded dreams) compared to plain replay and real-episode cloning; offline selection gauge for scoring failure modes.
AI.result: World model retains reward discrimination (~1.0 retention), value estimates, and termination structure; actor collapses. Frozen world model + standard imagination fails (0/3 seeds), graded dream rehearsal recovers skills (3/3). Graded dream rehearsal yields 3/3 four-task and eight-task chains; plain replay passes 0/3. Consistent gains over real-episode cloning (paired diff +0.13, 95% CI [0.07, 0.24]).
AI.conclusion: Forgetting in continual model-based RL is a channel (actor) problem, not a memory (world model) problem. Graded dream rehearsal provides a task-label-free, parameter-constant continual learning method. Dream-grading is critical; two failure modes identified and mitigated.

title: Train the Model, Not the Reader: Decodability Supervision for Verifiable Activation Explanations
summary: Natural-language autoencoders score explanations of hidden activations by reconstruction: an explanation is deemed faithful if the activation can be regenerated from it. The test is structurally insensitive to individual false claims: if flipping a claim does not change the reconstruction, the claim is never penalized. We show the test is passed in two ways, neither faithful. On a released Qwen-2.5-7B verbalizer, explanations reconstruct well above chance while ~2% of specific claims are reconstruction-dependent, so the score tracks gist, not specific facts. Under exact synthetic ground truth, the standard recipe develops co-adapted private codes (false wording the reconstruction depends on) in 5/5 runs, and fixes that leave the target model unchanged do not help. We contribute two audit protocols, the grounded-vs-true cross and the evaluator swap, and RECAP (Readable Encodings via Co-trained Auxiliary Predictors): linear heads trained alongside the target model to keep designated content decodable. On RECAP-trained sandbox models, fresh verbalizers state the designated content truly and the codes vanish, at a +0.001-nat cost. This replicates on a pretrained Pythia-160M: the content becomes reliably probe-decodable, though a fresh verbalizer conveys it only in part (truth 0.44-0.46 vs a near-zero control). For interpretability, high reconstruction does not certify individual claims.
