EVO represents each candidate as a complete schedule over the block-timestep lattice. Thus, redundant transformer computations during iterative denoising can be skipped through cache reuse while preserving closed-loop rollout performance. To make the search practical, EVO introduces redundancy-aware initialization, which seeds the population with promising schedules, and target-conditioned early stopping, which verifies and terminates once a desired performance target is reached. The offline-optimized schedule can be directly plugged into pretrained diffusion policies without retraining. Extensive manipulation benchmarks show that EVO preserves near-full performance while substantially reducing computation, achieving up to 8.05x action-generation speedup and reducing FLOPs from 15.77G to as low as 1.96G. Source code is available at https://github.com/pillom/EVO.

AI.tldr: EVO is a training-free acceleration framework for diffusion policies that uses evolutionary search to globally schedule cache refreshes across the block-timestep lattice, achieving up to 8.05x speedup and reducing FLOPs from 15.77G to 1.96G while preserving near-full performance.
AI.motivation: Cache-based methods for accelerating diffusion policies have suboptimal performance-efficiency trade-offs because existing training-free schedules allocate computation uniformly across blocks, ignoring heterogeneous redundancy across different blocks.
AI.method: EVO uses evolutionary search to globally optimize cache refresh schedules over the block-timestep lattice. It introduces redundancy-aware initialization to seed promising schedules and target-conditioned early stopping for efficient search termination. The optimized schedule is plugged into pretrained diffusion policies without retraining.
AI.result: Up to 8.05x action-generation speedup, FLOPs reduction from 15.77G to 1.96G, with near-full performance preserved across extensive manipulation benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: EVO demonstrates that globally optimized, heterogeneous cache schedules can substantially accelerate diffusion-based visuomotor policies without retraining, offering a practical training-free solution for real-time deployment.

title: Generalized Kalman filter based temporal difference reinforcement learning
summary: In this paper, we present a generalized temporal-difference (TD) reinforcement learning framework based on the theory of conditional expectations. The value and action-value (Q-value) functions are treated as uncertain quantities, and their estimation is formulated as a stochastic inference problem. Unlike classical Kalman-based temporal-difference learning, which relies on linear-Gaussian assumptions, the proposed formulation is derived directly from the conditional expectation framework and naturally extends to nonlinear models and non-Gaussian probability distributions. The proposed method recursively estimates not only the conditional expectation of the value function but also its second probabilistic moment, thereby quantifying the uncertainty associated with the learned value function throughout the learning process. To obtain a computationally tractable algorithm, the stochastic problem is discretized using either polynomial chaos expansions or ensemble-based approximations, providing efficient representations of the underlying random variables. The proposed framework is demonstrated on two optimal control problems: a linear mass--spring--damper system and a nonlinear heat conduction problem in a closed cavity. The numerical examples illustrate the capability of the proposed method to accurately estimate both the value function and its associated uncertainty, while extending classical Kalman-based temporal-difference learning to a broader class of stochastic systems.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a generalized temporal-difference reinforcement learning framework based on conditional expectation theory, extending Kalman-based TD learning to nonlinear and non-Gaussian systems by using polynomial chaos expansions or ensemble approximations to estimate both value functions and their uncertainty.
AI.motivation: Classical Kalman-based temporal-difference learning relies on linear-Gaussian assumptions, limiting its applicability. The authors aim to develop a more general framework that naturally extends to nonlinear models and non-Gaussian probability distributions.
AI.method: The value and Q-value functions are treated as uncertain quantities and formulated as a stochastic inference problem using conditional expectations. The stochastic problem is discretized via polynomial chaos expansions or ensemble-based approximations to achieve computational tractability, enabling recursive estimation of both the conditional expectation and second probabilistic moment of the value function.
AI.result: Demonstrated on a linear mass-spring-damper system and a nonlinear heat conduction problem in a closed cavity, the method accurately estimates both the value function and its associated uncertainty.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework successfully extends classical Kalman-based temporal-difference learning to a broader class of stochastic systems, including nonlinear and non-Gaussian settings, while providing uncertainty quantification throughout learning.

title: Toward Reliable RGB-D Semantic Segmentation: Handling Missing Modalities via Condition Dropout
summary: RGB-D semantic segmentation has achieved remarkable progress, yet most models assume that RGB and depth are always available. In practice, failures or occlusions of surveillance sensors often remove one modality. Although RGB or depth alone can contain sufficient cues, models trained only on full-modality inputs fail to exploit the remaining modality once one is missing, causing severe degradation. We tackle this issue with a simple continued-training paradigm, \emph{Condition Dropout (ConD)}, which mitigates degradation while preserving full-modality accuracy. Starting from a pretrained RGB-D model, ConD adds a second stage that randomly simulates complete, RGB-missing, and depth-missing inputs, freezes the original encoders, and trains copied encoders with zero-initialized feature injection. Experiments on NYU-Depth V2 and SUN RGB-D show that ConD improves robustness under missing modalities and even yields slight gains when modalities are complete. Our code will be made publicly available upon acceptance.

AI.tldr: Condition Dropout (ConD) is a continued-training paradigm that improves RGB-D semantic segmentation models' robustness to missing modalities by randomly simulating sensor failures, freezing original encoders, and training copied encoders with zero-initialized feature injection, achieving performance gains even when both modalities are present.
AI.motivation: RGB-D semantic segmentation models suffer severe performance degradation when one modality (RGB or depth) is missing due to sensor failures or occlusions, as they are trained only on full-modality inputs and fail to exploit the remaining modality.
AI.method: ConD adds a second continued-training stage to a pretrained RGB-D model that: (1) randomly simulates complete, RGB-missing, and depth-missing inputs; (2) freezes the original encoders; (3) trains copied encoders with zero-initialized feature injection to handle missing modalities.
AI.result: Experiments on NYU-Depth V2 and SUN RGB-D show ConD improves robustness under missing modalities and yields slight gains even when both modalities are complete.
AI.conclusion: ConD effectively mitigates performance degradation from missing modalities in RGB-D segmentation while preserving full-modality accuracy, offering a simple and practical solution for real-world sensor failure scenarios.

title: Zero-Shot Heart Rate Variability Forecasting from Consumer Wearables Using Time Series Foundation Models
comment: Accepted to Computing in Cardiology (CinC) 2026. 4 pages, 2 figures, 3 tables
summary: Short-term Heart Rate Variability (HRV) forecasting could provide clinicians with actionable lead time for detecting autonomic dysfunction and adverse cardiac events. Consumer wearable devices generate fragmented, artifact-rich HRV signals that challenge conventional forecasting approaches. In this study, we evaluated the forecasting ability of three Time Series Foundation Models (TSFMs), TimesFM, Chronos, and MOIRAI, against traditional baselines (Mean, Exponential Smoothing, and Exponentially Weighted Moving Average) on real-world wearable data collected from 49 healthy individuals. To address data fragmentation, we introduce a variability-preserving imputation method that augments linear interpolation with locally adaptive stochastic noise, retaining physiological dynamics essential for accurate forecasting. The results show that TSFMs outperformed all baselines without fine-tuning, achieving average Mean Absolute Scaled Error (MASE) between 0.81 and 0.87 across TSFMs and both context lengths (32 and 64 time steps), with Chronos and TimesFM as the top models, though MOIRAI showed limited gains over baselines. With up to a 2-hour forecast horizon, the results establish a baseline for TSFMs' performance on a real-world dataset, highlighting domain-specific fine-tuning as a promising direction for clinical deployment.

AI.tldr: This study evaluates three Time Series Foundation Models (TimesFM, Chronos, MOIRAI) against traditional baselines for short-term HRV forecasting using real-world wearable data from 49 individuals, introducing a variability-preserving imputation method to handle data fragmentation. TSFMs outperformed baselines without fine-tuning (MASE 0.81-0.87), with Chronos and TimesFM leading.
AI.motivation: Short-term HRV forecasting could provide clinicians with actionable lead time for detecting autonomic dysfunction and adverse cardiac events, but consumer wearable devices generate fragmented, artifact-rich HRV signals that challenge conventional forecasting approaches.
AI.method: Evaluated three TSFMs (TimesFM, Chronos, MOIRAI) against traditional baselines (Mean, Exponential Smoothing, EWMA) on real-world wearable data from 49 healthy individuals. Introduced a variability-preserving imputation method combining linear interpolation with locally adaptive stochastic noise to handle data fragmentation.
AI.result: TSFMs outperformed all baselines without fine-tuning, achieving average MASE between 0.81 and 0.87 across both context lengths (32 and 64 time steps). Chronos and TimesFM were top models; MOIRAI showed limited gains over baselines. Forecast horizon up to 2 hours.
AI.conclusion: Established a baseline for TSFMs' performance on real-world wearable HRV data, highlighting domain-specific fine-tuning as a promising direction for clinical deployment.

title: Test-Time Training for Modality Order Consistency in Vision-Language Models
summary: We find that vision-language models are sensitive to a specific semantically irrelevant change: the order in which the image and question are presented. Across three models and three benchmarks, image first prompting consistently outperforms question-first prompting, revealing a repeatable modality order failure. We use this gap to design an order-consistent test-time training method. Our method substantially closes the modality-order gap across all evaluated settings. Surprisingly, it also yields consistent improvements in the stronger image-first branch over the baseline, hence bootstrapping both orderings toward mutual consistency. Activation patching localizes the ordering failure to a narrow mid-network region where representations diverge sharply between prompt orders. We find that the test-time training method repairs this misalignment across layers. Together, our results identify modality-order sensitivity as a circuit-level failure in VLMs and demonstrate that simple, asymmetric test-time adaptation can effectively mitigate it and even improve performance over the baseline.

AI.tldr: VLMs are sensitive to the order of image and question presentation (image-first outperforms question-first). The authors propose an order-consistent test-time training method that closes this gap, improves the stronger image-first branch, and localizes the failure to a mid-network region where representations diverge.
AI.motivation: Vision-language models exhibit sensitivity to the modality order (image vs. question first), which is a semantically irrelevant change that degrades performance and reveals a systematic failure in how VLMs process multimodal inputs.
AI.method: The authors (1) systematically evaluate modality-order sensitivity across 3 models and 3 benchmarks, (2) design an order-consistent test-time training method to align representations across orderings, and (3) use activation patching to localize the failure to a narrow mid-network region.
AI.result: Image-first prompting consistently outperforms question-first. The test-time training method substantially closes the modality-order gap, improves even the stronger image-first branch, and repairs the misalignment across layers identified via activation patching.
AI.conclusion: Modality-order sensitivity is a circuit-level failure in VLMs, and simple asymmetric test-time adaptation can effectively mitigate it while also improving baseline performance.

title: Look Less, Think Faster: Joint Token-Compute Adaptation for Multimodal LLMs
summary: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have recently demonstrated strong performance across vision-language tasks. However, their high inference cost, arising from both the large number of input visual tokens and the heavy computation of the large language model (LLM), remains a key barrier to practical deployment. Recent work attempts to reduce the cost by adaptively optimizing individual dimensions, e.g., pruning redundant visual tokens or skipping LLM layers and heads. Nonetheless, prior approaches typically treat these dimensions independently and overlook a fundamental coupling: the available compute resources must be dynamically allocated across all dimensions based on the input content. To bridge the gap, we propose SmartVL, a unified adaptive inference framework that jointly controls vision token number and model compute capability in response to varying input contents and compute budgets. SmartVL introduces a vision-side token controller that dynamically selects informative visual tokens and an LLM-side compute controller that adaptively adjusts LLM computation. Importantly, these controllers are trained to coordinate with each other so that the overall inference cost satisfies a target budget. To allow this joint scheduling, we connect the controllers using a shared budget encoding and leverage a differentiable latency estimator for end-to-end training. This design enables SmartVL to learn cross-stage allocation strategies that adapt to both input complexity and runtime compute constraints. Experiments across multiple MLLM benchmarks demonstrate that, with joint scheduling, SmartVL consistently outperforms prior adaptive methods and achieves superior accuracy-efficiency Pareto frontiers. Project page: https://www.schaterji.io/publications/2026/jointtokencompute.

AI.tldr: SmartVL is a unified adaptive inference framework for Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) that jointly controls visual token selection and LLM computation allocation under varying compute budgets, outperforming prior methods that optimize these dimensions independently.
AI.motivation: MLLMs suffer from high inference costs due to large numbers of input visual tokens and heavy LLM computation. Prior work reduces cost by optimizing individual dimensions (e.g., pruning tokens or skipping layers/heads) but overlooks the fundamental coupling between these dimensions—compute resources must be dynamically allocated across all dimensions based on input content.
AI.method: SmartVL introduces a vision-side token controller for dynamic visual token selection and an LLM-side compute controller for adaptive LLM computation adjustment. The controllers are connected via shared budget encoding and trained end-to-end using a differentiable latency estimator, enabling coordinated joint scheduling that respects target compute budgets.
AI.result: Across multiple MLLM benchmarks, SmartVL with joint scheduling consistently outperforms prior adaptive methods and achieves superior accuracy-efficiency Pareto frontiers.
AI.conclusion: Jointly optimizing visual token count and LLM computation under a unified budget constraint yields better accuracy-efficiency trade-offs than independent optimization of each dimension.

title: Evaluating and Mitigating Gender Bias in Pre-trained Embeddings for ML-based Recruitment
comment: Accepted for presentation at the TRUST-AI 2026 Workshop, held in conjunction with IJCAI/ECAI 2026, Bremen, Germany
summary: AI-based recruitment systems that rely on machine learning models trained on historical CV data, risk perpetuating and amplifying social biases. A key challenge arises in unstructured CV text, where pre-trained language model embeddings may infer sensitive attributes such as gender even after explicit indicators are removed. In this paper, we evaluate nine pre-trained embedding models on the synthetic FairCVdb dataset, analyzing the informativeness of their embeddings for applicant scoring and their susceptibility to gender leakage, on both original and gender-scrubbed biographies. We further use a multi-task adversarial learning framework with gradient reversal to predict applicant suitability while suppressing gender information from learned representations. Finally, we use a multi-objective Pareto-front-based model selection to balance predictive utility and fairness. Our experimental results show that explicit gender scrubbing substantially reduces but does not eliminate gender leakage, while adversarial learning improves fairness mainly on original biographies and acts as a complementary strategy rather than a substitute for text-level debiasing.

AI.tldr: Evaluates gender bias in 9 pre-trained embedding models for CV scoring, showing that explicit gender scrubbing reduces but doesn't eliminate leakage, and adversarial learning complements but doesn't replace text-level debiasing.
AI.motivation: AI recruitment systems risk perpetuating social biases when trained on historical CV data, as pre-trained language models may infer sensitive attributes like gender from unstructured text even after explicit indicators are removed.
AI.method: Evaluate 9 pre-trained embedding models on synthetic FairCVdb dataset; apply multi-task adversarial learning with gradient reversal for debiasing; use multi-objective Pareto-front-based model selection to balance utility and fairness.
AI.result: Explicit gender scrubbing reduces but does not eliminate gender leakage; adversarial learning improves fairness mainly on original biographies; adversarial learning complements rather than substitutes text-level debiasing.
AI.conclusion: Adversarial learning and text-level scrubbing are complementary strategies; neither alone fully eliminates bias in AI-based recruitment systems using pre-trained embeddings.

title: Self Gradient Forcing: Native Long Video Extrapolation
summary: Recent autoregressive video diffusion methods are increasingly built upon Self Forcing, where the student is trained on histories produced by its own rollout rather than ground-truth video contexts. This reduces exposure bias, but the historical key-value cache is still used by future frames only as frozen rollout state. As a result, future losses cannot supervise how earlier generated latents should be written into more useful keys and values for later video-latent generation. We call this the historical context-gradient gap. We propose Self Gradient Forcing (SGF), a two-pass training strategy that restores this missing supervision signal without backpropagating through the full serial rollout. Pass 1 performs a no-gradient autoregressive rollout matching inference and, at a sampled denoising exit step, records both the self-generated context and the noisy latents fed to the model. Pass 2 performs parallel context-gradient reconstruction for the recorded exit step. The generated context is used as stop-gradient clean-latent input, while the model recomputes the context KV representations and future-to-context causal attention. Thus, SGF provides the missing memory-writing supervision within the native autoregressive training objective, using losses on future video latents to train the model to encode context into more effective causal memory. Across extensive long-horizon frame-wise and chunk-wise experiments under different initializations, SGF achieves stronger native long-video extrapolation than Self Forcing, especially in subject identity, background/layout consistency, and temporal stability. Remarkably, using only a 5-second training window, SGF can extrapolate to videos lasting several minutes. Code and models will be released to advance research on autoregressive video generation.

AI.tldr: Self Gradient Forcing (SGF) is a two-pass training strategy for autoregressive video diffusion that restores missing context-gradient supervision by having a no-gradient rollout (Pass 1) followed by parallel context-gradient reconstruction (Pass 2), enabling future losses to supervise earlier context encoding. SGF achieves strong long-video extrapolation (up to several minutes from a 5-second training window) with improved subject identity, background consistency, and temporal stability.
AI.motivation: In autoregressive video diffusion with Self Forcing, the historical key-value cache is used only as frozen rollout state, so future losses cannot supervise how earlier latents are written into keys/values for later generation — a problem termed the historical context-gradient gap.
AI.method: SGF uses a two-pass strategy: Pass 1 performs a no-gradient autoregressive rollout and records self-generated context and noisy latents at a sampled denoising exit step; Pass 2 performs parallel context-gradient reconstruction where the generated context serves as stop-gradient clean-latent input while recomputing context KV representations and future-to-context causal attention, enabling future losses to supervise memory writing.
AI.result: SGF achieves stronger native long-video extrapolation than Self Forcing across long-horizon frame-wise and chunk-wise experiments under different initializations, particularly in subject identity, background/layout consistency, and temporal stability. With only a 5-second training window, SGF can extrapolate to videos lasting several minutes.
AI.conclusion: SGF effectively bridges the historical context-gradient gap by providing missing memory-writing supervision within the native autoregressive training objective, significantly improving long-video generation quality without backpropagating through the full serial rollout.

title: Co-Evolving LLM Evaluators and Policies via DynamicRubric
summary: Post-training with evaluator feedback on policy-induced samples serves as a major mechanism for improving large language models. As policies improve, these sampled responses become close in quality. These close candidates create a bottleneck for policy optimization: collapsed relative evaluator score gaps yield weak or misleading policy supervision. We theoretically characterize why these gaps matter through a probability allocation view, showing that the directional gain of shifting probability mass from one response to another is exactly the evaluator score gap between them. This identifies relative score gaps as the policy optimization signals that guide updates. Motivated by this view, we propose DynamicRubric, a response-set-conditioned evaluator--policy co-evolution framework that generates weighted binary rubric items for each candidate set and aggregates the resulting judgments into response-level scores. In our experiments with 8B backbones, DynamicRubric improves evaluator performance and provides stronger policy supervision than baselines using a 70B reward model or a 235B static rubric generator. DynamicRubric-optimized policies also show gains on verifiable reasoning and coding tasks. A DynamicRubric-optimized model is fully deployed in WeChat Search's AI answering scenario, where it serves all online traffic across tens of millions of requests per day and improves key online metrics. These results suggest a principle for evaluator-guided post-training: evaluators should evolve with the policies they supervise.

AI.tldr: DynamicRubric is a co-evolution framework where evaluators and policies jointly improve by generating weighted binary rubric items for each response set, addressing the bottleneck of collapsed score gaps in post-training. Using 8B backbones, it outperforms 70B reward models and 235B static rubric generators, deployed in WeChat Search serving millions of requests daily.
AI.motivation: As policies improve, sampled responses become close in quality, causing collapsed relative evaluator score gaps that yield weak or misleading policy supervision signals.
AI.method: DynamicRubric: a response-set-conditioned evaluator-policy co-evolution framework that generates weighted binary rubric items for each candidate set and aggregates judgments into response-level scores.
AI.result: With 8B backbones, DynamicRubric improves evaluator performance and provides stronger policy supervision than baselines using 70B reward model or 235B static rubric generator; gains on reasoning/coding tasks; deployed in WeChat Search AI answering serving all online traffic with millions of daily requests.
AI.conclusion: Evaluators should evolve with the policies they supervise; relative score gaps are the fundamental policy optimization signals.

title: Persian Pixel: A large-scale synthetic OCR dataset for Persian language
summary: Optical Character Recognition (OCR) for Persian remains substantially less mature than for Latin-script languages despite Persian being spoken by more than 110 million people across multiple countries. This gap arises from two fundamental challenges: the intrinsic complexity of the Perso-Arabic writing system and the limited availability of large-scale, high-quality annotated datasets. Persian script exhibits obligatory cursive connectivity, context-dependent glyph shaping, extensive ligatures, diacritic placement, and stylistic variation across writing forms such as Naskh and Nastaliq, all of which significantly complicate text recognition. At the same time, the high cost and labor-intensive nature of manual annotation have created a persistent data bottleneck, limiting the development of robust OCR systems and slowing progress in Persian document digitization.In this paper, we introduce Persian Pixel, a comprehensive synthetic OCR dataset specifically designed to address these challenges. Comprising over 343,000 high-fidelity image text pairs, the dataset spans sentence, paragraph, and full-page document layouts generated from a carefully curated seven-million-word Persian corpus using the SynthOCR-Gen rendering framework. The generation pipeline faithfully models the typographic characteristics of Persian script, including contextual character joining, positional glyph variants, diacritic placement, and multiple representative Persian typefaces. To bridge the synthetic-to-real domain gap, the rendered images are further enriched with more than twenty-five stochastic degradation models that emulate realistic document acquisition artifacts, including ink bleed, paper aging, blur, illumination variation, scanner imperfections, compression artifacts, and multiple noise processes.By overcoming the long-standing scarcity of annotated Persian OCR data, Persian Pixel provides a scalable and openly available resource for training and fine-tuning modern OCR architectures, including transformer-based models such as TrOCR and Donut. The dataset establishes a strong foundation for research in Persian document analysis, historical manuscript digitization, and end-to-end document understanding, while demonstrating that programmatic synthetic data generation offers a practical, cost-effective, and scalable alternative to manual annotation for advancing OCR in low-resource and typographically complex scripts.

AI.tldr: Persian Pixel is a large-scale synthetic OCR dataset (343,000+ image-text pairs) designed to overcome the scarcity of annotated Persian data. It uses curated text, typographically faithful rendering, and 25+ degradation models to bridge the synthetic-to-real gap, enabling training of modern OCR architectures like TrOCR and Donut.
AI.motivation: Persian OCR lags behind Latin-script OCR due to two fundamental challenges: the intrinsic complexity of the Perso-Arabic writing system (cursive connectivity, context-dependent glyph shaping, ligatures, diacritics, stylistic variation) and the severe scarcity of large-scale, high-quality annotated datasets caused by the high cost and labor of manual annotation.
AI.method: The authors create Persian Pixel using the SynthOCR-Gen rendering framework, generating over 343,000 high-fidelity image-text pairs from a seven-million-word Persian corpus. The pipeline models typographic features (contextual joining, positional glyph variants, diacritics, multiple typefaces including Naskh and Nastaliq) and applies 25+ stochastic degradation models (ink bleed, paper aging, blur, illumination variation, scanner imperfections, compression artifacts, noise) to bridge the synthetic-to-real domain gap.
AI.result: A comprehensive synthetic OCR dataset of 343,000+ image-text pairs spanning sentence, paragraph, and full-page layouts with realistic document acquisition artifacts.
AI.conclusion: Persian Pixel overcomes the long-standing scarcity of annotated Persian OCR data, providing a scalable, openly available resource for training modern OCR architectures and demonstrating that programmatic synthetic data generation is a practical, cost-effective alternative to manual annotation for low-resource and typographically complex scripts.

title: Autonomous Collaborative Learning Among an Ensemble of Tsetlin Machines with Consensus-Based Inference
summary: Tsetlin Machine (TM) is a rule-based machine-learning algorithm comprising collectives of two-action Tsetlin Automata (TAs) that cooperatively form conjunctive logical clauses from Boolean inputs through stochastic feedback. Although few recent studies have examined TM Federated Learning, the broader area of distributed and decentralized TM learning has not received much attention in the existing literature and warrants further exploration. In this work, we propose a paradigm for decentralized collaborative learning under a vertical feature-partitioning setting among an ensemble of Tsetlin Machines using consensus-based inference. Within this decentralized paradigm, each agent maintains its own private TM model, and there is no exchange of raw data among agents. Inference combines individual agents model predictions into a global consensus. The paradigm accommodates heterogeneous TM-based agents with differing data acquisition means, local data distributions, or computational resources, thereby facilitating the integration and fusion of information in settings such as multi-modal sensing environments. Experiments conducted using two-dimensional grid and connected graph network topologies demonstrate that the classification accuracies achieved are comparable to those of centralized models.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a decentralized collaborative learning paradigm for Tsetlin Machines under vertical feature partitioning, where agents maintain private models and reach consensus through inference without sharing raw data, achieving accuracy comparable to centralized models.
AI.motivation: Distributed and decentralized TM learning has not received much attention; existing work only briefly examined TM Federated Learning, warranting further exploration.
AI.method: A decentralized paradigm using consensus-based inference under vertical feature partitioning, where each agent maintains a private TM model, no raw data is exchanged, and individual predictions are combined into a global consensus. Tested on 2D grid and connected graph topologies.
AI.result: Classification accuracies achieved with the decentralized paradigm are comparable to those of centralized models.
AI.conclusion: The proposed paradigm enables effective decentralized collaborative TM learning, accommodates heterogeneous agents, and facilitates information fusion in settings like multi-modal sensing environments.

title: PercepCap: Video Captioner with Structured Spatio-Temporal Perception
summary: Video captioning requires fine-grained spatio-temporal understanding of videos, including spatial perception of where objects are located and temporal perception of when events occur. Existing MLLMs usually generate captions directly from video inputs without exposing the perceptual evidence behind descriptions. As a result, mistakes in spatiotemporal perception are only observed in the final caption, making it difficult to identify the underlying perceptual errors directly. To address these issues, we present PercepCap, a perception-aware video captioning framework that makes perceptual evidence explicit before producing the final caption. Specifically, PercepCap follows a perceive-describe generation chain, where the model first produces a spatiotemporal perception trace comprising object trajectories and temporal events, and then generates the final caption conditioned on the perceived evidence. To support this, we design a two-stage training strategy. Perceive-then-Describe Supervised Fine-tuning adapts the model from caption-only generation to the proposed perceive-describe chain, while Perception-Grounded Reinforcement Learning optimizes perception trace and caption quality with joint rewards over perception chain and the final caption. To support our two-stage training, we introduce Caption-Anchored Perception Data Construction. This pipeline builds the SFT and RL training data by first generating a caption-only description, extracting the objects and events it mentions, and grounding them back in the video with boxes and timestamps. This yields caption-aligned perception data that provides solid training ground truth, ensuring that the explicit perception trace and final caption refer to the same objects and events. Across direct caption and caption-to-QA evaluation, PercepCap consistently improves upon the Qwen3-VL baseline and demonstrates leading caption quality.

AI.tldr: PercepCap is a video captioning framework that explicitly generates spatiotemporal perception traces (object trajectories and temporal events) before producing the final caption, using a two-stage training strategy (perceive-then-describe SFT + perception-grounded RL) and a caption-anchored data construction pipeline to improve perceptual accuracy and caption quality.
AI.motivation: Existing MLLMs generate captions directly from videos without exposing perceptual evidence, making spatiotemporal errors hard to diagnose because mistakes are only visible in the final caption.
AI.method: PercepCap follows a perceive-describe chain: first produce a spatiotemporal perception trace (object trajectories + temporal events), then generate the caption conditioned on it. Two-stage training: (1) Perceive-then-Describe SFT adapts the model to this chain, (2) Perception-Grounded RL optimizes both trace and caption with joint rewards. A Caption-Anchored Perception Data Construction pipeline builds SFT and RL data by generating captions, extracting mentioned objects/events, and grounding them back with boxes/timestamps.
AI.result: PercepCap consistently improves upon the Qwen3-VL baseline in both direct caption and caption-to-QA evaluation, demonstrating leading caption quality.
AI.conclusion: Making perceptual evidence explicit before caption generation improves spatiotemporal accuracy and overall caption quality, with the two-stage training and data construction pipeline effectively supporting this paradigm.

title: CURED: Creating, Understanding, and Repairing Errors Demonstrator
summary: Detecting and cleaning errors in tabular data is a prerequisite for data intense software applications. Recent research at the intersection of Machine Learning (ML) and Database Management Systems (DBMS) highlights the potential of statistical learning algorithms for error detection and cleaning. This paper combines our recent work on ML-based data cleaning and error models in a unified demonstrator. The web application allows users to upload tabular data, perturb the data with realistic data dependent errors and use modern ML methods to clean and understand error mechanisms in data. Our demonstrator helps to bridge the gap between theoretical advancements and intuitive practical insights in the context of error models and data cleaning algorithms for tabular data. The demonstrator is available at https://cured.demo.calgo-lab.de/

AI.tldr: This paper presents a web-based demonstrator that combines ML-based data cleaning and error models, allowing users to upload tabular data, inject realistic dependent errors, and apply modern ML methods to detect, clean, and understand error mechanisms in data.
AI.motivation: Detecting and cleaning errors in tabular data is essential for data-intensive applications, and there is a gap between theoretical ML-based data cleaning advancements and practical intuitive insights.
AI.method: The authors built a web application where users upload tabular data, perturb it with realistic data-dependent errors, and apply modern ML methods to clean data and understand error mechanisms.
AI.result: A unified demonstrator that bridges theoretical ML-based data cleaning research with practical, hands-on exploration of error models and cleaning algorithms.
AI.conclusion: The demonstrator helps bridge the gap between theoretical advancements and intuitive practical insights in error models and data cleaning algorithms for tabular data.

title: ATSplat: Compact Feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting with Adaptive Token Expansion
summary: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) achieves high-quality novel-view synthesis by optimizing freely placed primitives in 3D and adaptively densifying them in under-reconstructed regions. However, this scene-adaptive capacity allocation is largely lost in existing feed-forward 3DGS methods, which commonly regress Gaussians at input pixels and lift them along camera rays. Such pixel-aligned formulations make the number and placement of primitives depend on image resolution and input viewpoints rather than scene complexity, resulting in dense and often redundant Gaussian sets. We present ATSplat, a feed-forward 3DGS framework that restores the adaptive allocation capability of 3DGS optimization through Adaptive 3D Tokens. ATSplat first lifts coarse patch-level depth and camera cues into sparse 3D anchor tokens, forming a compact scaffold of the scene. Each token is then regressed into local Gaussians with learnable 3D offsets, decoupling primitive placement from input image grids. An Adaptive Token Expansion module predicts a token-level uncertainty score, supervised by rendering error maps, and selectively expands high-uncertainty tokens through learnable expansion layers. This sparse-to-adaptive formulation enables ATSplat to concentrate primitives in challenging regions while maintaining a compact representation. Experiments on two representative datasets, RealEstate10K and DL3DV, show that ATSplat achieves state-of-the-art rendering quality while reducing the number of Gaussians by more than $5.7\times$ compared with dense feed-forward 3DGS methods. From 12 input images at $512 \times 960$ resolution, ATSplat completes reconstruction in less than a second using a single commercial GPU, and renders high-quality novel views at 1136 FPS ($512 \times 960$) with only 311K Gaussians.

AI.tldr: ATSplat is a feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting framework that restores adaptive capacity allocation by using sparse 3D anchor tokens and an Adaptive Token Expansion module, achieving state-of-the-art rendering quality with 5.7× fewer Gaussians than dense methods, reconstructing in <1 second and rendering at 1136 FPS.
AI.motivation: Existing feed-forward 3DGS methods regress Gaussians at input pixels in a pixel-aligned manner, making primitive count and placement depend on image resolution and viewpoints rather than scene complexity, leading to dense and redundant Gaussian sets. This loses the scene-adaptive capacity allocation that makes optimization-based 3DGS effective.
AI.method: ATSplat uses (1) coarse patch-level depth and camera cues lifted into sparse 3D anchor tokens forming a scene scaffold; (2) each token regressed into local Gaussians with learnable 3D offsets, decoupling primitives from input grids; (3) an Adaptive Token Expansion module predicting token-level uncertainty supervised by rendering error maps, selectively expanding high-uncertainty tokens via learnable expansion layers.
AI.result: On RealEstate10K and DL3DV, ATSplat achieves state-of-the-art rendering quality while reducing Gaussians by >5.7× vs dense feed-forward methods. From 12 images at 512×960, it reconstructs in <1 second on a single GPU, renders at 1136 FPS (512×960) with only 311K Gaussians.
AI.conclusion: The sparse-to-adaptive formulation effectively restores scene-adaptive capacity allocation in feed-forward 3DGS, enabling compact yet high-quality novel-view synthesis with significant efficiency gains.

title: Active Inference as a Convex Markov Decision Process
summary: Active Inference (AIF) frames adaptive behavior as the minimization of expected free energy (EFE), combining epistemic and pragmatic objectives within a single variational principle. We frame AIF as policy optimization and show that, for closed-loop control policies, EFE minimization can be formulated as a convex Markov decision process (MDP). In this formulation, the pragmatic terms are linear in the predictive state marginals and therefore equivalent to reward maximization in a latent MDP, while the epistemic value introduces a nonlinear component that distinguishes EFE minimization from standard reinforcement learning. This perspective further reveals the epistemic drive of active inference as a policy-dependent (performative) reward. We analyze finite-horizon, discounted, and average-reward formulations of EFE and derive a mirror descent (MD) algorithm that locally linearizes the objective around the current state marginals, yielding a policy-dependent reward that is compatible with actor-critic methods and dynamic programming. Finally, we argue that coupling world-model learning with policy optimization gives active inference the structure of performative reinforcement learning, providing a route toward grounding active inference within modern reinforcement learning and optimization theory, including convergence analysis and principled policy improvement guarantees.

AI.tldr: This paper reformulates Active Inference (AIF) as policy optimization in a convex Markov decision process, showing EFE minimization combines linear pragmatic terms (equivalent to reward maximization) with nonlinear epistemic value, and derives a mirror descent algorithm compatible with actor-critic methods and dynamic programming, ultimately framing AIF as performative reinforcement learning.
AI.motivation: To bridge Active Inference with modern reinforcement learning and optimization theory by providing a formal connection between EFE minimization and convex MDPs, enabling convergence analysis and principled policy improvement guarantees.
AI.method: The authors frame AIF as policy optimization, formulate EFE minimization as a convex MDP where pragmatic terms are linear (equivalent to reward maximization in latent MDP) and epistemic value is nonlinear/policy-dependent. They analyze finite-horizon, discounted, and average-reward EFE formulations and derive a mirror descent algorithm that locally linearizes the objective around current state marginals.
AI.result: The epistemic drive of active inference is revealed as a policy-dependent (performative) reward. The mirror descent algorithm yields a policy-dependent reward compatible with actor-critic methods and dynamic programming. Coupling world-model learning with policy optimization gives AIF the structure of performative reinforcement learning.
AI.conclusion: Active Inference can be grounded within modern reinforcement learning and optimization theory, providing a route toward convergence analysis and principled policy improvement guarantees through the lens of performative reinforcement learning.

title: Local Stability and Gaussian Smoothing of Quantized Neural Networks
comment: Accepted at the 23rd IFAC World Congress (IFAC WC 2026), Busan, Republic of Korea, 2026; 6 pages, 2 figures
summary: We study Gaussian averaging as a smooth surrogate for quantized neural models. Under bounded local oscillation, we derive a local dimension-dependent bound on |f-g|, linking Gaussian smoothing to the stability analysis of discontinuous networks. We compute closed-form Gaussian averages of the rectified linear unit (ReLU) and sign activation functions, and illustrate the mechanism on a high-dimensional binary perceptron, where layer-preactivation aggregation under an explicit quantization-noise surrogate yields the Gaussian envelope used in inference-side smoothing and training-side smooth surrogate gradients.

AI.tldr: The paper studies Gaussian averaging as a smooth surrogate for quantized neural models, deriving dimension-dependent bounds linking Gaussian smoothing to stability analysis of discontinuous networks. It computes closed-form Gaussian averages of ReLU and sign activations, and demonstrates the mechanism on a high-dimensional binary perceptron.
AI.motivation: To address the discontinuity in quantized neural networks by using Gaussian smoothing as a differentiable surrogate, enabling both inference-side smoothing and training-side smooth surrogate gradients.
AI.method: The paper derives a local dimension-dependent bound on |f-g| under bounded local oscillation, linking Gaussian smoothing to stability analysis. It computes closed-form Gaussian averages of ReLU and sign activations, and illustrates the mechanism on a high-dimensional binary perceptron with layer-preactivation aggregation under an explicit quantization-noise surrogate.
AI.result: Closed-form Gaussian averages of ReLU and sign activation functions are derived. A local dimension-dependent bound connecting Gaussian smoothing to stability analysis of discontinuous networks is established. The Gaussian envelope is demonstrated as an effective surrogate for quantization-noise in both inference and training.
AI.conclusion: Gaussian averaging serves as a principled smooth surrogate for quantized neural models, providing theoretically grounded bounds and practical computational forms for handling discontinuities in neural networks.

title: Self-organizing Architecture of Receptron Units: a Hardware-Aware Framework for Edge Intelligence
comment: This work has been submitted to NeuroPHY 2026
summary: The growing demand for intelligent processing at the edge of IoT networks is constrained by the severe computational and memory limitations of microcontroller units, which render impractical conventional deep learning approaches. We propose a neuromorphicinspired classifier based on the Receptron model, a single-unit architecture capable of implementing non-linearly separable decision boundaries, without resorting to multi-layer networks. The model is designed for direct deployment on mid-range MCUs, while supporting continuous on-device adaptation. Experimental evaluation on basic dataset benchmarks yields cross-validated accuracies compatible with standard machine learning method baselines. These results position the Receptron as a viable and interpretable alternative for resource-constrained neuromorphic edge systems operating in dynamic, non-stationary environments.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a Receptron-based neuromorphic classifier that implements non-linearly separable decision boundaries in a single unit for direct deployment on mid-range MCUs, achieving accuracy comparable to standard ML methods while enabling continuous on-device adaptation for resource-constrained edge IoT systems.
AI.motivation: The growing demand for intelligent processing at the edge of IoT networks is constrained by the severe computational and memory limitations of microcontroller units, which render impractical conventional deep learning approaches.
AI.method: A neuromorphic-inspired classifier based on the Receptron model, a single-unit architecture capable of implementing non-linearly separable decision boundaries without multi-layer networks, designed for direct deployment on mid-range MCUs with continuous on-device adaptation.
AI.result: Experimental evaluation on basic dataset benchmarks yields cross-validated accuracies compatible with standard machine learning method baselines.
AI.conclusion: These results position the Receptron as a viable and interpretable alternative for resource-constrained neuromorphic edge systems operating in dynamic, non-stationary environments.

title: Instance Hardness-Based Relevance for Imbalanced Regression
summary: Imbalanced regression problems arise when the target variable has an asymmetric distribution, resulting in underrepresented value ranges in the dataset. Traditional approaches for identifying rare instances rely on a relevance function that assigns higher importance to specific regions of the target distribution. However, the effectiveness of imbalance-aware learning methods depends strongly on how relevance is defined. In more complex scenarios, such as bimodal distributions, traditional relevance functions struggle to capture rarity, as they assign fixed relevance values based solely on target values, thereby compromising the distinction between truly rare and normal instances. To address these limitations, this study proposes an Instance Hardness-based relevance function (InHaR) for identifying rare instances in regression problems. Unlike traditional relevance functions, the proposed approach incorporates learning difficulty, allowing rarity to be inferred not only from the target distribution but also from the difficulty of instances for the learning algorithm. This property is particularly important in bimodal scenarios, where rarity cannot be accurately inferred from target values alone. Experimental results demonstrate that the InHaR correctly identifies rare regions under bimodal distributions and, when used to guide resampling strategies such as Random Oversampling (RO) and Gaussian Noise (GN), leads to significant improvements in predictive performance compared to traditional relevance-based approaches. The code, dataset, and further details about the proposed method are publicly available at https://github.com/VitorLeitao/instance-hardness-Imbalanced-regression.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes an Instance Hardness-based relevance function (InHaR) for imbalanced regression that incorporates learning difficulty to better identify rare instances, particularly in bimodal distributions where traditional relevance functions fail.
AI.motivation: Traditional relevance functions assign fixed importance based solely on target values, which fails to distinguish truly rare instances from normal ones in complex scenarios like bimodal distributions.
AI.method: The proposed InHaR function incorporates learning difficulty (instance hardness) to infer rarity from both the target distribution and the difficulty of instances for the learning algorithm, rather than relying solely on target values.
AI.result: InHaR correctly identifies rare regions under bimodal distributions, and when used to guide resampling strategies (Random Oversampling and Gaussian Noise), it significantly improves predictive performance over traditional relevance-based approaches.
AI.conclusion: Instance hardness-based relevance is more effective than traditional relevance functions for identifying rare instances in imbalanced regression, particularly for complex distributions where target-value-only approaches are insufficient.

title: On Optimization Complexity of Second-Order Certified Unlearning
summary: We study machine unlearning: the removal of memorized training data from a trained model. Specifically, we investigate the algorithmic complexity of certified unlearning from an optimization perspective. We formalize the goal of an unlearning algorithm as simultaneously achieving certified unlearning and optimization accuracy. Utilizing the notion of uniformly convex regularizers, we prove new bounds on the distance between initial and unlearned models using a novel substitute for generalization error. Thus we theoretically demonstrate that if the removed data is well-predicted by the unlearned model, the corresponding optimization problem is simple. Furthermore, we develop a new second-order unlearning algorithm with an anisotropic Gaussian mechanism and state-of-the-art global convergence. We prove fast rates for our method in achieving certified unlearning for linear models with quasi-self-concordant losses. As a direct application, our theory covers unlearning for logistic and exponential regressions and shows a provable benefit of utilizing second-order information compared to first-order unlearning methods.

AI.tldr: This paper studies the algorithmic complexity of certified machine unlearning from an optimization perspective, proving theoretical bounds linking unlearning difficulty to data predictability, and proposing a new second-order unlearning algorithm with anisotropic Gaussian mechanism that achieves state-of-the-art global convergence, particularly for linear models with quasi-self-concordant losses like logistic and exponential regression.
AI.motivation: To formally investigate the algorithmic complexity of certified machine unlearning from an optimization perspective, providing theoretical guarantees on the trade-off between certified unlearning and optimization accuracy.
AI.method: The paper uses uniformly convex regularizers to derive new bounds on the distance between initial and unlearned models via a novel substitute for generalization error, and develops a second-order unlearning algorithm with an anisotropic Gaussian mechanism that achieves state-of-the-art global convergence. The method is proven to achieve fast rates for certified unlearning in linear models with quasi-self-concordant losses.
AI.result: Theoretical demonstration that if removed data is well-predicted by the unlearned model, the optimization problem is simple. The proposed second-order unlearning algorithm achieves state-of-the-art global convergence with fast certified unlearning rates for logistic and exponential regressions, showing provable benefit over first-order methods.
AI.conclusion: The work provides a rigorous optimization-theoretic foundation for certified machine unlearning, demonstrating that second-order information yields provable advantages for unlearning in generalized linear models, with concrete application to logistic and exponential regression.

title: OLEDLM: A Unified Language Model for OLED Molecular Design
summary: The development of organic light-emitting diode (OLED) materials faces the compounded challenges of an astronomically large chemical space, stringent quantum-chemical constraints, and a scarcity of labeled data. Although the question of OLED generation is important, few models have been trained effectively for this specific domain. We propose an inverse molecular design framework based on causal language models: given target optoelectronic properties (e.g., excitation energy, oscillator strength), our model directly generates OLED SMILES sequences satisfying the specified constraints. We employ a multi-stage strategy: first, we establish a foundational chemical language model using a LLaMA-style transformer architecture. To the best of our knowledge, this represents the first successful adaptation of LLMs specifically for the OLED domain, bridging the gap between generic molecular generation and the stringent structural requirements of optoelectronic materials. Second, we fine-tune property predictors based on a BERT model pre-trained on our large-scale OLED dataset. Then, we perform Reinforcement Learning on our fine-tuned model, leveraging our property predictor, for better SMILES generation. Finally, through DFT verification, we demonstrate that our framework can efficiently navigate the OLED chemical space, generating novel candidates with high structural validity and optimized optoelectronic properties.

AI.tldr: A causal language model-based inverse molecular design framework (LLaMA-style + BERT predictors + RL + DFT verification) generates novel OLED SMILES sequences with targeted optoelectronic properties, addressing the challenges of large chemical space and scarce labeled data.
AI.motivation: OLED material development faces an astronomically large chemical space, stringent quantum-chemical constraints, and scarce labeled data; few models have been effectively trained for this domain.
AI.method: (1) Foundational chemical language model using LLaMA-style transformer; (2) BERT-based property predictors fine-tuned on large-scale OLED dataset; (3) Reinforcement Learning on the fine-tuned model guided by the property predictor for optimized SMILES generation; (4) DFT verification for validation.
AI.result: The framework efficiently navigates the OLED chemical space, generating novel candidates with high structural validity and optimized optoelectronic properties, verified via DFT.
AI.conclusion: This is the first successful adaptation of LLMs specifically for the OLED domain, bridging generic molecular generation and the stringent requirements of optoelectronic materials.

title: The Quadrilateral Loss: Additivity as a Measurable Behavior of Dense Neural Networks
summary: Additive models buy interpretability by forbidding feature interactions, a constraint that neural instantiations enforce architecturally. We introduce the quadrilateral loss, a differentiable penalty that treats additivity as a measurable behavior instead: a second-order mixed difference on pairs of training points swapping one coordinate, which vanishes if and only if the coordinate carries no interaction, remains informative for piecewise-linear networks, and equals in expectation the per-coordinate interaction mass of the interventional Shapley-GAM. The loss turns additivity into a dial - most learned interactions prove removable almost for free, and on small datasets a moderate penalty improves accuracy and additivity simultaneously - and into an online observable: its per-feature surrender curves show, across seeds and datasets, that pre-regularization interaction magnitude barely predicts what a regularized model retains, undermining post-hoc interaction rankings. Against this instrument we compare routes to exact additivity, spanning structural masks, behavioral penalties (optionally crystallized into exact structure), weight decay, backfitting, the shared-section model, and bagged boosted stumps: constraining behavior before structure dominates weight-space constraints, rankings reverse between data regimes, and converging routes agree on the shape functions themselves. Three silent failure modes we document share one anatomy: guarantees imported into settings that quietly void their preconditions.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces the quadrilateral loss, a differentiable penalty that measures feature interactions in additive models, allowing additivity to be treated as a tunable dial rather than a hard architectural constraint. The authors analyze interaction removal across various regularization routes and identify three silent failure modes where guarantees break due to violated preconditions.
AI.motivation: Additive models enforce interpretability by forbidding feature interactions, but neural network implementations impose this architecturally. The authors seek to treat additivity as a measurable, tunable behavior rather than a hard constraint, enabling more flexible trade-offs between interpretability and accuracy.
AI.method: The quadrilateral loss is a differentiable penalty based on a second-order mixed difference on pairs of training points swapping one coordinate. It vanishes iff the coordinate carries no interaction, remains informative for piecewise-linear networks, and equals the expected per-coordinate interaction mass of interventional Shapley-GAM. The authors compare structural masks, behavioral penalties (optionally crystallized into structure), weight decay, backfitting, the shared-section model, and bagged boosted stumps.
AI.result: Most learned interactions are removable almost for free; moderate penalties improve both accuracy and additivity on small datasets. Pre-regularization interaction magnitude barely predicts what regularized models retain, undermining post-hoc interaction rankings. Rankings between regularization routes reverse across data regimes; converging routes agree on shape functions. Three silent failure modes are identified.
AI.conclusion: Constraining behavior before structure dominates weight-space constraints. The quadrilateral loss enables additivity as a dial and an online observable. Three documented failure modes share the anatomy of importing guarantees into settings that quietly void their preconditions.

title: ELSAA: Efficient Low-Rank and Sparse Attention Approximation for Training Transformers
summary: The quadratic $N\times N$ attention score matrix remains a central obstacle to extending Transformers to longer input lengths. Existing efficient attention methods usually reduce this bottleneck by either imposing sparsity, so that each query attends to only a small subset of keys, or by using low-rank/kernel sketches, so that global interactions are compressed into a lower-dimensional representation. We propose \emph{ELSAA}, an efficient low-rank and sparse approximation of attention. Importantly, ELSAA does \emph{not} decompose the learned projection or output matrices of the Transformer into sparse and low-rank factors. Instead, after dense projections produce $Q,K,V$, ELSAA approximates the induced attention score operator itself: a sparse branch captures selected high-similarity interactions, while a low-rank branch summarizes diffuse global interactions. Since the two branches can be normalized over supports with very different denominator mass, ELSAA introduces a denominator-aware fusion term that scales the sparse branch according to its estimated attention mass relative to the low-rank branch. This gives a practical framework for constructing low-rank and sparse attention outputs without materializing the full quadratic score matrix, aiming to enable longer-context training while preserving both sharp token-level interactions and broad contextual mixing.

AI.tldr: ELSAA approximates the quadratic attention matrix with a sparse branch (high-similarity interactions) and a low-rank branch (diffuse global interactions), fused via denominator-aware scaling to avoid materializing the full score matrix.
AI.motivation: The quadratic $N\times N$ attention score matrix is the main bottleneck preventing Transformers from scaling to longer input sequences. Existing methods reduce this via sparsity or low-rank/kernel sketches, but often sacrifice either fine-grained token interactions or global context.
AI.method: ELSAA decomposes the attention score operator itself (not the learned projections) into a sparse branch (top-k similar keys per query) and a low-rank branch (global compression). A denominator-aware fusion term scales the sparse branch by its estimated attention mass relative to the low-rank branch, ensuring proper normalization across the two heterogeneous supports.
AI.result: A practical framework that avoids materializing the full quadratic attention matrix, enabling longer-context training while preserving both sharp token-level interactions (via sparsity) and broad contextual mixing (via low-rank).
AI.conclusion: ELSAA offers a novel, operator-level decomposition that fuses sparse and low-rank attention with proper normalization, aiming to extend Transformer context length without sacrificing interaction quality.

title: User-Centric Modeling of Transactional Sequences with Explainable State Space Models
summary: We propose a hybrid approach for user-centric modeling of transactional event sequences that combines contrastive representation learning (CoLES) with State Space Models (SSMs). While contrastive methods yield high-quality compressed user representations, existing encoders -- RNNs and Transformers -- suffer from vanishing gradients or quadratic complexity, respectively. Mamba, a selective SSM, efficiently handles long-range dependencies but remains underexplored for personalized user analysis. We investigate two integration strategies: (1)~initializing the Mamba hidden state with a CoLES embedding, and (2)~prepending the projected CoLES embedding as a prefix token to the input sequence. Both approaches supply the model with an informative user prior from the first step. Experiments on three public datasets -- Age (multiclass age-group prediction), MBD (multi-label product acquisition), and Taobao (binary purchase prediction) -- demonstrate consistent improvements over standalone Mamba and CoLES with a linear classifier, with the hybrid models converging 2--3$\times$ faster than the plain SSM baseline. Explainability analysis via discretization-step maps and Integrated Gradients reveals selective event filtering on behavior-rich datasets and identifies the most informative transaction features.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a hybrid model combining contrastive representation learning (CoLES) with State Space Models (Mamba) for user-centric modeling of transactional event sequences. Two integration strategies are explored: initializing Mamba's hidden state with CoLES embeddings or prepending CoLES embeddings as prefix tokens. Experiments show faster convergence (2-3×) and improved performance over standalone models on three public datasets.
AI.motivation: Existing encoders (RNNs, Transformers) for modeling user transactional sequences suffer from vanishing gradients or quadratic complexity. Mamba (selective SSM) handles long-range dependencies efficiently but is underexplored for personalized user analysis. The authors aim to combine the strengths of contrastive learning (high-quality user representations) and Mamba (efficient sequential modeling) to create better user-centric models.
AI.method: Two hybrid integration strategies: (1) initializing the Mamba hidden state with a CoLES embedding, and (2) prepending the projected CoLES embedding as a prefix token to the input sequence. Both provide an informative user prior from the first step.
AI.result: Consistent improvements over standalone Mamba and CoLES with linear classifier on Age (multiclass age-group prediction), MBD (multi-label product acquisition), and Taobao (binary purchase prediction) datasets. Hybrid models converge 2-3× faster than plain SSM baseline.
AI.conclusion: The hybrid CoLES+SSM approach effectively improves performance and convergence speed. Explainability analysis via discretization-step maps and Integrated Gradients reveals selective event filtering on behavior-rich datasets and identifies the most informative transaction features.

title: PIER: Physics-Informed Environmental Retrieval for Time-Series Modeling
summary: Accurate modeling of environmental systems is fundamental to scientific understanding and decision-making, yet remains challenging because observations are limited and physical dynamics vary across systems. Retrieval-augmented approaches offer a natural path to transfer knowledge across systems, but standard embedding-based retrieval does not guarantee consistency of underlying physical processes, since scenarios with similar embeddings may arise from different underlying mechanisms. We propose Physics-Informed Environmental Retrieval (PIER), a model-agnostic framework that augments embedding-based retrieval with a physics-aware stream that scores candidates by flux-response consistency with the target, using local verifiers trained on physics-derived flux features. A weight adjustment mechanism then learns per-scenario weights that adaptively balance the two retrieval streams based on diagnostic features summarizing physics-stream reliability. Experiments on 356 lakes across the Midwestern United States spanning 41 years show that PIER consistently outperforms baselines for water temperature and dissolved oxygen prediction, and serves as a general augmentation strategy across diverse backbones.

AI.tldr: PIER is a physics-informed retrieval framework that augments standard embedding-based retrieval with a physics-aware stream and adaptive weight adjustment, consistently outperforming baselines in water temperature and dissolved oxygen prediction across 356 lakes over 41 years.
AI.motivation: Accurate environmental modeling is limited by sparse observations and varying physical dynamics across systems; standard retrieval methods fail because similar embeddings may correspond to physically inconsistent mechanisms.
AI.method: PIER combines embedding-based retrieval with a physics-aware stream that scores candidates via flux-response consistency using local verifiers trained on physics-derived flux features, plus a learnable weight adjustment mechanism that adaptively balances both streams based on diagnostic features of physics-stream reliability.
AI.result: On 356 lakes in the Midwestern US over 41 years, PIER consistently outperformed baselines for water temperature and dissolved oxygen prediction, and served as a general augmentation strategy across diverse backbone models.
AI.conclusion: Physics-informed retrieval with adaptive balancing improves environmental modeling by ensuring physical consistency in knowledge transfer across systems.

title: PhaseAware: Interpretable Human-in-the-Loop Rehabilitation Scoring with Boundary Monitoring
comment: 22 pages, 4 main figures, 3 tables, and 17 supplementary figures. Supplementary Information is included in the same PDF
summary: Rehabilitation scoring systems are most useful when their outputs can be reviewed and interpreted within clinical workflows. This study presents PhaseAware, a compact framework for continuous rehabilitation quality assessment that combines a temporal backbone with phase- and body-group descriptors through a backbone-conditioned gated residual pathway. The model was evaluated on the UI-PRMD deep-squat protocol and further tested on the KIMORE squatting subset. On UI-PRMD, PhaseAware achieved an RMSE of 0.0230, corresponding to an 88.9% reduction relative to the accepted baseline. It also maintained favorable performance on KIMORE, suggesting that the phase-aware design transfers across related squatting protocols. In addition to score prediction, PhaseAware generates structured review cues based on phase- and body-level sensitivity, highlighting the movement stages and body regions most relevant to each prediction. The architecture employs a backbone-conditioned gated residual mechanism to stabilize feature representation, supporting use in resource-constrained settings. These cues are intended to support clinician review, boundary-case monitoring, and human-in-the-loop triage rather than autonomous decision-making. Overall, PhaseAware offers a practical and interpretable approach to rehabilitation scoring that may help integrate automated assessment into information systems while preserving clinician oversight.

AI.tldr: PhaseAware is a compact, interpretable framework for continuous rehabilitation quality assessment that uses a backbone-conditioned gated residual pathway with phase- and body-group descriptors. It achieves 88.9% RMSE reduction on UI-PRMD, generalizes to KIMORE, and generates structured review cues for clinician oversight.
AI.motivation: Rehabilitation scoring systems need to be interpretable and integrable into clinical workflows, but existing automated assessment methods lack structured, phase-aware outputs that support clinician review and boundary-case monitoring.
AI.method: PhaseAware combines a temporal backbone with phase- and body-group descriptors via a backbone-conditioned gated residual pathway. It generates structured review cues based on phase- and body-level sensitivity to highlight relevant movement stages and body regions.
AI.result: On UI-PRMD, PhaseAware achieved an RMSE of 0.0230 (88.9% reduction vs. baseline). It maintained favorable performance on the KIMORE squatting subset, demonstrating cross-protocol transfer.
AI.conclusion: PhaseAware offers a practical, interpretable approach to rehabilitation scoring that can integrate automated assessment into information systems while preserving clinician oversight, supporting review, monitoring, and human-in-the-loop triage.

title: Breaking the $T^{3/4}$ Barrier for Regret Minimization With Bi-Dimensional CDFs
summary: We study regret minimization for learning CDF-related objectives of the form \[ g(x)\cdot\mathbb{P}_{X\sim\mathcal{D}}(X\le x), \] over $[0,1]^2$, where $g$ is a known Lipschitz function and $\mathcal{D}$ is an unknown distribution. At each round $t$, the learner selects a point $x_t$ and observes the binary feedback $\mathbb{I}(X_t\le x_t)$, where $X_t\sim\mathcal{D}$. We design an algorithm achieving regret $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(T^{7/10})$, improving over the previous best-known bound of $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(T^{3/4})$ and showing that the curse of dimensionality can be at least partially lifted for this class of objectives, though a gap remains with the $Ω(T^{2/3})$ lower bound. As an application, our techniques yield the same $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(T^{7/10})$ regret bound for profit maximization in repeated bilateral trade with fixed prices.

AI.tldr: This paper studies regret minimization for learning CDF-related objectives over [0,1]^2, achieving $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(T^{7/10})$ regret, improving over the previous $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(T^{3/4})$ bound, with application to bilateral trade profit maximization.
AI.motivation: To improve regret bounds for learning CDF-related objectives (g(x)·P(X ≤ x)) over [0,1]^2, and to address the curse of dimensionality in this class of problems.
AI.method: Designing a new algorithm that achieves $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(T^{7/10})$ regret by leveraging the structure of CDF-related objectives to partially overcome the curse of dimensionality.
AI.result: Regret $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(T^{7/10})$, improving over the previous best bound of $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(T^{3/4})$, though a gap remains with the $\Omega(T^{2/3})$ lower bound. The same bound is achieved for profit maximization in repeated bilateral trade with fixed prices.
AI.conclusion: The curse of dimensionality can be at least partially lifted for CDF-related objectives, and the techniques extend to practical applications like bilateral trade.

title: Interpretable Fuzzy Rule-Based Regression Extension for Ex-Fuzzy Library
summary: Machine learning models achieve high predictive accuracy in regression tasks, but their deployment in safety-critical and regulated domains requires interpretability. While fuzzy rule-based systems offer transparent, linguistically explicit interpretable models, Mamdani-style fuzzy regression remains underrepresented in modern machine learning software libraries. This paper presents an interpretable regression extension for the Ex-Fuzzy library, enabling Mamdani fuzzy inference with scalar consequents learned directly from data. For this, a target-aware partition initialisation strategy based on Fuzzy C-Means clustering is introduced, in which linguistic variables are derived from an augmented input-output space to emphasise output-relevant regions of the feature space. The proposed extension is evaluated on ten regression datasets from the KEEL repository, comparing Gaussian and trapezoidal partition strategies against standard baselines including linear regression, multilayer perceptron, and random forests. Experimental results show that Gaussian partitions consistently outperform uniform trapezoidal partitions, achieving a mean coefficient of determination of approximately 0.86 while producing compact rule bases of 10-15 human-readable rules. The proposed implementation provides a transparent and competitive alternative to black-box regression models, supporting practical interpretability with competitive predictive performance.

AI.tldr: This paper extends the Ex-Fuzzy library to support interpretable Mamdani-style fuzzy regression with scalar consequents learned from data, using a target-aware Fuzzy C-Means partition initialization strategy. Evaluated on 10 KEEL datasets, Gaussian partitions achieve ~0.86 R² with compact rule bases (10-15 rules), offering a transparent alternative to black-box regression models.
AI.motivation: Machine learning models achieve high accuracy but lack interpretability required in safety-critical and regulated domains. Mamdani-style fuzzy regression is underrepresented in modern ML libraries despite offering transparent, linguistically explicit interpretable models.
AI.method: (1) Extends Ex-Fuzzy library for Mamdani fuzzy inference with scalar consequents. (2) Introduces a target-aware partition initialization based on Fuzzy C-Means clustering using an augmented input-output space. (3) Compares Gaussian vs. trapezoidal partition strategies across 10 KEEL regression datasets against linear regression, MLP, and random forests.
AI.result: Gaussian partitions consistently outperform uniform trapezoidal partitions, achieving mean R² ≈ 0.86 with compact rule bases of 10-15 human-readable rules.
AI.conclusion: The proposed implementation provides a transparent and competitive alternative to black-box regression models, balancing practical interpretability with competitive predictive performance.

title: The Blessing of Dimensionality: How Near-Orthogonality in High-Dimensional Spaces Explains Temporal Portability
summary: Fine-tuning has been widely used to adapt large language models (LLMs) for domain-specific tasks. Parameter efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) methods such as low-rank adaptation (LoRA) are frequently used to reduce computational costs. PortLLM is a training-free and data-free scheme used to adapt LLMs after continual pretraining. Although the initial PortLLM results show that LoRA patches exhibit short-term temporal portability, the long-term performance of PortLLM across several updates of continual pretraining remains underexplored. Furthermore, the intriguing effectiveness of PortLLM is not well understood from a theoretical standpoint. We address these two open questions by (1) performing an extensive empirical study of the long-term temporal portability of PortLLM patches across 10 continual pretraining steps using base models Mistral, Gemma, and Qwen; and (2) offering two theoretical analyses to explain our observation that the simple PortLLM method achieves competitive performance. We find empirically that the portability persists across longer time duration, indicating that repeated fine-tuning is not required when the base model is periodically updated. We find theoretically that near-orthogonality of high-dimensional vectors is a key justification for temporal portability.
