Our analyses also demonstrate a geometric perspective of the loss landscape in facilitating the theoretical comparison of different adaptation options.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates the long-term temporal portability of PortLLM (a training-free, data-free LLM adaptation method) across 10 continual pretraining steps on Mistral, Gemma, and Qwen, and provides theoretical justification based on near-orthogonality of high-dimensional vectors and loss landscape geometry.
AI.motivation: To address two open questions: (1) whether PortLLM's temporal portability persists over long-term continual pretraining updates, and (2) why PortLLM achieves competitive performance from a theoretical perspective.
AI.method: Extensive empirical study across 10 continual pretraining steps on three base models (Mistral, Gemma, Qwen), plus two theoretical analyses: near-orthogonality of high-dimensional vectors and geometric analysis of the loss landscape.
AI.result: Empirically, PortLLM portability persists over longer time durations, eliminating the need for repeated fine-tuning. Theoretically, near-orthogonality of high-dimensional vectors justifies temporal portability.
AI.conclusion: Repeated fine-tuning is not required when the base model is periodically updated; high-dimensional vector near-orthogonality and loss landscape geometry explain PortLLM's effectiveness.

title: Classical Hardware Acceleration of Quantum Autoencoders for Real-Time Anomaly Detection in Collider Experiments
summary: Quantum machine learning (QML) algorithms in high energy physics (HEP) can efficiently represent and leverage long-range, high-order correlations in high-dimensional collider data, potentially with fewer parameters and favorable scaling relative to classical models. Deployment of QML in real-time collider applications such as trigger systems requires the ability to emulate and compile quantum circuits classically, then synthesize the resulting quantum gates onto low-latency hardware accelerators, namely field-programmable gate arrays (FPGAs). We present a study of variational quantum autoencoder models for real-time anomaly detection triggers in modern collider experiments. The models achieve performance comparable to state-of-the-art classical approaches and, after FPGA synthesis, satisfy resource usage and timing constraints consistent with trigger applications in future colliders. This work provides one of the first FPGA implementations of QML models for HEP triggers, enabling higher-capability models in today's classical data acquisition pipelines while advancing quantum readiness of collider experiment infrastructure.

AI.tldr: This paper presents FPGA-implemented variational quantum autoencoders for real-time anomaly detection triggers in collider experiments, achieving classical-level performance while meeting hardware resource and timing constraints.
AI.motivation: QML algorithms in HEP can capture long-range, high-order correlations in high-dimensional collider data with favorable scaling, but deployment in real-time trigger systems requires low-latency hardware implementation.
AI.method: Variational quantum autoencoder models were designed and then emulated/compiled classically, with resulting quantum gates synthesized onto FPGA hardware accelerators.
AI.result: The QML models achieved performance comparable to state-of-the-art classical anomaly detection approaches. After FPGA synthesis, they satisfied resource usage and timing constraints required for future collider trigger applications.
AI.conclusion: This is one of the first FPGA implementations of QML models for HEP triggers, enabling enhanced models in classical data acquisition pipelines and advancing quantum readiness of collider infrastructure.

title: Multi-modal transformer for signal classification in nanopore blockade experiments
summary: Nanopore devices have emerged as powerful tools for single-molecule sensing, with potential for rapid, portable diagnostics. They detect changes in ionic current as analytes enter nanometer-scale pores, providing a means of identifying diverse biomarkers from their characteristic signal patterns. However, these signals are highly complex, and reliably assigning them to specific molecules remains a major challenge. Here, we address this by introducing a multi-modal deep learning architecture that jointly processes multiple signal representations, including raw time-series data, wavelet-based images, and static feature vectors. Our approach surpasses existing methods by more than 10 percentage points on a 42-peptide benchmark and transfers to a 20-amino-acid dataset with near-perfect accuracy. The model integrates complementary information from these representations, with attention analysis showing that the time-series and wavelet-image inputs emphasize different features of the same event. Together, these results demonstrate the potential of machine learning to enable robust, high-accuracy molecular identification with nanopore sensors.

AI.tldr: A multi-modal deep learning architecture that jointly processes raw time-series, wavelet-based images, and static feature vectors improves nanopore-based molecular identification accuracy by over 10 percentage points on a 42-peptide benchmark and achieves near-perfect accuracy on a 20-amino-acid dataset.
AI.motivation: Nanopore signals are highly complex, and reliably assigning them to specific molecules remains a major challenge, limiting the practical application of nanopore devices for single-molecule sensing and diagnostics.
AI.method: A multi-modal deep learning architecture that jointly processes three complementary signal representations: raw time-series data, wavelet-based images, and static feature vectors. Attention analysis was used to examine how different input modalities emphasize different features.
AI.result: The approach surpasses existing methods by more than 10 percentage points on a 42-peptide benchmark and transfers to a 20-amino-acid dataset with near-perfect accuracy.
AI.conclusion: Multi-modal machine learning can enable robust, high-accuracy molecular identification with nanopore sensors, demonstrating the potential of combining complementary signal representations to overcome the challenge of complex signal interpretation.

title: Interval and fuzzy physics-augmented neural networks (iPANN and fPANN) for uncertainty quantification and propagation in constitutive modeling
summary: Constitutive modeling under uncertainty remains a central challenge for reliable mechanics simulations, particularly when the available stress-deformation data are sparse, noisy, or heterogeneous. We propose interval and fuzzy physics-augmented neural networks (iPANNs and fPANNs) for uncertainty-aware hyperelastic constitutive modeling. iPANNs learn sparse lower, mean, and upper free energy density branches whose stresses, obtained by automatic differentiation, ultimately enclose noisy stress observations. In contrast to this deterministic interval description, fPANNs embed the learned iPANN branches into a fuzzy-set representation through alpha-cut interpolation, yielding a nested family of admissible responses. iPANNs and fPANNs encode mechanistic constraints - preserving objectivity, consistency and promoting polyconvexity - and smoothed L0 regularization promotes interpretable energy representations. The bound models are trained through a two-stage transfer-learning procedure in which a sparse mean constitutive response is learned first and then fine-tuned into lower and upper energy branches. We evaluate the framework on synthetic isotropic hyperelastic data with heteroscedastic noise, varying random realizations, shifted noise means, and varying noise magnitudes. The results show that the learned bounds enclose noisy stress observations while generalizing to the test set. Further, we examine the propagation of uncertainty through the mean, upper and lower bound predictions of the learned iPANN models in a finite element setting. The proposed framework provides a compact, physics-consistent route for distribution-free aleatoric uncertainty quantification in hyperelastic constitutive modeling, and propagation in downstream finite element simulations.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes interval and fuzzy physics-augmented neural networks (iPANNs and fPANNs) for uncertainty-aware hyperelastic constitutive modeling. These models learn bounded free energy density branches that enclose noisy stress observations, embed mechanistic constraints (objectivity, consistency, polyconvexity), and use transfer learning and smoothed L0 regularization for interpretability. The framework is validated on synthetic data and shown to propagate uncertainty through finite element simulations.
AI.motivation: Constitutive modeling under uncertainty remains challenging when stress-deformation data are sparse, noisy, or heterogeneous, motivating the need for uncertainty-aware hyperelastic models that can handle distribution-free aleatoric uncertainty.
AI.method: Proposes iPANNs (deterministic interval bounds) and fPANNs (fuzzy-set via alpha-cut interpolation). Both encode objectivity, consistency, and polyconvexity; use smoothed L0 regularization for sparsity; and employ a two-stage transfer-learning procedure (train mean response first, then fine-tune to lower/upper branches).
AI.result: Learned bounds successfully enclose noisy stress observations on synthetic isotropic hyperelastic data with heteroscedastic noise, varying random realizations, shifted noise means, and varying magnitudes. The framework generalizes to test sets and propagates uncertainty through finite element simulations.
AI.conclusion: iPANNs and fPANNs provide a compact, physics-consistent, distribution-free approach for aleatoric uncertainty quantification in hyperelastic constitutive modeling and downstream FE simulations.

title: Variance-reduced Domain Adaptation using Paired Sampling
summary: Correlation alignment and the maximum mean discrepancy are two widely used distribution-matching frameworks for unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA). However, high variance in these losses has been shown to undermine their effectiveness in minibatch optimisation settings. Furthermore, the losses lack finite-sum structure, which renders them incompatible with classical stochastic variance reduction (SVR) methods. This paper proposes Paired Sampling for Domain Adaptation (PSDA), a novel SVR technique tailored to such objectives. PSDA pairs observations both within and across domains, to form quadruplets that are always sampled together during training. The pairings are designed to minimise expected gradient variance, and reduce to solving a set of linear assignment problems. Our simulations demonstrate reduced variance compared to related methods, and experiments on three domain shift datasets show improved target domain accuracy.

AI.tldr: PSDA proposes a paired sampling variance reduction technique for distribution-matching losses (CORAL, MMD) in unsupervised domain adaptation, forming cross-domain quadruplets via linear assignment to reduce gradient variance and improve target accuracy.
AI.motivation: Distribution-matching losses like CORAL and MMD suffer from high variance in minibatch optimization and lack finite-sum structure, making them incompatible with standard stochastic variance reduction (SVR) methods.
AI.method: PSDA pairs observations within and across domains to form quadruplets that are always sampled together. The pairings minimize expected gradient variance by solving linear assignment problems.
AI.result: Simulations show reduced variance compared to related methods; experiments on three domain shift datasets demonstrate improved target domain accuracy.
AI.conclusion: PSDA is an effective SVR technique for distribution-matching losses in UDA, addressing their variance issues and improving performance.

title: Online Variance Reduction for Domain Adaptation on Streaming Data
summary: This paper studies the problem of stochastic variance reduction (SVR) for the maximum mean discrepancy (MMD) and correlation alignment (CORAL) loss functions. Although various offline SVR algorithms for these losses have been proposed, these are incompatible with online, distributed, or incremental learning settings. This paper presents Adaptive vaRiance Reduction via Online reWeighting (ARROW), the first online SVR algorithm for the MMD and CORAL for streamed data. The method maintains moving average references of the alignment statistics, and adaptively reweights incoming minibatches so that the minibatch and reference statistics are aligned. Further, we propose a relaxed reweighting scheme so that the ensuing weight-optimisation problem is tractable. In experiments and simulations, we show that ARROW performs competitively with offline algorithms in terms of runtime, degree of variance reduction achieved, and target domain accuracy.

AI.tldr: ARROW is the first online stochastic variance reduction algorithm for MMD and CORAL losses, using moving average references and adaptive minibatch reweighting to achieve competitive performance with offline methods.
AI.motivation: Existing SVR algorithms for MMD and CORAL are offline and incompatible with online, distributed, or incremental learning settings.
AI.method: Maintains moving average references of alignment statistics and adaptively reweights incoming minibatches to align minibatch and reference statistics, with a relaxed reweighting scheme for tractability.
AI.result: ARROW performs competitively with offline algorithms in runtime, variance reduction degree, and target domain accuracy.
AI.conclusion: The proposed ARROW algorithm successfully enables online SVR for MMD and CORAL losses while matching offline performance.

title: PG-KINN: A Physics-Informed Petrov-Galerkin Kolmogorov-Arnold Network for Solving Forward and Inverse PDEs
summary: Physics-informed learning of partial differential equations (PDEs) has been dominated by multilayer perceptrons (MLPs), whose spectral bias and dense parameterization limit both accuracy and interpretability. Kolmogorov Arnold Networks (KANs) mitigate these limitations because their learnable spline activations are structurally aligned with the piecewise-polynomial bases of classical discretizations. However, the way a PDE is cast into a loss functional is as decisive as the choice of approximator: strong-form residual minimization requires high-order derivatives and heavily weighted losses, the energy (Bubnov-Galerkin) form is restricted to self-adjoint operators and, as we show, collapses to a trivial solution for parameter-identification problems, and boundary integral forms require a known fundamental solution. We propose PG-KINN, a physics-informed KAN built on a Petrov-Galerkin formulation in which the trial space is a KAN and the test space is an independent, compactly supported, piecewise-polynomial space evaluated with Gauss-Legendre quadrature. Integration by parts lowers the differentiation order while retaining applicability to general non-self-adjoint, nonlinear, and inverse problems; the localized test functions turn the global residual into a set of element-wise weak residuals with favorable conditioning. On a suite of benchmarks spanning crack singularities, stress concentration, Neo-Hookean hyperelasticity, inverse parameter identification in heterogeneous media, and complex geometries, PG-KINN consistently outperforms legacy MLP baselines and state-of-the-art KAN-based strong/energy/inverse formulations (PIKAN). These results position the Petrov-Galerkin coupling of KAN trial spaces and polynomial test spaces as a robust and accurate route for AI-based computational mechanics.

AI.tldr: PG-KINN is a physics-informed Kolmogorov-Arnold Network that uses a Petrov-Galerkin formulation (KAN trial space + piecewise-polynomial test space) to overcome limitations of MLP-based PINNs and KAN-based strong/energy/inverse formulations, achieving superior accuracy across crack singularities, stress concentration, hyperelasticity, inverse problems, and complex geometries.
AI.motivation: MLP-based PINNs suffer from spectral bias and dense parameterization limiting accuracy and interpretability. Existing KAN-based methods still rely on suboptimal loss formulations: strong-form requires high-order derivatives and loss balancing, energy (Bubnov-Galerkin) form is restricted to self-adjoint operators and fails for parameter identification, and boundary integral forms need known fundamental solutions. A more robust formulation is needed.
AI.method: PG-KINN couples a KAN trial space with an independent, compactly supported, piecewise-polynomial test space evaluated via Gauss-Legendre quadrature in a Petrov-Galerkin framework. Integration by parts lowers differentiation order while retaining generality for non-self-adjoint, nonlinear, and inverse problems. Localized test functions decompose the global residual into element-wise weak residuals with improved conditioning.
AI.result: PG-KINN consistently outperforms legacy MLP baselines and state-of-the-art KAN-based formulations (PIKAN strong/energy/inverse) across benchmarks including crack singularities, stress concentration, Neo-Hookean hyperelasticity, inverse parameter identification in heterogeneous media, and complex geometries.
AI.conclusion: The Petrov-Galerkin coupling of KAN trial spaces and polynomial test spaces is a robust and accurate approach for AI-based computational mechanics, positioning PG-KINN as a superior alternative to existing physics-informed neural network paradigms.
